title: Find your tree
author: Arnav Jain
article_text:
At Duke, nature is everywhere, from the Sarah P. Duke Gardens to our namesake giant forest. Yet it is often overlooked. 

We navigate East Campus with earbuds in, rush from classes to Perkins and spend downtime staring at our phones. We’re constantly told to “touch grass,” but that’s easier said than done when our schedules are packed with classes, clubs, problem sets and coffee chats.

Two weeks into Duke, I realized I’d fallen into this routine. I spent the day hurrying across campus without noticing its trees and green spaces. I was surrounded by nature, but my mind was somewhere in my last class, homework or phone. 

One day, though, with a few extra minutes before class, I stopped beneath a calming tree I pass regularly right outside WU, and, for the first time, actually paid attention to where I was. I noticed the cool shade beneath its branches, the leaves shifting overhead and the noise of campus fading into the background.

I began to question the advice to simply “touch grass.” It tells us to go outside, but not where or how to actually stop and notice nature. Maybe students don’t really need more nature spots, but one they can return to regularly.

It’s well-founded that nature can refresh a weary mind. A 2008 University of Michigan study found that participants scored nearly 20 percent higher on working memory and attention tests after walking in an arboretum than in a busy downtown. 

Researchers explain this through “attention restoration theory,” which states that our ability to focus is limited and quickly depleted, while nature replenishes it by engaging us more gently through soft fascination. For example, something as simple as listening to birdsong for six minutes can reduce anxiety and paranoia. 

The reason we should choose one spot specifically is that familiarity makes nature easier to access. “Touch grass” requires us to make a decision. Where do we go? When? With all that friction, we often end up not going. 

But “go to my spot” is automatic. It’s easily accessible, so requires little effort. Even a brief visit to a green area helps relieve stress. A place five minutes from our dorm or class is much more likely to become part of our lives than an occasional nature excursion.

Returning to a place in nature makes us notice details we otherwise would miss. A 2018 research article in “Ecopsychology” reports that repeated nature walks increase people’s awareness of natural beauty. 

The tree we notice in September will not look the same in December or April. For instance, we may notice the leaves changing. Having one familiar spot makes these changes much easier to notice, allowing nature’s restorative benefits to be experienced more fully.

No studies suggest that one familiar tree is scientifically better than 10 different ones. That is not the point. But a familiar place transforms the abstract suggestion to “touch grass” into a palpable routine that incorporates nature and its benefits into everyday life. For me, that calming tree in front of WU has started to become that place. 

So this week, look for your spot. Use Duke’s Tree Viewer, an interactive map of campus trees, to find a nearby tree, or choose a bench, garden corner or patch of grass you pass regularly. Sit there in both stressful and ordinary moments. After some time, notice what has changed. 

You might find that, as you become attached to a little chunk of Duke’s nature, Duke starts to feel a little more like home.

Arnav Jain is a Trinity first-year.

title: ‘I hate Barack Obama’: Mitt Romney encourages political retribution, urges extremism in Sanford lecture
author: Monday Monday
article_text:
Editor's note: The article below is satire.

Former Republican Senator Mitt Romney brought his “Should’ve Been Me” tour to Duke campus last week to share insights from his career with aspiring public leaders.

“I’m convinced the American people, at our core, hate Barack Obama,” Romney told a packed Page Auditorium. He added, “Some people just can’t move on from the 2012 election. Obama is a despicable man, and I hope he burns in hell.”

Best known for his failed presidential run, Romney began his career as a businessman before bursting onto the political scene as Governor of Massachusetts. After he successfully closed tax loopholes and passed universal healthcare in the state, the Republican Party demoted him to Co-Senator of Utah.

From the center of the auditorium stage, Romney emphasized that both sides of the aisle share responsibility for the present political moment. “The thermometer is simply running too hot,” he conveyed. “What we ought to do — Democrat and Republican alike — is take a step back, seize that thermometer and whack Barack Obama over the head with it.”

Reflecting on the planning behind the flagship lecture, the Sanford School reported that they faced an agonizing choice between Romney and an AI hologram of Mao Zedong. “Though our personal loyalties lie with Chairman Mao, Mitt’s speaker fee won the day,” a Sanford spokesman explained. Investigative journalism from Monday Monday revealed that Romney paid $14 million for the opportunity to speak.

When the event moderator prompted Romney to discuss his renegade impeachment vote against President Donald J. Trump, the ex-senator replied, “Minemine, it should’ve been mine, Mitt Romney should’ve had oval office, not Trump. Mine, minemine.” Romney subsequently curled up into the fetal position screaming “GO TO HELL BARACK” before returning to his chair like nothing had happened.

After the inflammatory event, Duke Centrists staged a “no-test” on Abele Quad with signs reading “We Are Here,” “Come Together Now,” and “Mitt Romney Is.” Sophomore participant Marco Branch articulated, “Who checks up on the status of the status quo? We are a big block of ice freezing everything exactly as it is.”

Monday Monday reached out to Former President Obama for comment and was honored to receive a reply: “Mitt’s a decent man and a solid American. I’d be happy to have a beer with him at my billion-dollar Obama Shrine here in Chicago.”

Monday Monday is serving the first of eighteen lifetime sentences due to President Trump’s latest press ban.

title: Duke’s Roots of Faith
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
I know we live in a time when people of religious faith can get a bad rap, especially considering the rise of Christian nationalism, which distorts an authentic Christian life of service. I know religious people from all types of religious traditions have done horrific things in the name of God for centuries. That’s a historical fact.

Yet, it is also a fact that people of faith have done a lot of good in the world — founding schools, hospitals, orphanages, civil rights movements and liberation movements on behalf of the poor in the face of oppressive regimes. Faith fueled the fire of this goodness. My point is to encourage you not to fast from faith because it is food for human freedom and flourishing. 

I say this on the heels of Founders’ Weekend at Duke, knowing that Duke, alongside many other universities in the world, was established by people of faith. Three key founders are laid to rest in the Memorial Chapel inside Duke Chapel — Washington Duke, Benjamin Duke, and James B. Duke. They founded this institution with faith and in faith. 

Washington Duke was a devout and active Methodist. His eldest brother, William James, was a lay preacher known as “Uncle Billy of the Old Ship” because he loved singing his favorite hymn “The Old Ship of Zion.” Uncle Billy was a farmer, preacher and mentor of Washington Duke, and so faith became important to Washington, which in turn shaped the lives of his sons and, through them, the contour of Duke University to this day.

In the 1924 Indenture of Trust, James B. Duke says, “I have selected Duke University as one of the principal objects of this trust because I recognize that education, when conducted along sane and practical, as opposed to dogmatic and theoretical, lines, is, next to religion, the greatest civilizing influence.” Education and religion. But notice the priority religion has. 

Then further on, he says, “And I advise that the courses at this institution be arranged, first, with special reference to the training of preachers, teachers, lawyers and physicians, … and second, to instruction in chemistry, economics and history….” Notice that the training of preachers is first. You may also know that the first professional graduate school established at Duke University in September 1926 was the Divinity School (originally named the School of Religion).

Education and religion are the historical beating heart of Duke, which is why in April 1925 when James B. Duke was walking through a forest with his friend and president of Trinity College, William Preston Few, he paused at the highest point of the land and decided that the chapel should stand here at the center of the university’s new campus. He said, “I want the central building to be a great towering church which will dominate all of the surrounding buildings, because such an edifice would be bound to have a profound influence on the spiritual life of the young men and women who come here.”

At the center of the university is a towering chapel, symbolic of faith and the spiritual life, alongside a school of divinity. The historic motto of Duke is the Latin phrase "eruditio et religio," meaning “knowledge and religion.” Even in the current university bylaws, in “Article I: Aims,” the very first stated aim of Duke University is “to foster a lively relationship between knowledge and faith.” That’s "eruditio et religio."

Why am I saying all of this? The importance of faith and religious expression at Duke historically reveals that Duke has become a world-class, research I university, not despite faith, but because of faith. Like the spires of the neo-Gothic Duke Chapel, faith leads us to aspire beyond what we know or see, beyond ourselves and even beyond our imagination. Thus faith — religion — has sown the seeds of Duke’s future, one in which education and knowledge are conjoined with faith and religion.

Faith or religious belief and practice at Duke is not only historical but actual. It is alive and well today, even as the religious traditions on campus have become more diverse over the years. Thousands of Duke employees and students are faith-filled or religiously practicing individuals, representing all the world’s religions. Thus, religion is not solely studied at Duke; it is practiced, lived and embodied — it is how many find purpose and meaning in their lives. 

Duke’s roots are steeped in faith. That’s a fact. I encourage you to water those roots to keep Duke grounded in its historic identity and to cause it to grow more fruitful in its second century.

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: Music’s connection to the self and the past
author: Robert Wallace
article_text:
I’m a nostalgic man. I love to ruminate. Sometimes I wonder if I think too much about the past, isolating certain events or frightening discoveries so that they become larger than they really are, rather than a part of a more forgiving whole. Maybe that happens when you turn 70? 

It was 1979. Fall. My future wife Roberta and I pulled into Durham, North Carolina, taking the exit to Duke Hospital, then only a southern campus. I was driving a two-toned green Ford Maverick — a car purchased in 1975 — new at the time. It only had an AM radio. I kept the dial set at WLS, a station out of Chicago, which played the songs of my youth. I can still hear Wildfire, by Michael Murphy, in my head. In 1975, I was dating the mayor’s daughter at the time, and this was “our song,” until it wasn’t, and that’s when I knew I was also no longer the one for her. 

Robert Miller, my future father-in-law, was in Duke Hospital when Roberta and I arrived in Durham nearly fifty years ago. I was twenty-two-years old when I first met him. When we walked in — Roberta and I — he was sitting on the edge of the bed, a fancy green robe gathered about him. From the beginning I liked this man. He wore wire-rimmed glasses, and he was mostly bald and had a twinkle in his eye. 

Once, years later, while he sat at the dinner table, he took a windup toy — a pair of red lips — wound it up and let it go, and we watched the lips rapidly go up and down. “I swear this thing has a soul,” he said, and I laughed. When he did things like that, I could see the mischievous boy in him. 

After Roberta and I married, my father-in-law used to take me down in the basement of his house and play reel film movies about his days in World War II. These were films projected on a white physical screen wound around a circular spool. He never talked a great deal about the war, but I could tell the war had affected him greatly. I used to listen to the stories he did tell, and I think he took great comfort in that fact.

The movies were often silent films. Sometimes he would play a record, mostly Frank Sinatra songs, on the record player, and the juxtaposition of watching the devastation and listening to Sinatra’s crooning voice I found immensely plaintive and strange. This, of course, was the music that my father-in-law held to his heart, so for him it brought back deeply held memories. 

Since last year, in this column, I began an exploration of memory through stories, not as a search for personal meaning, but as a way to connect through stories. Marcel Proust, in his Contre Sainte-Beuve (the book that eventually morphed into À la recherche du temps perdu), titled a chapter “Return to the Present.” He connected talent in writing to music and memory. 

In Sylvia Townsend Warner’s translation, he said, “When I began to read an author I very soon caught the tune of the song beneath the words.” He considered music to be the deepest memory. And so did E. M. Forster, who claimed in an address at Harvard University in 1947 that "music is the deepest of the arts and deep beneath the arts." This address was unrecorded but was eventually published not only by Harvard University Press but also separately by Forster in an essay titled "The Raison d'Être of Criticism in the Arts," which he later included in an essay collection.

Music is often used as a metaphor for memory. Nietzsche called it “the direct language of the feeling.” Proust, for example, made the solicitation of his memories his life’s work. Furthermore, in his essay, he distinctly claimed that we each have a story to tell, and that to not write it down, would be like never knowing “the tune that beset you with its intangible delightful rhythm.”

I was born on Christmas day. When I was a boy, before I began living with my grandparents, all the family would gather at my grandparents’ house for Christmas. I had a much older cousin, a beautiful young woman, who would always come into my grandparents’ house, and, usually while I was sitting on the sofa, bend over and plant a sweet-smelling kiss upon my cheek. I remember these kisses fondly. I also remember one time she came in singing Blaming it on the Bossa Nova, by Eydie Gorme. To this day, I think of Lucille as a woman firmly planted in 1963.

There has been a movement afoot, known as Music & Memory. It is based upon the concept brought forth by Dan Cohen, who surmised that older adults suffering from Alzheimer’s disease or other cognitive disorders could connect with memories through personalized music. It has come to see forms of numerous chapters, including one at Duke, and a film about the movement which gives full breath to how music works with memory Alive Inside. 

Memory, though a very individual phenomenon for each of us because our lives are unique, nevertheless, is something that we all ponder as part of being human. For Proust, it was everything. The political theorist Hannah Arendt, too, wrote significantly about memory in her posthumously published Life of the Mind. In the first volume of the planned trilogy titled “Thinking”, she had this to say about memory: “the mind’s power of having present what is irrevocably past and thus absent from the senses.” 

Furthermore, Arendt noted how Kafka specifically used music as a touching point for memory, such as in the story “Josephine the Singer, or the Mouse Folk,” where Josephine’s squeaking voice promotes togetherness for the mouse community that engenders “strength between the people,” which goes far beyond the capacity of any “single individual.” For Arendt, a memory constituted from music was more than a mere remembrance; it could be an aid for a call to reflect on one’s current state, even a retrospective call to action in the face of tyranny. And even Arendt — who was all about the political — believed that in order for music to live beyond the present and the individual, it must be collectively experienced. 

Arendt, of course, knew as well as anyone that this collective experience with music or sound could also be exploited against any notion of plurality, such as in the case of the Nazis’ manipulation of Wagner.

Musical rhythms were vital to Auden’s poetry, though he believed music was a present experience and that it had no cognitive effect on memory. But science has proven otherwise. Despite his belief, perhaps Auden subconsciously understood the connection when he wrote in “Hymn to St. Cecilia”: “O law drummed out by hearts against the still / Long winter of our intellectual will / That what has been may never be again.” 

Robert Wallace is a second-year graduate student of liberal studies. His column, 'Telling Stories', typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: Response to the DukeEngage Ghana Revelations
author: Charles D. Piot
article_text:
I write as a Duke faculty member who served as Program Director of DukeEngage Togo for 15 years (until 2024) and as Faculty Director overseeing the larger program from 2019-2023. During that time, I took more than 100 students to villages in northern Togo, a West African country which borders Ghana, where they conducted community engagement projects — setting up a local health insurance system, implementing a microlending program and building a cyber café where they taught computer literacy. 

Our students lived with local families and made a real difference in the lives of those they encountered, while themselves drawing irreplaceable lessons from the program. They not only experienced immersion in life abroad but also learned about local culture and history, witnessed first-hand the effects of global inequality and challenged their preconceived notions of Africa and the world beyond. 

I felt privileged to be able to run the Togo program and spend time each summer with such dynamic and compassionate students, and came to feel that DukeEngage fully deserved its reputation as one of Duke’s signature undergraduate programs.

I was therefore dismayed and deeply troubled to read the Sept. 11 Duke Chronicle article, “A Terrible Failure: How DukeEngage Ghana underpaid, underfed students and staff for years.” Outside of what I read in that article, I am not familiar with the facts of that case and so won’t be commenting on them here. 

Nevertheless, I was saddened by what the students and Ghanaian assistants to the program report. These students expected the experience of their lives and seemed to get something much different, and local assistants — who are often key intermediaries responsible for the success of DukeEngage programs — deserve generous remuneration for the time and services they provided.

At the same time, I hasten to add that I believe this to be an isolated instance. It is not the DukeEngage I know, and it does not adhere to the program’s otherwise high standards. 

As Faculty Director of DukeEngage, I supervised over 40 program directors who arranged projects all over the world each year, not only running impactful community engagement activities but also providing Duke students with unparalleled experiences of the world beyond. These faculty members were deeply dedicated educators who gave generously of their time and expertise.

Most germane to the case at hand, these faculty members were squeaky clean in running their programs. From what I saw, they attended fastidiously to the daily needs of their students, spent generously on their food and care and kept accountants’ records of what they spent. In my experience, DukeEngage is one of the tightest-run ships I’ve been associated with at Duke, and its administrative staff are exemplary stewards.

Again, I feel deeply sorry for what the students and the assistants in the Ghana program report. But I sincerely hope that DukeEngage’s well-deserved legacy is not irreparably tarnished by this account, and that the program can learn and improve from the reported problems in Ghana to ensure students continue to gain invaluable life experiences.

Charles D. Piot is the former Peter Lange Faculty Director of DukeEngage and current professor of cultural anthropology & African and African American Studies

Editor’s note: This column was updated Sept. 28 to replace the term “failures” with “reported problems” per the author’s request.

title: Sacrality of the University
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
This semester I’m teaching a Divinity School course at the federal men’s prison in Butner, North Carolina. It is titled “Music in the Air: Poetry and Preaching from Prisons.” The first day of class coincided closely with the death of the esteemed poet and writer Wendell Berry. Because of this, I started the class by reading his poem, “How to Be a Poet.” The following portion struck me:

Shun electric wire. 

Communicate slowly. Live 

a three-dimensioned life; 

stay away from screens. 

Stay away from anything 

that obscures the place it is in. 

There are no unsacred places; 

there are only sacred places 

and desecrated places. 

In the context of a prison, it was the last three lines that especially stood out to me: “There are no unsacred places; there are only sacred places and desecrated places.” Sacred means ‘holy’ or ‘to be set apart.’ Berry suggests (and I would agree) that all places are sacred, ultimately even a prison.

That may sound far-fetched, but the curriculum for the course I am teaching draws on poems and exhortations written from prison. The New Testament letters of St. Paul provide a lot of material because 40% of them were written from prison. One of the most famous texts from the U.S. Civil Rights Movement is Martin Luther King, Jr.’s “Letter from Birmingham Jail.”

Another source we are using is the collection of prayerful poems “Psalms from Prison” by the civil rights leader Benjamin Chavis, Jr., who preached at Duke Chapel in 1979 while serving time for a crime for which he was eventually pardoned. If prison can be the setting for these beautiful and prophetic texts, then surely it can be sacred.

If prison can be sacred, then so can a university like Duke. Many might refer to Duke as a “secular university,” but I have never sat comfortably with that notion. I understand on one level that “secular” can refer to being non-religiously affiliated or to a characterization of institutional values, but it is problematic from my perspective since all of life is sacred; therefore, a divide between secular and sacred is false. There may be desecration, but that is different from the so-called secular.

Duke is a sacred university, and by that, I mean in this place, heaven can meet earth, the Divine can touch the human, mystery meets the mundane. Think about it. The “ah’s” from learning in the classroom. The meaningful conversations about life on the quad or in hallways. Eating together and lingering for a while without being pressed for time. Playing together and laughing out loud in freedom. Joining together in solidarity to witness against wrongs in the world. Researching and discovering medical pathways for human healing. The list can go on and on. These are glimpses of sacred moments here at Duke.

I know some may say that I am venturing into hyperbolic language, so let me explain. To experience the sacred doesn’t mean there can’t be challenges or sadness or difficult times. The sacred is life, all of life. It permeates places; here on campus, it is not limited to the Divinity School, Duke Chapel or Religious Life at Duke. The sacred can’t be put in a straitjacket. “There are no unsacred places.”

As you walk around campus, you may be surprised to find yourself on sacred ground. If so, you are in good company. A founding father of ancient Israel, Jacob, had that experience. He was traveling and lay down for the night to sleep in a location described only as “a certain place.” There he had a powerful dream in which God promised to bless him with land and many descendants. “Then Jacob woke from his sleep and said, ‘Surely the Lord is in this place — and I did not know it!’” (Genesis 28:16).

The realization of our campus as a sacred place can change your perspective. You don’t solely see grades given but you see goodness when help is offered to get better; that’s sacred. Duke doesn’t just have labs; love is here and that’s sacred. We have corporate p-cards but to be sure, there is also human community at sporting events, receptions, book groups, clubs and more; and that’s sacred.

Most important to this perspective is the sacredness of life. Throughout campus, there are only sacred people who are lit with the sacred Light. In this place, we are stewards of each other as we handle one another with grace, understanding, care, love and delight.

I hope you know where you are. Lift your eyes up and away from screens and toward the sacred screaming aloud to be seen.

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: The Chronicle’s Board of Directors supports student press freedom
author: Duke Student Publishing Company Board
article_text:
Pressure comes with the territory in journalism.

Student journalism is no exception, and all sorts of people from university administrators to parents to fellow students have strong opinions on what should (or should not) be in a campus publication. But while strong opinions are fine, government suppression of student media is not. Members of the student press in the United States, like all other members of the press, are guaranteed the freedom to report, write and publish as they see fit without government interference in their work.

Recently, however, there has been a growing trend of government attempts to suppress the work of student media. Government officials trying to censor the student press is not new, but lately there has been a surge of incidents that seem designed to chill student expression across the country. In the past couple of years, student journalists have been arrested, attacked by police, criminally investigated, threatened with academic discipline and obstructed in other ways by government officials simply for exercising their rights to free expression and a free press.

Late last year, the University of Alabama suspended two student magazines, “Nineteen Fifty-Six” and “Alice Magazine,” citing a non-binding memo from the U.S. Justice Department on diversity and inclusion efforts. Because the University of Alabama is a public university, this move contributes to the ongoing trend of government officials suppressing student media and chilling the free speech of student journalists.

The Board of Directors of the Duke Student Publishing Company, which publishes The Chronicle, has voted to support an amicus brief organized by the Student Press Law Center in support of a legal effort to overturn these suspensions. A total of 40 student media organizations and 15 student media leaders have joined in support of the brief. The Chronicle is financially independent from the University and operates as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, with a board of directors as required by law. The DSPC board is composed of Chronicle alumni who oversee organization finances and policies but do not control what student reporters publish.

The Chronicle is not a party in this lawsuit. Signing the amicus brief means the organization is in support of the arguments made by the SPLC. Against the backdrop of ongoing and nationwide efforts to suppress student free speech, the DSPC board believes it is critical to support student media against efforts to suppress it and to push back against efforts to chill student expression.

Signed,

Duke Student Publishing Company, Inc. Board of Directors

title: Do you
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
At the beginning of this new academic year, I have two words of advice: “Do you.”

Those two words have been linguistic liberation for me ever since a friend said them to me about twenty years ago. I was a young professor at a seminary where I was once a student. When I became a professor, my former teachers became my colleagues. I was one of the youngest faculty members, so I made sure to wear a coat and tie every day to hopefully distinguish myself from the students. I wanted to show intellectual sophistication and demonstrate that I belonged in this new professorial peer group.

To be honest, I felt like an imposter. That’s when my friend — a PhD student at the time, now a university professor — encouraged me one afternoon with those words: “Do you. Just do you.” 

When my friend said those words, the light bulb came on and my heart listened. I didn’t have to “sound like a professor” or “act like a professor.” I was already a professor. My friend was encouraging me to embrace my voice and live into my vocation. I didn’t have to be someone else; all I had to do was be Luke. My friend’s two words put me on a path toward my freedom. From that time on, I have been attempting to “do me.”

The theologian Rev. Howard Thurman expresses the same idea when he says, “follow the grain in your own wood” and “follow the light on your path.” The grain in my wood and my path are mine. They aren’t yours, and they can’t be. You have your own wood grain to follow. Your own voice to lift. Your own gifts to share. Your own intellectual interests on your path.

In his book “Let Your Life Speak”, the writer Parker Palmer warns that sometimes the life we are living “is not the same as the life that wants to live in [us]” and that we may “live a life other than [our] own.” You may try to wear the face of another, when you should let your life speak — Your life.

The world needs you to be the genuine you. Why? The Muslim mystic and poet Rumi gives an answer: “If you are here unfaithfully with us, you’re causing terrible damage.” He’s referring to being faithful to your true self with integrity no matter what. It is the gift to the world only you can offer — you. If you aren’t you, then we can’t be fully who we are meant to be together. It is the blessing we all need.

You don’t have to be someone else just because you’re at Duke. Duke chose you because you are you! It is tempting to be someone else who appears smarter or more successful than you, but we don’t need counterfeits. There is enough fake news and identity theft in the world already. So, start this academic year in freedom and “do you.”

You do you and I’ll do me, and when we see each other on campus this semester, let’s turn to the poem “Ask Me” by William Stafford. It says, “Ask me whether what I have done is my life.”

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: Community members share remembrances for Alex Dittmar
author: Remembrances
article_text:
I was colleagues with Alex last year as part of the Peer Mentorship program at the School of Medicine’s Office of Biomedical Graduate Education. This is a year-long program where we ushered in first-year PhD students into the School of Medicine and co-facilitated discussions on the responsible conduct of research. In that short time, I remember Alex’s enthusiasm, helpful ideas and attention to detail as we worked together on tasks we got paired up to do. I also remember him being committed to his peer mentorship work and how he aimed to be able to provide the best experience to students. He will be greatly missed. My deepest condolences to his family, friends and colleagues at his department.



Jaifred (Jim) Lopez, PhD student in Population Health Sciences at Duke School of Medicine.

title: Duke should call the Justice Department’s bluff
author: Leo Goldberg
article_text:
Even by current White House standards, it has been a terrible, horrible, no good, very bad week for Donald Trump. U.S. munitions stockpiles are dangerously low following a spectacularly botched war against the Iranian regime. The equally botched Reflecting Pool renovations have turned into a national laughing stock, and progressive candidates are surging in elections across the country while the president’s abysmal approval ratings plunge even lower.

To save face, the Trump administration has retreated to an area where they’ve found some limited success over the last year: bullying universities. Unfortunately, that has once again roped Duke into the mess. 

On Aug. 6, the Department of Justice (DOJ) accused Duke Law School of illegally giving preferential treatment to applicants based on race, violating Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. To redress this infraction, the department demanded Duke reach a ‘voluntary resolution agreement,’ or face legal consequences. 

Our institution is now faced with a familiar choice. Duke can either do as it has in the past and sacrifice its integrity and freedom by complying with the federal government, this time to bogus charges brought by a politicized bureau, or it can fight to preserve them and almost certainly win. 

Needless to say, Duke must choose the second option. 

Part of the reason why Duke should not comply with the DOJ’s coercion is that they probably won’t have to. The Trump administration’s war on higher education is now far enough along that we know the president's success in getting concessions from universities has largely been because universities have willingly rolled over and capitulated without a fight. The Trump administration has succeeded because universities have been too scared to call its bluff when it threatens them without ample legal authority.

But developments over the last year have shown that when they do, they won resoundingly against the president’s unwanted advances. Take Harvard University, the most notable example.

In April 2025, the Trump administration froze $2.2 billion in federal grants to Harvard after the University refused to go along with the president’s demands for reform. A month later, the president froze another $450 million. 

Instead of immediately folding and negotiating for a settlement, as many other institutions did, Harvard took the case straight to the courts and won. In September 2025, a federal judge struck down the Trump administration’s freezing of Harvard’s funds as unconstitutional, delivering a major legal victory for the University. The case remains open as the Trump administration appealed the decision in December 2025. 

Harvard is not a standalone case. Along a similar timeline, in August 2025, the Trump administration tried to force the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) to pay a settlement worth $1 billion to resolve alleged civil rights violations. 

Like Harvard, faculty within the UC system marched to the courts, and, in September 2025, won a temporary legal victory when a federal judge ordered Trump to resume the funding of $500 million. The decision soon turned into a major landmark victory for UC schools when the same judge barred Trump from fining UC schools indefinitely in November.

In other words, when universities choose to call Trump’s bluff and fight him in the courts, Trump loses, badly. This has been consistent across public and private institutions.

Returning to Duke, the DOJ’s targeting of Duke Law is the first time our University has been majorly targeted by the federal government since these resounding legal victories. If there is any time to break from our cowardly and contemptible ‘strategy of silence,’ it would be now. 

Should Duke take the Trump administration to court, the odds of victory are overwhelmingly in its favor, and not just because of the now ample legal precedent. The DOJ’s evidence against Duke Law for racial discrimination in admissions is incredibly shoddy. 

According to the DOJ, there are two main pieces of ‘evidence’ of Duke Law having violated Title VI. The first is their categorization system for applicants’ short essay answers. According to the DOJ, Duke Law admissions categorized each response to the essay prompt asking how applicants would further Duke Law's mission with a label, one of which was “diversity/services.” 

Under this metric, a Black student who answered the question by writing about how their experiences as a Black American could benefit Duke Law by contributing to its ‘commitment to equal justice’ is unacceptable to the DOJ. 

To say that this admissions practice, one of several categories used to streamline applications, systemically prioritizes students based on race is self-evidently illogical. In reality, it is routine practice for a holistic approach to admissions — which happens to be used by every single major law school in the country. 

There is no way for Duke Law admissions to see a student’s race through this practice, let alone use it as a systemic admissions determinant. Considering diversity as a factor that could benefit an overall cohort of students, something which appears verbatim in Duke Law’s mission statement in the language of ‘diversity of perspective and experience,’ has nothing to do with racial preference.

The other piece of ‘evidence’ invoked by the DOJ is perhaps even more disjointed. According to the DOJ’s own analysis (a body which under Trump couldn’t even keep an Attorney General for more than a year), the median LSAT score for Black and Hispanic Duke Law applicants (164 and 170) differed by a few points from Asian and white applicants (173 and 172).

Again, this on its own proves nothing and fails to acknowledge the rudimentary fact that LSAT scores are just one of several factors in a holistic consideration of applicants. Personal statements, letters of recommendation and GPA are all factors that are considered by Duke Law. 

The DOJ’s alleged proof against Duke Law would easily fall in a court of law, which means they are counting on Duke not to push back. To conclude, I think there are a few facts that speak for themselves as to why Duke should.

Of the 227 students admitted to the Duke Law JD class of 2028, 15 were Black. That comes out to 7%. The current Black population in the U.S. stands at 14%, which means Black students are significantly underrepresented in Duke Law. Likewise, just 12% are Hispanic. The rest are Asian or white. The question now is whether Duke Law agrees with the DOJ that 15 Black students out of a class of 227 is too many.

If the Trump administration wants a fight, they should get one. It is now up to Duke to decide if they want to uphold the ideals outlined in their own law school’s mission statement, or not. The choice, in my submission, couldn’t be clearer.



Leo Goldberg is a Trinity junior.

title: Scott Dyreng’s AI classroom: Actually, we liked it.
author: The Students of Scott Dyreng’s Tax and Global Management Decisions Class
article_text:
We are a group of students who took Professor Scott Dyreng’s “Artificial Intelligence class” at Fuqua, also known as Tax and Global Management Decisions. We each had our own reasons for enrolling in the course. Some of us heard how popular it was. Scott is known for fostering great conversation and for delivering on his promise to help students “earn back the cost of their tuition in future tax savings.” 

Some of us got interested when we heard him explain the AI classroom to our entire cohort at the beginning of the year. We were tired of just talking about AI and wanted to experiment with it in novel ways. But none of us anticipated the criticisms we have read in the Chronicle over the past few months.

We thoroughly enjoyed Scott, his course and the value added by the AI classroom. We feel strongly enough that we want to respond to the criticisms he and the class have received. Three articles about the course have been published since the beginning of March. Two of the articles raised appropriate concerns about data privacy and the impact on the classroom environment. 

Those students took the course before us during its beta-testing phase, and we cannot comment on their specific experience. The third article, written by a student unfamiliar with the course or Scott, seemed to misinterpret those critiques and drew broader, harsher conclusions, going so far as to call the class “intellectual molestation.”

We feel differently and are more optimistic about the AI classroom’s value. We are also acutely aware of the public’s growing skepticism towards the value proposition of higher education. This skepticism will only grow if new, industry-transforming technology is shunned in the classroom. New technology should be tested critically, not rejected reflexively. The previous articles present valuable perspectives on the class, but we would like to tell a different story that should be included in this discussion as well.

Many of the criticisms centered on concerns about surveillance and psychological safety. But from our perspective inside the classroom, nothing felt unusual to us. Classrooms at Fuqua already record audio and video on Panopto. Participation in the classroom is already tracked manually, either by a TA or from a professor’s best recollection. 

The only thing different in this environment was that transcripts of recordings were submitted into an AI tool for feedback but without our names, voice recordings or any personally identifying information. The data is stored according to rigorous privacy regulations and deleted when the term ends. We think it is unlikely that a bad actor could access the data. But also, we wouldn’t care if they did. Anonymization ensures that statements can’t be traced back to the individuals who made them.

The observation we care much more about comes from our classmates. Psychological safety in that regard is influenced far more by the environment a professor actively cultivates. Based on the passionate conversations in our classroom, we think Scott did a great job. Students took strong policy stances both in favor of and against tariffs, fossil fuel regulations and wealth taxes. We heard arguments from Mamdani fans as well as Mamdani critics. We’ve rarely experienced classroom debates so open and lively while remaining respectful.

Yes, we had to record our weekly team meetings. But we controlled when the recording started and stopped and what we submitted. Some of our teams were comfortable with including their small talk as part of these recordings. Others preferred to chat and catch up during the first five minutes of a meeting before starting their recording and then focusing on the work. This replicated the corporate team environment many of us experienced in our summer internships. The AI classroom didn’t feel like surveillance to us. It felt like an improvement on the existing system, making it more accurate and consistent.

The more surprising outcome, though, was not how AI changed classroom monitoring, but how it changed teamwork. In business school, it can be difficult to get students together to work on a team assignment. MBA candidates have so many competing demands on their time between academics, recruiting, networking, student organizations and leadership positions; meeting with teams to do group projects offers the weakest incentive. 

Generative AI tools made it easy to “divide and conquer” work as individuals and then hastily patch it together to submit as a team assignment — that’s not what the business school is trying to teach us. Our professors want us to learn how to unlock the power of teams by working together on problem sets. 

In this time-constrained environment, though, the temptation to take the easy way out means many teams rarely do the work together.

However, Scott’s AI classroom changed that. Since there was an accountability factor, our teams met together to work on every assignment. Team members showed up prepared and took an active role in the discussion, because they knew the professor would find out if they didn’t. Anything students can learn about working together in teams is downstream of actually doing the work as a team.

The feedback we received from the AI tool was incredibly valuable. It provided an unemotional assessment of an individual’s contribution and the entire team’s performance. When one of our classmates was “called out” by the tool for only speaking for 5% of his team’s meeting (three minutes in an hour session), he participated more actively in the next team meeting. 

When another classmate felt like their input had been too quickly dismissed, other students couldn’t deny it, because the tool confirmed it with its meeting analysis. Even when a student gave Scott a negative course evaluation critical of one aspect of his teaching style, he had to accept that it was at least partially true, because the AI tool partly corroborated the criticism.

The tool did not replace our own individual judgment or diminish our humanity. It enhanced both. We used it as one data point of feedback that we could validate with our own perspective, with our classmates and even with Scott. In the friendly Team Fuqua environment, it can be difficult for classmates to give each other constructive criticism. Even when given, feedback is not always well received, taken as personal attacks or unfairness. But when an objective tool that is run through multiple models to eliminate hallucinations gives this feedback, it stings less, while being harder to ignore. 

It forced us to recognize how we were showing up in our teamwork and ultimately helped us learn more than just the fundamentals of tax policy and decision-making.

Underlying many of the criticisms of the AI classroom is a broader discomfort with being pushed toward AI tools at all. We understand that not everyone wants to use AI in this way. Simultaneously, not everyone wants to be “cold called” in class, give presentations in front of a crowded room or work together on team assignments. Business school has always required students to engage in uncomfortable experiences. That’s part of the reason we came here: to grow and prepare for our future work environment. 

Scott’s goal isn’t to force AI on students. It’s to make students comfortable leaning into AI and help them reconnect with their human strengths. We recognize that the tools and implementation were not perfect either. The beauty of academia is that we can experiment, debate and iterate to develop the right solutions.

After last term’s experiment, the ensuing debate brought up some valid criticisms. Fuqua is taking these criticisms seriously, as it should. The administration is engaging students as important stakeholders in shaping the future of the AI classroom. But our experience suggests that when used thoughtfully, like it was in Scott’s class, AI doesn’t diminish the human elements of education. We are proud to be part of an institution that is taking the lead in this frontier, and we look forward to observing and participating in future, improved iterations of the AI classroom that continue to reinforce positive elements while reducing and eliminating drawbacks.

title: Credit to my teammates
author: Sophie Levenson
article_text:
In my sophomore year of high school, I just barely made the JV basketball team, and I hated it.

It wasn’t the game — nobody on Sports staff would believe this now, but I played starting point guard all three years of middle school and loved it. The problem in 10th grade was my team, or the lack thereof. One of the other girls couldn’t stand me and made it clear as day. She was mean. She punched me once, after a game, for passing to someone else, and our coach pretended not to see. (I didn’t hit her back; I probably should have.)

I didn’t try out for varsity the next year — not that I would have made it — and I stopped running track, too. I had plenty of other things going on and team sports had lost their appeal.

But I spent most of my time at Duke writing about other people’s teams. I covered cross country, track, basketball, soccer and softball; lacrosse a handful of times, field hockey once. In every post-game interview, the athletes I spoke to had virtually the same thing to say every time, always some permutation of “Credit to my teammates.”

I see this everywhere in sports. I think Duke basketball’s success (both men’s and women’s) is largely due to the closeness of the players; it’s no coincidence that Cooper Flagg, Kon Knueppel and Khaman Maluach were best friends while they led the best team in the country last season. My friend Riya wrote a story about how the women’s soccer team climbed to No. 1 in 2024, and it was all about the players’ intense trust in one another. Marissa Young’s No. 12 softball team is much the same way: Those girls are a family.

There have been several times in college when I’ve thought about the strength of relationships that come out of sports teams and several more when I’ve lamented the fact that I was never part of one in any serious way. It must be so comforting to look around the court, or the field, or the track, and see a dozen or more people in the same uniform, working towards the same goal. 

And then at some point this year, I realized that I am on a team. We wear matching t-shirts and spend too much time together and our locker room is this sprawling, colorful place called 301 Flowers. Looking around the office during a Friday afternoon Sports meeting once, I thought to myself that I would go to bat for anyone in the room. Something had bound us together the way that the pursuit of championships bonds sports teams — it was this shared object of love, our newspaper, and the time which we had each, independently, decided to give to it.

One of the things that bonds teammates so deeply is their shared attention to little things to which people outside of the team aren’t privy. On a basketball team, maybe it’s the way the players are rebounding on offense. Maybe a soccer team needs to work on the way it communicates on the field. In The Chronicle, it’s the freshmen not knowing to alternate between “Duke” and “Blue Devils” in their gamers; it’s bad ledes; it’s the current status of our relationship with Duke Athletics communications staff. Sports teammates develop unique ways of talking to one another, and at The Chronicle, we speak in AP Style. Duke basketball players call Isaiah Evans “Slim” and we call Ranjan “Crooked Jindal.”

Our connection isn’t arbitrary, rooted only in these small, funny things. We do important work at The Chronicle, including in the sports department, where our work reaches beyond game stories to explore the bigger storylines behind sports. Our features tap into parts of the human experience best understood through sports stories: We have written about family, relationships, mental health, loneliness, diversity, and countless other human issues through the lens of Duke athletes and their teams. A student newspaper serves many purposes — holding power to account, keeping students and faculty informed, for two — but in my mind, its most important job is to keep its community tied together. Stories open our minds to the interior lives of other people, enabling our empathy and often making our differences seem less drastic.

My time in The Chronicle has been a testament to the way sports stories can bridge all sorts of gaps. The people who hang out in 301 Flowers are some of my closest friends in the world; we are also all pretty different. The sports hall is home to first-years and seniors, Eagles and Chiefs fans, liberals and conservatives, Christians, Hindus, Jews and atheists, frat boys, sorority girls, people who have never been to a Greek life function, some of the smartest people at Duke and some of the biggest fools you’ll ever meet. It is far and away my favorite room in the world.

On paper, the girls on my JV basketball team had a lot more in common than we do in the Chronicle office. But we are the much better team.

title: Duke is increasing writing course sizes again: Here's why that's a bad idea
author: Lecturers, Instructors and Professors of the Thompson Writing Program
article_text:
You chose Duke. Maybe it was Duke’s academic excellence — the opportunity to cultivate “bold ideas” and "relentless curiosity.” Maybe it was Duke’s commitment to learning beyond the classroom. Maybe it was the basketball. 

As professors, we like to think that your decision was rooted in a desire to have deep, meaningful connections with both faculty and peers, supported in large part by small class sizes.

Unfortunately, Duke administration is proposing to raise class sizes, again, in a course required for all first-year students in Trinity: Writing 120 (formerly Writing 101).

This small, first-year seminar serves many functions. It’s a place for new students to feel seen and heard by their professors and peers. It’s a place for students to receive individualized support while building the reading, research and writing skills needed at Duke and beyond. It’s a place to find new friendships, and a place where your professor notices if you’re struggling. 

Writing 120 class sizes have historically been small because individualized attention and support take time. Writing 120 professors don’t have TAs, and each professor teaches multiple sections per semester. Still, they commonly spend an hour or more responding to each student draft, across writing projects with multiple drafts. 

When students need help with a reading, a new skill, a particular writing challenge, their research or just college in general, the professors meet with them one-on-one. They also create and maintain writing communities in the classroom. Writing 120 classes are small because, in larger classes, this level of attention and instruction is untenable. 

Despite this, in fall 2026, university administrators want to increase the size of Writing 120 classes. From 2000 until a recent increase in 2021, these classes were capped at 12. In 2021, they increased to 15. Duke is now proposing to increase them yet again to 17. This would correspond to a 42% increase in class size since 2020. 

In the same time period, the cost of attending Duke has increased by 31%, from $73,519 in 2020-21 to $96,597 in 2026-27. The university recently announced a surplus of $74 million for fiscal year 2026, and an independent audit found it currently takes in over 4% more than it spends per year. Trinity College just had the most successful fundraising year ever. 

What are students paying for and what are Duke’s priorities, if not a world-class education? At a time when Duke should be renewing its commitments to students and faculty, it's squeezing them even harder. 

As Writing 120 professors, we care about our students and their success. In our petition, we strongly oppose the proposed increase in class size for several reasons. 

First and foremost, it would reduce student engagement and achievement. The proposed increase would diminish the level of individualized feedback we’re able to provide on drafts, revisions and research development, all of which are essential in helping students grow as writers. Writing instruction depends on sustained interaction between professors and students, including written and verbal feedback, conferences, office hours and check-ins. 

A larger class size would inevitably reduce the time available for these activities, weakening the effectiveness of our courses and the quality of the learning experience for students. More students per class means less connection time with faculty, one of the four pillars of Duke’s Student Experience. 

Larger classes would also lead to unequal student experiences and workloads. Writing 120 is an important opportunity for small-group learning, one of the very few during students’ first year. Writers develop in community with peers and their professor because writing is an inherently collaborative craft. Writers need the feedback of others to hone their ideas and expression through discussion, experimentation and revision. To create consistent opportunities and experiences for all students, class sizes need to be evenly divisible into small groups. 

They also need to be small, so professors can meaningfully interact with each group. The proposed class size of 17 isn’t evenly divisible into groups of any size. It would force groupwork to be asymmetrical, with some students doing more or different work than others. For example, during peer review, some students might receive less feedback and some groups would have less time to discuss their feedback. With the current class size of 15, professors already struggle to provide consistent experiences for each group.

Many of our courses rely on collaborative projects in which student teams work across weeks or months to conduct research, develop critical thinking skills and learn from one another. The benefits of collaborative project-based learning are well established. The proposed class size increase would disrupt this core element of our pedagogy. Under the increase, these projects would exacerbate day-to-day asymmetries in group size, workload and experience, making it difficult to ensure that all students are fully engaged in the collaborative process. 

Add to that the logistical struggle of cramped and overcrowded classrooms. Many of the Writing 120 classrooms on East campus are already struggling to accommodate the current class size of 15. 

Beyond developing research, reading and communication skills, Writing 120 courses are an important source of community and individual support. We help first-year students adapt to the norms, expectations and protocols of the university, and we are often the first to notice and act when a student is struggling academically, physically or mentally. The larger our classes, the less support we're able to offer, and the higher the risk that students begin to slip through the cracks.

Most of our peer institutions have first-year writing courses capped at 12 (Penn, Princeton, Yale, Johns Hopkins) or 15 (Dartmouth, Harvard, MIT, Vanderbilt). The proposed increase in class size could reduce Duke’s official ranking in US News & World Report, 11-15% of which is based on faculty resources like the 7:1 student-to-faculty ratio Duke advertises. Duke’s Writing in the Disciplines program is currently ranked #2 in the nation. Instead of investing in this key source of prestige and competitiveness, Duke is trying to undermine it by increasing the size of all Writing 120 courses. 

You chose Duke. Is Duke choosing you?

title: In defense of legacy admissions
author: Tate Arges
article_text:
Monday, March 31, was an important day in the life of our university. It was the day that we invited a new generation of Blue Devils to join our Duke family. This incoming class is sure to be as brilliant and accomplished as it is diverse, bringing together students from every corner of the globe and every walk of life. It will include first-generation college students and students from low-income backgrounds who are stepping onto a campus like this for the first time. It will also include students from immense wealth who represent the latest in a long line of Blue Devils in their families. These latter students are often grouped under a single, increasingly controversial label: “legacy”.

At Duke and other elite universities around the country, “legacy” has become a loaded word. In conversations about admissions equality, legacy students are often discussed as symbols of elitism: beneficiaries of generational privilege who take spots from more deserving applicants. This kind of criticism is not without merit. But in our haste to condemn legacy admissions, we have distorted the term into something it was never supposed to mean.

To understand why, it helps to start with how Duke and other elite universities actually build their incoming classes. Admissions committees are not simply trying to assemble the highest possible average SAT score. They are trying to build a community of roughly 1,700 students who will live, study and grow together over four years. That means practicing a form of holistic admissions that finds value in students who exemplify different kinds of excellence and different kinds of contribution to university life. A class made up solely of the highest academic achievers who are selected without regard to background, connection or communal contribution might look impressive on paper. But that class might also be fragmented, competitive to the point of isolation and lacking any shared identity. Community is not built solely on academic metrics: it is something universities must intentionally cultivate by examining the whole of each applicant. 

When thinking about admissions this way, there is a version of “legacy” that comes to mind that the public debate surrounding admissions has seemingly forgotten. This is not a defense of every legacy admission. It is a defense of a narrower category: highly qualified, already competitive applicants whose connection to the university is not transactional, but relational. 

They are students that we should want at Duke. 

They are the students who grew up with Duke being an irreplaceable core of their family’s story. They heard about thrilling games in Cameron and hijinks in K-ville. They walked through West Campus as children, and they see Duke not just for its ranking or what it can add to a resume or social status, but as the community that matters so deeply to the people they love. Their desire to be at Duke is not because of familial expectation; it is because of the relationship they inherited from their family.

This is different from the stereotype that often dominates our discussions about university admissions: the affluent student who applies because that's what their family has always done, who has rarely visited campus and who views attending Duke as a social distinction to brag about. These students exist. But they should not define what “legacy” means. 

One of the hard truths about attending any college is how disorienting it can be for students when they first arrive. Even at a place with as many resources as Duke, many students will still arrive unsure of how to navigate the university experience academically, socially and emotionally. First-generation, transfer and low-income students might often feel this the most intensely. Ideal legacy students can and should be resources in that process. Their familiarity with campus traditions, buildings, alumni networks and institutional quirks can help others find their footing. They can explain what “tenting” is, how to navigate the bus system or where to find support when a class goes badly. And their excitement to be here can be contagious, helping others to feel that Duke is not an impersonal machine but rather a community worth investing in, even when times are hard.

Legacy students can also serve as bridges between the student body and the alumni community. Critics are right to point out that universities often justify legacy admissions by pointing to the correlation between alumni donations and legacy admissions. This concern should not be dismissed. But alumni engagement is not only about donations. Students with deep ties to the university can draw alumni (their parents or their parents' friends) into increased active participation in the life of the university, not just as donors, but as mentors, volunteers and members of an ongoing community. In this way, legacy students can play a role similar to that of student-athletes, who energize alumni networks and sustain connections across generations.

This is not an argument that legacy students are inherently better or more deserving than other students. It is an argument that they can carry inter-generational social and cultural knowledge, which can strengthen the university community. 

And none of this is to deny the reality that donor influence exists in admissions. Preferential treatment for families who can write seven-figure checks is wrong. It undermines trust in higher education and perpetuates inequality. But calling these kinds of admissions “legacy” muddies the conversation. Paying for admission is not legacy. It is influence and favoritism. If we want to reform the admissions process, we should name that practice directly rather than just lumping it into a broader category that includes genuine intergenerational connections. 

Clear language matters. If the problem is donor preference, we should call it donor preference. When we label everything as “legacy,” we can obscure what we are actually trying to fix.

Reclaiming the term “legacy” does not mean defending every legacy admission policy. Universities should be transparent about how legacy status is considered, and they should ensure that it does not threaten commitments to equality, access and academic excellence. But reform does not require erasing the value of intergenerational university connections. A legacy should mean more than just a checkbox on an application or a line on a donation spreadsheet. It should mean that a student comes to Duke already deeply shaped by the university’s story and is ready and eager to shape that story in return. 

The task then is not to pretend privilege doesn’t exist, but to distinguish between transaction and relationship. If we are serious about making Duke a university that fosters both academic excellence and meaningful community, this is a distinction we cannot ignore.

Tate Arges is a second-year graduate student at Duke Divinity School.

title: Sanford, I can’t change the world
author: Jasmine Fan
article_text:
Earlier this semester, an editorial by Sherman Criner described the Sanford School of Public Policy in a “crisis of meaning.” 

While I wouldn’t necessarily deem the School in a crisis, I do believe Sanford needs to reevaluate its adherence to its values and principles. One in particular feels noticeably absent from the undergraduate experience: service. 

First, let me preface by saying that I’m incredibly grateful for Sanford. As a school, it offers resources most departments can’t come close to matching. The alumni network is unparalleled, the research opportunities vast and the professors brilliant. Journalists, authors, scholars, senators and ambassadors pour onto our campus. I’ve had some of the most fascinating discussions within Sanford’s walls. And I’ve traveled to Washington, D.C. on Duke’s dime — twice. 

Let me be clear: It is only because I value Sanford so deeply that I am critical of it. And it is precisely because of its wealth of resources that I know it is capable of more.

I agree with Criner that the curriculum needs reworking. But the issue isn’t solely what Sanford teaches — it’s how it teaches. People don’t form lifelong moral commitments from PowerPoint slides and institutional slogans. Drilling in moral dogma every Tuesday and Thursday from 1:25 to 2:40 p.m. to a room of 18- and 19-year-olds is probably not going to be very effective. 

Sanford’s defining value is service. Community engagement is what sets public policy apart from the theoretical focus of a political science degree. And yet, experiential learning remains largely absent in the undergraduate core, particularly Public Policy 155, Introduction to Policy Analysis.

Like many prospective public policy students, I heard the rumors about the gateway course during my freshman year. 

“Definitely take an elective first.” 

“155 is why I switched to Political Science.” 

“The gateway is the most boring class I’ve taken at Duke.”

To my surprise, I ended up loving the class. The group discussions were engaging, and the assignments pushed me to master the fundamentals of memo writing. Above all, my professor was thoughtful, genuine and kind.

There was really only one qualm I had with the course. 

On the first day of class, we discussed poverty. The issue wasn’t the topic itself but how it was taught that felt off. We were listening to someone preach about poverty, all while sitting in a gothic castle backed by a $12.3 billion endowment. The disconnect was impossible to ignore.

If you asked for my favorite poem, I would point you to Walt Whitman’s “When I Heard the Learned Astronomer.” In short, we don’t learn astronomy from staring blankly at diagrams in a lecture hall. We step outside, tilt our heads and stare “in perfect silence at the stars.” 

That is all to say, Sanford simply cannot manufacture moral purpose within the boundaries of a lecture hall. Inside an ivory tower, the view looks pretty different from above.

Sanford students need a new vantage point.

Right now, the public policy major risks placing too much emphasis on policy and not enough on the public. Hands-on application is central to every discipline. In chemistry, that means lab experiments. In theater, performances. For public policy, community engagement. 

Former Dean Judith Kelley, celebrating 50 years of Sanford, echoed the School’s mission “to change the world.” And while that sentiment is certainly inspiring, it also presented me with a dilemma: How can I begin to change the world when I don’t understand it yet? Even the more attainable calling to “serve my community” seems a dizzying undertaking, especially when the “Duke bubble” is stubbornly difficult to pop.

The truth is, there are already more than enough people who aspire to change the world. There are considerably fewer who first seek to understand it. 

I’m young and naive. I’m not exactly sure how to understand the world. But I do know it requires stepping outside a lecture hall.

Though Sanford’s internship requirement is intended to push students beyond the classroom, it falls short of experiential learning. An internship doesn’t necessarily guarantee meaningful engagement. One student can devote their summer to a local nonprofit while another spends 300 hours behind a desk, drafting policy memos. Both experiences fulfill the requirement, but only one connects policy to the public it is meant to serve. 

Sanford’s internship also becomes a burden to students who aren’t able to carve out their summers, and meeting the 300-hour requirement during the school year is even more daunting. More importantly, the requirement outsources hands-on learning to a single, isolated experience. If Sanford truly wants students to gain real-world perspective, that learning should not be confined to an internship. The experience should be embedded within the core curriculum itself, rather than stacked on top of summer obligations. 

What we’re really missing isn’t more policy analysis. We’re missing perspective. 

Duke’s service-learning model aims to build this perspective. And while service-learning courses include some public policy electives, they are nowhere to be found in the undergraduate core.

Sanford should embed community engagement within the gateway course. To understand education policy, students could partner with public schools. For civil justice, they could speak to legal aid organizations. Local partnerships would allow professors to draw from real case studies and allow students to pop that ever-so-stubborn “Duke bubble.” After all, without an understanding of our local Durham community, how can we expect to understand the world beyond it? 

Still, it is important to acknowledge the many pitfalls of service-learning. Service can easily become performative and inauthentic. When poorly designed, the approach risks serving the institution more than the community. 

Community engagement, then, shouldn’t begin with the intent to serve, but with the intent to understand. Students might start by having conversations with local government officials and nonprofit leaders. Or maybe they begin by simply observing: attending a Durham City Council meeting could be just as valuable as attending a lecture. Perhaps this is what Whitman has been trying to tell us all along — step outside, tilt your head and stare at the stars. 

Until then, it feels like Sanford is training undergraduates to legislate the world before we’ve even encountered it. 

I want to first understand the world. And I’d like to walk in more shoes than just my own.

Jasmine Fan is a Trinity junior.

title: Things I’ve found in a second review
author: Andrew Negus
article_text:
“2-ing” is a bit strange to be so enthusiastic over. Yet, I patiently check my inbox each Thursday for emails from Abby DiSalvo. Which articles would I have the privilege of reviewing? 

I vividly remember the day Sophie Levenson brought me to my first meeting, where she assured me that I’d fit right in with my love of sports and mild interest in writing. Sitting down in the main hall of 301 Flowers, we introduced ourselves (name, class year, hometown), shouted out a piece of writing and something we looked forward to. This would range from sporting events, seeing people or finishing course work. 

For the past year, although I never mentioned it in the meetings, I’ve always looked forward to my weekly associate editor shift. This may come off as strange, since some might see it as tedious fact-checking. Yet “2’ing” has revealed how much I value being a part of The Chronicle. The additional day outside of meetings to fact-check provided a greater introduction to the strong community of this newspaper.

It has allowed me to find the sanctuary that is the Chron office — somewhere to watch games and eat cookie cake; to study if you don’t want to go to the library; to reminisce on Duke’s athletic success, and most importantly, to spend nights with friends. 

I have always said The Chronicle is the most welcoming organization at Duke because the process to join is quite simple. One might assume that such a low barrier might decrease the overall commitment between its members. After four years, that has proven to be the opposite. Every writer, photographer and creator makes a tangible difference. Beyond output, The Chronicle has a deep connectedness — these people value me as a friend more than as a writer.

I’ve found opportunities for dream-like experiences. I’ve been lucky enough to travel across North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida twice and back home to Tennessee to cover games. 

I’ll never forget the nailbiters, from my first interview ever with retired head-coach Jamie Green to prepping for my USF coverage on Clearwater Beach. I’ll never forget Shake Shack in Miami, Home Team BBQ on the drive home from Clemson. I’ll never forget asking event staff where the media room is in each new arena, raising my voice to ask Jon Scheyer a question and being a guest on the Blue Devil Beat podcast.

I’ll never forget shaking Kara Lawson’s hand over winter break, co-writing in Koskinen with Sophie and last year’s women’s tennis victory over North Carolina on the road. I’ll never forget my blog posts for women’s basketball, men’s soccer and Duke legend Maliq Brown.

I would have never thought I would cover a men’s basketball game in Cameron. When that game was Cooper Flagg’s 42-point game, the most ever by a Duke freshman, I couldn’t believe my luck. Sitting in the press row with the Crazies just inches behind, no basketball game in my life has flown by that quickly — there was barely time for me to digest the moment’s gravity, especially since it was my first time writing for the sport.

That experience was unique, unlike anything from any of my previous work, because it felt like I was writing in a team. Ranjan edited my writing in real-time and I worked alongside Rodrigo at the table and in the press room. I credit my desire for writing about women’s basketball to the energy and the excitement of that game. 

That’s the necessity of reflection and review; sometimes, you discover the true effect the second time around.

I’ve found that I’m surrounded with incredible talent. As a university, we’re accustomed to excellence, and I think we should appreciate that more. The students, the athletes we report on, are worthy of excellent coverage. 

Searching through the voice memos on my phone, I see a portfolio of interviews with future tennis professionals, a USA national team coach and NBA players. I understand that we’re a men’s basketball school by nature, but nothing could compare to the joy of sitting amidst a packed Ambler Tennis Stadium for the women’s match against North Carolina. It is undeniable that some of the best events I’ve watched as a student were soccer games, tennis matches and women’s basketball. 

This excellence goes beyond those we cover. After all, all Duke students are talented. The staff of The Chronicle themselves have appeared on ESPN, CNN and many even go on to pursue journalism full-time. 

Being a part of this team means we get to learn from everyone’s strengths. Seeing their writing, how each person describes and tells a story, has helped me approach articles in new ways. Conducting interviews with other beats has shown me the value of crafting excellent questions. Having my work live-edited by uppermast is like a direct coaching session. All the extra analysis from the people of The Chronicle has made me a better writer. 

There’s a great importance to double-checking every detail that goes beyond writing. It’s called “2’ing” because it refers to the second set of eyes that reviews the work before it’s published. Those eyes ensure the quality in every part of our paper. 

I’ll miss being those eyes on Thursday afternoons, but I’ll always be grateful for the things I’ve found.

Andrew Negus is a Trinity senior and served as a sports associate editor for The Chronicle’s 121st volume. He thanks Jonathan Levitan, Andrew Long, Ranjan Jindal and Abby DiSalvo for their leadership and friendliness that truly embody The Chronicle spirit.

He’s grateful for every senior in The Chronicle for their unwavering support and friendship.

He’d like to thank Dom Fenoglio for training him how to be an associate editor. He’ll always remember Martin, Myles, Asa and all the women’s basketball beats for their coverage of an amazing season. He cannot wait for his trip with Myles to Phoenix one day.

Lastly, he thanks Sophie Levenson for inspiring him to keep writing.

title: The weight of the story
author: Lucas Lin
article_text:
Journalism is an assembly line. 

A story goes through a series of work stations in the newsroom. After a story is ideated, the reporter lays out its structure and gathers the necessary components to meet a deadline. The draft is then subject to rigorous and iterative testing. AP style is the protocol of standardization. Fact-checking is our quality control; we catch any potential mistakes before publication. 

Once we press the “publish” button, the story is out to the world. 

To boost a story to customers, we devise distribution strategies via Instagram. Sales figures are measured in likes. To update our subscribers, we also provide delivery services. Subject lines are our labels. However, not everyone opens the box at the doorstep. Occasionally, we issue recall notices, when stories leave the floor with a minute error.
