My three years at The Chronicle has taught me that the life cycle of most news stories is relatively short. In fact, most stories go unnoticed. Breaking stories generate immediate peaks for a few hours before fading the next day. Human interest features can stretch over a week. They show instead of tell. They evoke imagery and curate photo galleries. Even so, they can still be forgotten. There are exceptions, of course.

I may be more pessimistic, but I have doubts about the future of journalism. At a time when people receive snippets of information from chatbots and TikTok, the countless hours we pour into crafting stories can feel obsolete. Sometimes, I fear that the assembly line will one day close. 

I found it difficult reconciling this reality with my love for stories. 

As reporters, we pick up stories and complete them under a deadline. The same process goes on and on. As editors, we verify every piece of information, refine ledes and nutgrafs and draft the headline. But the fast-paced news cycle keeps demanding that we set our sights on tomorrow and not today (literally, when we publish at midnight after a six-hour shift).

I found myself writing stories about people I’ve never met, drafting articles over a phone call and exchange of emails. I was hardwired to meet deadlines, verify facts, publish three stories a day, break news and repeat. 

I rarely sit down and consider the weight of the story. 

Hundreds of stories have passed through me, in a continuous stream along the belt. Yet, I failed to closely examine them. I felt attached to storylines but detached from the story. 

Launching the paper’s first multimedia section aimed at audience engagement, I’ve traded genuine emotions with bite-sized hooks, hoping that students with ever-decreasing attention spans would pause their scrolling for even a few seconds. I wasn’t happy when I had cheapened a story for clicks. 

But journalism isn’t an assembly line. After all, we are human, too. 

My most memorable stories were not long-term investigative hit pieces or centennial features. They were obituaries where I saw the inevitability of loss in this ephemeral world. They were raw emotions of happiness, spontaneity and sorrow that one would miss in the blink of an eye. In those moments, I felt a genuine human connection, sharing in their emotions and preserving them on the record. I let the line of “objectivity” loose and allowed their experiences to register as my own. 

My favorite memories with my fellow editors and staff were moments when we allowed ourselves to simply be human. I couldn’t have asked for a more talented editor-in-chief, whose spontaneous backflips, playing catch and selfie bombs at the office brighten my day. I couldn’t have asked for a more brilliant and effortlessly funny news editor, whose voice and personality shine through every story she writes, despite weathering difficult times. I couldn’t have asked for a better lineage of managing editors, though I’ve clearly inherited their nonchalant outlook on life. (Note: I have found our successor.) Lastly, I couldn’t have asked for a better audience engagement director who shares my obsession with patrolling follower counts. We were this close! 

Managing editor was not my favorite job. We charted the growth of our digital presence and held power accountable, but that wasn’t what drew me to journalism. I missed my first-year staff reporter self, arriving as an international student and full of curiosity about this campus. My first stories brought me to unexpected corners of campus, from DKU study abroad students to the local Durham Public School board. I knew I wanted to learn more, talk to people from different backgrounds and look them in the eye. 

I have an opportunity to love journalism again. This may mean taking a break. This may mean getting to know my fellow staffers beyond the walls and stairs of 301 Flowers. This may mean writing stories I truly care about, not stories others think I should care about. 

Lucas Lin is a Trinity junior and served as managing editor for The Chronicle’s 121st volume.

He extends his gratitude to Ana Despa for her trust and for guiding the volume with bravery, clarity and patience, and to Claire Cranford for shaping 301 Flowers into a space of warmth and passion while mentoring a new generation of reporters and editors. He is thankful to Ranjan Jindal for indulging him in his crazy plans and forgiving him for stealing countless SD cards. 

He is grateful for Dylan Wang, Jackson Kitts and the staff of multimedia who believed in the power of video in telling stories. Multimedia would not be possible without its incredible staff who were not afraid to bring the camera to strangers on the streets. 

Lastly, he is confident that Vol. 122 is in capable hands with Dylan Halper, Ella Moore and Abby DiSalvo at the helm.

title: Farewell columns 2026
author: Staff Reports
article_text:
"I came to The Chronicle the way you come to anything when you're running from a question you don't know how to answer," wrote Ana Despa, a Pratt junior who served as the editor-in-chief of The Chronicle’s 121st volume.

"But journalism isn’t an assembly line. After all, we are human, too," wrote Lucas Lin, a Trinity junior who served as managing editor of The Chronicle's 121st volume. 

"The Chronicle is, objectively, an unserious institution — we are 18 to 22-year-olds running a large public service experiment with very little professional oversight, giving you the facts, holding ourselves to an exceptionally high standard that nobody required of us except ourselves. And yet we have done so much; we can do so much," wrote Claire Cranford, a Trinity junior who served as news editor of The Chronicle’s 121st volume.

"I don’t think I would have ended up in the third-floor Chronicle office writing this column if I weren’t lucky enough to have people who also believed in me," wrote Abby DiSalvo, a Trinity junior who served as sports editor of The Chronicle’s 121st volume.

"However, photography at The Chronicle is not just about the fleeting moments that come and go. It is about perspective: where you stand, what you choose to see, and what you decide stays in the image matters," wrote Amy Zhang, a Trinity junior who served as photography editor of The Chronicle’s 121st volume.

"The arts try to capture the moments in between the events that define our lives. They ask us to see the beauty in the mundane and the comprehensible in the infinite — to find meaning in the attempt itself," wrote Kadin Purath, a Trinity senior who served as recess editor of The Chronicle's 121st volume.

"The Chronicle brings to itself people with ideas, with passions and with courage. A courage to be bold, to think unlike others," wrote Shambhavi Sinha, a Trinity junior who served as opinion editor of The Chronicle’s 121st volume.



"The Chronicle has been the excuse I get to use to find the answers to my own questions, the opportunity I’ve had to grow as a communicator and a leader in a newsroom that prides itself on impact and excellence," wrote Zoe Kolenovsky, a Trinity senior who served as news editor of The Chronicle’s 120th volume and data editor of The Chronicle’s 121st volume.

"The Chronicle has given me so much more than life lessons; it has defined my Duke experience," wrote Ranjan Jindal, a Trinity senior and audience engagement director and multimedia editor of The Chronicle’s 121st volume, as well as sports editor of The Chronicle’s 120th volume.

"Art demands more from us than passively scrolling TikTok or mindlessly watching some trash TV. But that doesn’t mean we should abandon it and drift to the path of least resistance, to a world of low-quality trash," wrote Zev van Zanten, a Trinity senior who served as Recess managing editor for The Chronicle's 121st volume and Recess editor for The Chronicle's 120th volume.

"My friends from The Chronicle are often the first to find out about any job offers, good grades or moments of victory, but more importantly, they have listened to me complain, bemoan and otherwise grumble about everything from intramural sports to deep personal obstacles," wrote Dom Fenoglio, a Trinity senior who served as a sports managing editor for The Chronicle’s 120th volume.

"There’s something to be said for the urge to seek out stories from strangers — and to listen for no other purpose than listening. I only wish I had done it sooner," wrote Mia Penner, a senior who served as the audience engagement editor for The Chronicle’s 120th volume and Editor-at-Large for The Chronicle’s 119th volume. 

"To the writers who will be around next year and long after I’m gone, keep harnessing that love. Let it flow through you in everything you do, in The Chronicle and elsewhere," wrote Martin Heintzelman, a Trinity senior who served as sports managing editor of The Chronicle’s 121st volume. 

"What The Chronicle gave me back was that sense of joy that comes from writing about things that make you passionate, from crafting stories that have a piece of your soul inside because that’s how much you care about telling them," wrote Mackenzie Sheehy, a Trinity senior who served as Blue Zone Editor for The Chronicle’s 119th volume and sports associate editor for The Chronicle’s 120th and 121st volumes.

"Three years on, my time at The Chronicle became more than just chasing stories for a student newspaper; it became a place where I found a loving community of fellow writers and shared some of my most treasured memories at college," wrote Jun Tan, a Trinity senior who served as associate editor for the sports department in The Chronicle's 121st volume. 

"In that vein, perhaps most of all, writing and editing for Opinion has made me more inquisitive and less comfortable in certainty. This, I am happy to say, won’t end with graduation," wrote Anna Sorensen, a Trinity senior and an associate opinion editor for The Chronicle’s 120th and 121st volumes.

"The Chronicle pushed me to explore Durham in ways I never would have otherwise," wrote Arnav Jindal, a Trinity senior who served as Recess culture editor for The Chronicle's 119th and 121st volumes. 

"These experiences, albeit paling in comparison to those of varsity and club athletics, helped us to grow as writers, understanding the complex emotions that go into competition," wrote Luke Jovanovic, a Trinity senior and sports writer for the 118th, 119th, 120th and 121st volumes. 

"I get a huge wave of satisfaction at putting my ideas into words, and I love seeing the cute blue box on The Chronicle website with my name on it," wrote Anna Garziera, a Trinity senior who served as an opinion columnist for The Chronicle's 119th, 120th and 121st volumes.

"Being a part of this team means we get to learn from everyone’s strengths. Seeing their writing, how each person describes and tells a story, has helped me approach articles in new ways," wrote Andrew Negus, a Trinity senior who served as an associate sports editor for The Chronicle's 121st volume.

"Our connection isn’t arbitrary, rooted only in these small, funny things. We do important work at The Chronicle, including in the sports department, where our work reaches beyond game stories to explore the bigger storylines behind sports," wrote Sophie Levenson, a Trinity senior who served as Sports managing editor for The Chronicle’s 120th volume.

title: For the first time, I couldn't pick a bead
author: Ana Despa
article_text:
I opened the top drawer of my bathroom sink in my childhood home. Among the clutter of scented hand sanitizers, scrunchies and neon nail polish that my parents couldn't bring themselves to throw out, my eyes caught a bracelet I wore proudly to middle school. It was one of those Lokai bracelets with one rubber bead that supposedly carried water from Mt. Everest and one with mud from the Dead Sea to represent the highs and lows in life.

I held that bracelet on countless rides to school, pressing my finger on whichever bead felt like me that day. Holding it then on spring break, I couldn't choose one.

I came to The Chronicle the way you come to anything when you're running from a question you don't know how to answer. I was a Duke sophomore who didn't know what the future could hold, watching everyone around me seem more certain by the day. I couldn’t fully find my place in my biomedical engineering classes and needed somewhere where I could still be exceptional — where the metrics weren’t grades but were mine to set. So, I spent my waking hours campaigning for editor-in-chief, and I won, and for a while that was enough to drown out everything else.

For the past year, I've spent 6 p.m. to midnight in 301 Flowers editing stories, planning coverage and managing a staff that has become family. I've tended to a filled inbox that made me dread Monday mornings and kept me anxiously refreshing Outlook on Friday afternoons when Duke administrators and President Donald Trump famously find the time to announce moves on higher education.

The news cycle didn’t pause for exams, exhaustion or inexperience. I learned that quickly — calling a source between classes or making sense of a policy change on the floor of Hudson Hall, laptop plugged into whatever outlet I could find. Duke genuinely struggles with transparency, and we covered it during a year when higher education felt like it was shifting underneath everyone. I pushed assignments to the side, skipped dinners and sleep, and lost a friendship I held close because I kept choosing the office. 

There’s a particular kind of loneliness that comes with being in charge that nobody warns you about. Newspapers are filled with readers, and at times, staff who believe with complete sincerity that they could do the job better than you. You cling to the idea that if everyone is happy, you’re probably not doing the job right. Some nights that’s reassuring. Other nights, it's just something you say.

Sometimes, someone who barely knows you misconstrues your character so blatantly that someone might believe it. That’s when I wanted to yell. Not defend myself or explain, just yell. "That's not me. That's not who I am." 

Those nights I wondered whether I had chased this role because I loved journalism, or because I was seeking proof that I was still great at something.

Being editor has thrown me into conversations I never thought I would encounter. I never thought I would spend hours on the phone with a lawyer on the weekend of my 21st birthday. I never thought I would be on the receiving end of repeated texts and calls from a professor upset that I reported on his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein. 

There were nights I sat in the newsroom while people laughed and argued and teased me about a missed comma, and I was quietly wondering whether I was going to have to take a witness stand in court. The room was full and loud, yet I was completely alone in it.

That’s when I wanted to leave.

The Chronicle doesn't really let you, though. Not because of any obligation or contract, but because, at the end of the day, the people make it impossible to walk away cleanly.

The quotes added to the quote wall during nightly production that made no sense to anyone outside the office. The late-night conversations with my news and managing editor after the front page was set, when we were finally just people again. The times my closest friends waited for me to click "Start RSS" on the Daily Rundown so we could all walk back to the dorms together. Nobody had to, they just did. The times Duke communications was mad we got a story out and we laughed anyway, because we knew it meant we had done something right.

We broke stories that went national. I heard thank yous from staff members who said Duke's cost-cutting was being done in secret and felt our coverage gave them a voice. I never thought I would be in a position to hear those words either.

The Chronicle showed me that the world is not always fair or happy but doing the work anyway, in a cramped attic office with people who care about a front page most of campus will scroll past in thirty seconds, is its own kind of answer to the questions I was avoiding.

This paper brought me my closest friends and a sense of purpose I hope to find again somewhere else. I took the work seriously in ways that sometimes cost me the lightness of it, and I found that out too late. There’s something quietly beautiful about making your biggest problem how to layout the front page of a student newspaper. 

I put the bracelet back in the drawer. 

Maybe I was really at the top, surrounded by people I love, doing work that mattered. Or maybe the loneliness was the whole truth.

For the first time in a long time, I didn't need the answer.

Ana Despa is a Pratt junior and served as the editor-in-chief for The Chronicle’s 121st Volume. She would like to thank her managing editor Lucas Lin and news editor Claire Cranford for helping her steer the ship through this chaotic year. 

She would also like to thank Abby DiSalvo, Shambhavi Sinha, Kadin Purath, Amy Zhang and Anabel Howery for their steady leadership and contagious passion that kept the paper thriving. Nightly production would have been lifeless without senior editors Ryan Kilgallen and Aseel Ibrahim and the best lowermast she could have asked for, filling the room with laughter.

When all is said and done, the volume would’ve fallen apart without Vol. 120’s news and sports editors, Zoe Kolenovsky and Ranjan Jindal, who were always the first people to give a nod of reassurance or pick up a frantic phone call. She also owes a great deal to general manager Chrissy Murray, who guided her through the hardest moments of her editorship, and to the professors in the DeWitt Wallace Center who kept their doors open.

And most of all, she cannot wait to see where Volume 122 takes The Chronicle.

title: It was all a gift
author: Amy Zhang
article_text:
There are moments you don’t recognize as gifts until much later, until you’re standing at the edge of something ending, trying to gather what it all meant. As I write, so many things in my life are in flux: a potential early graduation, trying to navigate my career and the realization that some chapters, like this one, close before you are fully ready to say goodbye.

My time in The Chronicle started as a first-year with a borrowed mirrorless camera and a love for finding “the shot.” It’s when everything aligns for just a split second — the light, the motion, the feeling — and I realize I’ve just witnessed something irreplaceable and irreplicable. 

In portrait-taking or graduation photos, you can usually ask someone to re-pose or re-do a shot. There is a level of comfort in that kind of control — the ability to adjust the angle, fix the lighting and refine the imperfections in post-production to create a specific vision. You can always pause, step back, re-evaluate and try again. 

In photo-journalism, however, more often than not, once a moment is gone, it is usually gone forever. 

There is no asking a Duke basketball player to re-do a free throw or requesting a protester to recreate the exact moment their voice cracked mid-speech, the crowd gathering around them in a way that cannot be staged or repeated. There is no rewinding of a vibrant pink sunset over West Campus in the last few minutes before dusk.

There is no recreating the joy, the celebration and the confetti for a football team after an unlikely underdog victory at a championship game. There is no backtracking when the cherry blossom petals begin to fall and gather quietly along the paths of the Duke gardens. There are no words for and nothing you can do when a heartbreaking injury flashes across your viewfinder. 

However, photography at The Chronicle is not just about the fleeting moments that come and go. It is about perspective: where you stand, what you choose to see, and what you decide stays in the image matters. But more often than not, perspective came from chaos — from learning how to exist, and even thrive, in strange places.

A few perspectives I’ve learned while at The Chronicle are literal: the fourth floor of Wilkinson has a terrace with the best views of the Chapel. Courtside of Cameron Indoor, next to the visitor’s bench, is the best place to be for capturing Duke’s offense in the first half of any game. Courtside of Dean Dome in the seconds after a UNC win over Duke is less than ideal (you’ll probably be trampled in a court storming). And standing on a shaky wooden media stage in Bryan Center is probably unsafe, but it is the best shot you can get of Tim Walz at a campaign rally.

But perspective also means learning what to include — and what to leave out. Cropping, I learned, is its own kind of storytelling. A few pixels to the left or right can completely change an image, like isolating a player in a moment of focus, widening the frame to show the encompassing chaos of a student section, cutting out distractions in the edges of a shot, or deliberately leaving them in to tell a fuller, messier truth. 

I’ve done my fair share of bad crops and have seen plenty more while editing photos shot by staff photographers. However, unlike how other editors can issue a “The Chronicle regrets the error” note, there is no correction I can do for a published photo: it simply lives on the internet or in print, permanent and uncorrected. Every frame is a choice, and every choice reveals something about what the photographer thinks is worth noticing. And over my three years as a photographer here, I slowly realized that what you exclude can matter just as much as what you keep. 

Over time, The Chronicle gave me something else, too: perspective on what matters. At Duke, it is easy to get caught up in grades, deadlines, recruiting, the metrics of success. But my time behind a camera taught me that so much of college life isn’t measurable at all. It is in the joy and the stress, the games and the losses, the vibrant protests of student discourse, the camaraderie of late nights in The Chronicle office, and the quiet mornings in the blooming Duke gardens. It is in the way this campus uniquely breathes. 

And that perspective, more than anything, was a gift.

Amy Zhang is a Trinity junior and served as photography editor for The Chronicle’s 121st volume. She is deeply thankful for the mentorship of the editors and photographers who came before her — Alyssa Ting, Karen Xu and Abigail Bromberger — and credits them for setting examples of excellent leadership. 

She expresses the most heartfelt gratitude to Anabel Howery, the best co-editor she could have ever asked for. Thank you for being a constant — always just a text away, always ready with clarity, care, and perspective when it mattered most.

She is endlessly grateful for her dream team of Andy Jiang, Lena Nguyen and Wanyu Zhang for their tireless dedication and endless support throughout the year, but also, for sharing her love of hotpot and humoring all of the crazy ideas. 

To Katie Tan, she’s deeply grateful for the steady advice, constant reassurance and unconditional friendship from afar.

She is thrilled about Wanyu Zhang and Alex Long leading ChronPhoto next year and deeply believes that the department is in wonderful and capable hands. It has been an immense joy to witness the growth of Cynthia Canabal Comabella, Logan Swanner and Kevin Li as photographers, and she cannot wait to see how they shape the future of the photo department.

Lastly, she is deeply grateful to her parents and brother for their unwavering love and support — for embracing her side quest of chasing stories, specific shots and running a photo department, and for patiently enduring the long days and late-night calls that came with it.

title: A house of glass
author: Shambhavi Sinha
article_text:
I have always liked a lot of things — perhaps, too many. 

From physics to economics, from visual art to cinema. What some chide as a weakness has allowed me to be open — to other people, their eyes, their lives. 

I had learned at a young age that compromise is a core pillar of the social contract. Every opinion I had held strongly had brought me to circumstances where I could do nothing but give them up. Being proven wrong, time and time again, does wonders for one’s inner understanding. Expectedly, I became a person who could not answer a question without a “You see, it’s complicated because …”

I had, since then, come to believe opinions to be an object of fluid state — like liquid glass, hot to touch and glimmering to see, strengthened with time. Those who held them with strength, then coveted a delicate reality that was to be inevitably broken.

And yet, I found myself enamored with Opinion when I came here. In a world of flux that never ceases to accelerate, each student on this campus attempts to fulfill the self-centered (though not always ill-intentioned) motive of “doing something great.” Some involve themselves in campaigns to bolster change that doesn’t need to happen. Some demand real change. Some create cinema. Others create B2B SaaS “startups.” 

These things have happened for countless decades. Yet, it all seems so new. After all, every four years, Duke is the same, yet it is what it’s never been before. All that remains of the past are words, thoughts and ideas that we can find glimpses of. And that to me is what Opinion is. The birth of an idea, a person, of a lineage — one that extends beyond the momentary four years we have here. 

This notion is why I often said, during recruitment or otherwise, that I think Opinion is the voice of Duke. Where social media exists as a blip in our time here — posts on Fizz are hardly remembered after a few days of shock-filled disgust — and official records exist as a sterile, clinical write-up, Opinion stands somewhat like a picture frame on a wall — telling you the story, identity of its owner in a look. 

I have always been a writer first and foremost. I, too, wanted to be a part of this history we are recording at The Chronicle. It was a selfish desire; to be a picture on that larger wall. I remember the first peer to compliment my column in person. I remember each alum and faculty who I've talked to about my pieces. 

If writing was a task that brought immense fulfilment from its instant gratification, editing was the opposite. Editing is a long meditation, a conversation deep within two ideas, two people, at their cores. It is an act of exploration. 

The Chronicle brings to itself people with ideas, with passions and with courage. A courage to be bold, to think unlike others. I have met columnists who care not what the response to their work is. Professors who will stand by their words. Alumni who hold their beliefs across decades. The best part about my job is that I get to see that up close. I get to challenge them. To test the extent of their beliefs, their thoughts, their ideas. But also, to bring them to life. To let their words shine, lend my own. 

It is an understatement to say that now is a great time to have opinions. And I believe Opinion has done a great job showcasing that. Discussions on surveillance, on birthright citizenship, immigration and free speech. On institutional neutrality. On the cataclysmic impacts of funding cuts. On the imposition of AI. All these are problems being faced around the country, but also on our campus. 

All the while doing so, we have not compromised on the diversity of our views, ideas and thoughts. We haven’t compromised our identities as Duke students, but rather reformed them. Asked what that even means. What it means to be queer here. To study here, when departments are falling apart and research is being dismantled. To have a community here. To change over time. To choose who represents us. To belong here, even in a sea of privilege and pretense.

I will not say that it has not been difficult. After all, the nature of our polarized present does not lend itself very well to the challenging of ideas. From careless insults and legal concerns to offense at the notion of fact-checking or the choice of a word over another at 1 AM in the night, it has, in some sense, reinforced to me that people hold their glass balls close, lest someone shatter them. It has allowed me to see polarization at its absurd extreme.

But despite all of that, my love for liking things and liking people has allowed me to savor each of these columns, and so many more. My love for a challenge has allowed me to poke and prod at these intricate pieces of glass, allowing me a chance to imagine a life as a metaphorical gaffer. 

It is this love that allowed me to step back from the selfish desire to write endlessly, to claw endlessly, hoping to leave my mark on this campus. Instead, I want each and every single one of my writers, my editors, to be remembered and immortalized for their burning passions, courage and ideas. For them to be the framing pictures on Duke’s wall. 

Just like they are on my mind. 

I have always liked a lot of things — perhaps, too many. 

And what a gift The Chronicle’s Opinion section has been, to be able to like so many things that I never thought I would, to be able to think so vastly and so deeply. To challenge, and to be challenged. To think freely, to speak even freer. Even if your answer is complicated. Especially if your answer is complicated.

Shambhavi Sinha is a Trinity junior and served as opinion editor for The Chronicle’s 121st volume. She would like to extend her thanks to everyone who has supported Opinion, from readers to guest writers to columnists; they are the reason why she cares so much about this section. They make Opinion what it is.

She also extends her deepest, most loving gratitude to her team of associate editors, who lent their most amazing minds and ideas most Sundays; to Landen Meier, for being the bravest and funniest first-year she knows (even if his 10 PM Monday Monday drafts were traumatising); to Tanish Kumar, for his opinions on her opinions, to Leo Goldberg, for his excellent sense of humor and his even greater understanding for Shambhavi’s poor response time in texting.

She is immensely excited to see the adventures Devyn Deschamps will take Opinion on in the coming volume, led by Dylan Halper and Abby Disalvo, even if in a different timezone. 

She wants to thank the people who are also the reason she is proud to belong to The Chronicle: Ana Despa, Lucas Lin, Claire Cranford, Abby DiSalvo, Kadin Purath, Amy Zhang, Anabel Howery, Ryan Kilgallen, Alice Qin, Abby Spiller, among many more. But especially to Alice Qin, opinion editor of The Chronicle's 120th volume, who believed in her endlessly and without a day of doubt.

Finally, she would like to thank her family and friends who have sat through agonizing dinners and conversations about columns, writers and editors. Hopefully, they’ll hear less of that now.

title: On buzzer-beaters and belief
author: Abby DiSalvo
article_text:
There’s a special kind of silence that accompanies a buzzer-beater. Over the course of my year as sports editor, I got to know it well. 

I sat on press row of Cameron Indoor Stadium as Isaiah Evans launched his last-ditch 3-pointer against Florida, sealing a 67-66 victory in front of breathless Cameron Crazies. I held my breath in Charlotte as Luke Mergott caught an interception that clinched a historic ACC Football Championship. I edited the basketball gamers for late collapses against Texas Tech and North Carolina, a magic win against LSU and the final heartbreaker against UConn.

But what I will remember most vividly from the past year are not those split-second silences, when the crowd caught its breath in anticipation, nor the frantic edits or click of a publish button that inevitably followed. For every highlight-reel shot I was lucky enough to witness, there were a dozen other moments that made the past year worth writing about.

In my tenure as a student journalist — with heavy emphasis on “student” — I got a front-row seat to some of the best coaching in the country. I’ll admit that I skipped a few classes to hear Jon Scheyer give press updates before a rivalry game, and I turned in several subpar homework assignments as I followed Duke football and basketball around the country. In exchange, my tattered reporter’s notebook accumulated cliché words of wisdom: Value persistence over perfection. No game is a masterpiece. We still get to write our own story. 

I had the privilege of covering Duke’s sports teams with a group of incredibly talented writers, many of whom became my closest friends. We spent dozens of late nights in 301 Flowers tweaking print layouts, assembling newsletters, arguing over AP style and dissecting NIL lawsuits. I was far from perfect as an editor, but they made me want to return to our cramped little sports hall every day and keep learning.

Through it all, I often still felt like the shy, quiet first-year who sat on the floor of the office for her first Chronicle meeting, unsure whether she knew enough to write a simple football blog. When championship confetti swirled down in both Bank of America Stadium and the Spectrum Center, I wondered not only how each buzzer-beater had landed so perfectly, but why I was the one there to capture its path.

I think Manny Diaz got it right in Week 12 of the football season when he said: “At Duke, sometimes, our issue can be perfectionism. We'll play uptight because we're trying to be perfect. But we've been at our best when we've made games grimy. We've been at our best when we've stuck it out.”

At times, I got so caught up in meeting the deadlines of the day-to-day — editing my fourth gamer of the night, writing another recruiting brief (just in case), requesting another round of credentials — that I forgot to take a step back and appreciate the growth that made each story possible.

The truth is that no Blue Devil who made an important buzzer-beater over the course of this year overthought it. They took the shot because a coach put them on the floor and a teammate passed them the ball. They took the shot not because they hoped it would go in, but because they — and the people around them — believed it would. 

I don’t think I would have ended up in the third-floor Chronicle office writing this column if I weren’t lucky enough to have people who also believed in me. Without the editors who first welcomed me into the office and offered endless encouragement, I never would have dared to take on this role. And without the writers who trusted me with their words, none of the coverage we collected over the last year would have been possible. I would not have learned important lessons about preparation or dedication or confidence or friendship, as cliché as that all feels to say now.

So as the proverbial clock on my time as sports editor runs out, I can only hope that the future writers who pass through 301 Flowers eventually discover a similar belief in themselves. It’s because of The Chronicle that I found my voice and made memories that will last far beyond Volume 121. If there’s one lesson I will take away from all those buzzer-beaters, it’s this:

Next time the game hangs in the balance, take the shot. You never know where you might land.

Abby DiSalvo is a Trinity junior and served as sports editor for The Chronicle’s 121st volume. She would like to thank Martin Heintzelman for his infinite advice, Elle Chavis for her mind-reading powers and Caleb Dudley for every coverage adventure. 

She is forever grateful to Ranjan Jindal, who believed in her first, and Sophie Levenson, who probably believed in her most. She wishes the best to Alex Min, who she knows will do amazing things as the leader of the sports department next year. 

She still looks up to all the women who came before her in the press box — especially Sophie, Mackenzie, Anna and Rachael. She couldn’t be more excited to see so many underclassmen ready to follow in their footsteps.

Her final thanks go to Ana Despa and Dylan Halper, who somehow convinced her to do more work next year. She can’t wait for the tipoff of Volume 122 and all the stories it will bring.

title: All my favorite singers couldn't sing
author: Kadin Purath
article_text:
It’s hard to love a singer who can’t sing. What’s harder still, is to see and foster love and passion in the unkempt, quixotic aspects of another. One thing beyond (or maybe, more fittingly, below) production, in all of its forms, that is ignored, like the myriad arts offerings on campus that we cover, is earnest passion. It’s easy to see passion practically enacted in long hours and high output — similarly to how it’s easy to love music from a pretty voice. What’s difficult is to see and foster passion where it isn’t immediately compelling.

And yet, that process is exactly what made my year as Recess editor so meaningful. I’ve truly loved my editorship, from learning a lot about the dynamics and structures of the paper — something that I guilelessly avoided as a low level editor and writer — to, most importantly, witnessing the continued engagement of our writers in the parts of campus that can often be overlooked. Seeing our production this year and being the benefactor of a crop of sophomores and first-years passionate about local arts has been my greatest pride as editor.

I hope that my time at The Chronicle has been one example of what will amount to a lifetime of searching for what is not quite obviously there. It’s so difficult to write truthfully (in both the personal and essential senses of the word) about a performance, album or film. As a writer or reviewer, you have the difficult dual task of synthesizing the expression of another and intimating it with your own perspective. In many ways, this is what we’re all doing all of the time — it’s just that what we’re processing isn’t as impersonal and easily detestable as a recent Bruce Springsteen biopic.

Being able to write about art and show a genuine passion for the self-discovery found in another is a growing necessity, especially at a place like Duke. When competition, comparison and compensation drive attention and efforts, navel-gazing becomes the only place our eyes know where to look.

Recess, like any individual, can only offer a small but meaningful chance for others to step beyond solipsism and look outward at the continual striving around them. There are so many broad opportunities in every form of art at Duke and in Durham, but these are just a structural example of the everyday chances we have to look and feel deeper, especially in the areas where we least expect it.

The arts try to capture the moments in between the events that define our lives. They ask us to see the beauty in the mundane and the comprehensible in the infinite — to find meaning in the attempt itself. In that way, engaging with art centers the insistence behind something that doesn’t fully work but still instills emotion. This type of engagement is uncomfortable. It’s hard to intellectualize or verbalize. Yet, when we start to look this way, we begin to train ourselves to look at others, and at ourselves, with a little more patience and a little less certainty.

Passion is so easily rewarded when there is a metric output: GPA, exam scores, interview invites. It’s hard to sense the passion that leads to a lighter outlook, more graceful presence, simpler understanding. It’s just this type of yearning passion that engaging with the arts as both the subjugation of your personal perspective to another’s and an internal struggle toward greater self understanding can offer. It’s the ability to endeavor towards meaning while finding satisfaction in knowing you can strive. It’s a passion that doesn’t come out in the wash or go on a transcript, but it’s the passion that others can feel when you tell them about your day. It’s the passion I’ve learned to live by at Duke and through Recess.

Kadin Purath is a Trinity senior and served as the Recess editor for The Chronicle’s 121st volume. He would like to send a special thanks to Bhavika Verma and Zev Van Zanten for being his right hand throughout this year. He knows that, without them, nothing would be possible.

He would also like to excitedly thank Evan Poradzisz, Kyra Pahwa, May Hsu, and Jenna Arafeh for the writing work that they have done this year — their work has been the highlight of Recess this volume.

Lastly, he looks forward to everything that Olivia Prusky will do as editor of Recess next year and to the wonderful direction he knows that she will take Recess as editor.

title: Why I’m staying
author: Claire Cranford
article_text:
I have not particularly enjoyed Duke.

I find the social atmosphere stifling, beholden to some antiquated idea of status and hierarchy that I never quite figured out how to care about. For many months after arriving in the fall of 2023, I became very depressed and, frankly, set on transferring. I want to be honest about that, because I think honesty is the only thing that makes a farewell column worth reading.

Well. Then came The Chronicle. And I stayed.

This is not the part where I tell you I fell in love with journalism and everything clicked into place. That would be too clean, and it would also not be true. The truth is messier and, I think, more interesting. The truth is that I have spent the better part of this year being pulled toward this newsroom against what sometimes felt like my better judgment — late into the night, early into the morning, back again the next day. I did not always want to go. I went anyway. And I could never quite explain why, until about two months ago. 

I was lying in my bed, crying rather hysterically, convinced I had failed at this job — that I wasn't good enough, that I had let people down in ways I couldn't take back. And in that quiet, miserable moment, in the darkness of my Edens dorm, I realized that what I wanted more than anything was to be in 301 Flowers.

Why? Why would I want to go to the place that was supposedly the source of my anguish?

Because it wasn't. Lying there, I figured out what I was actually upset about — not that 301 Flowers had hurt me, but that I wasn't living up to the kind of leader I wanted to be inside it. The newsroom itself had never, ever been a problem. It was where I had watched people grow into reporters who asked sharper questions than they thought they could. Where late-night edits turned into inside jokes and where I’ve grown closer to some of the most important people in my life.

What I was mourning wasn't the idea of doing the job going badly. It was the distance I felt from that version of the newsroom, and from the version of myself who could walk in there, take a breath, and try again, in the presence of my closest friends.

The latest I left 301 Flowers this year was 5:43 a.m. The earliest was 10:11 p.m. I want to be clear: I did not always enjoy those hours. Sometimes editing a story is the bane of my existence, and that is just the truth! 

But I kept showing up — and what I learned, slowly and often painfully, is that there is a difference between enjoyment and fulfillment I had never quite understood before. I did not always enjoy this work. I am proud of it in a way that has settled somewhere deeper than enjoyment ever could. 

Part of what kept pulling me back is that I am a naturally curious person. Not because I enjoy asking questions — although I do — but because I absolutely abhor not knowing things. That is partly why I took this job. It is the perfect excuse to be constantly learning, even when I am not formally in a classroom. But curiosity alone does not explain the pull. 

Plenty of things make me curious. Outer space, for example, or the squirrels on campus (why do they scream like that?). But only one thing has ever made me want to stay up until 2 a.m. on a Wednesday, when I should be sleeping, because a story isn't quite right yet or because I need to send some follow-up emails and interview requests.

I have failed, in many ways, often fantastically. I have missed things I shouldn't have missed. I made calls I would probably not make now. The Chronicle is, objectively, an unserious institution — we are 18 to 22-year-olds running a large public service experiment with very little professional oversight, giving you the facts, holding ourselves to an exceptionally high standard that nobody required of us except ourselves. And yet we have done so much; we can do so much.

Which is why — and I recognize this may be difficult to understand — I am coming back in the fall to do it again.

Not because it has been easy. Not because I have always been good at it, or because the nights were short, or because I never once thought seriously about going home instead of to shift. I am coming back because this job is the only thing at Duke that has ever made me feel like the discomfort was worth it. Because I still want to be worthy of this amazing newsroom. Because, if I am honest, I do not think I know how to stop being pulled toward it.

I do not measure the success of this past year by awards or social media engagement. I measure it by whether you — reading this, on campus, in Durham, wherever you are — ever felt more informed because of what we reported. If you did, even once, I consider that a success. So thank you.

I'll see you in August, and I couldn’t be more excited. I’ll probably have something more profound and introspective to share next year, when my time at The Chronicle finally comes to a close. I reckon this isn’t much of a farewell column anyway. Until then, I can only hope that I continue to hold the standard.

And to the staff of Volume 121: you are the reason that even at my lowest, I still wanted to come back to 301 Flowers. That has to count for something. I think it counts for everything.

Claire Cranford is a Trinity junior and served as news editor of The Chronicle’s 121st volume.

She would like to thank Ana Despa for her remarkable bravery and strength over the past year, of which she wishes she could emulate even half; Lucas Lin, for his steady presence and cunningly creative guidance; Zoe Kolenovsky, for being her lab clone, closest mentor and friend; Aseel Ibrahim and Ryan Kilgallen, for their energy, attitude and support that keeps her going; Audrey Wang, Jazper Lu, Michael Austin and Abby Spiller, for leaving comically large shoes to fill; and finally, Dylan Halper, Abby DiSalvo and Ella Moore, for agreeing to take over what she knows will be a bright year ahead. 

She would also like to thank her grandparents, Honey and Papa, who read The Chronicle newsletter every day, even when they have no reason to care about the subject matter, and her parents and little brothers for loving and encouraging her always.

title: I’ll read this when I’m older
author: Anna Garziera
article_text:
Most journalists will tell you that opinion writing is not real journalism. You might be surprised that I sort of agree. 

At least the kind I’ve been doing for the past three years. For better or for worse, these columns have been my space to vent about my life at Duke. I’ve written about all sorts of things: friends, classes, boyfriends, teachers and most of all, about the books I’ve read during my college career. It’s been cozy, like a one-member book club. 

Have you been keeping up with my columns lately? Maybe since the start? I don’t mind, either way. Friends and strangers have often surprised me, saying they’d read my last column. I have often looked at them stupidly, like I’d forgotten these things get published at all.

Opinion writing didn’t use to appeal to me. It’s really uncomfortable, putting your opinions out there, knowing they’ll get read and judged, or worse — not read at all. I’ve since changed my mind. For me, opinion writing has turned into a sort of diary, and I don’t really care who reads it. Writing for Opinion is one of my favorite things I’ve done at Duke. It’s been therapeutic, being able to write about anything I wanted, as long as it was Duke-related. (Since my whole life is at Duke, it’s really easy to write anything, and then give it the “old Duke spin” later — a handy trick for future columnists.) 

Writing has really helped me keep the scary thoughts at bay. It works like this: I ruminate on the big questions, and once they’ve semi-matured, I sit down and write. Being on a biweekly schedule has kept my mind flowing for years. I get a huge wave of satisfaction at putting my ideas into words, and I love seeing the cute blue box on The Chronicle website with my name on it. Then, I move on. 

Last publication cycle, I wrote about a poem I found in “The Unabridged Journals of Sylvia Plath.” Reading this book freshman year made me think about my own collections of diaries — if I were cool like Greg Heffley, I’d call them journals, but who am I kidding — and how I threw them all away last summer.

If you’d asked me two years ago, “In a fire, what would you save?” I would have probably said, “My diaries.” Silly me didn’t know I’d be sending them off to the Charleston County Landfill just a few months later. I don’t want to get into all the reasons why I did that, nor whether or not I regret it. But in short, they were too personal. I didn’t want future me to read them.

Which takes me back to these columns, and what they’ll mean to me going forward. 

I’m not a big picture-taker. As my friends know, if I have six pictures of you on my phone, it means I really like you. I have some sunsets, some portraits of my dog, some selfies with my dog and some useful things, like my driver’s license. Not much else. Since getting my phone in October of freshman year, I have taken 832 photos. More than the average grandma, but far less than the average college girl. 

Since throwing away my diaries, which chronicled my life from ages 14 to 20, I haven’t started journaling again. So, since starting my undergraduate degree at Duke, I am up 832 photos and down 3.5 diaries. Many would argue, that’s a net loss. Photos tell you where you’ve been, but not how you felt. 

If my memory were better, I wouldn’t worry too much about it. But it’s not very good. I’d try to make a joke and say I’m like Dory from “Finding Nemo,” but it’s been years since I’ve seen that movie and can’t remember if Dory’s the one with short-term memory loss. (She is, I just googled it. What was I saying?)

You know how some women forget the pain of childbirth? My brain has similarly wiped out all accounts of Spring 2024, when I took Math 212 (Calc 3) freshman year. I’m sure there were some good moments that semester, but who knows.

How will I remember my time at Duke? Overall, fondly. I’m confident I’ll remember some highlights, like that brunch at Elmo’s on Ninth Street and that jazz night at Kraft, and that long walk I took trying to locate the Durham Craft Market. But as I get on in my years, I might lose some bits and pieces. That’s when I’ll turn to my beloved columns.

Dear Chronicle Opinion, thank you. Thank you for gently pressuring me to write down how I felt about my life every couple of weeks. I couldn’t ask for a better graduation gift. (Though, if you really want to send me a Franklin, let me know.)

To all seniors: If you haven’t documented your time at Duke thoroughly — no diaries, few pictures — then write a couple of pages tonight. Sit down in front of your Untitled Document and just start typing. You might feel silly doing this if you don’t write often, but it doesn’t matter. Do it. If you need a leg up, begin like this: “It is the last week of my senior year at Duke. Freshman year me would not believe…”

Anna Garziera is a Trinity senior and an opinion columnist for The Chronicle's 119th, 120th and 121st volumes.

title: The things we love
author: Martin Heintzelman
article_text:
I have not liked every minute of my time in The Chronicle.

I’ve been reflecting a lot on these last four years as a chapter comes to a close, and I think there’s no better statement to sum up how I’ve felt about this organization. That might just be my demeanor — I’m not known around here for my optimism. 

But that’s the truth about this gig. The work we do is hard, and it demands a lot from us. It’s challenging to really enjoy editing a 1500-word baseball game article down to 1000 in the moment, the same way it’s difficult to spend an hour scrolling Orbitz trying to concoct a plan to get a trio of 19-year olds from Durham to West Point, N.Y., the same way it’s hard to like staying up in the office until the early hours of the morning watchdogging a print edition.

When you join this organization, you give something up — sometimes a lot of things. News staff and editors give up their weeknights for production shifts, our sports associate editors spend hours fact-checking everything from a standard lacrosse or soccer gamer to an 1800-word feature on the Duke club equestrian team. Chronicle sportswriters often forfeit their rights to cheer at Blue Devil sporting events and, most brutally, to drink before North Carolina comes to town for a basketball game. 

I’ve moved midterm exams, awoken in the earliest hours of the morning and watched helplessly as writers get stranded in airports across the country due to missed connections. If I were a cooler person, I probably would’ve had to skip a lot of parties for The Chronicle, too. There are a plethora of moments where this all feels more like a job than it does a student organization, and I can guarantee that nobody on The Chronicle’s staff, present or past, has liked every single minute of their time here.

But there’s a difference between liking and loving something. As this year’s sports budget monkey, I’ve loved getting to book travel across the country so that our writers can cover Duke teams wherever they go — providing the sort of opportunities most other student papers (including the folks down the road) can’t even come close to. As an editor, I’ve loved the chance to help newer writers find their own journalistic voices through live edits and plenty of comments on Google Docs. As a person, I’ve loved late nights in 301 Flowers with my friends and colleagues, perfecting a special print edition or just hanging out and playing pong or Mario Kart.

As student journalists, we don’t do this job because we like all of it, or even sometimes most of it. We do it because we love it. Too frequently, the training we receive from the well-meaning editors of The Chronicle is to take the emotion out of our writing. We want to be unbiased, objective sources of information from around campus and beyond — and we often take that to mean that there should be minimal feeling in our work. My best work, from a feature about a coach I’ve covered for all four years of my time here to my column about the end of the road for two of my classmates on Duke women’s basketball, has always been about the people and teams I love — in other words, the articles with the most emotion captured, not the least.

The reality is that, in an era where more and more people get their sports information from AI-generated game summaries or quick clips on TikTok, our love is what makes our writing appealing. Our readers can feel it when it’s there, and it brings people in like nothing else. There’s something uniquely valuable about content created by a writer who really cares. 

So, to the writers who will be around next year and long after I’m gone, keep harnessing that love. Let it flow through you in everything you do, in The Chronicle and elsewhere. Let it guide your hand as you pump out gamers and sidebars and blogs and every other type of article we publish. Regardless of how hard the individual nights are — long editing shifts, interpersonal conflicts, brutal travel days — you’ll ultimately arrive at the same conclusion I did: 

I have not liked every minute of my time at The Chronicle, but I’ve certainly loved it. 

Martin Heintzelman is a Trinity senior who served as sports managing editor of The Chronicle’s 121st volume. 

He would like to thank Abby DiSalvo for taking a flyer on him despite his advanced age and for always listening to his ramblings, as well as Elle Chavis and Caleb Dudley for being there through all the ups, downs and Microtels of the year. 

He also wants to thank the rest of the Chronicle sports senior class — Anna Newberry, Elliott Jarnot, Mackenzie Sheehy, Garrett Spooner, Luke Jovanovic, Andrew Negus and Jun Tan — who have seen him through thick and thin. In particular, he’d like to shout out Ranjan Jindal and Dom Fenoglio for being excellent, patient friends and always providing voices of reason. He thanks Sophie Levenson for everything. 

He thanks Em Adler for trusting him to take over her prized women’s basketball beat, and Jonathan Levitan and Andrew Long for setting stellar examples of what Chronicle leadership can be. Finally, he’d like to thank Blake Ciresa, for always reminding him how serious Duke really is.

He wishes the best of luck to Alex Min, Colton Schwabe and Ryan Hamner as they gear up for another volume, although he knows they won’t need it. He’s sad he won’t get to see The Chronicle’s freshman class grow up in person, but he’ll never stop watching from afar. He knows that there is nowhere like 301 Flowers, and he’s treasured the opportunity to see a new group of people discover it like he did four years ago.

title: Chasing the story
author: Jun Tan
article_text:
It was a dark and cold night in December 2024. I remember the winter wind billowing through Cary’s WakeMed Soccer Park as the whole stadium held its breath. Then the sharp whistle for a penalty. And the crowd erupts. 

Half of them cheering for an early North Carolina lead, the other half groaning as the Blue Devils conceded against their archrivals in the most important game all season. Rubbing my hands and sighing in frustration, I kept calm and continued typing away on my laptop. 

Through the next two goals, I typed. My keyboard became a flurry of motion as I watched in anguish at how our team desperately rallied a comeback. But even the most fervent of perseverance could not help the number one team in the country. I almost cried when Robbie Church gave his final press conference, the legend retiring as the winningest soccer coach in Duke history. 

As I stood alone outside the stadium gates, watching the team bus leave, I wondered why I even bothered coming at all. I could have watched the game on television, with the rest of the sports department while eating mediocre hibachi. I could have even stayed in my dorm to study for my maths final. But freezing away on that Friday night, I knew exactly why I was there.

It was for the love of the beautiful game. More than that, it was the love I had for The Chronicle.

***

If there’s one thing The Chronicle has taught me, it’s that stories like these are never really about the result.

Sure, I have spent the past few years chasing them — the field hockey box scores, the basketball buzzer beaters and the occasional recess articles on Ted Lasso and Ed Sheeran. I’ve written about heartbreaks in Chapel Hill, historic triumphs for women’s soccer and some March Madness losses that lingered just a little too long. 

But somewhere between late-night edits and early deadlines, I realized that the real story was never just what happened on the court. It was everything around it: the people in 301 Flowers that continue to inspire me, encouraging me to keep chasing the stories.

When I first stepped into The Chronicle’s office as a sophomore, I faced a daunting challenge. I had a passion for writing and a love for sports, but I had zero experience in journalism and did not know anyone in the department. However, a warm welcome from the sports editor was all it took to convince me to stay and start my Chronicle journey.

I still vividly remember my very first live game coverage. Being the only reporter on campus, I was thrown into the deep end of writing a Duke men’s basketball game on New Year’s Eve. I cannot forget the deafening silence of Cameron’s press row before tip-off, my heart thumping as I prepare to race against time and the shot clock to see the Blue Devils thrash Queens 106-69. But amidst all the chaos, one small calm notification appeared on my phone: it was that same editor, texting all the way from Idaho to reassure me that he has my back covered, that he’ll be there for me no matter what.

Three years on, my time at The Chronicle became more than just chasing stories for a student newspaper; it became a place where I found a loving community of fellow writers and shared some of my most treasured memories at college. Indeed, I spent as much time writing for the paper as enjoying fellowship with my friends and colleagues, whether it be losing intramural soccer games or crashing out at trivia tournaments. I have found a place on campus that I truly felt belonged.

I would like to think that writing for The Chronicle was the best decision I ever made at Duke. Because writing here means writing for a community that deeply cares about you. It’s the feeling of being part of something bigger than yourself. And for a few years, I got to contribute to that story about all the wonderful people in 301 Flowers, and to leave my small mark on a storied publication that continues to deliver the very best of student journalism. That is a privilege I don't take lightly.

Moreover, The Chronicle fashioned my love of storytelling and gave me the platform and resources to do so, leading me to chase some of the wildest and most fascinating of tales. I would have never imagined covering that heartbreaking Final Four for women’s soccer, or writing a feature about Duke’s club equestrian team. I even had the privilege of traveling to Lake Wheeler in Raleigh, where an ex-rower like myself witnessed Duke clinch bronze in the ACC Rowing Championships.

It’s these stories and the community I found that gave me a real sense of purpose in the mundane daily life of a college senior. Every week I would look forward to picking up an article, or even just talking to people in the office. And now, having only two weeks left before graduation, I lament the fact that I should have joined The Chronicle sooner, that I could have stayed in the office just a little longer.

If I could leave one piece of advice, it’s this: chase the story, not the moment. The moment will pass. The story is what stays. The memories, the friendships I’ve made in 301 Flowers will forever remain the highlights of my four years at Duke.

Jun Tan is a Trinity senior and served as associate editor for the sports department in The Chronicle's 121st volume. 

He would like to thank his “boss” editors, Ranjan Jindal and Abby DiSalvo, for always believing in him and encouraging him to chase the stories; Zev van Zanten for introducing him to Volume 119 and their years of friendship; Dom Fengolio for all their deep conversations and the best tenting season he has had; Martin Heintzelman for always making him laugh, even in boring Econ lectures. 

Last but definitely not least, he would like to thank Andrew Long for being his mentor and friend throughout all these years.

title: An ode to Opinion
author: Anna Sorensen
article_text:
I joined Opinion in my sophomore year because I knew I wanted to get involved in journalism, but I wasn’t sure I’d be so good at the whole “neutrality” thing in news. I figured since I was already in a journalism class, and since I planned to complete the journalism certificate (now the JAM minor, neither of which I actually stuck with), I had my bases covered. 

And as a relatively vocal person who has written what feels like hundreds of argumentative essays, I was ready to tackle the next challenge. When I spoke to a member of Opinion at an info session, she basically told me that I could write whatever I wanted whenever I wanted to. So yeah, that sounded good to me! 

For a moment there, I also thought I wanted to start straight away with editing. As I quickly learned, that’s actually not how hierarchies work (RIP to the naivety of an ambitious sophomore). And there’s a reason for that, which I quickly came to learn. For my application to be a writer, I wrote a very flowery, sincere piece titled, “You are more interesting than your summer internship.” Well, yes, dear panicking sophomore, yes, you are! But let’s just say it was the kind of article I’d gently steer my writers away from now. 

That said, it was an article I needed to write for myself. And I’m glad I’ve returned to it today. Because right at the end, I wrote the following:

“The greatest value of college comes not from where we go afterwards, but from who we are when we’re done … However long ago, someone sat at a desk at 2138 Campus Dr. and thought that you would be a good person to have in the Duke community — that you would contribute something special. Back then, you probably saw college as a destination you had to work towards. Don’t skip over it now in a rush towards the next one.” 

On the nose? Yes. Cheesy? Certainly. Stylistically accurate for The Chronicle? Sadly, no. (I had yet to learn of the war that AP style wages against Oxford commas, for one).

But it seems the Class of 2026 and I have now reached the moment where we can actually consider “who we are when we’re done.” We are almost ready for the “afterwards,” for the next destination. I don’t know exactly what that looks like for me yet (shoutout to job market and existential crises), but I can say with confidence that I am proud of the person I am moving in that direction — thanks to Duke, and thanks to The Chronicle. I have come a long way from this application article, as a writer, as a student and as a person. 

I would like to think that Opinion has been a place where I have contributed something special to the Duke community. But even if that weren’t true, even if it has just been a place for me to explore and connect with the Duke community without seismic impact, it is an experience for which I am endlessly grateful. 

My early pieces for Opinion — from articles on under-appreciation for the arts on campus, to cold water showers (perhaps a little rogue of me, I’ll admit), to working outside, to birthdays in college, to religious life at Duke — all provided me with the space to reflect on my place in the Duke community and to explore what mattered to me. Writing is thinking: and how lucky I am that the publishing cycle of an Opinion writer had me routinely thinking about my time at Duke. And how special it has been to share that thinking with a wider audience. 

When I became an editor a bit over a year ago, I naturally had less time to write. This was okay, though — welcome even — because it gave me the chance to think alongside my writers: to get out of my own head and cast my net more widely into the Duke community. Working with writers like Samantha George, Kareena Sukhnanan and Stella Kaye, for example, has exposed me to perspectives at Duke that I may have never otherwise accessed. 

It has also made me a better, more creative writer. What you read, after all, determines what and how you write. So, I want to also take a moment here to appreciate how writing for The Chronicle has forced me to read widely (a practice I think we all could use a little more of). These past three years, I’ve spent hours poring over newspaper websites, Substack blogs and long-form journal articles in order to both inform myself on the issues the Duke community cares about and to engage with a diverse set of writing styles. 

Most recently, I’ve been lucky to have a front row seat to my sister’s budding career as a journalist for The Beiruter in Lebanon. I am proud of and touched by her dedication to the communities she works in, to genuine on-the-ground reporting and to journalistic humility. In a recent Substack post — which she uses as an expressive outlet outside of her news reporting (opinions run in the family) — she wrote, “I will happily sit with my doubt, before I ever proclaim a deceitful certainty.” I quite like that one.

In that vein, perhaps most of all, writing and editing for Opinion has made me more inquisitive and less comfortable in certainty. This, I am happy to say, won’t end with graduation. I will miss writing for all of you, but I am confident that this will not be the last op-ed I publish. 

I am proud of the questions I have answered during my time at Duke about who I am and what I care about, but I am equally proud of the questions I have, getting ready to leave Duke — about who I want to be and what it will take to get myself there. I look forward to exploring these questions and more in my future writing, wherever it may take me. Just look out for an abundance of Oxford commas going forward. 

Anna Sorensen is a Trinity senior and an associate opinion editor for The Chronicle’s 120th and 121st volumes. She would like to thank the entire Opinion and Chronicle team over the course of her time here at Duke — particularly Alice Qin and Shambhavi Sinha for being fearless section editors in her time with Opinion. She also sends her utmost appreciation to her writers, who have inspired her with pithy one-liners and thought-provoking pieces. 

Anna would also like to extend her gratitude to all her mentors — writing and personal — in her time at Duke; special thanks to Mike D’Alessandro for all the support these past four years.

Finally, she wants to thank Frank Bruni, whose work and teaching here at Duke (unbeknownst to him) inspired her to write for Opinion in the first place.

title: An ode to IM Chron sports
author: Luke Jovanovic
article_text:
Within the sports department of the Duke Chronicle, we take pride in our detailed coverage of all 14 women’s and 13 men’s varsity athletic teams. These stories include previews, gamers, features and post-season reviews. We will even highlight club sports, ranging from the somewhat ordinary pickleball to the extraordinary equestrian. However, there’s one set of Duke sports that, for a select few in the senior class, trumps all. 

Intramurals. The landscape of washed-up high school athletes, not willing to let go of their childhood dreams. 

Like clockwork at the beginning of the semester, the texts will go out:

“Like this message to join Chron IM (insert sport here).”

Instantly, five likes appear on the message, with more trickling in as the minutes pass. A new GroupMe is created. Schedules are compared and contrasted, balancing school work, associate editor shifts and other club commitments until the desired date and time is set. 

If the sport is offered, it’s more than likely that we compete in it. Soccer, Kickball, Dodgeball, Flag Football (4v4 and 7v7) and Basketball (3v3 and 5v5), just to name a few. For a few hours once a week, we put down the pens and lanyards and lace them up, attempting to live out the on-field emotions we cover on a day-to-day basis.

The two engines behind the sports department of the Chronicle are also yin and yang in the intramural sphere. Ranjan Jindal and Dom Fenoglio led and starred on all of these teams, and their talent and motivation boosted our squads to heights far beyond their expected ceiling. Just like it worked in the office, their differences complemented one another perfectly on the field.

Dom is the heart of the team, and he wears it proudly on his sleeve. The 6-foot-3 (which in IM at a school like Duke might as well be 6-foot-9) product translates his high school talents into a bruising TE, punishing center or fierce dodgeball hurler. He will stop at nothing to win, even testing the durability of his own noggin against the Brodie Gym wall, diving for a ball going out of bounds (Hint: the wall won.) 

Dom expects the same of every single one of his teammates, never mincing words if someone isn’t performing up to his standards. He personally benched the (incoming) sports editor during a championship football bout. Dom loves nothing more than dishing out a good tongue-lashing, exposing his St. Louis roots with his brutal trash talk to opponents. And God bless any poor graduate student referee, trying to supplement their six-figure tuition by officiating some games, who crosses his path. 

Ranjan is more of the soul of the operation. The 5-foot-8 man from Greenville, South Carolina, doesn’t scream athlete upon first glance, but he is probably the most skilled guy on every team. His ball placement with a pigskin? Immaculate. His talents on the hardwood? Smooth as butter. Heck, he was the only ball handler we had for 3 seasons of IM hoops. Ranjan is just as competitive as Dom, but expresses it quietly with just a fist pump or a shake of his head. He’s the first to pick you up when you’ve made a mistake, reminding you there’s plenty of time left in the game, and after all, it is just intramural sports.

Ranjan’s best superpower, however, might be that he is the only one who can control Dom and set the tone for the team. When the emotions run hot, he’s able to wrangle us into line. It’s a quiet confidence he exudes that fits so perfectly with the strong authority of Dom that leads to success.

Over the four years, we’ve had our highs and lows. Winning on a Hail Mary in a scrappy 7-0 quarterfinal football game our sophomore year, just to lose the semifinal by forfeit due to Chronicle traveling commitments. Advancing to the quarterfinals of 5v5 basketball in our junior year, just to lose in a two possession heartbreaker in the following contest. Triumphant in the 7v7 football championship this year on a game-sealing interception in triple overtime, just to turn around and blow a 12 point lead in the final 40 seconds against the same team in the 4v4 playoffs.

These memories remind us of why we love and cover sports. Sports bring out the kid in each and every one of us. They remind us of the beautiful spectrum of emotions that life yearns for us to feel and live. They give us happy and sad memories, but memories nevertheless, with the people we admire and love. 

My girlfriend, a Chronicle writer herself, always asks me, “Why do you care so much about IM Chron?” I’ll admit she has a point; it sounds ridiculous to take it this seriously, or to dedicate my last written words to them in my farewell piece.

For a few moments every week, we writers were reminded once again what it was like to be on a team. To have a practice on the Quad or in Wilson. To travel to the faraway land of East Campus for games or eat postgame meals together, regardless of the outcome. To hug one another in pure ecstasy, or not even bear to look one another in the eye after a bad miscommunication leads to Duke Basketball-esque collapse. 

These experiences, albeit paling in comparison to those of varsity and club athletics, helped us to grow as writers, understanding the complex emotions that go into competition. They created lifelong friendships and stories we will undoubtedly recount at every Duke reunion to come. But most importantly, IM Chron, and The Chronicle in general, gave us four extra years of being kids, exploring our passions, and learning from our mistakes. 

And for that, I’m forever grateful.

Luke Jovanovic is a Trinity senior and was a sports writer for the 118th, 119th, 120th and 121st volumes. He’d like to thank Jonathan Levitan and Andrew Long for welcoming him to Chronicle with open arms. 

He’s indebted to the graduating seniors, also known as the Jai Bean Fan Club, and knows that graduation won’t be a goodbye. 

He’s grateful for every member of the 2025 7v7 IM Football Championship roster and hopes the leftover travel money from Duke’s shortened basketball season can be utilized to buy the banner they deserve.

He’d like to also thank Chrissy and all of the Chronicle benefactors for providing him an incredible opportunity to travel and cover games. 

And lastly, he’d like to shout out his favorite Chronicle love, Caleb Dudley.

title: Do things for the plot
author: Arnav Jindal
article_text:
I think I joined The Chronicle because I wanted to write food reviews for local restaurants. Ultimately, that did not pan out (I have a wonderful Beli to use for that instead), but the people I emailed convinced me to show up to a Recess meeting. I excitedly picked up a pitch and went to report on a concert. I was young and dumb, and almost got The Chronicle sued by the venue. I had my very first article retracted.

There I was, a nervous first-year, born and raised in India, brand new to America and Duke, sitting in front of my then-Recess editor Jonathan Pertile and the editor-in-chief of The Chronicle. I did not think I would write again. But Jonathan convinced me to stay. It was my fault. The advice of "Maybe don't do live events or concerts, but write about music in other ways" was something I could work with. It wasn't the start I had planned, but it was a great story.

Eventually, I wrote my first published piece, one about Carly Rae Jepsen. Along the way, I felt super supported by the rest of Recess. It felt great to go into a meeting and meet all these cool and interesting people. People who still believed in me despite my many mishaps.

I think I'm glad I stuck with it. First as a staff writer, then as culture editor, then back to being a staff writer before becoming culture editor again. Recess's greatest strength will always be the people it attracts, and they're what kept me showing up every Monday evening.

I usually tended to surround myself with people from my major or with similar backgrounds to mine. At Recess meetings, I met people outside my Duke bubble: people who listened to music by artists I'd never heard of, people with majors or clubs very different from mine, people I would never have crossed paths with otherwise. I found a community that gave me great movies to watch, restaurants to try, music to listen to, perspectives I hadn't considered. It expanded my worldview in ways I had never imagined.

Something I got to do freshman year was cover Dreamville. It was my first ever music festival. The whole experience was mesmerizing: I got to listen to performances I still think about, discover music and artists I still listen to, and most of all, have the strange privilege to write about it all. I had signed up on a whim. It turned into one of the most formative weekends of my first year (including a ride in a police cruiser).

It inspired me to stay in The Chronicle, to cover local arts and small businesses. To interview interesting people, I would never have stopped to talk to otherwise.

In my sophomore fall, I interviewed and profiled a new small business opening up near campus. I met Isaac from Isaac's Bagels and was one of their very first customers. Through that piece, I found a weekly ritual: a great bagel and a place to take my friends every Friday. It's been so inspiring to watch the shop become a staple for Durham and the Duke community.

The Chronicle pushed me to explore Durham in ways I never would have otherwise. I never would have gone to so many EDM shows at The Fruit had The Chronicle not sent me to my first one. It's a nice venue, with some really great artists, and I think more Duke students should check it out. I got to interview people who inspire me, like Alison Chen; rank every boba shop in Durham, chase down the guy Mr. Beast flew to Paris for baguettes. In the grand scheme of things, I'm really proud of what I've written. I wrote about things I care about and I got to have a lot of fun doing it.

As an international student, Recess made me more culturally aware. As culture editor, I was keeping track of everything: new movies and music, cultural trends, weird celebrity news. One week, I was pitching a piece on Starbucks Bear cups, the next on the NewJeans’ breakup. You can't be Recess culture editor without being aware of what's happening and I'm glad I get to graduate with a ton of niche knowledge.
