As I finish senior year, I'm grateful The Chronicle was part of my Duke experience. It sparked a real love of journalism in me, enough that I took journalism classes because of it and ended up reading and consuming so much more news than I used to. It nudged me out of my comfort zone and gave me the confidence to walk in and interview people.

And that's what I really want to emphasize: just do things for the plot. You can sidequest your way into experiences you'd never have planned for. I came to Duke thinking I'd cover food, almost quit, and somehow ended up with four years of stories and memories I didn't see coming. I'm leaving with a Beli full of restaurants, a notes app full of half-finished pitches and a whole lot of sidequests. 

Arnav Jindal is a Trinity senior and served as Recess culture editor for The Chronicle's 119th and 121st volumes. 

He would like to thank Jonathan and Tessa from Volume 118 for giving him a chance to stay; Jules, Anna and Derek for being wonderful editors to work with; Zev for being a Chronicle staple for four years; and Kadin for really taking charge of Recess.

title: Driving through the storm
author: Zoe Kolenovsky
article_text:
I’ve always felt safest behind the wheel.

I love everything about being alone in the driver’s seat — choosing the radio station, deciding when to turn and when to stop, getting exactly where I need to go without ever checking a map. There, I am completely independent and completely in control.

I didn’t really know what it meant to drive blind until my senior year of high school, when Hurricane Ida ripped through the city and tore us all right out with her. At about 6 feet below sea level with levees on all sides, New Orleans is literally shaped like a bowl. That August, it filled up then started boiling, its contents whisked to and fro by 150-mile winds under a 100-degree Louisiana sun.

As Ida carved through the coast, I ended up in my favorite place, alone in the driver’s seat, but for my brother to my right and our dogs in the backseat as we evacuated down I-10.

Six hours into the drive, the clouds darkened. A small sprinkle of droplets quickly grew into a ceaseless wall of water pummeling my windshield and turning the freeway into a free-flowing river. Soon, I couldn’t see a thing — not the road, not the taillights of the car ahead, not even the reflection of my own headlights on full blast. I gripped the wheel with white knuckles and prayed for my tires to keep their traction, for the trees on the shoulder to stay standing, for everyone else on the road to just keep driving.

Right as I thought I would lose my hold and we’d spin out in the downpour, the clouds broke. The wind stilled, the rain slowed, and I caught a glimpse of the sun. We were in the eye of the storm.

The reprieve only lasted a few minutes. But it was just long enough for me to catch my breath and make sense of my surroundings before I drove back into the spiraling chaos to get through to the other side.

Over the past four years at Duke, I’ve felt lost in the storm more than I’d like to admit.

But through it all, The Chronicle has been my clarity and my center.

I came to the paper later than most, trekking up the (ridiculously steep) steps to 301 Flowers for the first time on a sweltering August day in my sophomore year. I didn’t know it at the time, but the lovingly worn-down office I found at the top of the climb would soon grow to become my home.

There’s nothing quite like the satisfaction of having a question that you know is important to someone, hunting down its answer, fitting that information together into a narrative that not only makes sense but is actually interesting to read, and then sending that story out into the world so it can reach those who need it. Once I got that first, electrifying taste, I was hooked.

Since then, writing for the paper has given me the keys to unlock journeys I never expected to take. My reporting has brought me to corners of campus I couldn’t find on a map — shining headlights down the back roads of Duke’s administrative decision-making or the flashing construction signs of federal policy changes one day before opening up to the rolling hills of colorful community features the next.

When I got to serve as news editor for Volume 120, every day turned into one of those adventures. You really can’t predict where the next 24 hours will take you in the job; the news never stops, and it seems to have a funny way of breaking at the absolute worst times. Some stories were more fun than others — I definitely had my fair share of days where it felt like 18-wheelers were flying into our lane without warning. But every time, the next morning would bring the thrill of a new dawn and an open road.

I was always eager to get back in the driver’s seat with the hope that wherever I went next, I’d be able to tell a story that would do somebody some good — whether that meant digging through University archives to explain the history behind a new initiative, building and analyzing datasets that could illustrate the nuances of North Carolina politics or interviewing community stakeholders to make sense of the different perspectives shaping a contentious campus debate. After 200 bylines in two-and-a-half years, there’s definitely some truth behind the long-running joke that I never leave the office. But I’ve never minded the good-natured teasing. If I get to choose how to spend my time, I’ll always pick the spot behind the wheel.

Because however much good my reporting has ever done for any of our readers, it’s been exponentially more beneficial for me.

Chasing down storylines for the past three years with the goal of helping people understand the complexities of fast-unfolding news events has also been my method of making sense of the world and my place in it. 

The Chronicle has been the excuse I get to use to find the answers to my own questions, the opportunity I’ve had to grow as a communicator and a leader in a newsroom that prides itself on impact and excellence, and the birthplace of countless friendships that will last long after my byline is lost on the website. And whenever I feel like my tires are losing traction and I can’t see through the torrent, the paper has been there as a place where I can step back, take a breath and take stock of my surroundings to find the best way through.

Our office in 301 Flowers has truly been the eye to a life that can feel like a hurricane. It is my refuge from the mess of everything else as much as a vantage point from which I can see where I am — and where to go next.

So as my three-volume joyride comes to an end, all that’s really left to say is thanks for the lift.

Zoe Kolenovsky is a Trinity senior who served as news editor of The Chronicle’s 120th volume and data editor of The Chronicle’s 121st volume.

She has too many people to thank to possibly fit within one paragraph — though, let’s be honest, she’s never been one to stick to a word limit. She will, of course, start with Michael Austin and Abby Spiller, her other halves during a tumultuous and beautiful year for three blind mice. 

To Ana Despa, for leading the charge this volume with immeasurable grace and letting her stick around even though she’s washed and unc, and to Claire Cranford, for being the best successor (and possible clone) a girl could ask for.

To the rising juniors of the news department, for being her guinea pigs when someone had the ridiculous idea to put her in charge of them during their first year — especially Dylan Halper and Ella Moore, who she knows will chart an exciting path for V. 122.

To Anna Newberry, for convincing her to finally bite the bullet and come to Flowers for god’s sake (and for being her first and forever Duke friend). To the rest of the senior class, who have all set the bar so damn high.

To everyone else at The Chronicle who welcomed her with open arms and became the community she reaches for every day. She’ll always be proud of the stories we told, but it’s the laughter she’ll remember.

And to her brother, for always trusting her to keep her hands on the wheel and her eyes on the road.

title: Journalism is the best teacher
author: Ranjan Jindal
article_text:
During my freshman year with The Chronicle, I happened to be the only women’s basketball beat that didn’t have class Tuesdays at noon. Naturally, I got the assignment of attending Kara Lawson’s midweek Zoom press conferences every week. 

I remember rigorously preparing for those calls and scouring ESPN for trends to find the perfect question to ask Coach Lawson. I realized that was probably over preparation, but I wanted to represent The Chronicle’s name well in my first year with the paper. Sometimes, there would be only one other media member who would consistently ask questions. Other times, it was just me.

My first ever Chronicle feature story included an amalgamation of quotes from those midweek Zoom sessions that I compiled into a piece taking a journey through the team’s season, Lawson’s most successful at that point. Those few months were when I learned some of my most formative lessons. Not just because of Lawson’s way with words, but because it taught me a tenet of journalism and life: It pays to show up. 

And over the years, I’ve realized The Chronicle’s strength is in our numbers. I’ve watched our sports department grow to more than 50 writers who show up to cover all 27 varsity sports. That’s what makes us special, and our paper’s motto of “We were there” has never rang more true. 

My senior year as audience engagement director and multimedia editor has allowed me to pursue a new passion of mine to expand our digital presence with audio and video journalism. I’ve picked up a slightly embarrassing hobby of monitoring our Instagram account’s follower count. I set goals for 10,000 followers during last year’s volume and 20,000 this year (we’re close!) We even have an audience engagement group chat called “Scroll Patrol.”

But despite those quantitative goals, the reason I am passionate about multimedia content — and why I think it’s so essential — is because it means we show up. We show up and show off what makes the Duke student body wonderful, from backstage looks at student arts showcases, campus multicultural events and spontaneous student events. Our open mics give students a chance to feel connected, and I hope that those interviews made someone smile. 

My work with multimedia has also led to my second takeaway from journalism: It’s important to take a chance. During my summer before junior year in D.C., then-news editor Zoe Kolenovsky and I filmed reels in my dorm building and in front of the White House to advertise our coverage — the unofficial birth of Chronicle multimedia. Caleb Dudley and I started a Duke football podcast three years ago, and while we put our best into the very first episode, the product from then to now is completely different. We navigated the bumps of video production and the embarrassment from hearing our voices on an audio. 

Starting the multimedia section also had its own challenges, from educating people about the section to recruitment and retention efforts. However, looking back, I’m so glad that I took these chances, undoubtedly bolstered by the confidence I gained from the unwavering backing of our general manager, Chrissy Murray, which I am forever grateful for. 

And finally, as I’m completing my senior year, I realize how much of journalism is a lesson in empathy. I’ll never forget a line from “Walk Two Moons” by Sharon Creech, a powerful and poignant story I read in elementary school. A version of the line is oft-mentioned: “Don't judge a man until you've walked two moons in his moccasins.” One of my favorite TV show lines puts the lesson more directly. As Ted Lasso said, “Be curious, not judgmental.” 

It’s our natural instinct to judge; mine too. I’m far from perfect in this department, but nothing has helped more than journalism. 

I used to be scared to initiate conversation, but interviewing people from all walks of life has instilled in me a love for uncovering unique angles in every topic. Some of my favorite stories have stemmed from individual curiosities. In every piece we write, we’re telling someone’s story. What is more powerful than that? We dig deep to make more sense of our campus and the world around us. 

So thank you to The Chronicle for teaching me the value of showing up, taking a chance and practicing empathy. And now, because of the tremendous classroom that is four years in 301 Flowers, I realized I can’t let journalism go. I’m now going to work in TV news for some of the same hosts who were constants in my living room growing up. 

The Chronicle has given me so much more than life lessons; it has defined my Duke experience. It has provided me with my four-year best friends, a community of fellow sports-watchers, intramural teammates (and champions), pick-up basketball, tennis and golfing partners and study buddies. I can’t put into words the gratitude I feel towards every single member of this paper. I’m forever thankful to the sports and multimedia sections for believing in me these past two years and putting out content I am so proud of. 

Besides sleeping in my room at night, I was probably in 301 Flowers more than any other building on campus during my four years at Duke. If I did college over one more time, I wouldn’t have it any other way. 

Ranjan Jindal is a Trinity senior and audience engagement director and multimedia editor of The Chronicle’s 121st volume. He was formerly sports editor of The Chronicle’s 120th volume.

title: Finding my way back home
author: Mackenzie Sheehy
article_text:
Like so many late millennials and early Gen Zers, I was a big fan of Hannah Montana growing up. I watched the later seasons of the show on Disney Channel, and I even donned a blonde wig one Halloween and sang what I’m sure was a very out-of-tune rendition of “The Best of Both Worlds.”

And like so many Hannah Montana fans, I’ve seen “Hannah Montana: The Movie” several times. In the film, Miley Cyrus feels like her pop star alter ego is taking over her life and must return to her roots to rediscover what matters most to her. At the end, as with any Disney movie, everything works out as Cyrus sings “You’ll Always Find Your Way Back Home.” The song symbolizes that no matter how much changes about you, you will always find your way back to your true home.

Until I got to Duke, I honestly didn’t really resonate with the song. I was more than ready to leave my small Massachusetts home for Durham, even though I knew I would miss my family terribly. My entire motivation for four years in high school was simple: work as hard as you possibly can so you can go far away from this place. If you can’t tell, high school was pretty horrific for me. Making friends wasn’t easy, and I felt many of my passions die while I was constantly stressed out and anxious. I love to write, but after a year of serving as editor-in-chief of my high school paper, which was a very negative experience, I was nearly ready to kiss journalism goodbye.

That is, until I learned about The Chronicle. I decided to give journalism one more shot and attended a Sunday afternoon news meeting in my first week on campus. As a nervous first-year and a person who has never been good at dealing with change, I figured the consistency of working at a newspaper would be good for me, at least until I felt more settled. 

After attending that first news meeting with plenty of nice people, I still felt slightly adrift. I wasn’t entirely sure about returning to journalism after such a negative high school experience. My friends from orientation week, Martin and Caleb, were going to the sports department meeting the following Friday. I decided to go and check it out, especially as a former competitive athlete who has always loved watching sports.

If I could go back and tell my first-year self anything, it would be this: do whatever you can to go to that meeting. It will change your life.

From the minute I sat down with the rest of the sports department, I knew I was finally finding that home Miley Cyrus thought was worth singing about. I instantly felt like I had found my people after four years in high school, where I never obtained that true connection. Everyone was so welcoming, and it kept me coming back.

It took that sports meeting for me to make my way back to what has always been my true home: writing. I’ve always been able to express myself better on a page than talking to another person, and I think I like spending my time among words more than among people. But what The Chronicle gave me back was that sense of joy that comes from writing about things that make you passionate, from crafting stories that have a piece of your soul inside because that’s how much you care about telling them.

That first year, I grew as a writer, without a doubt. More importantly, I learned that journalism — and writing as a whole — is supposed to be fun. Whether it was on the side of my first field hockey game or sitting courtside in Cameron covering the women’s team, I found myself once again enthralled with the world of journalism. In fact, I loved it so much that I pursued it as a minor and in two internships for the rest of my time at Duke.

In hindsight, though, it doesn’t surprise me that The Chronicle brought me back to my home of writing. What surprised me more was the home it created for me while in college.

I struggled for much of freshman year to find my place, but the sports hall in 301 Flowers was always somewhere where I could find a friendly face who would listen to my rants or give me a hug when I needed it. I learned the value of putting away my laptop for a little while and watching sports on the office monitors or chatting about my life. I formed friendships with some of the most important people in my life, all because of a newspaper I was initially wary of joining.

It took leaving The Chronicle to study abroad; however, that made me realize the true home I had created at the paper. During my sophomore year as Blue Zone editor, I struggled immensely with the decision to study in London instead of staying with the paper. I knew in my heart of hearts I needed the break and the growth that would come with going to a foreign country, but I carried immense guilt and anxiety about the decision. 

I’ll never forget sitting down with Ranjan, then the incoming sports editor, and telling him my decision. I was so stressed about the entire thing, until his first reaction was: “That’s awesome. Where are you thinking of studying?”

Ranjan probably doesn’t remember that, and most people who know him aren’t surprised by the kindness he showed in that moment, but to me, his reaction told me something bigger. I had finally found a home that I would willingly come back to, over and over again. And that home would always be ready to welcome me with open arms. I finally did find my way back home after studying abroad, and while my relationship to the paper looked different, the lifelong friendships were still there, ready to pull me back in like I never left. 

The Chronicle has given so much to me over four years. It’s given me a group of friends I’m thankful for every day. It’s given me my sorority little, who has become one of the most important pieces of my life at Duke. It’s given me back my love of writing. It’s even given me a boyfriend, which first year me would never believe.

But most importantly, it’s given me a home. A home I’ll always find my way back to, and a home that will always welcome me when I need it.

Miley Cyrus was ultimately right in the end. We always find our way back home, to the people and the places that embrace us as we truly are and make us the best versions of who we want to be.

Mackenzie Sheehy is a Trinity senior and served as Blue Zone Editor for The Chronicle’s 119th volume and sports associate editor for The Chronicle’s 120th and 121st volumes.

She’d like to thank Jonathan, Andrew and Rachael for being the first editors to believe in her and have confidence in her abilities. She would like to thank Ranjan, Dom and Sophie, for making lower masthead such a fun and rewarding experience. 

She congratulates all of the graduating seniors, who became some of her closest friends at Duke. She’d also like to thank Abby for being one of her best friends and favorite journalists to read. 

Lastly, she thanks Luke. Of all the things to come out of The Chronicle in the last four years, our love story is my favorite.

title: Art is for everyone
author: Zev van Zanten
article_text:
I have a confession: before I came to Duke, I had never seen a play, attended a total of one musical (at my high school), listened primarily to country and rock and had at best a tangential grasp of film. Despite this shocking lack of any pop culture knowledge, I found myself the Recess Editor.

Indeed, it has been a running joke within Recess that I was the least culturally adept person on campus, despite ostensibly being in charge of knowing the most, or at least enough to manage the department responsible for cultural coverage. Yet for the last four years, I have had the incredible privilege of learning about arts and culture from some of the most talented writers and artists, be they students, staff, Durhamites or visitors. 

Why write about art then? I knew I wanted to get better at writing and saw writing more as an instrumental part of that (my advice: if you want to be a better writer, write as much as possible as frequently as possible). Equally important, I’ve always loved a very particular aspect of art: the written word. Be it poetry, books or blank verse, if it’s readable, I’ll at least try to take a look at it. 

But while I love to read, I am abysmal at writing anything particularly good. I consider myself the Sancho Panza of creative writing, producing good prose only by chance. Just like his constant commentary in Don Quixote occasionally produced little nuggets of profundity, I, by chance, scratch at the surface of producing good work by merit of churning out a lot of text. Though I never manage to produce anything good for more than a few lines.

Yet, while I could never be an artist myself, I still love the arts. Why? Why love something that you want to do but know you’ll never be good enough to do yourself? The answer to that question is the same reason the arts are something that should belong to us all. It’s also why, regardless of whether you are good or not at art, you should engage in it.

Like with many things, the arts can only be advocated for in one of two ways. The first and more common way is instrumental, looking at art for what it brings. The second is for its own sake. 

From an instrumental standpoint, art is and will always be one of the most important parts of education. By studying the arts, we can access and observe the lives and experiences of countless others, people whose shoes we would otherwise struggle to put on. More than that, art forces us to think, to grow, to debate and to critique. It is one of the best ways of shaping your mind, which is perhaps why art and the humanities more broadly were considered so integral to a liberal arts education. 

But art is also worth doing for its own sake. It represents an incredibly powerful and foundational human impulse, which is why the history of art stretches nearly as far back as overall history. Since we first figured out how to create color and make drawings, we have pursued this passion with vigor. Art is a means to an end, but it is also a meaningful end in its own right.

You may be asking yourself, why do I need to know this? The answer is simple: We live at what is perhaps the best time in our lives to experience the arts. For those still in college, Duke is dense with opportunities to engage. 

We have literally dozens of performing groups on campus, covering everything from Chinese theater to a cappella to musical theater to Bollywood dance. Our campus has its own museum, dozens of mini exhibits are scattered around campus, and all sorts of performing groups regularly come to campus. I get that Duke is a busy place, but you may never again have this level of proximity to the arts. 

And regardless of whether you’re graduating or still in school, I can’t deny that we live in a time with so many competing demands for our attention. Art demands more from us than passively scrolling TikTok or mindlessly watching some trash TV. 

But that doesn’t mean we should abandon it and drift to the path of least resistance, to a world of low-quality trash. We must choose to strive, to pursue the meaningful things, to, in the words of the immortal Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, choose beauty and chase beauty.

That isn’t to say that only one type of art or only certain arts are worth pursuing. I will admit that I consider certain genres better than others, and some art forms better. But the beautiful thing about art is that we are all struck by different things (for example, I consider science fiction to be high art, something which most art buffs would find concerning). 

Regardless of what you engage with, you stand to benefit. Though I encourage you to at least try the Great Books and historically popular arts more broadly (after all, their enduring appeal suggests they have something unique to offer).

And the most beautiful thing about the arts is that the pursuit of them can mean many things to many people. It might mean walking to the Nasher and taking a look at the newest exhibit, or attending one of Duke’s excellent art shows. 

Maybe it means listening to some nice music on your phone, or watching a good movie or TV show. Or, in the case of someone like me, maybe you can just sit down with a book for a few hours. Find a way to engage with the arts that works for you, and pursue it relentlessly.

I may be done with my Duke journey, but I know that I’m far from done with the arts. Indeed, I’m incredibly thankful to Duke Arts and our campus’s many wonderful student artists for helping me really start on that journey for the first time. For all of you reading this, I hope you’re not done either.

Zev van Zanten is a Trinity senior and served as Recess managing editor for The Chronicle's 121st volume and Recess editor for The Chronicle's 120th volume. He would like to thank Jules Kourelajos, Anna Rebello, Derek Deng and Jonathan Pertile for nurturing him as a writer and editor and pushing him to be the best he could be. 

He’d also like to thank Abby Spiller, Ranjan Jindal, Zoe Kolenovsky, Morgan Chu, Karen Xu, Alice Qin and Michael Austin for being the best masthead of all time. 

Last but not least, he would like to thank Kadin Purath and Arnav Jindal for being his Recess buddies all these years, and Olivia Prusky, Bhavika Verma and Gabriel Olatomi for carrying on the torch.

title: Beyond the bounds of uncertainty
author: Dom Fenoglio
article_text:
I really hate being late.

Every morning, I have to make my coffee within five minutes of my alarm ringing so I can wait precisely 10 minutes for it to cool off before I drink it. Then, I pace myself at the gym with playlists exactly one hour long so that I can be home to shower, get ready and head out the door with enough of a cushion to get to class at least 15 minutes early.

Sure, it’s nice to be on time, but I recognize how unnecessary a lot of my habits are. In reflecting about the biggest lessons I’ve learned at Duke, I’ve come to think lateness is only a single manifestation of my dissatisfaction with a larger enemy: uncertainty. 

I like having a solution to a problem and knowing the steps I need to take to get there; one thing that drew me to the statistics major was the ability to quantify uncertainty and bound possible outcomes neatly with a few numbers. On the other hand, I struggle with questions that don’t have tidy answers. Why does Duke lose games it should win? How do I figure out what I want to do in my future? What really makes me happy?

After stubbornly digging myself into plenty of holes, I realized there’s no formula for optimally getting through college. Instead, the best way to work towards better answers to life’s frustrating questions is with help from others and The Chronicle has been the community at Duke to guide me. 

Throughout my time with The Chronicle, I covered my fair share of painful losses, and after each one I found myself taken aback by the team’s composure and level-headedness. Growing up, I always wore my heart on my sleeve — especially in sports — and often had emotional reactions to bad breaks. I desperately wanted to know why I struck out, gave up a home run or missed a free throw, but refused to accept any and all explanations. Observing classmates my age and younger exhibit such impressive poise changed my perspective; if Cooper Flagg and Kon Knueppel can talk to a sea of reporters after their dreams were ripped from their hands, who am I to yell and scream?

Writing about sports eventually helped me find the right words to ask for advice from my friends at The Chronicle about how to handle my own personal moments of failure. Going to school at a place like Duke can make it scary to talk about being uncertain, but The Chronicle helped me grow comfortable leaning on others. My friends from The Chronicle are often the first to find out about any job offers, good grades or moments of victory, but more importantly, they have listened to me complain, bemoan and otherwise grumble about everything from intramural sports to deep personal obstacles. 

I haven’t learned how to answer all of my questions and eliminate uncertainty, but I have been shocked at how much progress I can make simply by talking about them with someone else. This is one reason I see journalism as an invaluable piece of our society: it allows us to articulate and shed light on some of life’s hardest questions. Just by reading a great article, we unlock something about what drives the world around us. I will forever be grateful that I walked into The Chronicle office freshman year, and I have no idea where I would be without this amazing group of people.

In the spirit of the great Andrew Long, I’ll wrap things up with a song that I consistently find myself coming back to. Roughly four years ago, I opened my admission letter to Duke — so nervous I had to check it alone in my room — and when I ran downstairs to tell my mom, I was welcomed by the sound of “You Can’t Always Get What You Want,” by The Rolling Stones. 

Some kind of confidence she had in me, right? 

Contrary to what the lyrics may appear to suggest, I don’t think it’s a sad song, or even a sad message. To me, it’s a reminder of life’s uncertainty. Things will go wrong, and that’s fine. Our job is not to control the uncontrollable, but simply surround ourselves with the right people and try our best to navigate forward.

It still scares me to think of all the unknowns in my future, and I will likely stick with my over-the-top morning routine, but I now feel far more prepared for all the twists and turns that lie ahead, and extremely grateful knowing that I’ll have the support of friends along the way. 

Dom Fenoglio is a Trinity senior and served as a sports managing editor for The Chronicle’s 120th volume. First and foremost, he would like to thank The Chronicle’s intramural flag football team for bringing home a championship this season. Slightly lower on the ladder, he wants to thank all of the members of The Chronicle who made it his favorite part of Duke. 

He wants to thank Jonathan Levitan and Andrew Long for modeling what it means to be a compassionate leader, Ranjan Jindal and Sophie Levenson for helping shape the best experiences of his time at Duke on last year’s sports masthead, the entire senior class for being the reason he stuck with The Chronicle, and every person he has ever argued with over sports, life, or anything in between. 

Finally, he would like to wish the best of luck to Alex Min, Colton Schwabe and Ryan Hamner in leading the department next year and all of the underclassmen set to lead The Chronicle in the years to come. He’s confident you’ll do more than he ever could.

title: The stories I didn’t write
author: Mia Penner
article_text:
While many of my Chronicle colleagues found journalism in college, I’ve been at it since middle school. My first article was a very earnest account of my seventh-grade winter dance. So, although my subject matter has changed, there’s clearly something special about reporting that’s kept me in the business so long. It’s less romantic than you might expect.

Sure, I love that journalism pushes me far beyond my comfort zone — like the time I, a born-and-raised New Yorker, found myself shooting clay pigeons with the Duke Hunting and Conservation Club. I love the moments when reporting puts me ahead of the curve, like being among the first to learn the Class of 2028’s acceptance rate. I value the opportunity to cover consequential stories about Duke’s place in a volatile political landscape, including the shuttering of the Reginaldo Howard Memorial Scholarship Program. And I take pride in leading serious investigations — yes, including my hard-hitting coverage of the hand, foot and mouth outbreak that swept through the freshman class in 2023.

But if I’m being really, truly honest, what I love most about reporting is the flow state — the electric stretch when the story seems to write itself. My favorite interviews are the ones I leave already hearing the final draft in my head, knowing exactly which quotes will make the cut. And I’ll admit, I relish reading over a piece of writing I’m proud of, perhaps all too self-satisfied.

Suffice to say, I didn’t know what to expect when I was asked to report without the part I love most: actually writing the story.

After three and a half years of writing, editing and helping grow The Chronicle’s social media presence, my role at the paper took on a new dimension this spring. I’ve been leading a research project focused on helping The Chronicle better understand its undergraduate audience. We want to figure out where students feel uninformed, how news fits into their daily routines and what challenges shape the way they consume information. The ultimate goal is to identify how we can adapt our content and products to better meet students’ needs at a time when, perhaps unsurprisingly, many are turning away from traditional college media.

My research team’s approach was thorough, if a bit unconventional. We worked with Ariel Zirulnick, a news product consultant, to interview 17 students across campus for one hour each. I participated in most of those interviews. 

We asked the expected questions, like “What information do you find yourself looking for most often when it comes to life at Duke?” But we also probed deeper. We wanted to understand what actually shapes students’ days, the constraints they navigate, how Duke supports or strains their mental health and what motivates them.

Ariel primarily analyzed the content of the interviews, so they felt fundamentally different from the ones I’ve conducted as a Chronicle reporter. I wasn’t calling sources in search of a specific quote or angle, nor was I weighing how each conversation might fit into an article’s larger narrative. Aside from writing a brief summary after each interview, there was little writing involved at all. My role was simply to ask questions — and, more importantly, to listen.

As it turned out, listening was harder than expected. It felt unnatural to invite students to open up about their personal lives and struggles without offering something of myself in return. And it was even harder to quiet the instinct to start writing their stories in my head, as if I were on deadline.

But that restraint made the experience more valuable. It forced me to let go of my assumptions and take each story as it came, without trying to fit it into a prewritten frame. And it allowed me to reflect deeply on my own four years here. 

A lot of the first-years I spoke with sounded like me during my first year, quietly struggling to find their niche on campus and feel like they belonged. I was struck by how many students described the same loneliness and uncertainty, yet each seemed convinced they were the only one feeling it. I don’t think about my difficult first semester very often, but revisiting it now, as a graduating senior, felt unexpectedly cathartic. I just wish I had known then how many other people were going through the same thing.

The interviews also put my own challenges in perspective. It’s easy to get caught up in your own world and assume your struggles are singular. But again and again, I was reminded that other students are navigating extraordinary challenges alongside the everyday demands of school and social life. 

Before interviewing international students, I had never really considered what it might mean to arrive in the United States for the first time the day before freshman year begins. I’ve had my own frustrations with the job search, but I hadn’t fully grasped how few companies sponsor international students, or how the 60-day window after graduation to secure a visa can make the process feel urgent, even existential.

More than anything, these conversations left me with a deeper appreciation for the people around me. Every student I spoke with was strikingly open and honest, more so than I think I would be with a stranger. 

It’s easy to fall into the lazy narrative that Duke students are snobby and out of touch. It’s true that many of us lead privileged lives, but I think that’s far from the full picture. The students I met — even the ones you might least expect — were open-minded, genuinely passionate about their interests and curious about the world around them. Maybe that shouldn’t be surprising, especially given Duke’s rigorous admissions standards. But meeting such wonderful people in these interviews made me proud to be a Duke student, and it makes it even harder to say goodbye. 

Before this semester, I had never been one to provoke “deep” conversations with people I barely know. Quite frankly, I’ve always found those kinds of people annoying. But there’s something to be said for the urge to seek out stories from strangers — and to listen for no other purpose than listening. I only wish I had done it sooner. 

Next fall, I’ll be starting a job as a public sector consultant, which has almost nothing to do with reporting. And while I hope to find my way back to journalism one day, it will probably be some time before I get to reread an article I wrote with a self-satisfied grin. I’m glad I never have to stop listening.

Mia Penner is a senior and served as the audience engagement editor for The Chronicle’s 120th and volume and Editor-at-Large for The Chronicle’s 119th volume. 

She is grateful to Chrissy Murray for trusting her to lead this project and for her steady support along the way — their Monday afternoon meetings were a highlight of the week. 

She also thanks Ariel Zirulnick and her Chronicle research team — Zoe Kolenovsky, Dylan Halper, Claire Cranford, Mia Taubenblat, Sarah Diaz, Ella Moore and Lina Olazabal — for their thoughtful and thorough work. 

Finally, she is deeply appreciative of the students who participated in the study for their openness and honesty with a complete stranger. You all have made her proud to be a Duke alumna.

title: “Monday Monday is just like us!” cry adoring fans
author: Landen Meier and Monday Monday
article_text:
Editor's note: The article below is satire.

I can hear it already.

“Landen is Monday Monday? But he’s too conventionally attractive to be funny …”

“I mean, now that I think about it, I guess Monday Monday has always sounded intimidatingly intelligent and thoughtful in the same way that Landen is …”

“Is there any way I can send him money?”

I know, I know. The news that I, Landen Meier, am Monday Monday may come as a shock to many of the millions of people who have waited for this article with bated breath. 

When I originally applied to be Monday Monday, I wasn’t sure it was right for me. Similar to the Joker or President Donald Trump, I’ve always felt too cloistered by society to pursue my true passion: comedy. But I knew that I needed to step up once I saw the state of Duke upon my O-Week arrival.

We were on the brink of moral collapse (I scrolled Fizz once). The evil and power-hungry had eked their way into our highest and most sacred halls (my friends keep reposting Aaron Dinin). Much like a movie starring Gal Gadot, I was NOT going to sit by and watch it. I was going to make a difference; I was going to write anonymous satire.

Jokes aside, I’m truly grateful for the experience of being Monday Monday. It forced me to keep up with what was going on at Duke on a macro level, to consider every angle of the positions I was taking (since what you write can and will affect you), and, most importantly, make fun of UNC.

My fear in a lot of what I’ve done creatively this year is that I don’t have a distinct enough worldview to make my perspective (and whatever work I create) interesting. Being Monday Monday as a first-year has allowed me the opportunity to build that worldview (at least about Duke) in real time, to form strong opinions and convert them into parts of my belief system.

And the question of whether what I create is interesting or not worries me less now because, having created something, I know I can and will create more things and that I will get the opportunity to be interesting again.

I’m also very grateful to everyone who helped me find my voice as Monday Monday. I want to thank my editor, Shambhavi, who was consistently patient when I would send her Google Doc drafts at 10 p.m. on Sunday nights. I also want to thank the Duke community, who have collectively given me the experiences of the best year of my life so far. Although I’ve made a million jokes about Duke and the people in it over the course of the column, I consistently find that the people here have good intentions and want to do the best they can.

Finally, I want to thank the three funniest people I know. When I told my family I was picked to write satire for The Chronicle for a year, it got mixed reviews. My brother wondered whether anyone else had applied for the position. My mom requested that I reconsider a STEM major. My dad, however, was excited and has since read all my articles when they come out every Monday.

He also gave me the idea and several of the jokes for what became The Chronicle’s most-read story of 2025. In a school that sometimes seems like a graveyard for artistic ambition, I have leaned on him and his insistence that a commitment to creativity was a matter of principle, not preference.

Thanks, Dad.

So now, I’ll face every Chronicle Opinion writer’s worst fear and let someone else talk.

Thank you, and it’s been an honor to be your Monday Monday.

Landen Meier is a Trinity first-year and served as Monday Monday, The Chronicle’s long-standing anonymous satirical columnist, for its 121st volume.

title: In suspending SJP, Duke administration gets its long-desired, cheap victory
author: Leo Goldberg
article_text:
It was only a matter of time before Duke’s chapter of Students for Justice in Palestine (SJP) was suspended by the administration. Given our university’s neurotic aversion to anything that could draw political scrutiny and the equally neurotic search of the pro-Israel factions to report the tiniest slip-up on the part of the pro-Palestinians as antisemitic, it was inevitable that the two would eventually converge to oust the small yet vocal SJP.

In March, the opportunity arose when the SJP made the mistake of posting a vile cartoon showing a pig holding a torch with the Star of David to promote a general body meeting. Though explained away by SJP as a criticism of Zionism exclusively, not Jews, the cartoon followed a long and revolting history of Jews being antisemitically depicted as pigs, beginning in the 13th century with the German Christian drawing Judensau. 

Duke’s SJP chapter has, for a long time, shown poor judgment of this kind, which has undermined its important and genuine cause. They refer to Palestinians killed by Israel as "martyrs," as if there isn’t enough fanatical religious language on this issue already. In a September memorial held for those killed in Gaza, they inflated the Palestinian death toll tenfold by adding an extra 0 to 68,000 and cited a fringe source claiming this to be the true casualty rate in Gaza. 

During a walkout demonstration in protest of former Secretary of State Antony Blinken’s visit to Duke’s campus in December, SJP congregated on Abele Quad and denounced his list of transgressions, which included placing sanctions on what they deemed the “democratically-elected government of Nicolas Maduro in Venezuela,” according to a Chronicle recording of the protest. The posting of the cartoon is another disappointing instance of this general pattern of carelessness.

Nonetheless, the reactionary decision of Duke Student Affairs to suspend SJP’s recognition as a campus organization and freeze funds before a proper investigation has taken place, and after SJP complied with its request to take down the cartoon, is ludicrous. 

To frame this whole affair in its full absurdity, the complaints filed by students were referred to the Office of Institutional Equity (OIE) for alleged violation of the Policy on Prohibited Discrimination, Harassment, and Related Misconduct (PPDHRM). The authority to take action under PPDHRM is delegated specifically to the OIE, yet jurisdiction has now been dubiously handed over to Student Affairs, represented by Ben Adams, senior associate dean of students for QuadEx. Adams, on behalf of Student Affairs, requested SJP take down the cartoon, which they did in full compliance, to which Adams responded by revoking their recognition status and freezing their funding. 

The reasoning behind the decision is extraordinarily suspicious and bizarre. In an email to SJP leadership, Adams claimed the authority to conduct “independent assessments of whether interim measures are warranted to protect the health, safety or welfare of the university community or any member of it” and took refuge in the condescending reasoning that organizational recognition is a “privilege” which comes with responsibilities. This is the kind of rationale, which has just a bit too strong a whiff of convenience and self-justification to it, that one would expect from someone who has an ulterior motive.

The dubiousness is compounded by the fact that, through emails reported on by The Chronicle, OIE has thus far corroborated all of SJP’s statements and denied any part in disciplining SJP under the punitive measures over which Adams is wrongly appropriating jurisdiction. Upon SJP’s submission of an inquiry to Adams to ask the reasons behind this hysterical overreaction, Adams, according to The Chronicle, “has not responded ... He declined The Chronicle’s request for comment on the matter ‘since it's still under review by Student Affairs.’”

The whole affair is a scandal, but it’s hardly surprising. There has, for many years now, been a flagrant double standard when it comes to Palestinian vs Israeli activism on college campuses, something which has come to be known as the “Palestine Exception.” Under this unspoken rule, the free speech of individuals and groups advocating for Palestinian rights, especially that involving criticism of Israel, is selectively targeted and suppressed. 

Over the last several years, universities, especially elite ones, have either rewritten disciplinary codes or implemented policies that heavily favor pro-Israel factions on campus and punish Palestinian activism under the guise of “antisemitism.” Duke’s version of this came in the form of its “Pickets, Protests, and Demonstrations” amendment in September 2024, which required student groups to submit planned outdoor protests 15 days in advance for administrative approval. Anyone who could read between the lines would know this was a clear attempt to suppress the kind of pro-Palestinian activism that got peer institutions like Columbia into so much trouble.

This trend, of course, is a legacy of the post Oct. 7, encampment protests where universities weathered substantial hits to their reputations and finances from the public and faced extortion from the federal government following the protests. Universities became terrified to permit anything that could put them at risk of being accused of enabling anti-Jewish hatred.

What this has come to mean is that any expression of support or solidarity with Palestinian rights or self-determination, and the often-concurrent criticism of Israel and Zionism, has been equated with antisemitism (one cannot say enough that the two are not, and have never, been the same). This is then easily abused by pro-Israel factions to claim a toxic environment of discrimination on campus. 

There is, of course, no corresponding or equivalent provision made for supporters of the Palestinians. Palestinian activism, in this alarming atmosphere of ideological policing that heavily favors one side, is canceled and censored by universities for the slightest transgression, while pro-Israel groups are able to get away with the most unbelievable types of behavior. Examples like the UCLA Zionist counterprotesters demonstrate this. 

This hypocrisy is evident at Duke, an institution that has made clear it will unhesitatingly sacrifice any and all moral principles in exchange for keeping its head down. SJP is held to a standard to which no other campus group or event is, and the cartoon incident is the most recent demonstration of this. 

All it takes to prove this is to look at the impunity with which similar objectionable actions carried out by other groups/events on campus are met. In September 2025, Jerry Seinfeld was allowed to come on campus primarily under the sponsorship of Chabad at Duke and claim that people standing for Palestinian rights are worse than KKK members. Was Chabad, or a single other group, suspended or even threatened with suspension for allowing such slander? Of course not. No disciplinary action from the University was ever taken, and many students criticized Duke’s lack of response as “massive hypocrisy.”

Can you imagine what the response would have been if the situation were reversed, and a Palestinian speaker sponsored by SJP had accused Israeli settlers of being worse than white supremacists? I can already hear the bloodcurdling shrieks of those who cry antisemitism whenever they can.

The clearest example, though, of Duke’s hypocrisy when it comes to SJP’s suspension comes from a remarkably similar instance where the situation was more-or-less inverted. In 2021, Duke’s chapter of Students Supporting Israel (SSI), amid the process of trying to get re-recognized as a campus group, reposted a tweet from a specific student objecting to Israel’s settler colonialism and used its social media platform to personally target them. DSG president at the time, Christina Wang, denied the group recognition because of this, based on the group’s singling out of individual students. 

SSI proceeded to stir up such a storm of outrage, including unfavorable national attention for Duke, that not only did Vincent Price put out a statement explaining that the Duke administration had nothing to do with the decision, but also proceeded to personally intervene and offer SSI alternative forms of funding outside of DSG, which would allow the group to exist on campus. Now, I personally disagree with Wang’s decision and would not have denied SSI’s recognized status, but it is astounding to see this kind of partiality on the part of the University towards campus groups based on their identities or views.

Simply disappearing SJP was the easy, cheap way for Duke to prevent having to deal with the hard questions and problems it posed in the future. The fact that the administration willingly chose hypocrisy and censorship to do so is deeply disappointing. In no way, though, is it surprising. 

Leo Goldberg is a Trinity sophomore. His pieces typically run on alternate Mondays.

title: Flourishing from an integrated education
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
Today is the last of three “Blue Devil Days” for admitted students considering coming to Duke (you’ll love it!). It’s also the last week of classes, including for our seniors who will be graduating in a few short weeks (every blessing on your final days of studying!). So it’s a good time to consider what a college education is for. What larger purpose does an education serve that extends beyond an individual student’s four years at Duke?

My hope for the Class of 2026 and the Class of 2030, as well as all the classes in between, is that you will seek out, or have already received, the integrated education that is offered here at Duke. Rigorous academics are, of course, at the heart of any college education. Building on that foundation, it will look different depending on who you are as a student and a person, but the Duke campus offers some clues about an education that promotes the flourishing of the whole person.

Let’s start with the Sarah P. Duke Gardens (with its newly opened Garden Gateway). My chapel colleagues, Rev. Dr. Lyn Pace and Rev. Leah Torrey, recently gathered a group of graduate students at the gardens as part of our “Interfaith Campus Pilgrimages” program. They led a session on spirituality and the natural world with students, including a discussion and a walk through the gardens to record their reflections and observations. 

The gardens are the perfect place, especially at this time of year, to be reminded of the beauty of the natural world. And it’s not just there where we find beauty; Duke has a robust arts program through which we can encounter the expressiveness of poetry, the elegance of dance, the artistry of painting, the delight of music and so much more. Through these experiences, we get a glimpse of how we can recognize, contribute to and even create beauty that transcends any one person.

Next, let’s go to Cameron Indoor Stadium (you may have had to camp out for weeks to get inside). This is, of course, the home of our double-ACC Champion basketball teams. There is so much to learn from sports; after all, you have to build a team. As Coach K told us when he spoke at the Chapel in the fall: “The most important speed that I worked on when I coached … was the speed to trust — how quickly will you trust me?” 

Sports require the kind of discipline that is needed in any endeavor in life, from working a job to practicing a religion to cultivating long-term relationships. To persist in athletics, you have to develop humility and perseverance. You won’t win every game or make every shot, and yet, as the Bible’s Letter to the Hebrews puts it, we are called to “run with perseverance the race that is set before us.”

Sports is one of the reasons I am still at Duke after 14 years, and it’s not just because of the impressive records of our teams. I remember my first Duke-Carolina football game in my first fall semester here. It was a tight and exciting game. Duke eventually came back to win near the end. 

I was sitting in the president’s box with my family, and the place exploded when Duke scored. I had my six-year-old son sleeping on my lap while vice presidents, deans and other Duke leadership jumped up and down, slapped high fives with one another and the dean of the Divinity School turned to my wife and gave her a huge bear hug. I knew then: Duke was for me! 

Our final stop on campus is — you may have already guessed it — the Duke Chapel. It is a symbol of the university’s motto, “eruditio et religio,” or, as we interpret it in the Chapel’s mission statement, “bridg[ing] faith and learning by nurturing and embodying the intellectual, ethical and spiritual life.” 

The soaring spires of the Chapel tower, the radiant stained-glass of its windows and the vaulted ceiling capped with a trumpeting angel all point to our highest aspirations. We are more than just thinking heads on a stick; we are whole persons who seek purpose, meaning and well-being.

That pursuit is not confined to Sunday services inside the Chapel. Throughout the week and around campus, students participate in the communities, rituals and prayers of two dozen Religious Life groups, ranging from Christian to Jewish to Hindu to Muslim — plus the courses and programs of campus partners such as the Kenan Institute for Ethics, DuWell and others. Duke wants humans to remain human even while in school and to live into an integrative vision; to be whole.

Whenever I think about places and buildings at Duke, like the Chapel, I am reminded of how former Duke President Richard Brodhead would talk about all of the campus construction projects that were underway during his time. He said buildings are means, not ends. 

The “telos,” the end, is human; buildings have human purposes. This is what I have found at Duke. You can have what former President Terry Sanford called “outrageous ambitions” and yet still embrace your humanity as a whole person (mind, body, spirit) because of the integrative approach here. 

The final piece of this holistic approach — and here I’ll quote one more former Duke president — is “greatness through service,” as William Preston Few said. An integrative education seeks not just “my good” but “our good;” it is in transcending ourselves that we find true human flourishing.

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: Stop saving “yes” for senior year
author: Gabrielle Mollin
article_text:
The best thing about senior year at Duke is a small but mighty, three-letter word: yes. 

“Do you want to get dinner tomorrow?” Yes. 

“Do you want to go to the game tonight?” Yes. 

“Do you want to hang on BC?” Yes. 

“Do you want to distract ourselves from the fact that graduation is somehow a month away????” Yes!!!!

The word “yes” has been an undeniably resounding force throughout senior year, and I’m happier for it. When I look back on the past semester, I’m grateful to have had friends who were motivated by the fleeting nature of college. Together, we’ve made the most of every game day, study session, meal, night out and so on. We say yes because we know our time is finite, and we can’t bear the guilt of passing up precious last moments. We say yes because why would we say no? 

But the concentration of all these yeses in senior year doesn’t sit right with me. It makes sense that we become more intentional once we’re faced with the reality of leaving, but I can’t help wishing that spirit carried through the entire Duke experience, not simply its end. Why do so many of us wait until the clock is running out to start showing up?

I’d argue that Duke students are a little too comfortable with the idea of “protecting your peace.” Freshman through junior year, it’s highly normalized to choose yourself over the moment. It’s okay to skip that hangout if you’re a little bit tired. It’s understandable to miss a friend’s birthday because you have a midterm later that week. It’s acceptable to cancel dinner plans because you think you’d better get more work done. Throughout these first three years, it’s the norm to put yourself first rather than show up for someone else. In my view, it’s been taken too far. 

To be clear, rest and boundaries matter. It’s a good thing that we’ve learned how to say no and do what’s best for ourselves sometimes. But the danger in “protecting your peace” sometimes is that it’s never really sometimes, but the majority of the time. What was meant to be occasional becomes habitual, and saying no is no longer what’s necessary but rather what’s comfortable. With the exception of senior year, saying no is easier than showing up because showing up doesn’t feel pressing. We are reasonably inclined to prioritize what feels urgent in those first three years: deadlines, exams, internship applications. Whereas we readily sideline dinners, birthdays or hangouts because we figure there will always be another one sooner or later. 

Senior year seemingly disrupts this logic. Suddenly, time feels scarce, and the plans that once seemed easy to pass up no longer come with the promise of a next time. 

But there isn’t anything inherent about senior year that warrants such a shift; it’s all a matter of perspective. Time in college is always finite, but we only really reckon with it at the end. And with some exceptions, seniors are just as busy as in other years, with job applications, graduate school exams and the usual classes. 

Seniors choose to recognize the urgency of their Duke experiences and memories alongside the urgency of their responsibilities. And the truth is, there’s nothing stopping underclassmen from striking the same balance. 

Rather than wait until the urgency of senior year creeps in, underclassmen should say yes more now. The people, opportunities and moments are already there. The only difference is whether you make the choice to treat them as a priority now or wait until the urgency really sets in. Of course, it should be okay to still say no sometimes, but don’t get too comfortable and wait until senior year to truly show up. 

Showing up is rarely perfect or easy. It often comes at the end of a long day or interrupts your routine. It asks something of you. But it’s also something you can’t make up for later. Senior year has taught me that college is so much more than the big events and milestones. College is truly defined by the ordinary moments we chose to be present for: casual WU dinners, sporadic walk and talks around campus, last-minute coffee runs and times we showed up even when we didn’t feel like it.

Senior year has shown me that saying yes really does matter. Our time at Duke has always been limited; we just waited to realize it until it was impossible to ignore. But you don’t need to wait that long to start showing up. You can and should start saying yes more now. Your senior year self will thank you.

Gabrielle Mollin is a Trinity senior. Her pieces typically run on alternate Thursdays.

title: Duke Mi Gente condemns the removal of Latino Student Recruitment Weekend
author: Aaron Andino, Yeddailin Gonzalez and Krishna Shah
article_text:
Mi Gente, as the largest Latine student organization at Duke University, condemns the administration’s decision and lack of transparency in making such a decision to halt Latino Student Recruitment Weekend (LSRW). Since 1999, LSRW has been integral to welcoming newly admitted Latine students at Duke and encouraging these admits to attend the University.

The establishment of LSRW was modeled after the Black Student Alliance Invitational Weekend (BSAI). Thus, to hear of BSAI’s cancellation this year is further disheartening when considering the opportunities the initiative provided for other cultural groups. 

The purpose of LSRW was an intentional step for undergraduate admissions in “realizing the future potential of this underrepresented population at Duke University,” referring to the increasing Latine/Hispanic population in the US that was not reflected on campus. It was a way to actualize Duke as an attainable pathway for these students. This began with having them on campus, meeting fellow Latine recruits, and living — instead of simply imagining — life as a student. LSRW is a catalyst for accessibility for students, for them to realize that Duke would not be an intangible concept to be never reached. 

“I felt very hesitant that Duke would be a space where I could feel welcomed and connected to home. LSRW introduced me to so many wonderful individuals and programs,” said sophomore Sofie De La Cerda when talking about her experience with the program. 

The impact of this initiative was seen following the first annual LSRW in 1999, where 21 out of the 46 students who participated in the program matriculated to Duke in the fall (46% yield). It is also important to note that LSRW students made up 23% of the incoming class of Latine students following the 1999 admissions cycle. The success of the LSRW program has only increased, with 56 out of 84 students who participated in 2024 choosing to commit to Duke. 

The share of Latine students admitted to Duke has increased from 5% in 1999 to 17% within the class of 2026; with a recent drop to 11% in the class of 2029. Concerns regarding the admission of Latine students have increased following recent rulings and executive orders against Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) initiatives, with the University itself having shifted its focus towards “Inclusive Excellence” in response to federal government scrutiny. However, it is clear that these changes only undermine the importance of ensuring a vibrant, present Latine community on campus. 

LSRW has allowed students to bond over language, culture and customs with each other. It has helped countless families feel much more at ease about their student's transition into a new place. For students like sophomore Mariangel Mendez Perez, "LSRW opened doors that [she] had no idea existed for the Latino community at Duke”.

Since 1998, Mi Gente has played a pivotal role in LSRW's main goals. Our organization has arranged meals, host assignments and event programming with limited funds and assistance from non-student staff. Before 2016, Mi Gente had used at least 35% of the organization’s funds to subsidize LSRW, with planning beginning in the fall through meetings and space bookings. There has been a historical trend of lacking proper institutional funding and support, which has continued to persist even a decade later. 

In 2016, these pressures reached a head with Mi Gente choosing to boycott that year’s LSRW due to the continued unmet demands of Latine students at the time for a cultural space and increased hiring of Latine faculty. 

In recent years, Mi Gente’s contributions have been conducted through hosting Mezcla, a large celebration with performances and activities during LSRW and providing volunteers in tabling and for working events. Even so, there has been increased frustration about how administrative offices have planned and communicated the LSRW timeline. This lack of proper communication, such as when students are expected to arrive on campus, limits our abilities and the time necessary to acquire resources for and plan events.

Planning for LSRW was intended and has generally begun in the fall semester. Before 2024, communications began in early January. In 2024, they began at the very end of January, and in 2025, it was early February. This year, the cancellation of LSRW and transition into Blue Devil Nights was not communicated with LSRW co-chairs — students who spearhead the weekend’s programming, funding, and coordination of hosts — until late February, with planning not beginning until after spring break. 

In addition to these truncated schedules, acquiring the proper funding and space reservations to host events for incoming students has been continuously constrained, becoming more prevalent in recent years. The decision to do away with LSRW is not accidental nor an unfortunate circumstance, but rather a continuation of Duke’s encroachment on this tradition, now halting it altogether, by limiting and, in ways, preventing students’ capability to properly plan LSRW. 

More importantly, the decisions regarding LSRW — or the lack thereof — have been made without the knowledge or inclusion of Latine students within and outside of Mi Gente, despite the long-standing contributions and collaboration that have been made in the past and are still ongoing. This lack of transparency is disrespectful and does a disservice to the experiences of the Latine student body.

It is important to understand that the initial proposal for LSRW was not a standalone initiative towards Latine recruitment, but one pillar in a greater effort to improve financial aid packages, offer Latine studies courses and establish Latine alumni networks. The program has allowed students like first-year Dianela Rodriguez to “meet the majority of my friends right now and make my first year at Duke the best experience ever.” It is critical, above and beyond the continual emphasis, that for some students, this experience forms the first and most impactful involvement with their community, overcoming bounds set by courses, majors and organizations. 

Although Mi Gente is proud of the progress that has been made from increased Latine students on campus to the establishment of La Casa, as a part of the CMA’s student affinity spaces, many of these other mechanisms of support have been left unfulfilled. Now, without LSRW, this year Mi Gente is pushed once again to reiterate the importance of our Latine community on campus. 

Former president Nannerl Keohane had outlined Duke’s commitment to diversity “in and out of the classroom” to “provide a greater understanding and appreciation for the complexity of the human experience and enhance our students' capabilities to become leaders in a heterogeneous democratic society.” 

Such multiplicity in identity is not solely cultural, but is still sought out through the recruitment efforts, and the ubiquitous support made available for athletes, STEM-specific programs, and scholarships solely for students living in the Carolinas. Yet initiatives such as LSRW and BSAI are facetiously categorized as ‘special treatment.’ When considering Duke’s own culture, from student demonstrations against apartheid to performing cutting-edge research to intense basketball rivalries, diversity forms the cornerstone of the Duke experience. 

Mi Gente will continue to publish demands to hold the Duke administration accountable to their promises, as we have in 1997, 2003, 2005, 2016, 2022 and now. 

These demands are meant to showcase that Duke’s support of Latine students goes beyond recruitment and truly encompasses the college experience and beyond. As iterated by several Duke alumni following Mi Gente’s 2016 statement, “We hope to welcome future Latinx students to a Duke that is concerned not only with showing their faces on brochures but with their academic success and social well-being as well — a Duke that is dedicated to creating an inclusive and equitable learning environment with Latin-x students in mind.”

For decades, Latine students at Duke have had to fight for visibility, resources, and respect. Time and time again, decisions impacting our community are made without our voices in the room. These demands are not excessive. They are the minimum required for Latine students to thrive on this campus.

Aaron Andino is a Trinity junior and the co-president of Duke Mi Gente.

Yeddailin Gonzalez is a Trinity junior and the co-president of Duke Mi Gente.

Krishna Shah is a Trinity junior and the political chair of Duke Mi Gente.

The Duke Vietnamese Student Association
