title: Is WU eating healthy?
author: Naima Sheikh-Mohamed
article_text:
Pad Thai from Ginger and Soy. Buffalo chicken wrap from Devil’s Krafthouse. Mac and cheese with salmon from Farmstead. Who wouldn’t be fond of these iconic meals?

It is not surprising that Brodhead Center, or “WU” as students call it, has food that is something to be in awe of. With diverse options and a Chef’s Kitchen on the second floor that changes regularly, what is not to love?

While I agree that these meals are very delicious, I have to wonder: are we getting every nutrient we need from them, or the right amount of specific nutrients, like sodium, sugar, etc.? 

Duke does provide NetNutrition, a service that lets you know what nutrients you are getting in your food. It is especially useful if you have to be careful about what you eat due to health conditions; but how easy is it to navigate?

NetNutrition is a website that allows you to “hover” over a food option to view its nutritional facts or assemble your meals (i.e. tacos) to see the overall nutritional value. It can be confusing, yes, but the reality is that for some students like myself, it is a resource I have to use daily.

Given my chronic condition, Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), I am a student who relies on NetNutrition heavily because I constantly need to watch what goes on my plate; and when navigating meals and their nutrient amount, I tend to see a common trend of high sodium foods and suspicious amounts of sugar. 

To show NetNutrition’s numbers, let’s take a look at some popular Wu meals.

Beginning with Ginger and Soy, let’s look at Pad Thai, a past favorite of mine. I was questioning what I saw: 31 grams of sugar, 1780 milligrams of sodium, but only 13 grams of protein? The first time I read this, I couldn't believe my eyes. I used to think it was healthy, but as it turns out, the sodium protein ratio is completely off balance. 

If you thought it couldn’t get worse, one meal from Gothic, the Teriyaki chicken sandwich, has a reported 12760 mg of sodium, which is 532% of the daily value. This is completely and utterly shocking.

The first thing someone would do when looking at these numbers is panic. I panicked. Seeing these kinds of numbers would make anyone, including myself, question everything you think you know about what you're eating — and it is a lot at first. However, what matters most is first not feel overwhelmed by these discoveries. 

With my specific diet, for example, it is not very advisable to have tons of sodium, as well as carbohydrates. When confronted with numbers like these, I had to do a lot of research on NetNutrition to find the perfect balance with my meals. 

So, a question emerges. How would I, a student with food restrictions, navigate these meals at WU? How could I both enjoy a delicious meal while maintaining the diet I need? 

At first, I would find myself mixing and matching from sometimes two or three places. The amount of time I spent doing so speaks to a deeper problem at hand: having a dietary restriction felt like a time-consuming task in a dining hall that is known for its accessibility and convenience. Navigating dietary restrictions should not be this difficult for our dining hall, which promises to serve students efficiently. 

On the one hand, I do believe Duke does a very good job of adhering to allergies and providing food without artificial dyes. For example, It's Thyme provides a variety of options, given that its food list is free of the top nine allergies and boasts relatively low-sodium options. But beyond allergens, Duke needs to start paying more attention to the nutrients they are serving within their foods.

This matters because for many students, dining halls are the only accessible option for food. With limited food options on campus besides Wu, it becomes the primary place to eat for many students. The challenge when trying to eat healthily becomes not choosing where to eat, but trying to navigate food restrictions that limit what you can eat. 

But beneath these difficulties, I’d like to point out some of Wu’s hidden, delicious options! Here are some of my favorites:

For those who need to maintain their sodium intake: I would recommend the Southern fried chicken sandwich from Gothic, which has only 730mg of sodium, but it has the recommended amount of protein — and it is delicious. Some other contenders are the Arugula chicken and goat cheese salad from Kraft: my personal favorite, with only 580mg of sodium, and the fresh berry grilled PB&J from Red Mango: a great source of fruit and protein.

For those who need to maintain their sugar intake: you need to avoid anything with Teriyaki, acai bowls from It's Thyme and all foods with sweet sauces (i.e. Sweet Thai Chili). A personal favorite of mine is the grilled yellow fin tuna/grilled salmon with mashed potatoes from JBs Roast & Chops. NetNutrition reports it has no sugar at all and the grilled salmon with mashed potatoes is underrated. 

Although the numbers on NetNutrition can seem alarming, the issue is not as simple as attacking the nutritional value of the food, but rather the lack of transparency behind it — students should not have to rely on a website to understand what it is they are eating. This reveals a broader systematic failure in Wu’s presentation of nutritional information. Without clearly disclosing the nutrients in its food options, it leaves students without the key information they need to make informed choices.

The dining hall needs to start displaying basic nutritional facts, such as sodium and sugar, directly in front of the student as they order, rather than putting it on an external website. This issue is one that clearly needs to be addressed and fixed immediately, because although Ginger and Soy is delicious, I think all students would think twice when being confronted with what their favorite bowls contain. 

Naima Sheikh-Mohamed is a Trinity sophomore.

title: There can be no liberal arts at Duke, without the arts
author: Stella Kaye
article_text:
In March, one of my peers, Jasmine Fan, published an article titled "At Duke, we are not getting a liberal arts education". She argued that Duke’s claim of delivering a well-rounded liberal arts curriculum falls short in comparison to other top universities. The consequence of such an unstable system? One that allows students to fill burdensome distributional requirements with “easy A” classes. Fan claims that each student who walks across the stage at graduation does so having received a different education.

I largely agree with Fan’s points, particularly those noting that the liberal arts curriculum has allowed students to take the “easy way out” in subjects they aren’t particularly interested in, leaving a select few departments with empty seats in every class. But something clearly remains missing from the conversation.

What I am here to add is the much needed perspective regarding the arts here at Duke. When I refer to arts, I mean both visual and performing arts, of course; but since I spend most of my time involved in the performing arts at Duke, I will focus mainly on that here.

So, let’s circle back to the empty chairs at empty tables scenario (Ha! See what I did there?). Take, for example, a comparison between enrollment in my music theory and psychology classes. 40 spots opened for MUSIC 261, Theory and Practice of Tonal Music, in the fall, and a total of three seats were filled. Meanwhile, PSY 101, Introductory Psychology, filled up 200 seats within the first few hours of course registration. I don’t highlight this to discount the merits of psychology, nor to criticize those interested in it. Instead, I mean to demonstrate that this disparity reflects the lack of encouragement Duke students feel to take part in the vibrant arts scene, even as Duke has space for the arts to flourish. 

What’s especially telling in cases like this one is that this enrollment gap doesn’t seem to stem from students’ lack of curiosity about the arts, but from the signals students receive about what is “worth” their time. At a school where pre-professional paths dominate day-to-day conversations among students and staff, advisors and peers seem to be steering students (sometimes implicitly) toward classes that feel practical, high-impact or legible to future employers. Large lecture courses like PSY101 appear to be foundational and broadly useful, while arts classes like MUS261 can come across as specialized or even risky in an already tight schedule. Without intentional administrative encouragement, then, the arts become something students feel they have to justify, rather than something they feel invited to explore.

At an institutional level, Duke also does not make a prominent effort to give students sufficient access to arts spaces. Anyone who has tried to reserve a dance studio on campus knows it’s almost as hard to secure as a ticket to a men’s basketball game. Four studios sit in the Rubenstein Arts Center, and more often than not, dance classes, teams or restricted access blocks general student use. I can recall at least ten times this semester alone when I tried to get into a dance studio and the auto-locking doors stopped me.

Duke students clearly carry a myriad of artistic passions. Weekly performances from student groups on BC Plaza alone make that evident. So, why do we lack access to the proper resources to practice and hone these passions? Dance studios and practice rooms serve as so much more than places to perfect one’s craft; they also serve as spaces to decompress and reflect amid the hectic pace of daily life here.

At a school that boasts about prioritizing mental health services, Duke should make a grander effort to grant students the proper spaces to devote time to their artistic hobbies — activities that often serve as de-stressers in simple daily practice. While CAPS and other psychological services may help students keep their cool during stressful weeks on campus, I know many others who would prefer to dance it out, play the piano or rock out with their band to ease the stress of school. With a campus of over 17,000 total students, do 25 practice rooms in Biddle suffice? I don’t think so.

So, while it’s true that Duke’s liberal arts education may be stunted in a broad sense, what stands out even more clearly is how that failure takes shape in students’ everyday experiences. When access to creative spaces is limited, when studios are locked and practice rooms are scarce, Duke is sending the powerful message that these forms of expression are not a priority. Over time, that message begins to shape not just how students spend their free time, but how they build their academic paths. The arts become something to work around, rather than something to pursue. Duke administrators may not say, “don’t take arts classes,” but they certainly don’t tell us to take arts classes — and that silence carries just as much power.

If Duke wants to uphold the values of a true liberal arts education, it has to do more than simply offer the arts — it has to actively invite students into them. That could look like prioritizing access to creative spaces, encouraging exploration through advising or marketing (and believing in) arts courses as essential rather than expendable. When students feel that invitation clearly, those empty seats in Biddle might finally start to fill.

Stella is a Trinity first-year.

title: AI for medical diagnosis: Where does Duke stand?
author: Anagha Gowda
article_text:
“Tomorrow’s doctors are going to be using ChatGPT.”

A joke often made by boomers and millennials as we make our way to the workforce.

A joke that is now getting pretty real.

On Jan. 31, researchers backed by the Swedish Cancer Society found new means to incorporate artificial intelligence into mammograms for breast cancer, improving the rate of diagnosis by a whopping 12%. In addition, on Feb. 12, scientists found that artificial intelligence machine learning models showed a 40% improvement in accurately diagnosing food allergies. 

Artificial intelligence is becoming progressively more prevalent in medical practice, celebrated for increasing accuracy and accelerating improvements in everything from diagnosis to research. For example, this research could change and save the lives of many breast cancer patients whose diagnosis may not have been originally possible under standard double readings.

However, the ethical implications of AI utilization in the medical field should be questioned, and as a school with an exceptionally strong medical reputation, Duke plays an integral role in asking these questions. Pre-med and current medical students at Duke must consider the place of AI in their careers and how their role in the medical community changes as a result.

So how do we at Duke, as a medical community, maintain that understanding of our place?

Despite the obvious success of AI in diagnosing patients, perhaps even better than human doctors can, it is still imperative to maintain regulations on the extent to which AI can be utilized in medical diagnosis. While AI can be dependable for analytical tasks (such as analyzing imaging), it should be avoided in deciding final diagnosis itself because it lacks the human and perception elements of diagnosis. Public regulation limiting AI use in medicine beyond quantitative measures could help with this drastically. 

First and foremost, medicine is a face-to-face field — one that relies heavily on perception and human interaction. While AI can be a helpful tool in diagnosing patients through imaging and testing (more quantitative measures), using AI to diagnose ubiquitously could be disastrous because of its inability to pick up on abnormalities. 

Studies have proven that doctor-patient conversations can have an especially significant impact on patients and their well-being as a whole. When a doctor is face-to-face with a patient, it is their connection and interactions that shape how a treatment or health outcome is viewed. A lack of regulation on AI in diagnosis could strip the process of its emphasis on holistic health in an effort to obtain efficiency. 

Secondly, the use of AI would overemphasize patterns in the medical industry, oversimplifying the individual experiences and needs of each patient in the field, which is critical to diagnosis. Even aspects of AI that “personalize” the approaches rely on patterns of how doctors have personalized similar patient treatments in the past; therefore, nothing in their technique of diagnosis will be new or novel. It is important to remember that each patient is different, and only humans can pick up on body language subtleties, tones, cultural nuances, and individual tendencies. The way each patient must be approached, the way they describe their symptoms, and the way they view healthcare are all intensely unique. 

Conceptually, AI and machine learning processes are based on pattern recognition and predictable paradigms, especially in medicine, where large language models (LLMs) are used to compile large amounts of data to provide the best outcome. In other words, AI learns from given examples to fine-tune its way of approaching a given problem.

Specific to medicine, this could mean that, should AI’s use extend beyond analyzing images and move towards in-person diagnosis, the LLMs predominantly used would examine data from the diagnoses of previous patients to determine the condition of any given person.

However, this would be fundamentally flawed because of differences in how patients describe their conditions and their own perception of what they think they need. The generalizations made within AI, while useful in the regard of analytics, would fail to adequately serve the medical community and capture the nuances between individual patients.

In the end, these nuances qualify AI to take part in the quantitative aspects of diagnosis: reading medical examinations, screenings, imaging, and quantifying what is shown or indicated. AI, specifically in medical settings, is not qualified to draw conclusions and final diagnoses — that should always be left to the doctor, who can perceive abnormalities and the overall demeanor of the patient, nuances that cannot be tracked through physical or medical examinations. 

To put this into perspective, it would mean, eventually, if the Duke Health Center and Duke Hospital take on the use of AI, they could use it to read tuberculosis tests, look for patient vaccinations, and compile the patient’s symptoms. However, during the final diagnosis, a Duke-employed doctor or medical professional should make the final call — AI would not be the one compiling the data and putting forth the medical opinion.

AI certainly has a growing role in both the medical community and in diagnosis efforts — the research from above proves that much. However, to allow AI to spread throughout the field could be a huge mistake. By increasing AI regulation in medicine, this novel technology could supplement our medical industry without taking away from what has always made medicine what it is: human-focused. People-oriented.

By keeping what is working and improving what is not, the medical industry could grow to do even more good than it already does — with the help of AI. 

Anagha Gowda is a Trinity first-year.

title: Adventures in chaos
author: Robert Wallace
article_text:
In a wood, along a path, a dump of trash. 

A lone chimney stands not at attention but like the leaning Tower of Pisa, a forest of twigs sticking out of its crumbling mortar. Among the debris: ceramics and glass, some of it ornate and fine, even the handles still intact. Magazines and books, rubber balls, eating utensils, children’s dolls with clumps of bright orange hair rooted out of the skulls, the finely dotted holes filled with red earth. Boards of fine-grained oak attached to long, tapered legs, rotted on the ends. A desk? A cabinet? A cluster of cold, half-burned nuggets which, once stepped upon, disintegrates under a well-placed boot.

I search among the remnants of this destroyed house in rural North Durham County and wonder about who used to live there. The foundation remains in places, a severed square wall of blackened rock. In the southern corner, a narrow hole leads not to a buried basement, but more likely a rabbit’s den. I peer inside, imagine where it leads, and jokingly holler for Alice.

Alice might have jumped down the hole, but I do not. 

160 years ago, as the American Civil War was coming to a brutal end, Lewis Carroll’s Alice jumped down a rabbit hole, sending her on an adventure that can only be explained as nonsense, primarily, if for no other reason, because of its lack of logic. 

Carroll, like many writers, was an inveterate letter-writer. He had this to say of one of his stories when asked about its meaning: "I'm very much afraid I didn't mean anything but nonsense. Still, you know, words mean more than we mean to express when we use them; so a whole book ought to mean a great deal more than the writer means. So, whatever good meanings are in the book, I'm glad to accept as the meaning of the book."

Alice’s adventures can certainly be seen as chaotic. But is there more to them than a wild, hypnotic experience than they appear to be? It would be easy, in today’s world, just as in mid-Century England, to say “Yes.” Just as Alice’s adventures appear to be without rules, or the rules appear to be twisted and misshaped, — and Alice herself physically changed in accordance with no known valid reasoning — events over the last few years all across the globe point to a world that seems lawless and without order. Individuals, countries and groups kill for reasons that justify their own theories of survival, however wrongly mistaken. The Queen, for example, in “Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland”, decries, without the slightest provocation, “Off with their heads!” She repeats the phrase often, and it is her answer for resolving all differences. 

Everywhere violence appears to be the answer to disputes and contrived threats. When I was a boy, not more than eight years old, I listened to my parents talk once about a man who had killed his wife, leaving the young daughter without a mother. I was listening in on the secret world of adults, and their banter that can be so mystifying to a child. I stood behind the door to my parents’ bedroom, secretly listening. My mother was crying softly.

“He just shot her,” I heard my father say.

“How awful,” my mother said.

 I didn’t know who they were talking about. I assumed it was someone they knew, but it could have been a story they read in the newspaper. 

I have often turned to literature to help make sense of the world. The world can be a very frightening place, but literature, according to Mia Cuota, “is not only a way to affirm our existence. It is a permission to disappear and to allow the presence of those who seem to be absent.” Reading the stories of other cultures helps us to bridge the gap between the self and others. It humanizes us all. Even Raskolnikov, in “Crime and Punishment”, is made more human, despite Dostoevsky’s portrayal of his murderous deed, by the psychological depiction of his actions and the slow, irrevocable understanding of his guilty conscience. 

Still, when I go back in my mind to the rubbish that was left by the people that once inhabited the burned-down house I observed in the woods so many years ago now, I’m reminded that the names of things have meaning, and that the names of people have meaning. That behind every child is a toy; behind every home is a world; behind every person is a life, behind every bomb was a mother and a father. A school. A child. 

In a way everything is a mystery. How does all of this start? Someone believes in something. Someone else doesn’t. God(s) are called upon in defense. In Albert Camus’s 1946 address to students at Columbia University, shortly after the end of WWII, he had this to say about the state of the world: “Yes. [T]here is a human crisis because in today’s world we can contemplate the death or the torture of a human being with a feeling of indifference, friendly concern, scientific interest or simple passivity.” Has anything changed in eighty years? Camus argued we cannot be silent in the face of wrongs that “we must always speak frankly.” Revolt should not be mindless.

Now these are some of the things I have learned. The brain is composed of three main parts: the cerebrum, the cerebellum and the brain stem. Tucked into each hemisphere of the cerebrum is the temporal lobe. It is here where our memories are stored. Sometimes I wonder what we will all take from here. How do balls, once flung in the air, carry with them the anticipation of sudden return? How can a mound of dirt, once fallen upon, cause an angel to appear with the simple movement of one’s limbs? How can the heavens be viewed with a simple telescope or the naked eye? The gentleness of a caring hand upon a cold stomach. The scent of citrus in warm water. The fall of a child down a rabbit hole. Other random or nonsense things. 

I must end in kindness. For without it, where are we in all this chaos? George Saunders did this when he spoke to the graduating class of Syracuse University in 2013. At 55, he told students that his primary regrets in life were moments when he failed to be kind. What was important in his speech wasn’t just the moments when he had been explicitly unkind, but the failed opportunities where he could have demonstrated kindness to someone — the implicit wrongs, the moments when he could have reached out and offered a kind word or a helping hand. 

For it isn’t the tragedies that have happened to Saunders that may keep him awake at night, but the marvelous opportunities he failed — and all of us fail — to capitalize and be kind; not turn away from life in despair, not allow it to become psychologically and emotionally abbreviated, but embraced in hope, justice and equality.

Robert Wallace is a first-year graduate student of liberal studies. His column, 'Telling Stories', typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: Don’t give me the Duke answer: Say what you really think
author: Sarah Pusser
article_text:
In English 101, professor Thomas Ferraro always says, “Don’t give me the Duke answer. Give me your answer.” 

I remember feeling so embarrassed, angry even, the first time he told me I was flat out wrong. It was probably the second day of class. We were reading Willa Cather’s “A Lost Lady,” and I voiced my thoughts on the main character. I said that I believed Mrs. Forester to be a weak female lead, doomed due to her lack of power in a patriarchal society. Professor Ferraro simply looked at me and said, “No. That’s not who she is at all.”

I was flustered when what I thought to be incredibly articulate contributions were called out as statements masked in flamboyance. He saw through the overly verbose language that I, along with my peers, have been trained to respond with — words like “juxtaposition” and “dichotomy.” While these words may sound as though they have rhetorical value, in reality, they are meaningless fluff. 

Professor Ferraro wanted a classroom that felt passionate, not practiced. As I fought my way to prove myself to him and the class, I realized he was right. I didn’t know what I really thought. I was lost in the inflections and definitions, prioritizing sounding intelligent over critical thinking, and consequently lost sight of any sound argument. 

As students, we often create cycles of mindless babble, saying cliches that almost mean something and trying our hardest to sound like we know what we’re talking about. We go to great lengths to avoid appearing ignorant, one consequence of which is the mistaking of consensus for intelligence. 

While seminars supposedly function as spaces that facilitate debate and encourage discourse (isn’t that such an empty sentence?), Duke students are often afraid to say what they truly think. Thus, the origin of the classroom confirmation bias: Students echo the beliefs of their classmates and professors out of fear of saying something incorrect or different. 

How many times have you been in a class discussion that repeats the same ideas over and over and over … and over? Maybe there's a little “twist” on one idea, but beyond that, nothing new is contributed. “Building off of what xyz said …” “Piggybacking off of this person …” This form of mind-numbing classroom discussion reinforces in students the idea that thought conformity is not only appropriate, but intellectually correct. 

Students are leaving the classroom unsure of how to form their own opinions, interact with dissent and advocate for themselves through questioning what they don’t understand. In our society, where conformity of one’s outward beliefs and politics has become more important than understanding why one stands for what they do, the students Duke produces only help reinforce these constructs.

Duke students are smart, which is why this issue is so prevalent on campus. We know what our professors want us to say. We spend our time in class dedicating our performance to getting a good grade, and boom, our semester is done. But intelligence is different from smartness. It involves critical thinking and skepticism, not just the consumption of information for later use. No good conversation can be comprised purely of the reiteration of things previously said, and if you never question anything, you’re never acknowledging your previous beliefs or biases. 

At the beginning of the semester, I was struck by our professor’s bluntness. If we are wrong in his class, he straightforwardly tells us so. But I was surprised by how quickly we would move on. We didn’t linger on the incorrectness, as it quickly became clear how essential mistakes were to learning. 

There’s a prevalent fear of being the only one in class who thinks what you do, the assumption being that thinking a thought that strays from the collective mind of the classroom means you just “don't get it.” But as my classmates got more comfortable speaking their minds, they began asking questions I, too, had, but was too scared to ask. Our professor even praised them for their innovative thinking (which is a good way to learn a lesson — to wish you had been the one to say it). 

Why did I have it fixed in my brain that a professor telling me I was wrong was so terrible? Isn’t that the definition of learning? I’ve seen it in my classmates, too. They blush at their mistakes and frantically try to explain them away, or they’d get quiet for the rest of class, afraid of erring again. 

But as time passed, we got more comfortable being wrong; we adapted to our professor's anguish at our “Duke answers.” We took risks, we were sometimes wrong, but, most importantly, we were finally having engaging conversations. I was learning again. When individual students aren’t afraid to be wrong, then, and only then, can they move past the echo-chamber of reaffirming others’ ideas. 

Even though this example was started by the actions of a professor, it doesn’t mean you can’t be the example for someone else. It’s scary, but see what happens. Speak your mind. And, please, not in a grossly flamboyant way. 

Speak it how you think it.

Sarah Pusser is a Trinity sophomore. Her column typically run on alternate Thursdays.

title: Kant wouldn’t want you to be on your phone
author: Ryan Growney
article_text:
In 1764, Immanuel Kant published an essay with the curiosity-piquing title of "Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime." It discusses what Kant deems “feeling of a finer sort,” the positive emotions that go beyond simply making us happy. It’s free of the “philosophicalese” that pervades his more academic writing, and was originally published in a newspaper in his hometown of Königsberg. The school that became Duke wouldn’t be founded for another three-quarters of a century. The first handheld telephone wouldn’t be invented for another 220 years. Yet, I think Kant’s Observations teaches us something incredibly important about the way we live our lives here.

Kant leaves it up to the reader to intuit exactly what he means by sublime or beautiful, opting for pages and pages of examples in lieu of the dense technicalities that plague many philosophical works. Mountain peaks rising above the clouds, night and the pyramids in Giza are sublime, while meadows scattered with flowers and the “brilliant day” are beautiful. Walking through the blooming Gardens is beautiful, the solemnity inside the Chapel is sublime. Succinctly, “The sublime touches, the beautiful charms.” 

Before I continue, I want to recognize that in the last part of this essay, Kant twists these ideas to espouse some reprehensible views about non-Europeans. The only reason I considered writing this piece is because I think the ideas are completely divorceable from the racism and sexism that Kant asserts using them. As a recent biography of Kant argues, what makes Kant’s work powerful is exactly that quality. While the author himself believed things we now know to be hateful and misinformed, these beliefs are forced upon his work, not endemic to it. 

Reading this on the plane on my way back from spring break, I couldn’t help but think about attention. It’s the perennial battle we face, staying attentive against the constant prodding of the unread text messages burning a hole in our pockets or the emptiness in our ear that music could be filling or of course the next Instagram reel that could be the funniest thing you’ve ever seen. I couldn’t help but think about attention because the nuances of the beautiful and the sublime are exactly the nuances I feel like I miss when I’m inattentive.

In those moments when I do look up, I notice them everywhere. The bright green of the trees outside is beautiful; the way the older ones arc and enclose the sky is sublime. The affection of a head leaned softly on a partner’s shoulder is beautiful; the way a pair of close friends chat animatedly, flashing between profundity and stupidity and back again, is sublime. 

The beautiful washes down from your head, suffusing, while the sublime wells up from deep inside your gut, overpowering. When was the last time I paused to think of the way my feelings feel?

The second part of Kant’s essay turns these ideas on the subject of human nature. According to him, the positive traits we call beautiful and sublime exist on the same continuum as vices we abhor. The beauty of cheerfulness and humor can quickly become shallowness, the sublimity of honor can curdle into grotesquerie. “[T]here are never to be found praiseworthy qualities that do not at the same time degenerate through endless gradations into the most extreme imperfection.” 

What I continue to miss through inattentiveness isn’t action or events, but rather transitions. It’s the never-long-enough 20 minutes between classes, the star-speckled nighttime walk back to my dorm from Coffeehouse, bus rides laden with the unsown seeds of conversation: all those times where I seem to fear a moment of boredom more than anything. I write and speak of a want to learn everything, to do everything. Yet I continually let my dreams degenerate. 

But, Kant offers a way forward for us. He calls it “true virtue,” the only thing incorruptibly sublime. In a glimpse of his famous categorical imperative, he defines true virtue as simply the recognition of the beauty and sublimity inherent in all others. It’s the capacity for infinitesimals of noticing, the beauty in the texture of the way someone laughs, the sublimity of staid principle in the small dignities performed. It is only through nuance can one understand, much less attain, the highest morality. 

Where is the space to define the nuances I see around me? Where is the time to appreciate the differences that define us? So much of our conversation around the dangers of inattentiveness centers on missed opportunity. But we’re not standing outside a room we can simply walk back into again by fixing our habits. We’ve sold the house. We cannot feel the loss of nuance because nuance is precisely what you would need to feel it.

That is what Kant understood way back in 1764. The danger was never distraction. It was becoming someone for whom the difference between the beautiful and the sublime has quietly ceased to matter.

But again, Kant published Observations in a newspaper. It’s an idea for everyone, because beauty and sublimity are everywhere. And I think he’d call that prevalence beautiful.

Ryan Growney is a Trinity first-year. His column typically runs on alternate Wednesdays.

title: Community members share remembrances for Abigail Yohannes
author: Remembrances
article_text:
I met Abigail during orientation. We didn’t stay in touch after that, but I always remembered her. She was always smiling, always kind, and always someone who would wave when I saw her.

I’m honestly shocked hearing this, even four years later. I think the fact that I still remember those small interactions says so much about the kind of person she was.

I’m really grateful I got to meet her.

Aryaman Dalal, Trinity '26

~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Whenever I saw Abigail, she always had a smile on her face. She was just a warm presence to be around. I remember walking into the Mary Lou Williams Center and seeing her sitting with friends, and I was always greeted with her smile there too — it is something I will truly miss. We were in a Bass Connections class together during our junior year, and she was always great to work with and shared so many amazing ideas.

One of the things I admired about her the most was how creative her look and aesthetic were. She always had the coolest eyeshadow and eyeliner colors. They were such pretty and bold makeup looks — and this was just her casual everyday look. The way her bright, beautiful makeup paired with her smile did more than light up every room she walked into; it made everyone in it feel her presence.

Hearing about this broke my heart, and I can only imagine what those closest to her are feeling. My thoughts and prayers go out to her family, and all the close friends are impacted by this loss. Rest in peace, Abigail.

Chris-Ann D. Bennett, Trinity '26

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Abigail Yohannes was a student in my “Bodies at Work: Disability and Capitalism” class. We look at the dynamic relationship between labor and disability, and how different eras of capitalism transform how disability is defined and comes to be disabling through societal constraints. But deep down, and after having taught this class four times, I have witnessed what consistently makes this class transformative to students on both personal and intellectual levels: its critical interrogation of what makes a human have worth​. We come to an understanding that it is not productivity that makes us valuable, but that we are human.

The very first day, Abigail demonstrated she came into class already thinking about these questions. After we read an essay unpacking the idea that work should define whether one is worthy of a livelihood, the first words Abigail spoke in class were, “I do not dream of labor.” That is to say, Abigail challenged the notion — so unfortunately prevalent at Duke — that having all the internships, being in all the clubs, getting a great job, and working oneself to absolute exhaustion is the only thing one should aspire to.


Her thoughtfulness in class and critical approach to systems of power was a special thing. She had a quiet, steady, consistently pleasant presence, but she especially lit up when talking about her plans for her independent research project for my class, an analysis of sleep rhythms and exhaustion, and a critique of campus grind culture. I valued her presence a lot. I will miss it a lot. And I will think of our relatively short time together for a long time to come.

Emily Lim Rogers, assistant professor of cultural anthropology

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Abigail was my cousin. She was a guiding light to our family, always wise and intelligent. She was a model student and an even better person. She had an outstanding ability to look out for others and ensure they felt seen and included, and I always admired how naturally that came to her. Her kindness and empathy are traits that I look to carry in my own life every day.

I was ecstatic when I heard she had been accepted into Duke, and I had the opportunity to show her and her parents around campus when they came for Blue Devil Days. It was dark and cloudy that day, but her wide-eyed excitement never faded. Countless moments like these are what I remember her by. Her passing was devastating to hear, and I still struggle to put into words the impact of this loss on our family. She was deeply loved, and we miss her warm presence every day.

Nathan Binyam, Trinity '23

~~~~~~~~~

I feel incredibly lucky to have had Abigail as a student of mine in Intimacies: Sexuality, Nation and the State (Fall 2025) and Race, Gender and Sexuality (Spring 2026).

Abigail was impressive in so many ways. She knew how to make her ideas radiate in writing. She also seemed to perfect that delicate balance between speaking up in class and taking a step back to let others speak. Her presence in class, always purposeful if not also profound, felt like a deliberate commitment to ensure the seminar was as equitable as possible. It did not take long for me to notice how introspective and generous she was.

A sincere, thoughtful and incisive speaker during seminar discussions, Abigail was also one of those few students who cared not solely about mastering the content of the class, but about making connections among the people she shared the classroom space with: her fellow students, her professor, and even the authors and artists we engaged in class. What I appreciated most about her, beyond her smile and warm presence, was the way she listened intently to other students. A sign of her emotional intelligence, Abigail knew how to string together the contributions made by others in a way that forged a genuine kind of connection. She particularly lit up when we discussed novels like Minor Detail and The Emperor of Gladness and the film Mississippi Masala.

There are a handful of memories of Abigail that I will long cherish. Some of them are rather ordinary, fleeting moments that stood out because they’re actually quite rare — like the way she’d always offer a caring nod of recognition or maintain eye contact with whoever was speaking. I hope I never forget how soft she spoke, and how that softness functioned like a vessel for her clear-eyed vision for a better world. Other memories are grounded in specific moments in which we shared space outdoors.

One day, an early September morning, I held class outside because the weather was perfect. Whenever I pass by Bivins, I’ll think of her and the entire class sitting on the grass, discussing the nuances between the nation and the state. I’ll remember walking around West Campus with her at the end of February. It was cold and she told me about her midterm plans and her work at the library. I learned about her lineage and her favorite Ethiopian dishes. Most of all, I’ll remember walking right behind her at a rally in February. She was one of three people holding a massive monarch butterfly, chanting and walking in solidarity alongside others.

I miss her. She left an indelible impact on me and so many. I hope she is resting easy, resting in power.

Anna Storti, assistant professor of gender, sexuality and feminist studies and Asian American and Diaspora studies

~~~~~~~~

The Rubenstein Library staff was deeply saddened to learn of Abigail’s passing. We were fortunate to have Abigail with us as a circulation assistant for nearly four years. Abigail was an absolute delight to work with. She was consistently responsive, responsible, and calm, bringing a steady and positive presence to every shift. Many of us will remember her quiet thoughtfulness, her willingness to help wherever needed, and the kindness she showed to those around her. We are deeply grateful for the time Abigail spent with us and for the contributions she made to the Rubenstein Library. She will be missed by all of us who had the privilege of working with her. Our hearts are with her family, friends, and all who knew and loved her.

Rebecca Pattillo, assistant university archivist for research services and student engagement

~~~~~~~~

I was fortunate to teach Abigail in Spanish 101 during her freshman year … what she didn’t know was that it was also my first time teaching at Duke. Throughout the semester, she was a star student whose presence helped me grow in confidence as an instructor. I was continually impressed by her work ethic, kindness and natural aptitude for the Spanish language. In the semesters that followed, it was always a joy to run into her on campus; she carried a warmth that came through in every smile and greeting.

My heart is with Abigail, her family, and her friends during this unspeakably difficult time. She will be deeply missed, both at Duke and far beyond.

Anna-Paden Carson Lagarde, fifth year graduate student in romance studies.

title: Under, but not over
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
This time of year, students — and faculty and staff, too — can feel under pressure. Maybe you feel underappreciated, underrated or under the weather. Maybe people have told you that you are an underachiever. Many of us are “under” something. But just because you are “under” doesn’t mean it’s over for you.

The poet and hymnwriter Susan Palo Cherwien gets at this in her poem “Suffering.” In the first few verses, she announces that suffering is not only about pain, misery and tragedy but instead means “to bear up under.” The poem builds on this understanding of suffering:

 There is an aspect of ascension to suffering:

it means not to be crushed.

There is an aspect of resurrection to suffering:

it means not to be defeated.

There is an aspect of eternity to suffering:

it means not to be destroyed.

But to bear up under.

“To bear up under,” Cherwien is telling us, means that things aren’t over. We are not destroyed; there is still the potential for ascension, resurrection and eternity.

You can see examples of this right now on campus. Those beautiful blossoms you have been photographing were just weeks ago hidden under bark. The flowers you see were seeds or bulbs underground. The theologian and poet Howard Thurman captures this in his poem “The Growing Edge.” He says, “The fruit ripens on the tree, the roots are silently at work in the darkness of the earth against a time when there shall be new leaves, fresh blossoms, green fruit.”

Growth is happening underground. There is life underground. I think of Harriet Tubman’s Underground Railroad to set the enslaved free. Just because you can’t see it doesn’t mean there’s not freedom underground, hope underground.

Buried hope is at the heart of the Easter message that Christians have just begun celebrating at this time of year. “[Jesus] was crucified under Pontius Pilate; he suffered death and was buried,” the ancient Nicene Creed declares about Jesus’s execution presided over by the Roman governor of Judaea at the time. Jesus was under, but his mission was not over. The creed tells us:

 [He] rose again on the third day
in accordance with the Scriptures.
He ascended into heaven
and is seated at the right hand of the Father.

The Jewish community is observing Passover this week. It’s a holiday that celebrates the liberation of the Israelite people from slavery under the tyranny of Egypt’s Pharaoh. The traditional foods for Passover, including unleavened bread (matzah) and bitter herbs (maror), are symbolic of how the Hebrew people bore up under the trial of fleeing Egypt and journeying through the wilderness to come to the Promised Land.

So, during this final sprint at the end of the semester, you may be “under” — under the gun, underperforming, under duress. The fruit of your labors may be hidden from others. If so, look to the poets, look to the scriptures, look to the natural world, and be reminded that, just because things are “under,” doesn’t mean they’re over. You can still bear up under.

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: Freedom of the press includes the right to offend
author: Leo Goldberg
article_text:
It physically pains me to write this, but I feel I have no other choice: I’ve come to defend the Daily Tar Heel (DTH). 

On April 1, our peer newspaper at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill became battered by controversy after publishing a series of satirical pieces in the spirit of April Fools' Day. One of the satire pieces, titled “Trump orders ALE in Chapel Hill to be replaced with ICE agents,” was met with outrage by the student body, and, alongside two others, titled “UNC brings back DEI - for whites” and “Hubert Davis rushes to find summer internship,” has ignited UNC into a conflagration of controversy. 

Several student groups at UNC posted joint statements on Instagram calling for the satire pieces’ immediate removal from both the DTH website and social media pages. Local outlets like CBS17 and Raleigh News & Observer also disgracefully used their decades of professional reporting experience not to help the DTH navigate a complex situation and stand up for themselves, but to attack a student newspaper by running unhelpful articles further stirring up tensions, replete with perspectives of students outraged by the articles and featuring not a single one in defense of press freedom.

So great was the resulting backlash that the DTH was forced to take down the ICE piece and publish a hasty, self-pitying public apology statement. The statement reads, “Our intention with an April Fools’ edition was to highlight the medium of satire, one that is grounded in centuries of journalistic tradition of holding structures of power accountable. But we have instead hurt the very communities that we intended to uplift and platform.” 

As a columnist at a student paper, I feel an obligation to stand in solidarity with the DTH in what I consider to be a clear-cut case of press freedom intimidation. Regardless of whether you thought the satire was unfunny or distasteful, the fact that an outlet of the free press, let alone a student newspaper, was bullied into self-censoring should concern us all. 

The right to publish material which some people may find offensive is one of the most basic and fundamental principles of freedom of the press, and, while the public has the right to be offended by such material and to criticize it, they do not have the right to demand it be taken down. 

The First Amendment crucially includes the right of the press to publish controversial material even and especially against an unfavorable public reaction. Real, hard conversations about important social issues are only possible when they are presented in ways which may on occasion make people uncomfortable. That is uncompromisable. How can we ever debate the rightness or wrongness of any idea if it is automatically precensored for the offensiveness it may cause?

This principle applies unconditionally to all published material, not just satire, but I want to give a brief word on satire specifically. The purpose of satire, in my submission, is to portray prominent social problems in so absurd a way as to cause people to reimagine the damaging and insidious effects of such problems which they may be currently overlooking. It is true that, on occasion, this is used to mask hatred and cruelty. The DTH pieces, however, did no such thing.

The ICE article, for example, was obviously not denigrating immigrants or supporting arbitrary and cruel immigration enforcement. In fact, it did the exact opposite by pointing out the mania of the Trump administration’s abuse of authority by using ICE to secrete fear across the country. If one were to actually read the article, they would know that it mocked ICE agents as oafs “lost as to what they should actually be doing” and taking orders from a mentally deranged tyrant.

It is important to remember that the capacity of people to be offended by ideas is inexhaustible. There is always someone who will find something to take issue with when anything is published in print. If the press were to censor itself in order to preemptively spare the potential hurt feelings of every individual, it would never be able to publish anything. The claims of people to be offended must never supersede the right of the public to have access to a free press.

It’s a shame that the DTH retracted a published article and released an apology letter asking forgiveness for things it shouldn’t have to apologize for. But they are not really to blame. They are, after all, a student paper that does not have the resources or bandwidth to engage in lengthy public opinion battles. That is why it is incumbent upon us to honor the unfettered right of the press to publish satire or any other content, short of hate speech or calls to violence, without worrying about being bullied into self-censorship. 

Bad satire, it is true, has the right to be criticized as distasteful (though, as far as bad satire goes, the DTH’s was really quite tame, I must say). But the solution to bad speech is not no speech; it is better speech. 

The proper point of action for students who may be upset by these articles would be to engage with them directly, through letters to the editor or other forms of written response, not indignant demands that the press retract what it publishes. It is precisely this concept, that certain ideas can be proven as better or more correct than others through vigorous debate and discourse, that progress in society has always been made. And it is the freedom of speech and expression that we have to thank for it.

Leo Goldberg is a Trinity sophomore. His pieces typically run on alternate Mondays.

title: The West House Barber: Why big impact starts with small cuts
author: Jacob Kim
article_text:
Chances are, you’ve seen a guy cutting hair by West House after stepping off the C1 on East Campus. That would be me. If you were to walk into West House, this is what you’d see: the West House lobby, whose furniture serves as a waiting room. A wooden chair beside trash cans. A wide open door. And me, the West House Barber. This is my story.

Hair is a powerful status symbol, so trusting your barber means trusting them to tell your story through your appearance. However, for as long as I can remember, my hair was a source of quiet dissatisfaction. Most East Asian men share a similar problem: our stubbornly straight hair practically grows perpendicular to our scalps. I spent years fighting my hair with every product imaginable, but nothing could make it cooperate. By my junior year of high school, I realized that crunchy gels and shiny pomades were like band-aids for a problem that needed a better solution. So, I did what others wouldn’t dare to try: I cut my own hair.

At Duke, my clients ask me how I learned how to cut hair, expecting me to say something along the lines of, “Much trial and a lot of error.” Instead, I taught myself by practically cutting it one strand at a time with my eyes glued to my bathroom mirror, making an effort to do better than the barbers I’d never go back to. Over time, I’ve shaved down my cutting time from two hours to twenty minutes, and my own haircut became a walking advertisement. My high school classmates would often ask me where I went to cut my hair, to which I’d often reply with a chuckle. By senior year, my friends figured that if I trusted myself enough to run shears through my hair, they could trust me with cutting their hair too.

When I packed my bags for Duke, I tucked my haircutting kit between my clothes, planning on only cutting my own hair. It was never my intention to bring the Barber to Duke; I didn’t think it would be possible for me to convince Duke students to receive a haircut from a peer. After O-week, however, there were more than a few shaggy heads of hair on East Campus. So, I didn’t wait for a permit or a professional studio. I set up behind the West House bench, blared house music, and turned the front yard of my dorm building into a barbershop. Students heading to class would stop and stare, and posts would pop up on Fizz, but the novelty soon turned into a thriving community. The West House Barber was born.

Jacob the Barber, the name my RA calls me, is more than a new alias. It serves as a creative outlet, a social incubator, and a job all wrapped together. People often ask me how much money I’ve made, but that’s not what pushes me to cut hair for four straight hours after a full day of classes. 

Haircuts are more than a transaction to me because a good haircut is the equivalent of a makeover. More important than the physical transformation, however, is the renewed sense of confidence that a haircut can give. I want to give my clients a reason to smile, whether it be when they run their fingers through their hair after they shower or when they receive compliments when simply walking through Perkins. I want to give my peers the confidence in their appearance that I once lacked in myself.

This year thus far, I’ve given haircuts to close to a third of the male first-year population at Duke. If I’ve learned anything from becoming the West House Barber, it's this: start small but think big. For me, cutting hair started not just small, but microscopic. I literally taught myself hair by hair how to reshape someone’s confidence, starting with my own. Now I do it for a living. If you want to make a difference, own your craft by doing the things others would never dare to do, even if that means cutting your friends’ hair in front of the East Campus C1 bus stop. 

Success isn’t about having the perfect circumstances; it’s about taking a leap of faith. It’s about learning how to ignore the noise of others’ doubts, and maybe your own, and focus on the people you serve. That’s how you can make a difference — working one hair at a time and seeing how far it can take you.

Jacob Kim is a Trinity first-year.

title: Why I would rather go live on a farm
author: Ryan Growney
article_text:
I would rather go live on a farm. Wouldn’t it be simpler, instead of sitting here in WU, banging my head against a wall of math problems, stressed about a summer internship or the amount of homework I have or the news that day or maybe all of them at once? Wouldn’t I be happier?

It’s not the farm itself. I could go live in the forest, or the mountains or build myself a nice shack on the beach somewhere no other tourist ever finds. Anywhere I could have just a community of the people I care about, anywhere away from everything else.

The thought keeps coming up because of a series of conversations I’ve had with some close friends here. It’s one of those “inactionables,” a what-if that flits through your mind when your set of options you have don’t feel sufficient for the challenge of your goals. It isn’t a particularly compelling one either — aside from the lack of basic amenities, everyone I’ve talked with about this loves Duke. I love Duke. I love the way of life here, I love who I am here, I love what this place is helping me become. We are among the most privileged people in the world to be here right now, and no one I’ve talked to about this is at all ungrateful for these opportunities. So why does a rural life seem so enticingly simple?

When I think of the times I was happy, I think first of camping. There is a moment, once you’ve wormed your way out of your sleeping bag, put back on the shoes you’re definitely going to throw away after this and unzipped the tent, that you get to fully stand up for the first time that day, smelling the crisp snap of mountain air before it makes you shiver and watching everyone else do the same. You get to see the people you’re with, look back towards where you camped the previous night, and point up at where you’re going to be in a couple hours. And then you get to do it all again. 

What is it about this time in my life? Why does it stand out to me more so than any other? Maybe it’s that I was surrounded by people I cared deeply about, but I feel that here at Duke too. It can’t be the place either, because you can camp anywhere. What stands out is really the tangibility of it all — what I remember most fondly isn’t a big achievement or event, it’s the times I was able to see, hear and feel exactly what I accomplished that day.

I was most happy when I could point to the mountain pass we were climbing towards. This is what is different at Duke. Here, our thoughts and goals are constantly abstracted away from what we can see. We’re here for the future benefit a college degree supplies us, for the skills we’re going to learn and the opportunities we’re going to get. We dream of a good career or success, whatever that means. We’re bereft of tangibility, swimming through life looking only at things we can’t really see.

My last article was about all the things I haven’t been able to do here at Duke, the hobbies and interests and potential pet projects I’ve put by the wayside because there aren’t 50 hours in a day. Playing the guitar, learning to paint; looking back now, each of those things are something tangible, something I can sit down and listen to or look at after an hour's work. This is what the farm provides. It’s a mental reaction to the distance we have from our work, a way of life where actions and meaning collapse back down into the same moment. It’s an attempt to make life tangible again, to be able to see the benefits of what I’m doing on the scale of hours instead of years. 

Here at Duke, we each struggle with so many amorphous dangers, our goals some indefinable collection of achievement or skills or “happiness.” The structure of this place, the very idea of preparing yourself for a career and a good life beyond school, is divorced from what we see day to day. This is the way it should be: we can’t only live in the here and now. None of us came here to live a small, simple life. But it feels really tempting to do so. It feels really tempting to be able to restrict your world to what you can see and touch and hear, to trade what we should do for control over what we can do, to forget about finding an internship or who’s in the White House or what job you want or if that job will even be around in three years when you graduate. As we navigate our time here at Duke, this is the balance we must strike. 

The question isn’t really if I should live on a farm, but how much of the farm I can bring back here.

Ryan Growney is a Trinity first-year. His pieces typically run on alternate Wednesdays.

title: My brain is rotting
author: Alex Berkman
article_text:
Hello, my name is Alex, and I am an addict. 

This is difficult to say out loud. My last few years have been truly terrible: compulsive behavior, deterioration of my brain and consistently choosing instant gratification over patient pondering. 

But, for the first time, I feel ready to start new. 

Standing at the edge of the shore in Somewhere, Dominican Republic, I stare into the horizon. I have nothing but the moonlight, and, with no sense of time or place, I reach slowly into my pocket. 

My hand wraps around a smooth, familiar object. A six-by-three-inch box that fits perfectly into my hand. We share a spiritual connection, he and I. Though this connection is not symbiotic. 

It is parasitic. 

And it must be severed. 

So I lift the object, draw my arm back and launch that brain-eating box as far as I can. 

Splash.

I feel liberated. Empowered. Alive. 

And completely stranded in the Dominican Republic without a phone, or any way to get home.

In fairness, before I decided to gift my phone to the fishes, I did lend the more conservative alternatives a chance. 

Time limits on phone usage — I bypassed them every time. 

Deleting Instagram and TikTok — I found myself scrolling X, YouTube Shorts and, most disturbingly, Gmail. 

I even considered switching to the "The Light Phone", which was designed to be used as little as possible. Of course, they’ve already begun adding music, podcasts and voice memos, and, in a year, a button that injects dopamine directly into your blood. 

Wonderful.

But, if there is one thing that gives me solace in my addiction, it is that you likely share it too: 

The real addiction, though, isn’t our phone; it’s our appetite for trivial, unchallenging content. Some call it mindless slop. Others call it:

Brain Rot.

An endless scroll of content designed to be consumed, not remembered. 

Brain rot can take many forms: edits of your favorite couple from Love Island, clips about looksmaxxing, even political commentary.

In my case, it means refreshing X to see what college basketball “experts” are saying about March Madness.

Ya … 

I wrote that two weeks ago.

The appeal of brain rot is quite simple. It is soft, frictionless and perfectly tailored to our tastes. It tells us what we already believe and gives us exactly what we want, exactly when we want it. 

Walking across campus, sitting in class, eating a meal, we do everything we can to fill the quiet with noise. 

But there is a problem. 

That space was never empty at all. It was where ideas used to be formed, where connections were made, where something original had a chance to emerge.

Albert Einstein once said that he would think for years on end, coming up empty 99 times, only to discover the truth on the 100th.

Darwin, Rousseau and Tesla all set aside time each day to do nothing but let their own thoughts occupy their boredom.

But, had Albert spent six hours a day on TikTok, would he have still developed the theory of relativity?

Doubt it. 

As a fellow addict, I understand that putting the phone down can feel unnatural. Our world is constantly innovating towards convenience. If Apple had it their way, we would all end up like the people in WALL-E: passive, distracted and permanently entertained.

And yet, thinking is not effortless. It is slow. It is uncomfortable. It requires sitting with questions that do not have immediate answers.

But that discomfort is exactly where something meaningful begins.

So here is a simple challenge: the next time you are standing in line, walking to class or sitting alone, do nothing. Do not reach for your phone. Do not fill the silence with scrolling. 

Just let the moment exist.

You don’t have to be a fool and toss your phone into the ocean. But, every once in a while, leave it in your room and see where your mind goes instead.

Alex Berkman is a Trinity senior. His pieces typically run on alternate Wednesdays.

title: The April myth
author: Anna Garziera
article_text:
Aaah, April. My favorite month. Why, you ask? Why, the flowers, of course. And the sun, and the breeze, and the scents the breeze carries. What else? Oh, the moon. It’s so round and creamy. The young grass, the stars.

Each year, I hope for an earlier spring. As I’m writing this, it’s been pleasant outside for about four days, though I’ve been wearing shorts since February to manifest the warmer weather. Look at me, spring, I am ready.

I read a lot, but my proudest read is “The Unabridged Journals of Sylvia Plath.” Exactly how it sounds, it’s a tome, containing all her diaries from when she started at Smith College in 1950 to May 1962, just before she took her own life in February 1963 at age 30. It took me all of freshman year to finish reading it. (Ironically, I have never read her only novel, “The Bell Jar,” but I heard it’s very good. Looking forward.)

On page 96, I discovered a gem — Sylvia Plath’s first sonnet. It starts like this: “you deceive us with the crinkled green / of juvenile stars, and you beguile us with / a bland vanilla moon of maple cream: / again you tame us with your april myth.”

As you probably know, Plath is best known for her poetry. Her magnum opus is “Ariel,” her final collection. Many of her poems are good, but my favorite, “Sonnet: To Spring,” was never officially published, never made it out of her journal. 

I don’t know about you, but I love a good sonnet. I’m childishly captivated by rhymed poems in the first place, and there’s something about the compact, intense language of a sonnet that feels like wrapping your hands around a hot pocket during a late-season game at Wallace Wade. Not all sonnets are good, of course. Most of them aren’t (including all of mine). But the good ones? They’re really good.

You can tell “Sonnet: To Spring” is a young poet’s attempt. Plath used big words like “beguile” and “juvenile” as a little show-off, and she probably thought the all-lower-case was cool. As green as this poem is, it’s at the same time very clever. It talks about the way spring enchants us and makes us forget another year has passed. Each spring, a clean slate, and we feel everything is “reset.” 

I love to talk about this feeling. As Duke students, we feel it every time a new semester rolls around. Shopping Carts Open day is like a national holiday. One friend recently admitted he was looking forward to it more than his birthday. The same feeling shadows starting a new notebook, or cracking open a packet of Duke Store gum. So satisfying.

In a way, spring gives us this feeling even more effectively than New Years. It’s hard to feel rebirthed when everything is dead outside. But in spring, you can see, literally see, each bud and leaf unfolding. The tree-you-thought-was-dead’s skinny branches are dotted in pale green and baby pink. Go to the Duke Gardens. You can feel (really feel!) life fighting and presenting you with its fragile young. There’s nothing like it. 

Plath is not the first poet to write about this. Another, similarly themed poem that comes to mind is Robert Frost’s “Nothing Gold Can Stay,” which tries to capture the precious and volatile essence of a new leaf. 

Like most sonnets, Plath’s has a volta, a punch line, that leaves you more aware of your gut than you’d like to be: “Again we are deluded and infer / That somehow we are younger than we were.” 

I’ve been repeating this couplet to myself for years, though it makes me sad and partly angry. It reminds me of everything I don’t want to but can’t help think about. The passage of time, aging, not being able to ever get back the years I’ve already spent. Spent! What an accurate word for what one does with time. Except, unlike money, you start off with a finite amount and your stash of minutes only decreases. 

But spring, as Plath points out, manages to trick me every year. Knowing it’s a trick doesn’t help. I see the flowerbuds and the young leaves, and I feel younger myself. I am 21, almost 22, supposedly at the prime of life, whatever that means. I might be “too young” to already feel the passing of years. But I do, I really do, and it really scares me.

But spring. Sweet spring. Thank God for you. Thank God, you are here. Thank God, I can take my shoes and socks off in the grass, and pretend I am a child again.

Anna Garziera is a Trinity senior. Her pieces typically run on alternate Sundays.
