title: Faculty oversight is a necessity for AI at Duke
author: Robin Kirk
article_text:
This academic year, Duke did not just experiment with artificial intelligence in the classroom. The University institutionalized OpenAI’s ChatGPT without consulting faculty. In June 2025, Duke signed a contract providing ChatGPT free to all students, staff, and faculty. This went beyond prior partnerships with Microsoft’s Copilot and Azure. After all, for tech companies, universities like Duke are a coveted revenue stream.

The University described the decision as a matter of equity, to make AI available to all. At the bottom of every ChatGPT session, a line of text reads that OpenAI does not use information provided by Duke users to train the model. In addition, Duke sponsors AI training and events, including debates on risks.

That’s laudable. But it does not change the fact that the fundamental first step is missing. Duke administrators did not involve faculty in the decision to contract with OpenAI (and not, for instance, Anthropic’s Claude or Google’s Gemini). According to the Duke University Office of Information Technology, Duke's AI Special Advisory Committee and Information Technology Advisory Council were involved in the process. However, Procurement and Counsel conducted the negotiation without much faculty participation or discussion in the Academic Council.

This is striking given AI’s enormous impact on Duke’s core purpose: education.

That needs to change.

Duke administrators often highlight that the faculty handbook enshrines faculty control of their classroom, yet fail to extend this principle to decisions that radically reshape teaching, including this one. Before the OpenAI license comes up for renewal, faculty must be at the table — and empowered to say no if a company’s record conflicts with Duke’s commitment to knowledge in the service of society.

We owe students the right to education — not just AI-generated slop. As Ronald Purser wrote in Current Affairs, the California State University (CSU) system’s announcement of a $17 million OpenAI partnership came at a “surreal” timing, just after the university announced $375 million in budget cuts. “While administrators cut ribbons on their AI initiative,” Purser noted, “they were also cutting faculty positions, entire academic programs and student services.”

Fortunately, Duke has a model for ensuring that its values are reflected in contracts. In 1998, students successfully lobbied the University to adopt a comprehensive Code of Conduct for university apparel to keep Duke from enriching sweatshops that abused workers.

Almost two decades later, the pressure continues to work. In one case, a company reopened a Honduran factory, rehired workers, and committed to respect worker rights. Today, we stand at similar crossroads. Duke should not partner with AI companies that decimate democracy and human rights, following our own precedent of refusing to do business with apparel sweatshops.

Some recent history underscores the urgency. Currently, the US government does not regulate AI companies. The companies’ own records on upholding rights is abysmal: OpenAI itself emerged from a fear that AI in the wrong hands could cause epic harm. But as a former OpenAI researcher wrote recently in the New York Times, the company is now “building an economic engine that creates strong incentives to override its own rules.”

On human rights, some tech companies already have a shocking legacy. According to a 2022 Amnesty International report, Facebook’s algorithms “proactively amplified and promoted content” that incited genocide against Myanmar’s Rohingya people as early as 2012. The company never apologized or paid reparations. When Anthropic made headlines for refusing to accede to Pentagon demands that the company lift restrictions on using the tech to surveil Americans and autonomously deploy weapons; OpenAI immediately stepped in and signed a deal whose terms remain secret.

Anthropic isn’t necessarily better. I’m an author currently awaiting a settlement payment from the company for pirating my books.

AI models depend on workers who receive low wages and face traumatic working conditions. According to Equidem, a human rights and labor watchdog, moderating violent content and training AI models for platforms like Meta, TikTok and ChatGPT exposes workers in Colombia, Ghana, Kenya and the Philippines to extreme occupational, psychological, sexual and economic harms. Locals and rights advocates are investigating huge data centers for polluting poor neighborhoods around the world.

Other universities see AI use as a decision requiring robust institutional oversight, not just a cool new tool. The University of California system implemented responsible AI principles that require transparency, equity impact assessment and clear data governance before the technology is deployed. MIT requires consultation with central IT and legal counsel before purchasing AI tools. Duke could also implement the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) principles to hold AI companies accountable for their respect for the rule of law, human rights, and democratic values.

To sum up, if Duke intends to lead in AI innovation, it must also lead in AI governance. This is not an outlier idea but a core principle of American higher education articulated by organizations like the American Association of University Professors, which has its own AI policy recommendations.

The University should empower faculty to review and revise or reject AI contracts that impact the classroom. Oversight should include educational and human rights impact assessments in regular reports. All partnerships should include sunset clauses requiring periodic review rather than automatic renewal.

This is not about being pro or anti-AI. This is about ensuring that teaching values are reflected in our relationship with a technology that has great potential benefit — and great potential harm. A recent report to the Provost from the AI at Duke Steering Committee lays out ambitious changes to better manage AI. Robust faculty governance — and the power to say no — must be a central pillar.

A university that teaches accountability needs to practice it.

Robin Kirk is a professor of the practice in cultural anthropology and directs the human rights certificate of the Duke Human Rights Center at the Franklin Humanities Institute.

title: Dear professors, stop force feeding us AI
author: Wendy House
article_text:
On March 15, an article came out detailing the AI policies practiced by one professor at Fuqua, Dr. Scott Dyreng. This news coverage had already been preceded by a letter to the editor from a concerned master’s student, whose comments I heartily agreed with. To make a long story short, Dyreng has begun using an outsourced AI model to analyze recordings of student speech in class and team meetings and give feedback. He pointed to the impracticality of giving personalized participation assessments in a class of 70, and claimed to have seen “significant benefits” in the spring.

Because I can’t resist it, I’ll go ahead and say the obvious: I don’t believe him. While I’m sure Dyreng believes sincerely that he has seen improvements, what I think he’s observed in class is nothing more than the parroting of whatever thrice-blended “analysis” his model has fed his students, and it’s more disheartening than I can say to think that someone of such professional prestige can’t tell the difference. Even if the learning gains he speaks of aren’t fiction, the degrading of student-professor and student-student trust which occurs when every classroom interaction, no matter how casual, is subject to the scrutiny of a nonhuman, non-accountable entity, has psychological implications the likes of which cannot possibly be predicted. 

Though I wish it weren’t, this is but one case in a sea of many more. While all professors certainly aren’t making AI the Big Brother breathing down students’ necks, the Provost’s Initiative has profoundly encouraged them to bring generative AI (gen-AI) into the classroom in some capacity. Already, others like global health professor Eric Green are forcing students to have long “conversations” with AI chatbots, or offering hastily-made alternative assignments for students who don’t use gen-AI, only after forgetting such a group even exists. 

Before anyone else says it, yes, I realize I am being a troglodyte. I know it, I’m proud of it. I don’t intend to talk down to anyone, and I don’t intend to let my confirmation bias produce an unsound argument. AI is evolving quickly, and it will probably be a part of many of our jobs, as these very qualified professionals have explained. I don’t take issue with the thought that professors should consider students’ use of gen-AI in the way they design their courses. I could even find it considerate for professors to develop class-specific models in order to let students use those instead of going rogue and being misinformed by ChatGPT’s hallucinations.

What I do take issue with is the forceful and inconsiderate assimilation of AI into class in a way that fails to offer a practical, equivalent alternative to using it. It is one thing to consider, or even to encourage; it is another thing entirely to require, or expect. 

There is far too much evidence that gen-AI reduces our capacity to think critically and erodes our tolerance for confusion for professors to be clawing to be “ahead of the curve” on this. We can’t see three feet ahead of us on this curve. This curve is a foggy mountain road where we should be reducing our speed, yet the very authorities we’re meant to put our faith in to drive our educational journeys are hitting the gas like their very lives depend on it. Though I haven’t encountered such a professor myself, it deeply scares me to think that those I trust to educate me are so desperate to pawn the most special part of their job — student connections — off on an algorithm. 

Even if you’re on the fence of the issue of AI’s effect on learning, which could be a reasonable place to be, there are environmental consequences to consider. The sustainability of AI’s water use is dubious, and its unique energy needs and exponential expansion require it to cause the output of actual tons of CO2.

To tell the whole truth, though, my problem with the force-feeding of gen-AI to students isn’t either of these things. My problem has to do with something much more basic than that: the fundamental right to choose. I do care about the environment, and my ability to think critically, but more than that, I care about my ability to interact with real people. I don’t care to “talk” to an AI bot, and I find it disrespectful to my identity as a human being to call that interaction a conversation. I think we are staring down the barrel of a grim future if we decide that the value of efficiency, in academia or anywhere, is greater than the value of humanity in our learning. AI may be inevitable, but to say “everyone needs to embrace it” is frankly cruel to those of us who won’t.

To decide that anyone who won’t assimilate will be left behind, before we’ve even had the chance to be left behind, is defeatist and not an attitude befitting of a Duke professor. To pressure students to use AI before its effects have been extensively studied, and in spite of their right to decline use of the technology, is frankly intellectual molestation. We as students came to Duke to learn to think independently, to think creatively, and coercive gen-AI classroom policies are antithetical to this purpose. I hope this article will encourage professors considering AI-integrating policies, and indeed, also those who have thus far been misguided in their enactment of such policies, to do so with consideration and ethical rigor. 

Wendy House is a Trinity sophomore. Her column typically runs on alternate Wednesdays.

title: Carbon offsets or net zero? The administration’s lack of transparency makes it difficult to answer
author: Carbon Reduction Resource Allocation Ad Hoc Committee
article_text:
In 2007, former President Richard Brodhead signed the American College and University Presidents' Climate Commitment and pledged that Duke University would become carbon neutral by 2024. Nearly 400 institutions signed, yet Duke is one of only 14 to have achieved this ambitious goal — and is the only Ivy+ university to do so. 

To achieve carbon neutrality, the University invested in efficient infrastructure and on-campus reductions, while spending $4 million to purchase high-quality offsets to counteract remaining emissions, all of which were retired in 2024. Over these 17 years, Duke reduced its greenhouse gas emissions by 31%, despite a 27% increase in its physical footprint and a 24% increase in its campus population. Thus, Oct. 24, 2024 — the day carbon neutrality was celebrated — was, indeed, a moment well worth marking.

However, Duke has struggled to articulate its next climate goal clearly and transparently. Last year, the administration announced a pivot away from neutrality to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050, noting that using offsets to achieve carbon neutrality was no longer the frontier for climate leadership and that the rarity of high-quality carbon offsets made this approach challenging. 

Despite this, the administration did not explain how the resources used to purchase carbon offsets would be reallocated to support its 2050 net-zero goal. Nor did it describe the consequences of Duke stepping back from its leadership role in promoting high-quality offsets. Many students, faculty and staff felt blindsided by the sudden and unexplained pivot, leading to demand for more transparency.

To address those demands — despite the initial decision already having been announced — executive vice president Daniel Ennis and vice president Toddi Steelman convened the Carbon Reduction Resource Allocation Ad-Hoc Advisory Committee (CRRAAAC) to advise the administration concerning its pursuit of the goals of its Climate Commitment. The deans from each of the University’s ten schools nominated faculty members to the committee, with undergraduate and graduate students nominated by the Office of Climate and Sustainability (OCS). 

Ennis gave the committee a limited, oddly binary charge to recommend which of the following two options Duke University should pursue: Continue purchasing carbon offsets to maintain carbon neutrality as it was doing, or reallocate all of those resources (i.e., move all the way to no purchase of offsets) to direct net-zero and sustainability initiatives supporting Duke’s 2050 net-zero goals.

During Spring 2025, the committee met regularly to gather information and deliberate. We heard from subject-matter experts on climate science and carbon-offset markets, as well as university representatives who shared Duke’s priorities and work to date for operations. Deliberations were complicated by the administration’s lack of clarity and transparency. For example, we requested the annual budget for offsets, interim targets for emission reductions, and capital improvements that would affect emissions. None of that information was provided before we were expected to make our decision. 

While still missing such contextual information critical for recommendations, we had to “reach consensus” — that is, vote between the two options offered, without any type of middle ground option — and we gave the Administration a written report in May 2025. We chose the option in which the University reallocates resources from carbon neutrality to direct net-zero and sustainability initiatives, with redirection of all the carbon offset funds to carbon reductions on campus.

In making this recommendation, we stressed the urgency of decarbonizing operations, the relative permanence of on-campus reductions, educational opportunities for students, staff and faculty, the University’s control over the quality and accounting of carbon reductions, the need to incorporate climate change, sustainability, and emission reduction into decision-making across the University. 

We also articulated complementary recommendations intended to ensure more durable climate benefits and accelerate timelines, given the urgency of the climate crisis. These included a strong recommendation that the University use the annual budget for offsets to fund efforts “additional” to existing or planned work, emphasizing internal and community-facing carbon reduction projects. 

The committee recommended that the University establish governance and accountability structures to guide future funding decisions involving the reallocation of resources away from carbon offsets and transparently communicate project outcomes and emission reductions.

Nearly a year later, the administration has not publicly released our recommendation, nor the full report. Months after our charge had ended, we received some of the information we had requested during committee deliberations about Duke’s capital plan. Yet we still have no response from the administration on which of our recommendations it thinks are feasible, which are not, and the rationales behind those determinations. (Those of us on the Academic Council appreciated the administration’s initial step toward transparency regarding recognition of our committee’s work when faculty members asked about the status of carbon offsets and our committee’s work in response to President Price’s annual address.)

We are troubled by the administration’s continued lack of transparency around our recommendations, its plans for achieving net zero and its process for seeking input and counsel moving forward. Universities need to stand out as beacons for evidence and critical thought in pursuit of stated values. Process matters – perhaps especially in these times. Our concerns are heightened because it fits into a pattern of a lack of transparency when previous campus initiatives — solar, biogas, transportation, and more — stumbled in implementation; those experiences have eroded confidence in the University’s Climate Commitment. We are worried that this effort is following a similar path.

While the ad hoc committee’s recommendations have the potential to deliver additional, catalytic and local benefits, in the absence of interim climate targets, transparency and accountability structures, it is difficult to trust that the Duke Climate Commitment will deliver a transparent, successful carbon-reduction strategy in terms of capital renewal — reducing carbon through reinvestment in existing infrastructure — a path that the committee was not able to consider due to the lack of information shared.

We understand the financial and political context for action on climate has changed significantly since the committee convened in January 2025, even more so since the University made its initial climate commitment in 2007. We sincerely appreciate the many things the Office of Climate and Sustainability is doing to move forward and set ambitious goals during a period of tremendous regulatory and financial uncertainty: from the Sustainable Operations Roadmap to address Scope 3 emissions, to bringing the Health System into the Climate Commitment. And we laud the University for these accomplishments, especially when its peer schools seem to have stalled on their own climate commitments.

Despite these challenges, the work of Duke University should be grounded in evidence, reason and clear communication. We urge the administration to provide greater transparency about its deliberations, rationale and implementation as it shifts its overarching climate goals from carbon neutrality to net zero emissions. Our community deserves a clear picture of options and tradeoffs as the administration chooses our path. As the need for smart decarbonization gets more urgent every day, the Climate Commitment is critical for not only Duke, but also society as a whole.

Editor’s note: This piece was co-authored by the undersigned members of the Carbon Reduction Resource Allocation Ad Hoc Committee.

Michelle Nowlin is a clinical professor of law and serves as the chair of the Carbon Reduction Resource Allocation Ad Hoc Committee.

Betsy Albright is the Dan and Bunny Gabel chair and associate professor of the practice of environmental ethics and sustainable environmental management.

Coral Giovacchini is an assistant professor of medicine.

Peter Hoff is the James B. Duke distinguished professor of statistical science.

Rick Larrick is the Hanes Corporation Foundation distinguished professor of business administration.

Fisher Mallon is a Trinity junior.

Jerusha Neal is an associate professor of homiletics.

Alex Pfaff is the Bernard Rhodes distinguished professor of public policy.

Avner Vengosh is the Nicholas distinguished professor of environmental quality.

Stefan Zauscher is a professor of mechanical engineering and materials science.

title: The Sanford School’s crisis of meaning
author: Sherman Criner
article_text:
In the Christian tradition, as with many other faiths, there is a common saying: “You will know them by their fruits.” This simply means that one’s internal character, their personal moral convictions, can be known by their output, through what it is that they actually do.

As a senior in my final semester, I have begun applying this axiom to many aspects of my life: from the people and institutions surrounding me, to, as of late, my education here at Duke.

Upon reflection, I have come to the realization that one of my majors (and the fourth most popular at Duke), public policy, does not justify its own existence in any real moral terms. Students do not learn why the discipline is important. Rather, we simply learn that public policy is a thing that exists and that leaders, for some inarticulable reason, ought to pursue it as a means for solving things that, for reasons we are never told, are known as “problems.”

There is no real articulation of what the Sanford School of Public Policy stands for — apart from the woefully vague values of collaboration, diversity, equity & inclusion, excellence, integrity and honesty, respect and service — let alone which policy ends the school wants students to pursue. Ask any professor at Sanford what any of these words mean, and each will give you a different answer. These “Sanford values” are not rooted in any cognizable moral philosophy or tradition, bucking the trend of most of America’s historic universities (e.g., Harvard College, founded “for the glory of Christ”) and a few stragglers today (e.g., Hillsdale College). 

The problem is not so much that these values are objectionable, but that they are so capacious and indeterminate as to provide zero substantive guidance to students. Sanford’s values do not mislead so much as fail to lead. Hamstrung by their stated commitment to affirm every value, the school commits to nothing, leaving students in a crisis of meaning. 

Such is the burden of the post-morality moralist.

Should we be surprised, then, that such a small portion of students in the Public Policy major actually go into government service jobs upon graduation — a fact that is often lamented by Sanford professors? It would be like training sailors for a voyage without ever telling them where they are meant to go, and then faulting them for going off course! 

Who could blame a PUBPOL student, then, when they are never given a real reason why they should value public service above, say, management consulting or finance?

Public service, after all, presupposes that public action matters, that there are immaterial goods worth pursuing (the family, commune, class, nation, goodness and fairness) and injustices worth correcting (poverty, crime and war) through political institutions. If students are never taught that a policy debate can be settled meaningfully — indeed, we are actively encouraged to believe that everything ultimately reduces to competing and equally arbitrary value systems — then public service becomes meaningless. Why pursue the common good when I can have confidence in my unconfidence that there is such a thing as the common good itself? 

Sanford is, to put it mildly, in a state of epistemic rot.

Perhaps an illustration will help tease out what this problem really looks like. 

Take Public Policy 155, Introduction to Policy Analysis, the major’s introductory course. The course is designed to introduce students to the discipline of public policy and give some tips (more aptly described as “fun facts”) along the way about various analytic and descriptive tools for working within the discipline. However, after you drill beneath this fluff layer of what Sanford perhaps intends the course to be, you realize that there’s something else afoot. 

At least when a far younger and spritely version of me took it a couple of years ago, PUBPOL 155 spent about half of the course critiquing past approaches to public policy (i.e. the classical/neo-liberal frameworks and McNamara’s “Whiz Kids”). There was a great deal of emphasis on deconstructing what was, without doing the good Chestertonian thing of asking why it was there in the first place.

Just look at the course’s description in Duke’s course bulletin. There is quite a bit about the “political and social context” of public policy and the field’s various “methodologies,” and there is even an allusion to “good decision-making.” But you know what you will not find in the description or in the class itself? 

A substantive definition of what it means to do “good” policy making. 

This is not to say that PUBPOL 155 does not at least hint at answers about what a “good” public policy framework might look like. We are introduced to some “transformational approaches” such as wellbeing economics, the use of stories to spur political action and facilitative leadership. Yet even when introduced to these supposedly “new” and “pioneering” approaches to public policy, we are never told by what measure these ideas are called “transformational,” while neoliberalism and the more quantitative analytical frameworks of yesteryear are considered “limited.” It is just assumed, in a palpable spirit of what C.S. Lewis once described as “chronological snobbery,” that because these approaches are “new,” they are necessarily better, again with no explanation.

Why then, in this grand introduction to Sanford’s Public Policy curriculum, are certain approaches to public policy treated with kid gloves and others denigrated, if it is truly just giving students an “overview?”

Is Sanford making an honest mistake, undermining its commitment to diversity and inclusion by accidentally emphasizing one perspective a little too zealously? Or is it what common sense suggests: some Sanford administrators and faculty truly want students to believe that the transformational approaches are indeed “better.”

At least we can work with the latter. 

A student coming into Sanford with the understanding that wellbeing economics and these other approaches are the school’s frameworks of choice would not have to wonder what good policy looks like. They would be able to work within these frameworks to attain policy ends that cohere with the moral goals of something like a wellbeing economics approach.

In this scheme, there would be no hemming and hawing — debating not just whether we’re allowed to say that some things are right and others wrong but whether we can even know any moral truths at all. Students would actually learn what it means to put policy to good use.

And, for what it’s worth, this change would also free professors to talk about what it is that they actually believe. Hint: there aren’t a lot of “based” MAGA policy analysts walking around Rubenstein Hall, if any.

Now, the typical counter to this suggestion — “So, what are you gonna do, force your beliefs on the students?” is entirely expected and reasonable. After all, every American has been taught that freedom for its own sake is what America was founded upon.

Yet, as I and the people who founded the modern university system see it, the only workable answer to this rebuttal is, quite frankly, yes. It defies reason to imagine a university that does not, in some form, impose its morals on its students. To design a curriculum is already to have made a decision about what is worth knowing, how it ought to be taught, and to what end. 

There are many university administrators who believe that a school preaching free inquiry and pluralism is, therefore, a school free from bias — but this claim does not even pass the sniff test. It bears a striking resemblance to the popular spiritual notion that “all paths lead up the same mountain.”

By this point, anyone familiar with the Public Policy curriculum is doubtlessly screaming at their computer, “WHAT ABOUT PUBPOL 302?”

PUBPOL 302, “Policy Choice as Value Conflict,” aims — according to the syllabus at the time I took the class — to “utilize moral and ethical frameworks to investigate and address tensions between different value systems and the ways policy decision-making influences and differentially determines justice and fairness.”

Note: the syllabus simultaneously suggests that there are tensions between value systems while also implying that we possess some shared sense of justice and fairness by which those systems can be judged. As with PUBPOL 155, it seems again that we are expected to know both what justice and fairness mean and agree that they ought to be pursued. 

When describing the course’s philosophy, the syllabus goes on to state that the class will examine whether:

“conventional western philosophy, ideology and policy decision making accurately reflects perspectives of socially diverse populations. Relatedly, we will explore how these processes have often been utilized to justify exploiting minority identity groups to the social, political, and economic advantage of majority identity groups while obfuscating these injustices.”

Again, why does the Sanford School neutrally describe the course as an introduction to “theoretical and practical problems in decision making in relation to conflicts of value and interest,” when the course itself approaches these conflicts through a clearly defined interpretive lens geared towards social diversity and combatting some degree of economic and racial injustice? 

Would it not serve students far better if Sanford simply called a spade a spade? If the school has a vision for what good policy looks like and who it ought to serve, say so. Own it. Students could then engage that vision critically, accept it, or reject it — rather than absorbing it unreflectively, never having been told it was there. 

But what of the class itself? Might the format of the course do a good job of remedying the apathy for public service by instilling students with a particular ethical outlook?

Most weeks in 302, our class would debate various controversial topics in a Socratic seminar eruditely facilitated by our professor (in my humble opinion, one of Sanford’s best). Topics included the meaning of meritocracy, racial justice, affirmative action and abortion, to name a few.

Throughout the semester, the professor was entirely transparent, providing a fairly detailed exposition of their hyper-specific moral philosophy. Be that as it may, we were never given the sense that any moral conclusion, even something as basic as “murder is bad,” could ever be right. The class was meant to press our philosophical buttons, open our minds, and cultivate appreciation for others’ worldviews. But is that good?

As much as I valued the discussions, I cannot help but think it is a woeful tool for moral education. The modern Socratic method, as practiced here, is well suited to leaving public policy students with a gaping hole in their moral reasoning, a vacuum that years in Washington will almost certainly fill with rather unsavory beliefs.

As G.K. Chesterton once wrote, “An open mind is really a mark of foolishness, like an open mouth. Mouths and minds were made to shut.” It is, therefore, the duty of a public policy professor to give students something real, something moral upon which chew.

People need real, moral reasons to pursue public policy. Ask yourself: would you die for the values listed on Sanford’s values page — not what they mean to you personally, but as they are described on the page and lived out through the School’s curriculum? No solider enlists for the sake of a vague, ivory tower notion of “inclusivity.” 

Today, Sanford’s “moral education” can feel like asking your girlfriend where she wants to eat and getting the same answer every time: “You choose.” We all know what that really signals, and it’s not selflessness. If you know what you want, you say it. What happens when a Public Policy student asks their school the same question? 

More importantly, what does that signal about the school itself?

So where do we go from here?

Aristotle argued, so I am told, that the end of education is to teach people what they ought to like and dislike, to cultivate virtue by habituating the young to a moral code. C.S. Lewis, in "The Abolition of Man", warned that failing to do so does not produce open-minded citizens. It produces people who can no longer uphold duty, act bravely, or love passionately — people who wander, bored and directionless, looking for something or someone to fill the void.

So who can blame the Public Policy major when McKinsey comes calling?

Sherman Criner is a Trinity senior.

title: Poetry during pandemonium
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
We are experiencing on Earth an unheavenly pandemonium. The word “pandemonium” literally means “the place of all demons.” In John Milton’s epic poem, “Paradise Lost,” it was the name reserved for the capital of hell. With the hell of war raging in our world, we are in a time of pandemonium. Some may feel the desire to reciprocate violence for violence, blow for blow, insult for insult, drone for drone. 

But, maybe it is time to drop a line of poetry rather than dropping bombs. Sometimes, the only way to sanctify our sanity is by writing poetry or at least creating art for our heart’s sake. Pen poems to pierce the chaotic depth of pandemonium.

I witnessed the power of poetry from our recent pluralism lecturer, poet Joy Harjo, who wrote a poem called “How to Write a Poem in a Time of War” in her book “An American Sunrise.” In it, she writes in verses laid out as jagged lines on the page with interspersed italics:

You can’t begin anywhere. It’s a wreck....

Soldiers crawl the city, 

the river, the town, the village,

the bedroom, our kitchen. They eat everything.

Or burn it….

This is memory shredded because it is impossible to hold with words,

even poetry.

This is the raw description of war in the first half of the poem. And then, without leaving the lament of violence, the poem takes a resolute turn towards the end:

Someone has to make it out alive, sang a grandfather

to his grandson, his granddaughter, 

as he blew his most powerful song into the hearts of the children. 

There it would be hidden from the soldiers….

He sang us back

to our home place from which we were stolen

in these smoky green hills.

Yes, begin here. 

From this, I have three observations. First, it is striking how the poem is laid out on the page. It’s almost as if the “memory shredded” is depicted through the fragments of lines and phrases, as well as the spacing between and within the lines. The words are not printed in the same consecutive manner as a normal sentence, but are disconnected or broken. There are gaps, and this is what war does. It births chasms. 

A second observation is the deliberate nonviolent act represented by choosing to write poetry during wartime. Rather than pulling a trigger, your fingers inscribe words to bloom, to protect the world. In this way, it functions like a prayer for peace, for humanity, for home.

A final observation: as with all poems, the reader is forced to slow down in order to reflect and ponder. The images, the words lead the reader to remember the past and the future, drawing them to the conclusion that times of violence are not the only possible realities them into a different sense of time. It is a reminder that a time of violence isn’t the only time present or possible. There is a time beyond this time. With this reminder, poems can aid in the transcendence of terror.

Harjo’s poem reminds me of others who, in their own pandemonium, wrote poetry. The list includes Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Benjamin Chavis, the Apostle Paul and even the Unknown Black Bards, the creators of the spirituals from a “slave prison.” Their creativity arose on the anvil of adversity.

Poetry is a balm amid bombs exploding in our lives. The ancient Greeks and their lyric poetry reveal this. Sappho of Lesbos, writing from exile in Sicily, wrote an “Ode to Aphrodite” to express distress and to plead for deliverance from suffering. Ancient “crisis” literature, like the Book of Revelation in the Bible, also includes poems or hymns. 

All of these are expressions of poetry during pandemonium. They are linguistic reminders that wars don’t have to be won. Suffering doesn’t have to devour us. Pain doesn’t have to pin us to the ground. There is a throughline of resilience in exilic experiences. The ancient sages will tell us that no matter how difficult our situations, keep planting gardens, building homes and creating families.

Keep on living! Keep on participating in life! Sing, dance, play or write poetry. Don’t allow the terror of our time to tear your soul apart. Don’t hesitate to create. Recreate. Do that in this time of war.

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: What’s missing at Duke: A curriculum of categories, not curiosity
author: Devyn Deschamps
article_text:
On Feb. 24, Ranjana Khanna, the director of the Franklin Humanities Institute, had a conversation with Duke President Vincent Price regarding the role the humanities play at research universities. Price dispensed his own thoughts on the imminent future of the humanities and pondered reconsidering what a liberal arts education should look like. Higher education is fighting an uphill battle against financial pressures, technological advances and constant legal battles, leaving universities at odds with the current administration. 

Duke is not immune to any of these issues, and in many ways has been forced to succumb to a new reality — out of necessity, not choice. When Price remarked on reconsidering what a liberal arts education should look like, the room for interpretation was vast. Perhaps a new approach could be exactly what the school needs. 

In 2025, Duke began initiatives to cut $364 million in a preemptive response to the Trump administration's vision of higher education. Duke operates as not only a university, but a health system — both of which felt the drastic impact of these cuts. After extending 940 voluntary retirement offers to staff and faculty members, a total of 499 individuals accepted. A whopping 5% of Duke’s staff workforce separated from the Duke community. 

The cuts came at the same time that another surprising change had begun at Duke: the revamp of Trinity College of Arts & Sciences’ undergraduate curriculum. After the previous curriculum had remained unchanged for nearly 25 years, the new curriculum has faced pushback, but it focuses on encouraging students to truly take advantage of multidisciplinary studies. 

The new curriculum requires students to complete two courses in each of the following categories: Creating and Engaging with Art (CE), Humanistic Inquiry (HI), Interpreting Institutions, Justice and Power (IJ), Investigating the Natural World (NW), Quantitative and Computational Reasoning (QC), and Social and Behavioral Analysis (SB). 

Students are also required to complete a three-course language sequence, and all first-years must also complete Constellations — a program of three thematically connected courses — or a FOCUS program. 

This choice to reimagine Duke’s curriculum at first glance ensures students go in headstrong with regard to the humanities. Concerns nationwide have been that there has been a steady prioritization of STEM over the humanities, and in many ways, the new curriculum sets itself as an equalizer. The domestic push for STEM has also left many departments in more niche departments to be neglected, with the criticism being that the humanities are among the most regretted majors. 

The new curriculum, particularly the first-year FOCUS and Constellation courses are in many ways a fleeting opportunity to have a larger group of students engage with smaller departments. The issue many first-years protest is that the flexibility to be in their first-choice cluster of classes is slim to none. 

Perhaps they are exposed to a breadth of new knowledge, but paired with disinterest, it creates a distasteful blend. Even more concerningly, this is the first impression that freshmen have of a liberal arts education. These mandatory clusters immediately impede on students' desired interests and create resentment towards a way of learning that Duke prides themselves for. 

Over the last year, while concurrently beginning the new curriculum, Duke has notably pushed initiatives such as 2025’s historic ‘Made for This’ campaign, which fundraised for Duke Sciences and Technology, the Duke Climate Commitment, the undergraduate student experience and Duke Health. The missing piece here, humanities, or even broader, the liberal arts, wasn’t even recognized. 

This fundraiser sought to “mobilize the entire Duke community" through philanthropy and “volunteerism and expertise.” Yet, it appears a sphere of expertise has been, arguably, selectively omitted. 

The pressing question now is, as cuts drastically affect overall budgets and Duke finds new ways to innovate, fundraise, and present itself as an institution, is it now fair game to reverse what the new curriculum set out to accomplish? 

A liberal arts education not only serves as a multifunctional degree but also as an immersive experience that steadily influences your choices for the duration of your life. It teaches not solely the importance of the humanities but also how to listen, understand, and connect concepts across the range of academia. 

Admittedly, I am a transfer from Vassar College in Poughkeepsie, NY, and it’s where I spent my first year at a higher education institution. Although not widely known, beyond being a Seven Sisters liberal arts college, Vassar has an open curriculum. Instead of being confined to a predetermined route, it ensures that students take courses outside of their sphere of comfortability. 

Transferring to Duke was incredibly hard for numerous reasons, with the most jarring and unexpected one being the well-known emphasis on pre-professionalism. At Vassar, we had joked about consulting being some sort of urban legend. Now, I’m acclimated to the rotation of Fortune 500 companies occupying the conference room of WU every week, holding a networking event. 

Of course, students value having a career at small liberal arts schools. But the nature of the “grindset” or “hussle culture” isn’t integrated into students' minds. One of my original criticisms of Vassar was the lack of structure; it felt almost too choose-your-own-adventure. Now I look back at it, compared to the culture of Duke, and I see the benefit. 

All students are required to take classes outside of their majors, with the constraints being exceptionally loose. Hence, when students took a class, there was genuine interest behind the content – there’s a perception of purpose while still being exposed to students from varying backgrounds. Lacking that flexibility of choice and interest leads to the issue we have at Duke, where many will try to cut codes, maximize class listings, and heroically defeat what a liberal arts education aims to be. 

Furthermore, higher education at a small liberal arts school was about creating a person excited to embrace differences sculpted through academic growth. In contrast, Duke at times acts as a transactional step before accepting a job offer. Not to discredit the community and spirit of the Blue Devils parade, but the college experience is much more multifaceted than just a career. 

University marks the point where traditional support systems are replaced by the friends you spend every day with. Classes and professors guide personal morals and integrity. College forces the jump from the bubble of your high school, where many had identical lived experiences, into a new school of thought that pushes your own perception of the world. Part of the experience is looking around and not seeing yourself in every other person around you, but growing from all of the dissimilarities of a college student body. 

Yet it seems that career opportunities and student success are often solely prized by Duke, and the quality of the student leaving is regarded as an afterthought. 

At Vassar, it was organically bred into students to take vastly dissimilar classes, and, more importantly, draw out connections between the courses. Not only was it academically conducive to get a plethora of views, but it also allowed me to expand my own interests.

It seemed so intuitive for higher education that I was truly shocked when faced with the constrained curricula that micromanaged course loads at Duke. Furthermore, many students around me were distraught by the idea of taking classes outside of their expertise. 

Although the definition of a “liberal arts education” cannot be easily defined, I argue that it is the organic integration of a breadth of disciplines where students leave with fundamental values of intellectual inquiry, imagination, and connection. Instead of chasing diversity of curriculum, students should first have the authority to explore their interests, and connect the dots moving backwards. 

An article in Forbes actually arguing for the necessity of STEM in a liberal arts education, also unpacked the core purpose of the impact the education provides — “Students should be able to analyze a situation, decide on a course of action, and advocate for their choice." 

Although STEM undoubtedly gives students the tools to understand the scientific process and how conclusions can be drawn, it’s within the equal priority of each discipline that gives a student, a community, and a world that develops empathy, communicativeness, and collective action. 

Those skills are not intuitive in the world of STEM, and even across the Duke campus, faculty and students alike notice the gaps. The San Roman Lab, where I work as an undergraduate science communicator, has been piloting a program focused on science communication to help broader audiences understand their genetic research. Although the lab’s science is perfectly sound, what purpose does that science serve if it cannot be understood by the masses? 

To me, the only suitable answer is a narrowed focus on staying aligned with the liberal arts education and relentlessly fighting for all disciplines to be represented. 

Although Price was wary not to undermine the importance of the humanities in civic life, his comments undermine exactly what the humanities go out to accomplish — by framing them as something that must justify their survival rather than something that inherently shapes the way we think, question, and live. They are a crucial part of the education we all came here to receive, and have an impact that surpasses simply fulfilling a credit requirement. 

Perhaps the value of a liberal arts education was never meant to be measured against the economy at all. Its worth lies in the way it shapes how we move through the world, not just what we produce within it. As Duke reimagines its future, the question should not be how the humanities survive, but whether we are willing to preserve the intellectual courage that makes them matter in the first place.

Devyn Deschamps is a Trinity sophomore. Her column typically runs on alternate Sundays.

title: Before ICE comes knocking: Duke must become a Fourth Amendment campus
author: Adam Rosenblatt and Leila Zak
article_text:
Duke administrators often position the University as a leader in its research, teaching and global reach. But what does it really mean to lead at this moment in our history, as democratic norms are shredded and wars without legal basis drive needless destruction and mass displacement? As federal agents execute protestors and immigrant community members and people die in ICE detention centers? What does it mean to educate a democratic citizenry that can face these crises, ready to pursue the “permanent good”? The answer might start right in our campus dormitories.

On Feb. 26, five plainclothes immigration agents arrived at a Columbia University-owned apartment building and told the superintendent they were police officers searching for a missing child, using fake badges. Once inside, they detained Ellie Aghayeva, a 29 year old senior majoring in neuroscience and political science, without producing a judicial warrant. After New York City’s mayor Zohran Mamdani personally intervened with President Donald Trump, Aghayeva was released.

This, or worse, could easily happen at Duke. We have already seen Duke employees forced out of their jobs into extreme precarity by the Trump administration’s cruel and discriminatory changes to immigration policy. After many years of bringing joy and dedication to their jobs, bus driver Luis Alonso Juárez and housekeeper Margoth Erazo have both lost their ability to work here due to the repeal of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Hondurans. 

Duke leadership, though quick to send emails with long tributes whenever a prominent administrator moves on or retires, has made no official statement about the sudden and traumatic departures of Juárez or Erazo. Nor have they offered them any legal, social-emotional, or financial support. Instead, students filled in the gaps: advocating alongside them, spending time with them off-campus and addressing their needs via mutual aid.

The incident at Columbia makes it clear that students living in university-owned housing are also vulnerable in ways that demand a real institutional response. Dormitories are private spaces. Under the Fourth Amendment, federal agents — including ICE — cannot enter private spaces without a valid warrant signed by a judge, specifying the name and address of the person under investigation. At Columbia, agents bypassed this protection through deception. Building staff let them in because they believed the story about a missing child.

The answer to this vulnerability is not simply acknowledging “uncertainty and concern,” while urging community members to contact the Duke University Police if federal agents seek to enter spaces on campus. That approach — which university leadership instated in April 2025 and upheld in November when Customs and Border Protection (CBP) began operations in North Carolina — does nothing to empower or educate our community. 

Private spaces, by definition, are not open to the general public; they require a designated key, Duke ID or permissive access for entry. In the campus context, this would include dormitory buildings, facilities exclusive to students and staff, offices, classrooms in session and spaces closed to the general public after certain hours. Without widespread communal awareness, a student or staff member could run the risk of granting warrantless access to a federal agent seeking to enter a private space by an act as well-intentioned as holding open a door. In an environment of fear and confusion, we need broad-based know-your-rights education and a commitment to providing as much safety as we can to all Duke students and workers. 

This is precisely what the Fourth Amendment workplace framework provides, and what over 250 businesses statewide, including the City of Durham itself, have already committed to. Fourth Amendment workplaces train employers and staff on how to recognize whether a warrant is valid, how to interact with federal agents without surrendering rights and how to avoid disclosing private information about employees. 

By agreeing to the framework, Duke would commit to explicitly distinguishing between public and private spaces on campus, and make these clear to all students and staff and create procedures to alert students and staff of ICE presence locally/on campus through university channels. In other words, being a Fourth Amendment workplace does not mean seeking conflict with immigration officials. It is fundamentally a commitment to sharing information and understanding of our constitutional rights. It reaffirms that Duke is a community where, above all, we learn together — especially in times of crisis.

That learning should start right where we live. For weeks, students with Duke Beyond Borders have been trying to arrange a Know Your Rights training specifically for Resident Assistants and Resident Coordinators in Duke Housing and Residential Life. These are the students and staff who serve as first responders in the dormitory environment — the people an undergraduate is most likely to turn to at 6 a.m. if immigration agents appear at their door.

The proposed training, to be delivered in partnership with Siembra NC — the North Carolina immigrant rights organization that has led Know Your Rights, ICE Watch and Fourth Amendment Workplace trainings across the state — would take 60 to 90 minutes. It would cover when federal agents are and are not permitted to enter public versus private spaces; the difference between a judicial warrant and an administrative warrant; current trends in North Carolina enforcement and local resources available to students.

Students from Beyond Borders, with the coalition Documenting Rights, have already led successful Know Your Rights trainings with Mi Gente, the Asian Students Association, DukeAFRICA and dozens of Durham community members and Durham Public School families. The organization has the expertise, the relationships and the commitment to communal education. What it needs is a green light from Duke Housing and Residential Life. Journalist Caitlin Dickerson has reported that ICE agent training is now “dramatically truncated” when it comes to understanding immigration law and constitutional rights. That means the burden falls on the rest of us to know our rights — and to know them well enough to assert them calmly under pressure when someone is banging on a dorm room door, or attempting to enter a private space on the basis of intimidation and deceit. The University — and not just student activists — should take ownership of this work, which belongs in the same category as Title IX training, sexual misconduct prevention modules and the Blue Book that every first-year student receives. Constitutional literacy is a shared responsibility, not a niche concern.

We are not asking Duke to take a political stance. We are asking it to do what universities exist to do: educate people, equip them with knowledge and affirm that the rule of law applies to everyone on this campus — regardless of where they were born, what they look like, or what their immigration status may be. 

Leaders don’t stay silent while the basic rights and safety of their own students and employees, and the democratic norms on which they depend, are threatened. They act. They teach. They find courage — the kind thousands of ordinary people, from Minneapolis to Durham, have shown as they defended their neighbors and took care of the most vulnerable in their communities. Duke should do the same.

Adam Rosenblatt is a professor of the practice of international comparative studies and cultural anthropology, and the faculty director of the Duke Human Rights Center at the Franklin Humanities Institute.

Leila Zak is a Trinity sophomore.

title: David James Duncan at Duke, silence and the search for meaning
author: Robert Wallace
article_text:
The movement in Samuel Beckett’s work constitutes the physical and the metaphysical. That is, his characters often wander on foot or by bicycle, searching for meaning. As often happens, they falter, eventually being unable to physically move. They become introspective, trying their best to understand their predicament, mostly, though not necessarily in theological terms, often in the negative. In other words, their suffering is discoursed in negation. In a literary sense, negative language has the ability — and perhaps more so — to draw attention to the subject all the more. After all, it may be easier to describe what something isn’t than what it is. From a language perspective, the mystics have a long history of using the negative. 

 Beckett had familiarity with the mystics, such as Meister Eckhart, Rumi, Teresa of Avila, Hildegard von Bingen, St. Augustine, Julian of Norwich, among many others. He read about them when he was young. He learned, as opposed to James Joyce, that “subtraction” was the way to confront the dilemma all writers have — how to express the “ineffable.” In his “Three Dialogues with George Duthuit”, he said, “The expression that there is nothing to express, nothing with which to express, nothing from which to express, no power, together with the obligation to express.” Perhaps the seventeenth-century mystic Angelus Silesius said it best: “The place and the word is one.”

This isn’t to say that someone like David James Duncan, who spoke at the Goodson Chapel on March 4, doesn’t have something to say on the subject of silence and language. Yet, his invocation of the ineffable comes with it, unlike Beckett, with behemoths, such as “Sun House” and “The Brothers K”. They certainly resemble Joyce in terms of wordage more so than Beckett. Yet, it is the ineffable — on the page — in which he is after. Unlike Beckett, however, his pursuit is with addition rather than subtraction. He may recognize — and even practice — silence as a way of life, but his characters often struggle with it. There is a lot of talk with them. And hunger for something better. This yearning, similar to Beckett’s “Molloy”, involves the “matter of [the] mother.”

For Duncan, the mother is Mother Earth.

Duncan lives in Montana, in the Bitterroot Mountains. There, when he isn’t writing, he traverses its trails, fly fishes its streams, and, perhaps most importantly, defends its right to exist through activism. This activism is spiritual in nature. While Duncan spoke very little in a direct way about how creative writing constitutes a spiritual practice (I believe it is here, where he invokes silence), he did discuss it obliquely: “Everything starts when we get out of our stupid way.” 

Here again, Duncan appeals to the mystics. In particular, he mentioned Julian of Norwich, who often defined the Divine through the feminine. He noted the Beguine movement too, which was prominent in the Middle Ages, particularly in the Low Countries, and still survives, though less significantly today. UNESCO has classified thirteen beguinages in Belgium alone. Beguine societies, then and now, are self-made communities of unmarried women who devote themselves to service to the poor and to spiritual practice. What the world needs more than anything, I would argue, is a devotion to the feminine, towards the matriarchal. 

I think what David James Duncan was unsaying was to notice. Be quiet and notice.

Stay active. Defend Earth and the less powerful. But find ways to give in to the accidental. 

I’m fascinated by light and water. Distance. And time. Space. One morning, years ago, hours before the rest of my family woke, I went outside and stared into the night sky, viewed millions of stars. The enormity of the universe is mind-boggling. 

One day, also years ago, while visiting my daughter in Cleveland, I spent an entire day reading a book of poetry by a local professor. I read it for the beauty of the language, such as this from Sarah Gridley’s “Green is the Orator”:

“Sink a chunk of salt on your tongue to name the ocean.”

There is a creek in my backyard which meanders its way — no more than half a mile — to the Eno River. It’s called Christmas Creek, and it often overflows its banks in heavy rains, but, much like the Eno River, it quickly swallows its bravado once the rains cease. 

There was a day once when a Great Blue Heron high-stepped its way through the creek slowly and methodically like some kind of ancient bird on a prehistoric hunt. I watched it through my binoculars for about twenty minutes, until it fished its way out of sight. 

My daughter, when she was born, had a full head of dark black hair.

I love to hear the owls in my backyard call to each other. Their calls stir me and remind me that I am not the only one alive; indeed, that humans are not the only ones that inhabit Earth. 

Kafka once said, “You do not need to leave your room. Remain sitting at your table and listen. Do not even listen, simply wait, be quiet, still and solitary. The world will freely offer itself to you to be unmasked; it has no choice, it will roll in ecstasy at your feet.”

Here is something beautiful: I have been married for forty-five years. Sometimes I can look at my wife and imagine that someday she will no longer be with me because I have either died or she has. This thought alone is enough to shatter any notion of disharmony. We are alive for such a short time and dead for so long.

We accumulate many things over our lives. Most of them: useless. Too many useless things. We think these things will make us happy. They do not. There are nomads who travel the earth with few possessions. I wonder if they feel somehow freer, unburdened by the things most of us carry around with us? 

Here is what I mean: A dog isn’t a possession. It is a living thing that curls up to you on cold winter nights, wags its tail when you come home, slips under the covers and unfurls its tongue any place and anywhere to show you how much you mean to it. A dog’s love is never disobedient. 

I used to run with my daughter in Duke Forest on Sunday mornings, our shoes brushing the gravel. She rarely talked while running, and that was okay. She is of me, but not me. We can’t possess a person any more than we can possess ourselves. Learning to love is learning to let go. 

When I was in the eighth grade, the football, basketball and track teams I played on went undefeated for the entire year. It was the first and only time this has ever happened. After the last football game, I walked home after showering, and the cheerleaders and other girls were outside waiting and some were walking home too. It was late fall in Michigan, cold, and my breath came out in puffs of white smoke. About halfway home, a girl was standing at a corner. She was waiting for me, and I felt my heart quicken.

“Good game,” she said.

“Thanks,” I said.

It started to snow. We looked at the first flakes of the year, and then simultaneously we stuck out our tongues to catch the delicate crystals. We laughed, and then she walked up to me. We kissed. It was the first time I had kissed a girl, and I felt this warmth move through me as I had never felt before, a shivering along my back. 

There is nothing like the first kiss.

Life is full of random bits of experiences and moments. Joys and sorrows. I have learned to confront my sorrows, but I do my best to wrap myself up in joys. It feels at times like streams of consciousness, as if words and paragraphs have swallowed me whole. 

Life isn’t ordinary. It is full of traces of the extraordinary. The serendipitous. Even in Beckett’s void, he knew this. So too the mystics. David James Duncan knows this. Like stars, animals, words and falling ice crystals. Kisses. 

Robert Wallace is a first-year graduate student of liberal studies. His column, 'Telling Stories', typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: The Chronicle is accepting endorsements for DSG presidential, EVP candidates
author: Ana Despa and Shambhavi Sinha

title: At Duke, we are not getting a liberal arts education
author: Jasmine Fan
article_text:
My dad exudes two relentless qualities: a love for learning and insatiable curiosity. He doesn’t merely read a book — he metaphorically devours it, ravenously. I watch him bite, carefully chew each page, swirl the words around with his tongue, scrape the nouns against the roof of his mouth and leave not a single vowel undigested. He seems to salivate for knowledge, and it is this voracious intellectual hunger that has always felt so profoundly palpable. 

I went to Duke to see if I, too, could begin to devour the world.

Duke grants students a coveted seat at the dinner table to satiate their intellectual appetites. Trinity promises each and every one of us a “world-class liberal arts education,” recently rolling out six new liberal arts categories. But since I’ve stepped foot on campus, Duke’s liberal arts curriculum seems to dissipate by the semester. Once in a while, it makes a guest appearance in a CZ or ALP class, but even then, it hangs quietly in the backdrop.

We may be attending a “liberal arts institution,” but are we truly receiving a liberal arts education?

When I asked my friends this question, most of them had no idea what a liberal arts education truly was. Others conjured an image of a blue-haired Democrat at a painting easel. In reality, the liberal arts have nothing to do with political ideology, nor are they solely focused on the arts.

The simplest explanation I’ve seen is from Dartmouth: “liberal arts were the skills (artes) taught to free men (liberales).” The liberal arts train us how to think, not merely what to think. They prepare students for a vast range of careers, encourage interdisciplinary exploration, push them to become lifelong learners and aim to build character and virtue, rather than just knowledge. Their goal is breadth and adaptability. 

In terms of how this definition actually manifests today, liberal arts schools are often private residential universities that come at much heftier price tags. They emphasize undergraduate education over faculty research, offer a wide spectrum of academic disciplines and keep class sizes small with discussion-based seminars. 

A common misconception is that the liberal arts is a push away from STEM toward the humanities. That is far from the case. The original liberal arts curriculum, rooted in classical antiquity, spanned seven disciplines: grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy. Any liberal arts curriculum that disregards math and science in favor of the humanities is, by definition, undeserving of the liberal arts title. 

Critics with more blunt assessments might characterize the liberal arts as a push away from “useful” skills toward “useless” ones. After all, compared to a repertoire of programming languages, “critical thinking,” “curiosity” and “creativity” don’t fit so neatly on a LinkedIn profile. In other words, some say our modern world renders a liberal arts education officially obsolete.

But I’m not here to argue for the superiority of a liberal arts education — there’s undeniable value in an engineering degree or vocational school. I’m here to discuss the universities that present themselves as liberal arts institutions, yet don’t fully live up to their label.

Duke prides itself as a liberal arts institution while disregarding its blatant pre-professional lean. I arrived at Duke, awaiting a liberal arts education, only to spend my first semester struggling to stay afloat in a sea of consulting clubs. There’s nothing inherently wrong with a pre-professional campus, but that’s definitely not how Duke markets itself to prospective students. To me, Trinity felt far from the “broad and deep liberal arts curriculum” plastered across the Undergraduate Admissions page. 

I wouldn’t go so far as to call Duke out for false advertising, but its curriculum certainly falls short of the liberal arts rigor offered by its peer institutions. While Trinity isn’t as lax as Brown’s Open Curriculum, it also doesn’t measure up to the Little Ivies, the Seven Sisters, or California’s beloved Claremont Consortium. Take Harvey Mudd, for instance: on top of its already demanding STEM Common Core with computer science, engineering, biology, chemistry, physics and math requirements, students must also devote around a third of their coursework to humanities, social sciences and the arts. 

Even schools more comparable to Duke offer first-year liberal arts curricula that dwarf Constellations and FOCUS. UChicago’s Core reaches across nine categories. Its curriculum requires at least two quarters of both Biological Sciences and Physical Sciences, which includes astronomy and astrophysics, chemistry, geosciences, molecular engineering and physics. Both the College’s Social Sciences Core and Humanities Core are sequential models, with courses centered around specific themes like “Greece and Rome” or “Classics of Social and Political Thought.” Columbia raises the bar even higher. The College’s infamous Common Core consists of literature, contemporary civilization, scientific inquiry, art history and even music courses. Its required reading spans from Shakespeare, Homer, Dante, Jane Austen and Toni Morrison — to Aristotle, Machiavelli, Nietzsche, Marx and even the Qur’an. With the exception of a few select majors, the typical Trinity student could cruise through their graduation requirements without having to even touch a single one of these works. Comparatively, Duke misses the mark.

Trinity describes its liberal arts curriculum as “flexible,” but in practice, “flexible” becomes synonymous with “avoidable.” I know because I’ve done it. I spent my freshman year ferociously scouring DukeHub, scrutinizing courses in my Shopping Cart and collecting T-reqs like they were infinity stones. In the process, I replaced philosophy and physics with R and Python. I picked the easiest NS course I could find, even when the topic didn’t interest me. When it came time to knock out my foreign language credit, I decided to kill two birds with one stone, opting for the one Chinese class that would fulfill both my FL and ALP (though the course had almost nothing to do with the latter). 

In maximizing my graduation requirements, I had minimized my education. I missed out on the breadth of a liberal arts experience. And for a while, I blamed Duke.

I’ve now come to a slightly different realization: yes, Duke markets itself as a liberal arts institution when it should recognize its pre-professional bias. But it’s not that Duke isn’t offering a liberal arts education — it’s that many of us don’t actually want one. The campus is swarming with students who are pre-med, pre-law and, as my friend likes to call economics majors, pre-wealth. 

I still remember my first college lecture: Economics 101. Griffith Theater was so packed that I had to stand on my tiptoes against the back door. Instead of asking about economics, I watched students pelt Professor Nechyba with finance questions, to which he would eventually throw his hands up and lament that he doesn’t actually know much about the stock market. 

When I thought about this more, I realized that Duke doesn’t prescribe pre-professionalism — students do. 

There’s a reason first-years aren’t ecstatic about the new Constellations program: It’s difficult to enforce a liberal arts curriculum on a student body that largely does not want one. Duke administration is often so lost in the minutiae of university policy that they have forgotten to take a hard look at student culture. Do Trinity students even want a liberal arts education and if not, why? That is the fundamental question administrators must first resolve. 

Perhaps the initial place to look is upstream. It could be the case that prospective students, particularly those from well-off families oriented toward pre-professional success, are self-selecting into Duke. The New York Times has already pointed out Duke’s low economic diversity relative to other elite institutions. This socioeconomic skew, along with Trinity’s pre-professional lean, can begin to mold university culture long before students even arrive on campus. Duke is shaped by who applies and who is admitted. 

The University may be able to dictate academic policy, but it cannot dictate student culture. If students don’t actually want to embrace a liberal arts curriculum, they won’t engage meaningfully with their courses. They won’t ask questions, challenge ideas, initiate discussion, apply feedback or think critically. Most importantly, they won’t be curious. And a seat at the intellectual feast means nothing to someone without an appetite. In this sense, a liberal arts curriculum, however well-intentioned, will remain hollow. 

The underlying problem with Duke culture is that many students are seeking a liberal arts degree rather than a liberal arts education. In theory, a degree and an education are synonymous. In practice, they are not. Someone can snooze through lectures, skim through readings and still scrape by with a diploma in hand. The assurance that “C’s get degrees” continually rings true.

We all end up walking across the same stage in May, draped in the same shade of navy blue. But when those caps go up in the air, it does not mean we all left Duke with the same education.

There’s a difference between earning a degree and receiving an education. That difference is stark: A degree culminates after four years — an education compounds over a lifetime.

At Duke, a liberal arts education is a choice. For those of you who want one, don’t hesitate. Choose it.

We may be attending a “liberal arts institution,” but are we truly receiving a liberal arts education?

Jasmine Fan is a Trinity junior.

title: Turnout trouble: Why aren’t women’s games a slam dunk?
author: Wendy House
article_text:
On Feb. 26, I was at a women’s basketball game. Shocking, I know. Shoulder-to-shoulder proximity? Eardrum-rupturing noise? Watching jocks throw around a ball for over an hour? Not typically my cup of tea. My friends are super-fans, though, and I thought it might be cathartic to scream my head off after the first round of midterms, so I went…

And I must say, I had a blast! The catharsis was indeed incredible, our ladies played admirably and we won the ACC regular season! I was even awarded for my brave endeavor with a Blue Devil plush (and got on the WBB Instagram page). What more could a girl possibly ask for?

Well, more attendees, for one. Those who were there cheered loud and proud, and it certainly felt like Cameron was full — but before and after the game, it was quite apparent that it wasn’t. I remember waiting for the pre-game countdown to run out, thinking “Alright, 15 minutes to go, people are really gonna start flowing in now … 10 minutes, it’ll happen now for sure … Five minutes … Are we serious?” I would say I don’t intend to blame Duke fans themselves for the incredible disparity between hype for women’s and men’s basketball games, but that’s not completely true.

I’ll start with the advertising issue, though. Duke does not show off its ladies like it does its gents. It seems you have to go out of your way not to know when a men’s game is happening, whereas to learn about women’s games, you must specifically seek them out. Many students get their information about games from the K-Ville Instagram, which either doesn’t post about the women’s games or posts about them day-of. 

For women’s games, section 17 (the student section) tickets are even sold to non-students, resulting in some unfortunate situations where fans of other teams dominate the very section specifically intended for Duke spirit. During last year’s WBB game against UNC, our student section was polluted with a massive amount of pale blue. Blue Devils found themselves surrounded by howling pastel-toting ghouls when they should have been a united front against that ancient scourge. 

We all know women’s games aren’t as hyped as men’s games — no one can possibly disagree with this. The question is why. For one, the latter is about 70 years older than the former. There is something to be said about reputation building with age, but the most iconic evidence of the glory of Duke men’s basketball is undeniably the phenomenon of K-ville, which only began in 1986 when both teams were well-established. 

So, why the disparity? This all takes me back to about a week ago, when a certain incident happened after the Olympics. 

After securing gold for the United States, the men’s hockey team hopped on a call with none other than President Donald J. Trump to celebrate. Maybe not the craziest party animal they could have called (well, at least when he’s on the mainland), but ok. The president extended an invitation to his State of the Union and, in typical fashion, made a joke that he was obligated to (but did not desire to) invite the women’s team as well, on threat of impeachment. The women’s team did not accept the invitation. 

The point is that everywhere I turn, women’s teams are being overlooked. Our WBB players are great this year, equally as well-performing as their counterparts. There’s no reason they should lack fans screaming their names and making the bleachers thunder. I could even accept some discrepancy, but the difference between coming at least an hour-and-a-half early to stay standing the whole game, and having a guaranteed spot even if you’re late, is simply unacceptable. We should be embarrassed.

I’m not really the right person to be delivering this message, yet delivering it I am. We need to start showing out for women’s games. We need to stop selling student section tickets to people who are not students. If there’s too much empty space, per my friend’s suggestion, we could grab fans who are already present and upgrade them to section 17. The K-Ville Instagram could post three days in advance, rather than mere hours, to give students enough time to plan to attend. Anything other than Duke blue on our court side seating should be utterly vomitous to anyone with even a hint of patriotism to our alma mater. 

After all, how can anyone call themself a Cameron Crazie if they’re only deluded for half the players?

Wendy House is a Trinity sophomore. Her column typically runs on alternate Wednesdays.

title: Reclaiming history: Memory beneath the Atlantic
author: Robert Wallace
article_text:
It would have been made of wood — often live oak or white oak — procured along the eastern coast of the United States. Live oak was durable and iron-strong. It could hold up against the harsh winds of the Atlantic. Its closed pores resisted decay. The masts, most likely made of pine, stood tall and straight and swayed in the breeze and rocked in blowing winds. In a tangled array of rigging and sails, the masts would bend but not break.

Down below lay the cargo.

In the gigantic ships, they were as many as 600 strong. The smaller ones held a few hundred fewer. They lay on plank beds, as little as sixteen inches apart. Above them was a solid wall of wood, so close that they often couldn’t sit up. They lay shackled together, a coffle of confiscated bodies. Black bodies.

In the hull, it was dark as night. All the time. They lost the sense of time. Daytime, nighttime, it was all the same. For a while, they looked for a stream of light entering the darkness, any stalactite of light would do, a spear across a frightened face, a candle-like spot on a swollen hand.

The inner glint had long disappeared.

There came the sounds of constant bodily adjustments, the pulling of chains, the yank of limbs, raw fingernails scratched across wood.
