Faces slumped against legs and arms and stomachs and feet, their ankles fettered together. Then there were the voices. The steady stream of death-defying misery: moans, wails, whines, sobs. Throughout it all was the water, continuously splashing against the ship, incessantly rocking them, like an enormous cradle of death. Still, they did not give up.

The Middle Passage.

The Atlantic Ocean covers 20% of the Earth’s surface. Imagine, if you will, thousands of ships, for nearly 400 years, crisscrossing this vast body of water, carrying stolen human beings from West Africa to the Americas and to Europe. Up to 12 million of them. Submerged in the tanks of ships designed specifically for the movement of enslaved people, millions did not survive the trips, dying enroute.

These slave voyages landed in ports far and wide: Liverpool, England; Nantes, France; Lisbon, Portugal; Havana, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; Charleston, South Carolina; Cuba and so many others. The last known slave ship docking in the United States was in Mobile, Alabama, around 1860, carrying some 110 African men, women, and children. It was an “illegal” voyage, as Congress had passed a law prohibiting the importation of enslaved people. The ship was subsequently burned in the bay to destroy the evidence.

And still there is the water.

Water can bring you home, but it can also take you away. It doesn’t want to remain still.

It can’t. There is, too, the inland waterways: streams and bays and, especially, the wide flowing rivers: the Paraiba do Sul, Amazon, Mississippi, Thames, Loire, Mersey. Many of these rivers flowed from ports where enslaved Africans were loaded onto barge-like, flatbed vessels, unceremoniously transported inland to work in mines and cotton and sugar plantations.

Water is life. But you can also die in it.

It is in the context of water's dualistic nature that Stephen L. Hayes, Esbenshade assistant professor of the practice of art, and Javier Wallace, instructor in the education program, have partnered to create the project “Reclaiming the Current.” This project aims to identify not only the many bodies of water for which the African diaspora were transported, but to lay claim to the truth for which the currents brought them.

Hayes, a sculpture artist, began his long-term alliance with water while in residence at Black Rock Senegal, a multi-disciplinary artist in residence program located in Dakar, Senegal. It was there that Hayes created “bio-art” and where he envisioned broadening his “collaboration with water” through an engagement with the places tied to the transatlantic slave trade.

Later, he met with Wallace in Barbados, where the project took its first step. On June 12, 2025, the first iteration was in memory of Barbadians’ failed attempt to install King Cuffee in opposition to British rule. Wallace's role, as a historian, in the collaboration is to “ensure each installation is rooted in meticulous historical research.”

Both Hayes and Wallace presented an overview of the project at Smith Warehouse on Feb. 23. Hayes intends to move the needle toward recognition of the transatlantic slave trade, so that this history isn’t erased. He plans to create busts, using actual living descendants of Africans, and submerge them in waters throughout the world. To that end, the first such sculpture was created in Speightstown, Barbados.

With the help of Speightstownians, including the hands of many children, two sculptures were submerged in 22 feet of seawater. There, the sculptures will stay for exactly one year, pointed in honor toward Africa. They will then be raised. Hayes, in his presentation, spoke about the importance of the art, the vitality of the waters and allowing the sea to do as it will to the sculptures.

“It’s a living memorial,” Hayes said. “The art is transformed by water.”

It is in the transformation, therefore, that “Reclaiming the Current” not only asserts its claim on the waters that brought Africans forcibly away from their homes, but demands a right to history itself. You can see this claim to history on the face of the bust that Hayes and Dr. Wallace brought to the presentation.

A sculpture bust created by Duke artist Stephen L. Hayes, part of the project Reclaiming the Current, shows the marks and discolorations left by time spent submerged in seawater.

The bust, an example of the work Hayes creates, stood on a pedestal. It had been in the waters along the coast of Senegal. At first glance, the young African woman appears colorless. There is a classical look to the sculpture. But if you take a closer inspection and walk around the bust, the viewer notices multiple colors. There are specks of blue, gray-blue, brown and reddish hues. Even off-white. It is dotted with markings and discolorations. The sea has absorbed it. The sea has become a part of the bust, and it is a part of the sea. They are one.

Throughout the project, after the busts have been raised from the sea, one will be left with the host country, and the other will return to the United States. Eventually, after a number of years, Hayes and Wallace plan to exhibit them.

The story is clear. The transatlantic slave trade isn’t just the story of Black people. It is also the story of white people. It’s the story of all of us.

As for “Reclaiming the Current,” says Wallace, “I am hopeful our contribution will be tied to the public memorization of this travesty in our history that centers the people who endured and their descendants who lived to talk about them.”

Robert Wallace is a first-year graduate student of liberal studies. His column, 'Telling Stories', typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: No, actually: ‘AI in the humanities’ is not our advantage
author: Anna Sorensen
article_text:
Last week, Duke President Vincent Price spoke at an event with the John Hope Franklin Humanities Institute. Among other topics, he discussed the role of AI in the humanities at Duke, and posited, in the words of a reporter at the event, “the role AI can play in the humanities as an example of an area where the University may have a comparative advantage over its peers, given its strong emphasis on an interdisciplinary approach.” 

It seems like we’ve been talking about AI for ages at Duke, and trust me, I’m the last person who wants to feed that flame. I roll my eyes whenever AI comes up in the classroom, and I often actively avoid conversations about it. As an English major and history minor, I can also say that I’m pretty well-versed in the ethos of the humanities at Duke and in higher education at large. So I wonder why it feels like we keep beating a dead horse, why we feel like we need to keep reiterating, agreeing with one another, that AI shouldn’t play a role in our humanities education. 

Statements like these from President Price make me reconsider this reality. It surprises and concerns me to hear AI asserted as a "comparative advantage” for the humanities at Duke. It makes me wonder: have any of the AI evangelists at Duke actually talked to anyone in the humanities recently? (The English department, I may add, shares a building with the (albeit walled-off) administrative suite, so it’s really not a far trek.)

Before I move on, I should provide some context on the rest of this event. Price also spoke about the difference between funding research in the humanities and STEM, noting that humanities research tends to be institutionally funded, while STEM research receives external support. That’s true, and it’s an unfortunate financial burden for our university. But I hope we can agree it’s one we must carry. To the point of research, I won’t try to assert that AI isn’t incredibly useful in humanities research. I’m all for embracing it there — not having to cite sources manually is a win for all of us. 

But I struggle to see a comparative advantage beyond that. 

I fear that AI in research at Duke is only the surface of its institutionalization. I can’t claim to know precisely what Price means when he talks about the role of AI in the humanities at Duke. And I wonder if this is part of the problem. As a student, I don’t feel we have a clear sense of the direction our university is heading with AI. Trust me, I’ve heard my fair share of complaints from faculty and staff — tales of long-winded angry emails to the administration — but it all feels pretty inaccessible to me. Ask students what Duke’s position is on AI, and you’ll probably get a wide variety of answers. Many will joke about their professors’ wars on AI, but I bet you few could articulate a clear, long-term administrative position. 

That scares me. So, perhaps in the absence of a cohesive position from the University, allow me to share my own perspective on what, at the very least, shouldn’t be happening. 

I want to be clear that I’m not anti-AI. (Yes, yes, this is the point in the article where I appeal to my opposition.) Do I think AI has incredible educational uses? Yes. But do I support it as part of the humanities' educational process? As something to be actively promoted in an institution of higher education? No. 

Shouldn’t a university like Duke be protecting us from the encroaching forces that threaten to degrade the value we place in higher education? Shouldn’t the humanities at Duke be a haven from the reduction of humanity itself outside Duke? 

In many ways, I feel like I’m shouting into an echo chamber over here. Most of the discussions I’ve had with English professors and fellow humanities students have been pretty conclusive in our collective disdain for AI in the college experience. I can feel like I’m preaching to the choir, but then I read news like this, and I wonder if these truths, which seem so obvious to us who work within the humanities, are actually that obvious. I wonder whether our university really envisions an enduring role of AI in the humanities.

I hope not. One upside (if we can even call it that) of AI’s meteoric rise and epic failures is the renewed belief in the value of the humanities — in the critical thinking skills which have always defined our value. As AI shows us all the amazing things it can do and the processes it can expedite, we, in turn, recognize its limitations and our own unique abilities. 

Price voiced this himself when he asserted that “the human skills, practices, approaches [and] perspectives that the humanities lend are absolutely critical.” Critical, maybe, but apparently not valuable — or should I say financially viable. Price also claimed that financial and technological developments are forcing Duke to consider alternative modes of supporting such scholarship. Let’s not be fooled here: economic efficiencies lie at the heart of this AI battle in higher education. If only we could recognize the urgent existential battles beyond that. 

As AI continues to erode our collective ability to think critically and to steal our intellectual property, it’s a gross overstep to position AI's role in the humanities as our competitive advantage. And such claims will only further ostracize Duke’s humanities community, which is already frustrated and sidelined in the wake of the “strategic realignment” we have faced over the last year. 

If we must adopt this corporate language of “comparative advantage” to talk about the humanities at Duke (which, I hope I’ve made very clear, I don’t condone), then let’s at least be clear about what this advantage really is. The “comparative advantage” of the Duke humanities should not be the extent to which we embrace AI; it lies beyond keeping pace with the AI machine. Our comparative advantage should be the students who graduate from our university with the critical thinking and writing skills necessary to engage thoughtfully in the world outside Duke. 

So maybe next time, before voicing our AI advantage on behalf of the Duke humanities, the administration should think twice about the message it sends to those of us belonging to it and to those who believe in the meaning of this discipline: understanding what it means to be human. 

Anna Sorensen is a Trinity senior.

title: Fuqua should focus on preparing students, not surveilling them
author: Shezaz Hannan
article_text:
Artificial intelligence continues to revolutionize the job market and how we work. Educators across Duke are being challenged to train students on how to use AI and prepare for careers that will increasingly depend on the technology. But the Fuqua School of Business is going beyond just incorporating AI in the curriculum, with its new experiments using AI systems in the classroom to assess student performance.

Here’s how it works: Fuqua classrooms are already equipped with cameras and microphones that record classes using Panopto, a video management system that then makes recordings available to students. Students generally check in to class using a Bluetooth and NFC-based “Fuqua Checkin” app. Under the new system, students would check in to class by scanning NFC tags at their seats, which then associates their student information with that seat. This information would be used in conjunction to additional microphones with the capability of ascertaining the exact position of speakers in the classroom. 

Transcripts are fed to an in-house AI system that "objectively" grades participation by assessing comment relevance and whether statements spur conversation. While framed as innovation, this transforms the classroom from a space of intellectual risk-taking into a monitored performance arena where spontaneity, vulnerability and genuine learning become casualties of surveillance.

The system illuminates just how artificial intelligence could change the practice of education. Scott Dyreng, senior associate dean of Innovation at Fuqua and the champion of this technology, claims that the system enables greater feedback for students and instructors alike.

Currently piloting in his "Taxes and Global Strategic Decision Making" course, his policy has expanded AI use beyond the classroom by requiring students to record and upload team meetings. The AI then provides feedback on speaking time distribution, contribution quality and team performance rankings across six dimensions — analytical rigor, intellectual diversity, topic coverage, conclusion quality, participation balance and collaboration dynamics. 

While this data could strengthen team discussions, it undermines vital workplace skills. Fuqua purports to teach students to be leaders of consequence with self-awareness and the ability to give and receive feedback. Replacing human feedback with AI undermines these very qualities. Students will face challenges in the workplace not only from technology, but from people — coworkers, clients, customers. Workplace collaboration requires teammates to communicate about what is working and what isn’t. Outsourcing communication to AI risks reducing meetings to easily measurable metrics misaligned with learning objectives.

In the classroom, the reduction of speech to data points has profound impacts on the quality of discussion. Some of the best classroom discussions, in my experience, come from half-baked ideas that are built upon by other students. When students are aware that their speech is being graded by AI systems with narrow instructions, the nature of classroom discussions changes. 

Learning requires a degree of vulnerability that is undermined when surveillance strips the classroom of psychological safety. Students in this system are incentivized to game the system by adhering closely to the AI rubric. This translates to students self-censoring and speaking less freely, especially when their comments might be provocative or when they feel they lack a genuine understanding of the material. Instead of incentivizing students to engage authentically in the classroom, students are encouraged to participate performatively in a way that is measurable by AI.

The system also erodes student privacy. While Dyreng and the administration can claim that students are already being recorded, the attribution and use of AI fundamentally escalates the surveillance of students. The AI system makes student viewpoints searchable and quantifiable for analysis. Patterns in students’ speech, their engagement levels over time, and even their lack of understanding about certain material become part of their education record.

Research on the use of surveillance in education consistently shows that systems that monitor students have chilling effects on student speech. While much of this research focuses on K-12 education, testimonials from prospective Fuqua students echo these impacts. After Dyreng recently presented about the AI classroom — and its impending expansion to all Fuqua core classes as soon as the upcoming academic year — to admitted students, they felt the system to be unnerving, remarking that the system may dismantle honesty in the classroom.

Proper implementation of the AI system could help dispel some of these student concerns. Basic data governance, the processes and policies that ensure data is used effectively and securely, is absent. Students haven't been told who accesses their data, how long it's retained or how to verify AI inferences. The syllabus claims that attribution of comments will only be used by the professor and teaching staff, ignoring that others, such as the developers of the technology, still have access to the data. Retention of data is important. While Duke surely has robust cybersecurity practices, imagine a scenario in which Duke is hacked and transcripts with attribution are leaked. Students, many of whom aspire to high positions of power and leadership, would have all their classroom speeches follow them throughout their lives.

Students lack the ability to meaningfully consent or opt out of the use of the technology in their classroom experience. When the first pilot of the classroom was conducted, students only found out about the experiment days before the start of class, when the syllabus was posted on Canvas. The syllabus read, “By taking the course, you agree to be part of this experiment.” There was no opportunity, at that point, for students to switch to a different elective offering at the same time slot. As the system expands, all students at Fuqua will be subjected to the AI classroom in their core classes. While admitted students were informed about the technology while visiting campus, in the absence of an opt-out mechanism, prospective students should be made aware of the technology system before they even apply.

To its credit, Fuqua is evangelizing the system through media attention in Poets & Quants and the Wall Street Journal. While Dyreng and the administration seem excited to make a big splash in the MBA world with the news, they should be more focused on making the value proposition clear to students and incorporating their feedback meaningfully — not just listening to concerns and responding defensively.

Many students are fascinated and excited by the new use of AI in the classroom. Others, like me, are appalled at the lack of care shown to students and the expansion of the surveillance apparatus within the classroom. Meaningful input means including students in implementation, making modifications for transparency, and alignment with learning incentives. Given the school's investment, scrapping the system seems unlikely. But there's still time to adapt its use in ways that benefit how students actually want to learn.

Better yet, Fuqua could focus on refining its AI curriculum. While many classes now promote the use of AI tools, few guide how to best make use of these tools, instead generically telling students to experiment with the use of AI tools. If Fuqua wants to prepare students to re-enter the workforce, it should prepare students for a future of working with technology — not being subjected to it.

Shezaz Hannan is a third year dual master’s student in the Fuqua School of Business and the Sanford School of Public Policy.

title: Nida Allam and the fight to change the Democratic Party
author: Wesley Knott
article_text:
Two days before Nida Allam publicly announced her campaign to represent North Carolina’s 4th Congressional District, Democratic House leadership appointed the incumbent she's challenging, Rep. Valerie Foushee, to co-chair the House Democratic commission on AI and the Innovation Economy. 

Now, AI-aligned PACs are spending more than a million dollars supporting Foushee’s re-election campaign. 

Voters across the district have likely noticed the sudden surge of ads flooding the airwaves. This is an all-too-familiar story for NC-04. In 2022, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) poured millions of dollars into the race at the last minute to defeat Allam. This year, the outside spending is from AI-aligned PACs.

There is a word voters use when industries regulated by Congress spend heavily to boost the campaigns of lawmakers overseeing them: corruption. 

Voters are not naïve. They understand how Washington works, and they don't like it — only 17% of voters approve of the way Congress is handling its job, with only 18% approving of the job Congressional Democrats are doing, a record low. How can it be that a party whose ideas consistently poll above 50% can have such a low approval rating? 

The party needs to go beyond messaging to address its unpopularity. Too many voters believe we say the right things about lowering drug prices, strengthening labor rights and regulating powerful industries, but fail to deliver when it comes time to actually take on powerful corporations and interest groups. The problem lies beyond ideology, but rather in credibility. Voters do not think Democrats are fighting hard enough to follow through on their promises, and when our campaigns are bankrolled by special interest groups, it only reinforces that skepticism.

At a time when most independent voters and even 1 in 10 Trump voters say they believe the Trump administration is corrupt, Democrats are rightly making Trump's corruption and self-dealing a central theme heading into the midterms. But if Democrats are going to prosecute that case effectively, we need messengers voters trust — leaders who will reject the self-dealing associated with Washington.

We cannot lament Citizens United while benefiting from industry-aligned outside spending. We cannot critique the military-industrial complex while accepting donations from Lockheed Martin and Raytheon. And we cannot claim to be a firewall against Big Tech's influence while taking money from Meta and Google. It is time for a change in our party.

That's why I’ve endorsed Durham County Commissioner Nida Allam for Congress.

Nida Allam understands the importance of restoring the trust our party has lost with voters, and she knows that trust is earned when voters know not just what you stand for but who you answer to. That's why she rejects corporate PAC money and is running a people-powered campaign.

As a county commissioner, Allam has a record of delivering for working families, but she understands that policy alone is not enough. Voters are looking for bold, progressive and independent leadership with the courage to take on concentrated wealth and power — not the corporate-dominated status quo that voters have grown tired of.

Nida Allam is the change the Democratic Party needs right now. By sending her to Congress, NC-04 can send a message that the future of our party will be defined by the people we represent, not the special interests bankrolling Washington.

Wesley Knott is the chair of the Wake County Democratic Party.

title: Meet Thom Tillis, your senator
author: Kris Sun
article_text:
Have you heard of Thom Tillis? Prior to 2025, I hadn’t heard of Thom Tillis.

I just surveyed my immediate friend group, and none of them had heard of him either. For most students at Duke, U.S. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., is either a foreign name or a sore subject. But recently, I, alongside many other politically obsessed students, had the chance to formally hear from our state’s representative in the US Senate on Feb. 20. And I, as someone who is liberal leaning, have to say: I don’t think we give Tillis the recognition that he deserves. 

So, for those that don't know him (or just hate him), I'd like to introduce Thom Tillis, your senator.

Tillis, a Republican, was first elected in November 2014 and has since served as North Carolina’s senior senator. He seemingly loves North Carolina, but I can’t honestly say that North Carolina has loved him back. Tillis has a 25% approval rating. Meanwhile, his disapproval ranges from 63% among Democrats to as high as 40% among conservatives. Tillis is so unpopular among his own party, that he was censured by an overwhelming two-thirds of the North Carolina GOP in 2023. 

However, Tillis’ 25% approval rating is not only unwarranted but a sign that North Carolinians are too polarized to understand the full weight of what he represents for politics. The departure of the senator ultimately represents another step in the death of independent voices and bipartisan politics. 

I had first learned of the senator in the summer of 2025 through coverage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. An obviously controversial bill, it faced contention from nearly all Democrats and a select few outspoken Republicans, including Tillis, who cited disagreement with the bill’s cuts to Medicaid. This struck me, as Tillis had historically been a consistent advocate against the 2010 Affordable Care Act and prohibited Medicaid expansion during his time in the North Carolina House. So why the switch? Is this ideological inconsistency? Or perhaps Tillis has some considerations reserved for the swing-state nature of his constituents. Based on his recent political history, I’d argue the latter.

Tillis has consistently shown a willingness to bend his own conservative beliefs in exchange for effective, and often necessary, political reform. Despite being considered a staunch Republican “warrior”, he’s also displayed surprising independence on hot-button issues like gun control and same-sex marriage. In 2022, Tillis was the primary Republican architect for the Respect for Marriage Act, which codified same-sex marriage as a backup to Obergefell v. Hodges, the landmark Supreme Court case protecting the right to gay marriage. The act passed with a 62-vote Senate majority. 

This was followed closely by what was, at the time, the first sweeping gun control legislation in 30 years: the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act. When circumstance calls, Tillis takes action — his gun control efforts came as a direct aftermath of the Uvalde school shooting. Meanwhile, the Lugar Center ranks him as the 68th most bipartisan Senator out of the 250 that have taken office since 1993.

And what is the consequence of bipartisan diplomacy? Plummeting approval ratings, hateful spite from the left, accusations of flip-flopping from the political center and censures from the right. After Tillis ended as one of three Republican senators to vote against the One Big Beautiful Beautiful Bill Act, President Trump took to Truth Social, threatening to back a challenger to Tillis’ re-election:

“Numerous people have come forward wanting to run in the Primary against ‘Senator Thom’ Tillis. I will be meeting with them over the coming weeks, looking for someone who will properly represent the Great People of North Carolina and, so importantly, the United States of America. Thank you for your attention to this matter!”

This, too, is a political trend: when politicians on either side of the spectrum attempt to diversify their positions beyond their party’s binary, they’re met with hostility from both sides of the political spectrum. Of the ten House Republicans who opted to vote to impeach President Trump in the aftermath of the Jan. 6, 2021 United States Capitol Attack, nine are no longer in office. Four members were “primaried”, including former Rep. Liz Cheney, and five opted to retire in the face of difficult election odds. 

Senator Tillis seems to be facing a similar fate, a sentiment he suggested in his dialogue at Duke University. When asked about re-election, he noted that the two considerations every politician must consider are fundraising capability and voter support. In consideration of the former, Tillis joked about the increasing price of entry into politics (and his hesitancy to spend more money), but ultimately decided that his team could have fundraised another election. To the latter, Tillis noted that his independent thinking no longer resonates with an increasingly partisan voter base.

Now a senator freed from the throes of campaigning, Thom Tillis has not been shy to make his independent stances known. In conversation with professor of political science Peter Feaver, he adamantly defended increases in support for Ukraine — to paraphrase his sentiment, it's a no-brainer to stand up to Putin, whose Russian forces are struggling, while simultaneously avoiding American on-the-ground intervention. He followed this stance by advocating for the independence of the people of Greenland. 

Online, he’s had a field day contesting members of the Trump administration, including badmouthing Duke’s own Stephen Miller and calling for the resignation of Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem. In-person, he reiterated similar messages, attacking Vice President JD Vance for what he described as a poor performance at a recent speech at the Munich Security Conference.

In total, I counted five curse words used during Tillis’ hour at Duke. His demeanor was calm, and he often interrupted his own sentences with swigs of water from his glass, which he audibly refilled whenever Feaver spoke (which wasn’t often; Tillis interrupted his questions rather frequently). As an individual who’s worked with dozens of politicians, I found his demeanor refreshing.

He says what he thinks. His default setting is “boring,” and when he’s not boring, he’s aggressive, douchey and cutthroat. Thom Tillis does not give a shit what anyone thinks. In every sense of the word, he’s independent — independent from his party, independent from the President and independent of even his own approval rating. And that makes him a powerful leader.

Meet Thom Tillis, your senator. I doubt anyone is going to miss his presence once his term ends — and I think that is a shame. Tillis’ voting record reflects both a dedication to incrementalism, which should appeal to the conservative half of North Carolina, and the occasional bipartisan jump, which reflects the 2.4 million Democratic affiliates in the state. To quote Paul Schumaker, Tillis’ political consultant, “North Carolina is the swingiest of all swing states.” I think it's only fair that we’re represented by a senator who is willing to swing all the same.

Is Tillis that senator? For some, he’s not even close. Even after retirement, Tillis, as Duke’s own professor Frank Bruni notes, still refuses to stand up against President Trump, opting instead to attack his inner circle, while continuing to vote in favor of President Trump’s policies 98% of the time. Still, we shouldn’t punish Tillis’ 2% of attempts to moderate his ideology, especially if he represents a swing state. And I’m devastated that politicians like Tillis are only able to speak up after announcing retirement, else they risk their jobs. 

In his departure, Tillis joins a growing population of politicians who are punished for defying their party. It’s easy to say that this is a problem exclusive to the supposed “RINOs” of Congress, but we’ve seen identical trends play out for retired Sen. Joe Manchin, a Democrat from conservative-leaning West Virginia, and more recently with Sen. John Fetterman, who has garnered widespread criticism from the Democratic Party for voting with President Trump 6% of the time.

This is a problem with how we, as voters, grade our politicians. We should judge Thom Tillis through the lens that his performance is meant to represent North Carolina’s politically diverse population. The reality is that the number of independent voters in the state outnumber both Democrats and Republicans. In Tillis’ audience at Duke, I spotted some conservative students and some who were liberal. Both populations found moments to applaud (and those moments often overlapped). Yet, at the debates and at the polls, we judge bipartisan individuals like Tillis with disdain. 

Let’s let Tillis’ departure from the Senate serve as a reminder to be more independent, whether that's in conversation or at the ballot box.

Kris Sun is a Trinity sophomore. His column, ‘Multitudes,’ typically runs on alternate Mondays.

title: ‘Abolish ICE!’ says Duke student who won’t vote
author: Monday Monday
article_text:
Editor's note: The article below is satire.

This Monday, The Chronicle documented a Duke sophomore posting “Abolish ICE!” to his Instagram story, despite having no intention whatsoever to vote.

“This administration DOES NOT care about you!! We have to do WHATEVER IT TAKES to make change!” wrote the student, reposting a news article about how children have been separated from their families by ICE to the song “DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS (Piano Version)”.

When asked who he would be voting for in the upcoming primary election, he said “What?”

It may seem like apathy, but The Chronicle confirmed that there was a woke and important political philosophy behind this. The sophomore said in an exclusive with Monday Monday, “My name is Inbred Moron and, although I have political opinions, I like to think of them less as belief systems that I must act on in order to make the world a better place and more as a kind of proof to myself that I am a good person.”

Is that how that works? The Chronicle fact-checkers have yet to confirm.

When asked about what he thought about the process of voting, the sophomore said “My vote won’t do anything important and I only do political action that’s important, like saving motivational Zohran Mamdani edits or overusing the word ‘hegemony’ in my discussion section.”

But what about your civic duty?

“Is it so bad to be someone who likes when things are good politically, but refuses to participate in even the most basic form of collective action when things are bad? A question for the philosophers, I suppose; I’m not a big thinker honestly.”

When The Chronicle last saw the sophomore, he was seen reposting a GoFundMe that he hadn’t donated to with the caption, “what you are seeing in gaza is a GENOCIDE!! we cannot continue to be complicit ^^.” Sources say hearing that his district representative, funded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), did not compel him to fill out a ballot, but he did verbally condemn the situation with significant gravitas.

Monday Monday is currently misquoting bell hooks to evoke an illusion of depth.

title: Don’t forget
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
On March 2, the Duke Chapel will host former U.S. Poet Laureate Joy Harjo for the second annual Pluralism Lecture in conjunction with the Provost’s Initiative on Pluralism, Free Inquiry, and Belonging. One of Harjo’s famous poems is titled “Remember,” in which she tells us to remember the sky, moon, sun, your birth, the earth, the wind and her voice, and more. Over half of the poem’s lines begin with the linguistic refrain “Remember.” 

Remembering can be a strange activity. Some people are unable to remember, or remember incorrectly. Some deliberately choose to remember things selectively and choose to forget that which is inconvenient or uncomfortable. 

What Harjo gestures toward is that remembering can remind us that we are part of a vast community, stretching from earth to sky. We are not alone, and all creation has “tribes” and “histories.” We are connected to this collective breathing and breath, a kind of “alive poem.”

When Jesus was locked in a struggle in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11), he quotes the Torah, his scripture, by reciting “It is written.” He remembers the ancient words of Deuteronomy, connecting him to his ancestors and their experiences and wisdom. He remembers. 

In this instance, he draws on religious memory of sacred texts. He demonstrates that there are words that have come before him that will sustain him in times of duress. He relies on the past to survive in the present and walk into the future. If we don’t ever pause to remember, we may, in turn, fail to make it through the rough patches in life. 

In this church season of Lent, I have been remembering the words that accompany the imposition of ashes on Ash Wednesday: "Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return." I am remembering a traditional Celtic prayer I learned from the Irish poet Pádraig Ó Tuama: “Dear God, Be good to me. The sea is so wide, and my boat is so small.” What words do you remember when challenges loom?

Wise words from prayers, poems and sacred texts point us to the fact that we are not alone in the world, but are a part of a long history of humanity and creation. We are tied to a human and non-human community, a web of wonder. So as you wander in the wonder of this web, know that we are interconnected to more stories and histories and legacies than we can ever imagine.

Harjo captures this interconnectedness of being at the end of her poem:

“Remember you are all people and all people
are you.
Remember you are this universe and this
universe is you.
Remember all is in motion, is growing, is you.
Remember language comes from this.
Remember the dance language is, that life is.
Remember.”

We’re at that time in the semester when you may forget these things because of exams, tests, projects, papers and more. And so it is all the more important to remember the words, sounds, music, and language we have each inherited. All around us, there are “alive poems.”

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: The real heated rivalry: Jewish Life at Duke
author: Stella Kaye
article_text:
You’ve probably heard of the battle of the sexes, the heated constitutional debate between federalists and anti-federalists and even the Reddit users dedicated to arguing over celebrities' heights.

But here at Duke, there’s a debate so drawn out and strong, even Reddit users can’t quite decide: which Jewish institution to go to on a Friday night. 

I’m not talking about a “chill night in or a fun night out” as the Class of 2030 Instagram page may suggest. Here, I’m writing about a subset of Duke’s community. The 12-13% of undergraduate students who identify as Jewish or allies who are looking for a Shabbat service, heading to a sanctuary for reflection, contemplation, prayer, food and (let’s be honest) wine. 

There are two main dining rooms for Friday night Shabbat dinners. One, located off campus at the Fleishman House (known as Chabad), a block off East Campus. The other, The Freeman Center (Hillel) located halfway between East and West Campus, a convenient stop on the C1 and Swift routes. 

As a Jewish student, I came to Duke unsure of which organization I should join (or at least attend events with). Each university’s Jewish student unions have their own reputations, and I feared affiliating with a group known for the wrong things. Although guided by the same religion, vast differences between Chabad and Hillel create divides within practices and specific beliefs. 

Chabad at Duke offers a tightly knit, tradition-centered space that can feel grounding for some. However, that same structure is rooted in a more rigid, traditional framework that doesn’t always reflect the realities or identities of a diverse student body. This structure draws on the long-standing teachings and interpretations of Orthodox Judaism as articulated by the Lubavitch movement. Leadership positions, ritual participation and certain religious responsibilities are gender specific, with men and women having different roles in services and communal rituals. 

For students who see their Jewishness as evolving alongside commitments to gender equality, LGBTQ+ inclusion and progressive social engagement, that atmosphere can feel limiting rather than comforting. In contrast, Duke Hillel prioritizes open community, creating a space where Jewish practice isn’t tied to a single ideological lane.

Events such as interfaith and intercultural dialogues, LGBTQ+ Shabbat dinners, service projects and even a Purim drag brunch allow students to explore Jewish traditions while integrating their broader values and identities. This openness allows students to bring their full selves into the room without needing to reconcile parts of their identity with institutional expectations.

After spending several nights a week at Hillel the past seven months, as well as stopping by Chabad, I’ve realized that the Freeman Center is where I, and many others, feel the most comfortable learning, engaging and ultimately, belonging. 

The choice between Chabad and Hillel thus illustrates something larger than Friday night dinners. It shows us the ways in which institutions shape religious identity and community engagement. While Chabad offers a structured and traditional approach, Hillel demonstrates that inclusivity and pluralism can coexist with meaningful practice. For students navigating complex identities, finding a community that aligns with their values is essential. For me, that community is Hillel, where faith and individuality can thrive together.

At the end of the day, the debate between Chabad and Hillel might never be fully settled. While some swear by the Fleishman wine, others can’t live without the Freeman family. In a world filled with overwhelming hatred toward certain groups — even within the same religions — it’s important to support the institutions that raise their voices on behalf of those who have long been silenced. At Duke, that institution is Hillel. 

Stella is a Trinity first-year.

title: Students can lead a new generation
author: Nida Allam
article_text:
I never wanted to spend my life in politics, but politics was always shaping my life. In 2015, I was an eager young student at North Carolina State University (NC State), probably much like many of you. I stayed up late studying for organic chemistry finals, went to basketball games, ate greasy food on Hillsborough Street.

Things changed, seemingly overnight. On Feb. 10, 2015, I got the horrible phone call that three of my closest friends, Deah, Yusor and Razan were murdered in Chapel Hill in a terrible hate crime. Walking into their apartment with a gun, their next-door neighbor ended three beautiful, successful, joyous lives in the span of just 36 seconds.

Unfortunately, local leaders and police did not see it that way. In fact, they were quick to label the situation a “parking dispute” — as if that is all their lives were worth. Entire futures swept under the rug, like just another petty disagreement.

Frustrated and grieving, I began to doubt all politicians. One day, they demonized Muslims; the next day, they explained away our deaths with the wave of a hand. I felt hopeless, and most of all, I missed my friends. As hard as it is to say, I even began to doubt my place here in North Carolina: my home for almost all of my life.

So I took to the streets. I started showing up to interfaith organizing events, joining hands with Moms Demand Action and other local groups advocating for an end to gun violence. I saw neighbors who looked nothing like my friends and I show up for us — and believe us when we said this was a hate crime. 

I began to see that we couldn’t simply count ourselves out or be shouted down — we had to stand up and demand to be treated with the dignity and humanity we deserved. We had to shape politics, or else they would keep shaping us. And rather than throw up our hands in defeat, we could find justice in community, tolerance, and compassion and in amplifying Muslim and immigrant voices in the public sphere.

Over the years, and inspired by my North Carolina neighbors, I found hope again. I joined the Sanders campaign and eventually decided to run for office myself. Today, I’m running for Congress to represent the 4th district — and I’m proud to be part of a new generation of progressive leaders, ready to demand better for our constituents.

We are living through troubling times. One man — Elon Musk — owns more wealth than the bottom fifty percent of our country. The median age to buy a home across the United States is 59, meaning our generations are more likely to be paying off student loans than a mortgage. Tens of millions of Americans are in a total of over two hundred billion dollars of medical debt.

To top it all off, our district is suffering the brunt of Trump’s authoritarian, unconstitutional and antidemocratic attacks. We faced the worst funding cuts in the country at the hands of DOGE, leaving thousands of USAID workers, FEMA responders and academic researchers at institutions like Duke unemployed for months. ICE has been in our streets, rounding up our neighbors and threatening our collective safety. And through it all, our member of Congress has been quietly maintaining the status quo.

Peaceful protestors are getting murdered in broad daylight, and yet I am the only candidate in this race who says loud and clear, Abolish ICE. 70,000 Palestinians civilians, including tens of thousands of children, have been killed by our tax dollars, and yet I am the only candidate says what’s happening in Gaza is a genocide and who has never taken a cent from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) — and never will.

My opponent is a Democrat, sure. But she’s cashing checks from all the same companies as a MAGA republican: Walmart, Lockheed Martin, AstraZeneca, Raytheon and Meta. So when it comes to governing … how will she hold them accountable?

This fundamental hypocrisy has defined the Democratic Party for far too long, and it’s made our leaders mealy-mouthed when they could have been taking bold stances. In this dark moment of inequity, authoritarianism and fascist control, it’s kept us from demanding Medicare for All, a Green New Deal, a fair living wage, and debt forgiveness — policies that have broad appeal across the political spectrum.

If you feel as cynical and alone as I did in 2015, I don’t blame you. But I am running today because we deserve better. We deserve a new generation of leadership that refuses to toe the party line or buckle under establishment pressure. We deserve a generation of leadership that knows what it’s like to live with debt, to choose between groceries and rent and childcare, and to wonder why our tax dollars are funding a genocide while we struggle to make ends meet.

This new generation of leadership will end the vice grip of money in politics. We will stand up for immigrants and workers, and all those who have felt cast out of the halls of power. To quote the late, great Jesse Jackson, leader of the Rainbow Coalition that inspired generations of progressives to come: “If my mind can conceive it, my heart can believe it, I know I can achieve it.”

We don’t have to give in to the tyranny of the status quo. We can be part of a new generation of leaders, changing our country for the better. Join me in demanding change on March 3 at the ballot box!

Nida Allam is the vice chair of the Durham County Board of Commissioners and the first Muslim woman elected to office in North Carolina.

title: Why Valerie Foushee deserves reelection
author: Michael Parker
article_text:
On March 3, the voters of North Carolina’s 4th Congressional District (CD-4) will, in effect, select whom they wish to represent them in the House of Representatives for the next two years of the Trump administration. Our district needs a fighter who will deliver, and Congresswoman Valerie Foushee is the clear choice.

As the area hit the hardest by cuts to federal research and education grants, we need a proven legislator who will continue to fight this administration in any way possible. Having served on the Chapel Hill Town Council, I know how critical it is to have leaders who will fight for our district’s priorities in Congress while delivering federal funding for our local public schools, services and community programs. 

Congresswoman Foushee has already been successful in pushing progressive legislation and delivering federal funding in spite of the Republican majority. Her ability to deliver for CD-4 can most directly be seen through her work to bring federal funding to the district. In fiscal year 2024 alone, she was able to secure $12 million for the district to support important projects such as affordable housing in Durham and Chapel Hill, needed reconstruction at RDU Airport, solid waste disposal in Durham County and public safety improvements throughout the district. She has also helped return over $5 million from federal agencies to residents of CD-4 through her and her staff’s casework and was able to secure $1 million for critical wastewater treatment infrastructure in Hillsborough in December 2025 in spite of being in the minority. 

In early February, she was able to secure an additional $21 million for our district to update water infrastructure, improve transportation and expand affordable housing access. These contributions to our district cannot be taken lightly. Foushee’s ability to deliver more federal funding than any other NC Congressional Democrat through the Community Project Funding process in 2026, while being in the Congressional minority, suggests she will be able to deliver transformative change for our district when she’s in the majority.

Foushee’s contributions can be measured in more ways than money, however. She has championed progressive legislation like the Green New Deal, the Block the Bombs Act, Medicare for All, College for All and overturn Citizens United v. FEC, which has earned her the endorsement of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. She and her staff have also been steadfast in assisting CD-4 residents in fighting back against ICE’s depredations by leading legislation to end local law enforcement cooperation with ICE, while assisting our immigrant community with casework related to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). She also hosts community Know Your Rights information sessions while fighting to defund the agency entirely.

At a time when many Democrats have been lacking a backbone, she did not capitulate to MAGA and stood strong against the reopening of the government without the continuation of Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies. She’s also consistently voted against the GOP’s heinous bills, including the Big, Ugly Bill, boycotted Trump’s State of the Union address and voted to advance Articles of Impeachment against Trump this past December.

Legislatively, she has led numerous bills, including the National Gun Violence Research Act, the Redistricting Transparency and Accountability Act and a resolution pushing Trump to act on the blockade on humanitarian aid in Gaza with Rep. Pramila Jayapal. Despite having only served with Republican majorities in her three years in Congress, she was still able to pass her climate bill, the IMPACT Act, to help curb the 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions that concrete production accounts for. She has also been party to nine amicus briefs challenging the Trump Administration’s blatantly illegal and unconstitutional policies in court filings and helped lead rallies outside of ICE headquarters, the U.S. Department of Education and the U.S. Department of Treasury to call out the administration’s tyranny.

Valerie Foushee has been able to rise in the ranks of the Democratic Party, leading the Space & Aeronautics Subcommittee and successfully securing proper funding in the NASA Reauthorization Act, which passed the committee by a unanimous vote, despite the widespread federal funding cuts we are seeing across government agencies. 

She is also the sole Black member of the House Democratic commission on AI and brought the commission to our local HBCU, North Carolina Central University, the very first commission roundtable outside of Washington. Her progressive voice is what we need at the top of our government in order to deliver progressive priorities for this district as Democrats regain the majority in Congress.

Moreover, Foushee continues to champion causes that may not capture headlines, but that make real change for our community. Notably, she has personally introduced the Democracy Restoration Act with Rep. Jasmine Crockett to end the denial of voting rights based on criminal convictions, the Second Chance Mental Health Access Act with Rep. Robin Kelly to expand mental health services for individuals transitioning from incarceration back into the community, the Prison Libraries Act with Rep. Emanuel Cleaver to expand library resources in correctional facilities and the Federal Prisons Naloxone Access Act with Rep. Lucy McBath to ensure life-saving opioid reversal medications. 

She is also leading a Congressional inquiry into FCC Butner, located in this district, on staffing and prison conditions. While the fight for prison reform and the reintegration of incarcerated individuals into society may not make headlines, they are important initiatives that can help save lives here in our district, and across the country.

Valerie Foushee is a tireless worker who has delivered for our district her entire life. She was born here and attended a segregated elementary school in CD-4, attended college in CD-4, raised her family in CD-4 and has fought for the people of CD-4 for almost 30 years throughout her career in public service. Now in Congress, in just a few short years, Congresswoman Foushee has passed legislation through a Republican majority, secured millions in federal funding for CD-4, and has pushed the priorities of our district forward.

While we see hundreds of members of Congress roll over and give Trump clearance to pass his illegal policies, we have an experienced fighter representing us who has never stopped pushing for our needs with real results for our district. When Democrats can regain control of Congress, we want to see real change, and that’s what Congresswoman Foushee’s track record says she’ll deliver.

She is a fighter who wins for the people of CD-4. That’s what we need in Congress — a fighter who wins. On March 3, 2026, she needs to be reelected.

Michael Parker is a former Chapel Hill town councilman.

title: Community members share remembrances for Olivia Ayiku
author: Remembrances
article_text:
I served as the teaching assistant for Olivia Ayiku in the course "Political Analysis for Public Policy". From the start of the term, my goal was to ensure she had a seamless experience during our weekly online classes and discussion sessions. I still vividly remember sharing the Zoom link with her before every class and staying attentive throughout our meetings to resolve any technical difficulties she might face immediately.

I recall a specific moment when her laptop had an issue and she reached out to request an extension on an assignment. The instructor granted it, and I was very hopeful that she would soon be able to join our classes in person again. I never imagined that the next update I would receive would be the news of her passing. Although our time together was only a few weeks, she was a valued member of my section. My heart goes out to her family and friends during this incredibly difficult time.

Muhammad Sawaiz Fatar, Fuqua '26

~~~~~~

Meeting Olivia this past fall and getting to know her was a gift of grace. She and I talked about faith and writing and life and death. And we laughed — she was funny. And selfless and outward-focused. Her presence and active participation on this campus made Duke better.

Olivia’s name could not have been more appropriate, since the name Olive is associated with peace and wisdom. The last time I sat with her was the Tuesday before she left for Chicago. When I entered the cancer unit, I was fearful of what I was going to feel during and after that visit. Instead, I felt peace — absolute peace and love. The rest of that day (and I write these words deliberately), I felt unexpected lightness in my soul. I didn’t feel anger that this disease was taking such an amazing young woman, which is part of what I had expected to feel. Instead, I felt moved that she gave so freely in living and in dying.

Even as her illness progressed rapidly, she showed no self-pity, no signs of giving up, yet absolute peace with what awaited her. She muted her physical pain for the sake of anyone in the room with her. And she shone brighter. Her smile and eyes radiated light. What a testament to how to live a life. We can learn from Olivia. She might as well have taught a class on the values this institution emphasizes: humility, connections, curiosity. With humble confidence, Olivia greeted each day ready to take on whatever challenges. Maya Angelou might as well have been foreseeing a future Olivia Ayiku, whose ability to connect with others brought to life Angelou’s words: “…people will never forget how you made them feel.” How she made others feel was unforgettable. She remains unforgettable. Olivia’s curiosity about the world and her place in it was limited only by time.

How much Olivia accomplished in a short time on this Earth is evident in how loved she was by her family and friends and those of us who only got to know her for what feels like a fraction of a second.

Thank you so very much to Olivia and her family for kindly welcoming me. I will never forget the peace Olivia shared, and I will work each day to share that peace forward. She lit a torch of hope, determination and gratitude in so many of us. That is a life well lived.

Ginny Ramirez-DelToro, Trinity '01

title: When history calls, will Duke students answer?
author: Gabrielle Mollin
article_text:
When I read the news every day, it feels like I could be reading the content of a future history textbook. With surging political violence, global brinkmanship and deep cultural divides, the 2020s are shaping up to resemble the turbulent 1960s, like some have already suggested. 

The ‘60s began with the world dangerously close to nuclear war during the 1961 Cuban Missile Crisis. The decade saw worsening Cold War tensions, exemplified by the construction of the Berlin Wall. Across the world, American involvement in Vietnam deepened during the Tet Offensive, with sobering violence broadcast directly to Americans’ TV screens. Political violence at home led to the infamous assassinations of President Kennedy, Malcolm X, Martin Luther King, Jr. and Robert F. Kennedy in a mere span of five years. 

Right now, Americans and Iranians are bracing for a ​​potential war. The Trump administration is increasingly militaristic in Latin America, while pursuing mass deportation through masked agents with military-grade weapons. In recent years, Americans have witnessed two assassination attempts on President Donald Trump, the murder of Minnesotan Rep. Melissa Hortman and her husband, the assassination of Charlie Kirk, arson at Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro’s residence and the killing of two Israeli embassy staffers in D.C. The list sadly goes on. 

Yet amidst this darkness, the ‘60s still saw significant progress because of people who were willing to go against the grain. The Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts were secured because of Black Americans’ courage and tenacity during lunch counter sit-ins, boycotts and marches. Likewise, second-wave feminists, environmentalists, anti-war activists and gay rights supporters all made meaningful inroads in this period. What each of these groups knew was that change would not come unless they stood for it in unconventional, often uncomfortable, ways. 

In the ‘60s and throughout U.S. history, change has been consistently driven by young people brave enough to step outside the mold that was pushed upon them. And that’s where the historical consistency falls off; because when I look around campus, I don’t see nearly enough Duke students who are poised to step outside the box. Overwhelmingly, I see students falling in line. I see students moving further away from the idealism and willingness to challenge the status quo that has proved a consistent catalyst for historical change. Rather than being the drivers of change that these times warrant, students are sidelining passions and curiosity in favor of “prestige” and high salaries. 

Just like the ‘60s, we are living in a decade that is sure to stand out in our nation’s history. That means what we choose to do with our time has never been more important. Similar to the young agents of change in the ‘60s, the choices we make as college students about how we want to engage with the world around us hold power. Unlike older age groups, we are relatively unencumbered and malleable thinkers. The choice of our classes, majors, internships, post-grad plans and so on holds the power to turn into meaningful perspectives and experiences. When students lock themselves into a career in tech or finance from as early as their freshman year, they lose out on meaningful opportunities to develop their worldview as people independent of their careers or future obligations. They lose out on the power of being a young, free thinker in a historic decade. 

In the ‘60s, college students took charge of the anti-war movement, helping turn the tides of public opinion against the Vietnam War. Though notably, former President Joe Biden opted out. A sport coat-wearing law student focused on his career, young Biden remained disengaged from the peace movements of the time. Passing by a Students for a Democratic Society demonstration on campus, he recounted “they were taking over the building. And we looked up and said, ‘Look at those assholes.’ That’s how far apart from the antiwar movement I was.”

Over 50 years later, student activism resurfaced in a similar manner surrounding the conflict in Gaza and he struggled profusely in connecting with either side. His case demonstrates the risks of turning away from history when it’s essentially waiting on your doorstep, ready for you to face it. Biden may be a lofty comparison for most students, but the key point is that turning a blind eye to important moments in college may contribute to an out of touch, institutionalist mindset, the very kind of thinking that the changemakers of the ‘60s successfully bet against. 

I say all of this not to demonize individual students who find themselves on this popular path through corporate America; it’s popular for a reason. There are serious advantages for students to weigh, like a salary that can help them pay off their student loans. I know it’s not easy to turn away from such opportunities and I struggle with my decision to do so often. 

But while it may not seem to matter if you individually decide to follow this path, the culture that your choice is a part of matters. Think of the half of Duke students who graduate each year to enter big tech, finance, or consulting. Now think about the freshmen and sophomores who see these results every year and choose to opt into the path, keeping the trend going. Now expand that to the other elite colleges in the country, where job rates in these industries can reach as high as 60%. That’s thousands of students each year, losing out on an opportunity to break out of society’s mold and make history. The more we lose students to these industries each year, the less collective force we retain to agilely challenge and demand reform like previous generations have.

But the decade’s not over, and there’s still time to make its comparison to the ‘60s more than a repetition of violence and division. Regardless of what you know or don’t know about your future plans, you can still work to emulate the catalytic idealism of the ‘60s so that it might supersede the violence and division of today’s world. If you’re already committed to your pre-professional path, I’m not here to guilt you or push you to change your mind. But do not abandon your capacity for idealism. Stay informed. Stay engaged. Debate. Organize. Give. Vote. Don’t let comfort or routine get in the way of your capacity to do great things outside of the corporate mold. 

For those of you who haven’t yet figured out your path, good. Consider the historical comparison and take inspiration from the SNCC and the Freedom Rides, where young Black students decided changemaking was their path forward through the ‘60s. Or think of the number of students who took the risk of joining PeaceCorps or Americorps, which are still options to you today. While in Durham, think about spending time with Durham Public Schools, the Emily K Center, Habitat for Humanity, DukeEngage, the 9th Street Journal and more. More broadly, there’s Teach for America, Fulbright, non-profit work, public service, research, community organizing, etc. And while you wait to make your choice and enjoy your time at Duke, read deeply, argue fiercely, protest when necessary, build community, create art and so on. 

Whatever you have decided or will decide, history is waiting for you. 

Gabrielle Mollin is a Trinity senior. Her pieces typically run on alternate Thursdays.

title: After Stephen Buckley
author: Noor Nazir
article_text:
I don’t know their name or their story. But someone at Duke reported sexual misconduct by a faculty member and endured an investigation. This piece begins with the acknowledgment that their story is not mine to tell. 

The first time I realized I wanted to be a journalist at Duke was in Stephen Buckley's classroom. In his “News Writing and Reporting” class — every Wednesday for two and a half hours — I sat in the Sanford School of Public Policy. 

In October 2025, Duke placed Stephen Buckley, Eugene C. Patterson professor of the practice of journalism and public policy, on administrative leave. Journalism students were notified of his leave on Oct. 23; the reason was kept quiet. Around early December, he resigned. 

On Dec. 13, The Chronicle published an investigation outlining his misconduct that was later reported to have been in direct violation of Appendix L of the Faculty Handbook. He also resigned from his position at the Dallas Morning News.

I was affected by the aftermath, though in a fundamentally different way.

In the classroom, Buckley would sit at the head of the table and wouldn't just teach us how to structure a lede or tighten a nut graf. He also taught us that words are not decoration, they are responsibility. To tell someone’s story is a moral act. The more I reported and wrote for the class, the more my faith in journalism grew. I left that class understanding how to listen. And how to remember. For many of us, those classrooms shaped how we understood journalism.

I kept returning to his office for advice and to work through considerable self-doubt. He was a person of color considered a veteran in the journalism world. He was my representation in the DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy. In early October 2025, I emailed him, hoping to visit his office. It bounced back with an out-of-office response.

That was the first sign something had changed.

I thought about the classroom, the drafts covered in comments, the office hours where I went when I wasn’t sure my reporting was good enough. Those memories did not disappear, but they no longer felt simple. They now existed alongside a confirmed violation and the knowledge that someone had been harmed. In that collision, my focus moved beyond personal disappointment to the larger question of how an institution responds when a mentor’s authority has been misused.

I reference the following policies not to question them, but to acknowledge their purpose and the protections they are designed to provide: due process and the integrity of investigations.

Investigations involving students are governed by federal privacy law, including FERPA, which restricts the public disclosure of identifiable student information. Those protections are essential. When a student is connected to a misconduct case, the University’s ability to speak publicly is constrained not only by employment policy but by law. 

Under Duke’s OIE procedures, when a faculty member is found responsible for misconduct, the outcome is handled as an employment matter. That means the decision is routed through university officials and Human Resources for discipline. Because these cases often involve protected student information, the University’s ability to publicly disclose specific details is limited.

That said, there are multiple parties in moments like this: the survivor, the faculty member, the administration and the students who were mentored, advised and shaped. And so, an institution can follow every rule and still fall short of what a community needs.

Centering survivors and protecting their privacy must remain the institution’s first responsibility. The University cannot and should not disclose confidential information. But it can acknowledge impact and it can create space. Accountability and care must coexist in the practices of an institution committed to justice. Creating space for students to process does not minimize harm to survivors; it instead recognizes that serious violations affect entire academic communities.

The absence of broader acknowledgment in this case left many students without guidance or space to process the disruption. We received announcements and read The Chronicle articles. The University declined to comment publicly, citing privacy and legal constraints. Moments like this test whether the values taught inside classrooms are reflected in institutional practice.

Buckley’s lawyer spoke to The Chronicle on his behalf, but did not address The Chronicle directly. What emerged publicly was partial and procedural, not relational. What followed was silence — the sudden removal of a faculty member following a serious violation disrupted academic relationships and mentorship pathways, possibly for many students. 

However, it does not need to be this way. 

When a faculty member is placed on administrative leave, the University can communicate that an investigation is underway and acknowledge the disruption to students, without discussing confidential details, a process followed by peer institutions. If the faculty member resigns or is found responsible, the school should then provide structured support for students who were directly mentored or supervised. 

There is precedent: when Harvard professor John L. Comaroff was placed on administrative leave following sexual harassment allegations, the university publicly confirmed sanctions after they finished their internal review. Still, universities should do more. 

Leadership should also proactively contact students who were directly supervised or closely mentored, offering one-on-one academic guidance. A sudden departure can leave research projects, career plans and recommendation pathways in limbo. Those practical gaps require prompt attention.

Finally, the school should also issue a follow-up communication. This should be separate from any disciplinary notice. It should reaffirm its values and clarify available support resources. Students should hear, clearly and publicly, that accountability and care are not competing principles.

These steps should not violate privacy or relitigate facts. They should simply recognize that students are stakeholders in the academic community and that when something serious occurs, silence compounds uncertainty.

A year into Duke, in that Wednesday classroom, I learned that words are a moral act and that accountability and care must coexist. If that is true inside the classroom, it must also be true outside of it.

Due process, survivor protection and community care are not competing values. A just institution must practice all three. The first sign that something had changed shouldn’t have been just an out-of-office reply. 

Noor Nazir is a Trinity junior. Her column typically runs on alternate Tuesdays.

title: Why can’t I do everything?
author: Ryan Growney
article_text:
I want to learn how to paint. 

I’ve never considered myself artistic — that was always my brother’s area of expertise. It’s simply always been one of those micro-ambitions that stack up like boxes in mental corners because I’ve let other parts of life become priorities. It’s not the only one. I want to pick up the guitar again. I want to read more about the Greek myths I once loved as a kid, to get more into chess, to dive into physics and to build my own version of Shazam to see how it works. 

In high school, it was easy to push those interests off — later, when I had more time, I would get around to it. Later, I would be in a place where the structure and community put exploration to the forefront. Later, I would be in college, where I would be able to explore all these scattered interests and more. 

Yet, as my second semester here at Duke flies by, I’m beginning to realize that time here is even more precious than it was in high school. It’s not even possible to explore all the beckoning crannies and niches and questions near my area of study, much less the far-off ideas that peek through dog-eared pages on my bookshelf. Yet, this feels like my last chance. I don’t plan on going to graduate school, so I can’t think of the next time I will be in a place where exploration is expected. I won’t have the ability to spend my days in courses taught by experts in their fields, nor the depth that comes from living amongst people purely focused on asking questions. 

I’ve already written about what kinds of activities I think Duke students should participate in, but I’m quickly realizing that an arguably more relevant question is what we shouldn’t do. More importantly, how much should we be okay not doing? 

Over the past few years, I’ve read a lot of biographies. John von Neumann, Bertrand Russell, Immanuel Kant; it’s so marvelously interesting to see these larger-than-life people put back into the context of the real world. While biographies are often sobering to their subject’s legacy in a number of ways, what always astounds me is the breadth of ideas their subjects touch. von Neumann created game theory, contributed meaningfully to quantum physics and statistics and helped invent the computer. Kant wrote on beauty, travel, politics and religion in between his contributions to metaphysics and ethics. These people were polymaths in the true sense of the word. 

When I think of true success, it is this type of person that comes to mind. I am under no misconceptions about being the next mathematical-scientific revolutionary, but I’ve always admired the idea of the “Renaissance man.” Exploring, discovering, understanding big questions unhindered by disciplinary bounds — that is what learning should be. At Duke, it feels possible too. Here, scattered interests are easy to justify. We are a liberal arts institution, and Duke earns that name every day through the innumerable multitudes of classes and clubs and organizations and opportunities we have to engage. You can’t walk two steps in any building without being bombarded with colorful posters and signs about this lecture and that club and the next opportunity to take advantage of. I can say unreservedly that Duke does an amazing job of creating the structure for exploration. 

The difficult part about biographies, however, is that they compress decades of life into dozens of pages. You need time just as much as structure to explore something you’re interested in, and any Duke student can tell you that time is a rare commodity. Maybe it’s arrogant to expect out of four years the diversity of someone working for forty, but that passion is exactly what I came to Duke to pursue. To sacrifice that would be to sacrifice the dream that makes this school what it is, the dream of what this school will let me be. It’s a standoff between who I want to be and the reality of getting there.

But it’s not really a standoff. It’s an unstoppable force versus a movable object. When our means can’t meet our ends, there are two options: scale down our ends or scale up our means. I can’t add more hours to the day, or somehow squeeze twice as much productivity out of the 24 I already have, so scaling down it is. I must be the one to change my views. I can’t do all my classwork, participate in clubs, tent with my friends and also spend the hour I want to with a guitar pick and a paintbrush in hand. I have to choose. Yet each choice closes off a version of who I want to be.

I can choose to pick up the guitar again. I can choose to foray into painting or chess or classics. But it feels like an hour spent on one interest is an hour not spent on the others. Behind each club I joined is 10 that I didn’t. I know in my mind that narrowing down my options, honing in on what I want to pursue is exactly what Duke and college in general is all about, but it doesn’t make it feel any less momentous. Any less scary. 

There’s no biography that covers the interstitial time between moments of becoming who we are. There’s no biography that discusses the nagging in the back of your brain about the hobby you never picked up, the dog-eared page never revisited. There’s no biography about the quiet ache of choice, of a million little doors closed on a million micro-ambitions. I could wax poetic about the polymaths I admire and how we remember them for the bold steps they took instead of the ones they didn’t, but that’s not the point. At Duke, we’re asked to live in the interstitial time, parse out who we want to be just as much as we expand it. 

Maybe this is what “growing up” is, living with the loneliness of choice.

I still want to learn how to paint. I still want to learn more about physics and to come back to the mythology I loved so much. I don’t know which of those doors I’ll keep open, or how many will quietly close without my noticing. But, slowly, moment by moment, I’m starting to become okay with simply not doing.

Ryan Growney is a Trinity first-year. His pieces typically run on alternate Wednesdays.

title: On writing
author: Anna Garziera
article_text:
This is now my final semester, and what better time to finally take a writing class to improve these biweekly opinion articles, which I’ve now been writing for almost three years.

Before “Intro to Creative Nonfiction,” my formal writing training was close to null. The last time I remember getting writing feedback was on a persuasive essay for AP English Language which I’d fashioned after Martin Luther King Jr.’s famous “I Have a Dream” speech. The feedback was curt: sentences too long; missing evidence; lots of deadwood.

As much as I wanted to, I couldn’t disagree with Mr. Martin. Junior year of high school was a time in my life when I read old English novels like Jane Austen’s “Emma” and “Pride and Prejudice” more to feel well-read, than because I enjoyed them. Inevitably, I started picking up some of Austen’s writing habits, hence the long sentences.

The “missing evidence” had to do with the way I voice my beliefs without always having a good reason to believe them. In my AP Lang essay, the evidence meant to persuade (about what, I don’t remember) must have been miles short of abounding. I tend to blabber on, thinking I’m being convincing when, in fact, I’m just being stubborn.

The last bit, the “deadwood,” referred to all the extra words in my sentences and extra sentences in my paragraphs Mr. Martin didn’t think I needed. Every good writer knows concision is King. Like clarity, it's non-negotiable. The reader will get bored if you don’t get to the meat of your argument within the first few lines.
