Which makes me think I should be moving on to that right about —

Now, here’s my argument: Writing matters not because we compose new ideas, but because we begin to see old ones in a new light.

During our first class, my creative writing professor told us, “To write is to think.” In other words, writing ideas down lets you understand, internalize, and release your thoughts.

Why do you think I write my articles? 

One answer could be that I am a modern Narcissus. The son of a river-god, I like to update you — society — the universe — with what’s been going on in my life because I’m self-obsessed. I revel in images of myself and can’t help but share them with the whole campus. That’d be pretty strange. I’d have to be completely out of options if the best way for me to vent my vanity is to an anonymous audience. 

The other way to see me is the right way — as a confused senior who is trying to figure herself out. I’m someone who always has too many thoughts in her head. Not to sound ungrateful. I’d probably get bored if my internal narrative were single-voiced or linear. But it’s a lot sometimes — I need to write my ideas down to make sense of them. So I extract my thoughts like an unmagical Dumbledore: pen and paper, my personal pensieve. 

My thoughts, though abundant, won’t blow your mind. They don’t stretch further than what you’d expect a fairly well educated 21-year-old’s thoughts to stretch. What I tell you through these articles, you’ve probably heard before. 

This shouldn’t surprise you. It has to do with the way writing has been used throughout the centuries. 

If I had to make a biased, non-evidence based guess, I’d say most of what’s been written by humans since the very start has to do with discovering our nature and the meaning of life. It’s inevitable. Our place in the world, our ambitions, our jealousies, are the kinds of things we both fully know and don’t understand. So we write about them.

Let me give you an example. I just finished reading Willa Cather’s “The Professor’s House” for a class, and I obviously loved it. Very roughly, the story explores a professor’s midlife crisis, triggered by his deceased, brilliant protégé, Tom Outland. What’s not to love — Cather brought up all my favorite topics, using words so beautiful they took my breath away. More importantly, they made me think.

This is just to say, if what I feed you every two weeks is food for thought, just know it’s been chewed, digested and regurgitated by generations of people before us. In fact, if you have some guts, you can hear the lore directly from the original philosophers. Plato, Socrates, Aristotle, knew what they were talking about. And what they were talking about are the same things we’re talking about, with our friends, lights off, till the early hours of the morning. 

More than you and me, these thinkers knew how to put their ideas into words. That has value. But if those tomes intimidate you, you can try taking the easier route. Ask your old friend Chat GPT: “What’s the meaning of life?” 

“Thinking …“

“That’s one of the biggest questions humans have ever asked. There isn’t one universally agreed answer. For many people, meaning is: Loving and being loved; Learning and growing; Experiencing life deeply; Being part of something bigger than themselves.”

Thanks, Chat. I think we had that much figured out.

The reality is, as explorers of life, we’ve just about run out of points to make. This doesn’t mean writing like I am doing now is useless. It serves a few purposes. Firstly, it helps me articulate complex ideas and therefore understand them. That’s the selfish part of this. Secondly, it may enlighten someone out there, a young reader, by exposing them to an idea they hadn’t encountered before. Lastly, it reexposes the rest of the masses to the same old ideas, but maybe framed in a new way that persuades them. 

Were you impressed by ChatGPT’s rundown of the meaning of life? I didn’t think so. But it’s not because its “ideas” are wrong. They’re just bleak and dry and abstract. 

The secret of life isn’t a secret. It’s just hard to internalize. Good writing inevitably helps us with that. It’s only when Tom, looking back on the summer he spent on the Mesa, says, “I was full to the brim, and needed dark and sleep,” that we too think, “That’s it. I have found it out.”

Anna Garziera is a Trinity senior. Her pieces typically run on alternate Sundays.

title: North Carolina’s Zohran Mamdani: Nida Allam is exactly what Congress needs
author: Leo Goldberg
article_text:
On Feb. 13, a niagara of political energy flooded into Durham as the Bull City became the latest stop on Senator Bernie Sanders’ nationwide “Fighting Oligarchy” tour. The rally served as a chilling reminder of exactly what ordinary Americans are up against in this country: their mass political and economic disempowerment at the hands of a highly stratified class of self-aggrandizing billionaires who own monopolies on media, information and political power, encouraged by a pliant, mercenary government.

Over 1,000 people turned out to hear Sanders echo his decades-long political message. But they also came to hear from a much younger, much more local political figure who is as committed to realizing his admirable vision: Durham County Commissioner Nida Allam. 

Running a fierce campaign to unseat current incumbent Valerie Foushee in the Democratic primary for NC-04’s House seat, Allam seeks nothing less than the rightful restoration of political power to the public. Drawing and proudly embracing comparison to NYC mayor Zohran Mamdani, her candidacy is based on the recognition that a massive political overhaul is needed to deliver to ordinary people the basic, common-sense political and economic policies out of which they have long been cheated by a dysfunctional and highly ossified establishment.

I spoke with Allam in an interview to learn more about what she hopes to bring to Congress and why. “I'm running for Congress because, as a commissioner, I couldn't sit idly by and tell my constituents in good conscience that you have to wait 3 years for change,” she said. 

She cited the increasingly exorbitant cost of living as well as the authoritarianism of the Trump administration as just some of the crises too important to postpone until a later election date. Allam sees her community in urgent need of what she termed “common sense” policies — a living wage, healthcare and a liveable planet, among others. “These are not partisan issues,” she stated.

Indeed, they are not. We often disregard and passively accept, due to propaganda and platitudinous talking points in this country, how truly appalling it is that Americans’ right to live or die is determined by their employment status, or how millions lack adequate wages to support a decent lifestyle in the richest country in the world. 

The U.S.’s venal, money-infested political culture operates on a class of concentrated elites who spend billions of dollars conglomerating media and buying off politicians to convince ordinary Americans to vote against their own interests. This political bribery was legalized by the Supreme Court in 2010, when it ruled in Citizens United v. FEC that corporations could spend unlimited amounts of money on advertisements for political candidates. 

To this day, the verdict remains one of the worst Supreme Court decisions in U.S. history. Under the ruling, for example, pharmaceutical companies can (and do) spend millions to help elect candidates in exchange for the promise to vote against subsidized health care and convince taxpaying Americans that they are lazy and entitled to expect standard first-world social services in return. 

For Allam, reforming this system is one of her top priorities. She was adamant in what she characterized as “getting this corporate corruption out of our political systems.” That is also what she views as perhaps the biggest difference between herself and her opponent, Valerie Foushee. To Allam, Foushee’s acceptance of financial contributions from corporations and Political Action Committees (PACs) undermines her integrity as a candidate. 

“Why, in a safe blue seat, are we even accepting corporate cash money?” she asked. “Corporations that have been lobbying and union busting across the country, like Walmart, have written checks to our incumbent. Meanwhile, North Carolina’s minimum wage hasn't been increased in over two decades, and is stuck at $7.25. To be able to afford the cost of living while raising a family here, you would have to be earning $24 an hour.” 

Foushee, it is important to note, has done many good things in Congress and is, by and large, on the better side of U.S. politicians. But because she willingly enjoys the lavish financial support of corporations and PACs, she belongs in the class of politicians in this country who are politically compromised. There is no way around that. And as Allam rightly points out, there is no reason why, in a district as reliably blue as NC-04, constituents cannot have a Congressional representative who is both right on the issues and has sound political integrity.

When elected leaders can safely rely on a reservoir of corporate wealth to sustain their tenures in power, it relieves them of the obligation to listen to and act in the interests of the people they represent. This is precisely the dilemma that debauches America’s governmental framework and estranges ordinary Americans from political power. The inability to make progress on every major issue in the U.S. today, independent of ideological stance, stems from this critical juncture. 

Perhaps no position is more undermined by this than foreign policy, specifically U.S. military aid to Israel. Numerous politicians gladly accept handsome checks from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), effectively buying unconditional support for the furnishing of the Israeli military and insulating such decision-making from critical thought or moral consideration. 

Once again, Foushee is grossly at fault. She happily enjoyed the patronage of millions of dollars of AIPAC financial support for years until August 2025, when she reversed course and announced she would no longer take AIPAC money. 

This change of heart, whether genuine or out of political expedience, did not impress Allam. “I know that [Foushee] has said she's no longer going to take AIPAC money. But to take that pledge now is not going to bring those 70,000 lives back,” she said in reference to the current death toll in Gaza. 

For Allam, this issue is personal. “As a mother of 2 young kids, I see my children in the eyes of the children of Gaza,” she said. “I had an emergency C-section for one of my daughters. It is unbelievable to think of the amount of Palestinian women who are having C-sections without any anesthesia, without any proper medical facilities, because all the hospitals have been destroyed. And we have an elected official who still refuses to call Netanyahu a war criminal.” 

Even for those who may instinctively object to Allam as too far left to govern (because inculcated defense mechanisms naturally kick in), her record illustrates an impressive success of passing progressive legislation even under tough circumstances. Reflecting on her time as Durham County Commissioner, she recounted with pride her hard-fought success in passing the low income homeowner tax relief program for Durhamites. 

“Passing that program took getting scrappy,” she said in reference to significant opposition from Republican attempts to exert authority on local government. “Even with all the restrictions and limitations, we were able to push through this policy and find a way to get relief to our residents who needed it the most,” she said.

She invoked this example not only to demonstrate her ability to negotiate with political opposition but also to push back against the narrative often put forward by Democrats that they cannot advance substantial legislation in Republican-majority chambers in Congress. “You can accomplish progressive things even in states like North Carolina, where the powers at the state level are trying to block you every step of the way,” Allam said. “But it's gonna take hard work. It's gonna take determination. That's what I want to bring to the halls of D.C.”

Indeed, the halls of D.C. are in desperate need of it. Currently, the political sentiment in America is one of dread, pessimism and fear. Donald Trump is a deeply unpopular and disliked president, and the establishment of the Democratic Party has nothing to offer to meet the moment. There is, and has been for decades, a dire need for massive political change in this country. Nida Allam, and what she stands for, has the potential to deliver it. And unlike Foushee, who embraces progressivism largely when it is suitable, Allam adopts it unconditionally.

As shown by Zohran Mamdani in New York, there do exist leaders capable of winning political office who both listen to their constituents and deliver substantial results, and do so with grace, wit and class. On March 3 (and during early voting), we have the chance to elect such leadership here, too. If we desire leaders who are both receptive and uncompromised, and fight for policies that combat the massive upward transfer of wealth and power in this country, it is those like Allam who offer the best chance of doing so. 

Leo Goldberg is a Trinity sophomore. His pieces typically run on alternate Mondays.

title: Within the stacks of books
author: Robert Wallace
article_text:
My first bookstore experience was in a strip-mall. It sold trinkets and other whatnots, greeting cards and posters, along with books. I was a sixteen-year-old teenager when I discovered the bookstore. The entire side wall was for books. It was a vast wall full of “classics” that I would spend hours perusing. It was a time in my life when I wondered who I was destined to become, what I was meant to be, like all teenagers. I wondered how I was going to survive multiple family traumas. 

And reading became my best friend.

It was at this bookstore — I forget its name — that I first discovered Steinbeck, Hemingway and Faulkner. Later, Morrison, Wright and Ellison. I loved to pick up the Bantam Books, with the red or black rooster on its spine. 

Just the feel of the books excited me. Steinbeck’s titles and the pictures on the front of the books, pictures of Lennie and George, the Joad’s, seasonal workers, those oppressed and exploited and the dark Vintage spines of Faulkner’s “The Sound and the Fury” or “As I Lay Dying”, which signaled something psychological or enigmatic inside. 

Back then, on cold, rainy days, I would spend hours looking at the books, pulling them off the shelves, reading the descriptions on the back. Sometimes I would sit on the floor, crossed-legged, a stack of books beside me, and often I would flip through them, reading whole pages and the time would pass. The owners never rushed me. Sometimes they would come by and smile at me and say, “Finding everything?” or “Quite a stack you have there!” But that was more out of politeness than anything. Mostly, they let me be. 

It was at this bookstore that I first discovered and purchased the Russians, mostly Dostoyevsky, but Turgenev and the shorter novels of Tolstoy, too. The books were thick and had pictures — especially those in Dostoyevsky’s — of people on the front who appeared tormented by inner demons. I used to stuff these books in the back pockets of my jeans, the books inevitably protruding out of the pockets, and, with them, often a back that ached because of the awkward positions they created while sitting. 

For a while, I carried “Crime and Punishment” and “Notes from Underground” in both back pockets, simultaneously flipping back and forth between Raskolnikov’s tortured soul and the “Underground Man’s” monologue ramblings. I don’t know if the balance helped my back or not, but I remember the excitement I felt carrying them around, just knowing that I was hauling whole worlds that were waiting to be discovered, and, hopefully, understood.

This year will mark the sixty-second anniversary of Brown v. Board of Education. Parents of children in Topeka, Kansas, brought forth the suit, claiming separate but equal was inherently unequal because segregation created a society that left the children of the underprivileged at a distinct disadvantage. They were right. 

And where have we come in the past sixty-plus years? Has anything changed? Has Durham changed? 

The city of Durham is a very diverse community, composed of 46 percent white and 54 percent non-white citizens,including over one hundred thousand Black Americans. Durham is improving in the proportion of adults with a high school diploma. So, too, are we improving in the number of Black Americans graduating from high school within four years. Yet, there is a lot more progress to be made. One in every four Hispanic students in Durham Public Schools is dropping out before finishing. One in five students from economically disadvantaged backgrounds does not graduate within four years. These are groups being targeted disproportionately by the current administration, which may only cause further harm. 

Without a doubt, Brown v. Board of Education has improved the educational lives of millions of minority children. This is a good thing. However, recent research has shown that children, regardless of nationality, culture or background, are reading for pleasure less and less. Sadly, this is also true for adults. Many children do not read for pleasure at all. Many don’t even have books at home. 

But even the privileged, despite having the resources, aren’t reading for the pure joy of the experience. Reading for pleasure is an act of play. Much in the same way children from generations past were free to engage in activities of their own choosing outdoors, reading for pleasure does the same for the mind that free play used to do for children’s bodies — it engages them, it teaches them empathy and it sets in motion the foundation for all sorts of learning and development. 

We must encourage our children to read. We must encourage everyone to read. This is all our responsibility. Reading is integral to human survival. Many would not have us read, to limit our access to books, to limit what we choose to read. To limit who gets to read at all. Ray Bradbury said, “You don’t have to burn books to destroy a culture. Just get people to stop reading them.” To read is an act of love and an act of political courage. 

And it is everyone’s responsibility to see that children have books in their homes to read. 

Even today, I still get a tingle when I enter a bookstore. When I go to The Regulator Bookshop, I enter with an open mind, browsing through the fiction, non-fiction, and literary journals. To look upon their shelves is as much an act of self-discovery as it is discovering something I didn’t know within the pages of a book. For that is what reading can teach us; it can teach us something about someone else, but, often, it teaches us more about ourselves. 

Robert Wallace is a first-year graduate student of liberal studies. His column, 'Telling Stories', typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: Um, so about those layoffs …
author: Wendy House
article_text:
Is it rude to say “I told you so?” Honestly, I couldn’t care less. I did tell y’all so. 

In 2025, Duke responded to sweeping federal funding cuts by immediately folding under pressure and buying out employees with “voluntary” retirement incentives, followed by layoffs. About 600 staff — constituting 5% of the workforce — and 82 faculty chose to accept the incentive. 

What is alarming on the surface of this is the total lack of transparency from the Duke administration. Regardless of the necessity of layoffs, or lack thereof, it is the obligation of any respectable employer to be very clear about how they are proceeding when layoffs do happen. We should not have to be rooting around for information on the who, what, when, and why of layoffs like truffle hogs. Yet, there have been no updates on the tally of terminated employees since September 2025; there have not been any breakdowns released of terminations by department — ever. 

When I wrote my article last October, ranting about Duke’s insufficient minimum wage, I briefly mentioned the layoffs. I questioned how it could be possible for seven-figure salaries to remain stagnant while overworked service staff, barely able to put food on their own table, are denied their right to be recognized and negotiate as a union. I also noted that I am by no stretch of the imagination qualified to analyze Duke’s finances. Well, I’m pleased to say that while I may not be an accountant, someone else went and hired one. 

Fed up with Duke’s overzealous cost-cutting (as compared with peer institutions), Duke’s chapter of the American Association of University Professors commissioned Dr. Howard Bunsis to give them the real dirt. Bunsis has a storied history of over two decades busting bloated university administrations, one which has not been met without pushback from said administrations. You might be able to guess what his review of Duke’s finances found:

The cuts were not a financial necessity.

To make a long story short, Bunsis pointed to billions in unrestricted reserve funds — tied up in assets — which we have failed to tap into during these times of strife. While recognizing the financial complexity of reserved funds, he questioned why the administration wouldn’t dip into this resource rather than disrupt entire livelihoods for money two orders of magnitude less significant. We’re talking 20 or 30 million compared to billions with a “b.”

I don’t see how there’s anything I can argue that would carry more weight than the well-researched analysis of an actual accountant. It is beyond debate at this point that the Duke administration has grossly overcorrected against federal cuts –– which they refuse to resist — and utterly singed the very people who keep our lights on. We have the math to prove it. What is more alarming to me is that the administration doesn’t seem overly concerned that we know this. 

At least at other institutions Dr. Bunsis has reviewed, administrations have responded heatedly with long statements defending their honor. Well, our guys are going on three weeks past D-Day now. And unless I’ve gone blind, I’m quite sure there has been no comment released. 

This is ringing with uncomfortable resemblance to the administration’s refusal to acknowledge the demands of Durham Rising in a timely or respectful fashion. I mean, what are they doing in their offices? Playing patty-cake? Poring over investment portfolios like Smaug over his golden hoard? Layoffs are anathema to a healthy university environment; they sow and spread fear faster than the freshman flu propagates. They should be the last possible resort during financial hardship, and the suggestion that they were treated as anything less than that should be felt as a personal insult to any employer with a remote interest in respectability. 

This also comes at a time when Duke is failing to protect its immigrant employees. As if Luis’ initial departure wasn’t enough of a stain on our commitment to hardworking, delightful employees, he was ousted a second time by another federal decision. Another employee, a housekeeper named Margoth Erazo, was almost identically affected by the citizenship struggle for Honduran immigrants. While our hearts get yanked around in the fight to keep valuable staff like Luis and Margoth, Duke goes on, neglecting to get them employment based visas.

This comes at a time when Duke is also failing to protect its immigrant employees. Two weeks ago, we were all elated to hear Luis Juarez was set to return to campus after a federal ruling voiding the revocation of his Temporary Protected Status. Even in this, Duke attempted to shortchange him by initially offering only entry-level salary and benefits, an offer which is completely beyond the pale to a veteran employee of nearly two decades. However, he was torn from us yet again by another judicial turn and could not come back to campus. Another employee, a housekeeper named Margoth Erazo, was almost identically affected by attacks on the protected status of Honduran immigrants; Margoth was denied her former job, even during the period when her TPS was reinstated. While our hearts get yanked around in the fight to keep integral staff like Luis and Margoth, Duke goes on neglecting to get them employment based visas. 

So, the next time you greet the person in WU making your breakfast, lunch or dinner, remember this. Remember, they are working for an administration that could respect them, but will not. Next time you interact with a professor, consider that someone in their department may have been pressured into retirement by a buyout. And next time you see that ugly monstrosity currently wrapping itself around what used to be the Rueben-Cooke Building, remember that there are about 700 employees who could have been kept on if our budget valued actual excellence instead of productive-sounding noise. 

Wendy House is a Trinity sophomore. Her column typically runs on alternate Wednesdays.

title: To any freshman who watched the North Carolina vs. Duke game
author: Hana Stepnick
article_text:
On Feb. 8, 2020, I witnessed a miracle. Two, actually. I was with my friend Sam and a hundred or so other freshmen in Trinity, watching the referee bounce the ball to then-sophomore point guard Tre Jones for his second free-throw attempt. There were 4.4 seconds left on the clock. 84-82, Carolina. “Everyone is standing in this building,” the announcer said of the Dean Dome. We were too. We had been down 13 with five minutes to go, down nine with two.

Jones doesn’t dribble. He chucks it up to the rim. Miss. He turns around, dashes over his right shoulder, catches his own rebound, steps back … swish, right at the buzzer. We scream as the game goes into overtime.

Four and a half minutes later. Joey Baker misses a three. Down three, 20 seconds to go. Baker fouls, down five. Jones gets a layup and gets fouled, down three, but he misses the free throw. Wendell Moore Jr. layup, down one. Jones fouled again. He makes the first one, tie game, then goes up for the second.

“A MISS” the announcer screams. “A TAP!” And it’s back in Jones’ hands for the game-winning jumper, a shot that veers so far to the left that every tenth of a second is physically painful. Except Moore, at the same time, is charging towards the basket. He tips it in — and that’s game, baby. I jump up and down with my friends whose names I hadn’t known seven months prior.

To all of the freshmen who witnessed the loss to Carolina last Saturday, I don’t tell this story to brag. Less than a month later, on March 7, 2020, Duke beat Carolina by 13 in Cameron. I watched my first bench burn, then I went home for spring break. 72 hours later, the University told us not to come back.

I won’t regale you with tales of being in college during Covid, but what were once indiscriminate gatherings in ridiculous numbers and disgustingly close proximity became a lot of time outdoors and on Zoom, still laughing but fully masked. It was a time of abrupt changes. One day, I woke up and realized one side of every swinging blue bench on campus was gone. College was still there, but it was less.

But life and basketball, synonymous on Tobacco Road, came back swinging. In May 2021, my fall study abroad program was cancelled. But while God may taketh away, he also giveth. And, for my entire life, my God was a man: named Mike Krzyzewski, who announced in June 2021 that he would be retiring at the end of the season.

2026 marks the first time in 47 years that no undergraduate remembers sharing a campus with Coach K, a man so famous that we literally bowed down every time he stepped onto a court adorned with his name.

I went to games whenever I could. Tuesday 9 pms. Saturday 3 pms. My friends and I didn’t even wait for them to announce if there would be a tenting test for the UNC game — we knew we would be there. We became certified stalkers to secure our place in line (My group was able to draw Trevor Keels’ tattoo, but we did not know Theo John’s dog’s birthday. We’ll always regret it.)

No one thought we would lose. Duke blew out UNC by 20 points in February. ESPN was slapping Coach K’s face on pizza boxes and coffee cups. This was our destiny. After the past year, we deserved it.

Basketball, of course, had other plans. The game started decently. Close, but we steadily led for most of it. It started to fall apart with around 10 minutes left. We were tied up, 61-61, and Paolo Banchero, a man who would be picked as number one in the NBA draft a few months later, turned the ball over. 

With 2:25 remaining, Jeremy Roach stood at the line, 82-75. Our hands went up, like a prayer. In. In. There was a collective feeling of divinity, only slightly influenced by the preceding 10 hours of drinking and the five weeks of sleep deprivation. But also the specter of Coach K’s 42 seasons as the winningest college men’s basketball coach of all time, his almost perfectly tied all-time record against our greatest rival and everyone like my dad, sitting three hundred miles north of me in his favorite Duke sweatshirt, soon to be disappointed.

About an hour after those free throws, I remember lying on my friend’s dorm room floor in Crowell, downing some Krafthouse chicken tenders, not speaking.

Hope, of course, found a way. We breezed through the first and second rounds of March Madness, then pulled it out against Texas Tech in the Sweet Sixteen. My friends and I, Stockholm Syndrome-d by waiting in line, camped out in Krafthouse all day to get a booth to watch the Elite Eight. (About five minutes before the game, other students started dragging tables in from Panera.)

Running around campus that night with my friends is one of my favorite memories from college.

The next day, Chapel Hill unsurprisingly knocked off the 15-seed Saint Peter’s Peacocks, setting up a Final Four meetup never seen before, despite our 36 combined appearances. The table was set for K’s swan song. Redemption was so close, we could taste it. 

But revenge, the Class of 2023 soon learned, is a dish best served successfully. UNC’s Caleb Love hit a three-pointer with 28 seconds to go that the internet lovingly describes as a “dagger.” Try a machete.

But I was a junior. I had more time. 

We won both games my senior year, after tenting again. I remember jumping up and down with my best friends when we won the home game, with Scheyer en route to going undefeated in Cameron that year. 

Last April, I sat in complete silence with many of those same friends in an apartment in D.C. as Duke broke down in the final two minutes against Houston. And last Saturday, I stood in a bar during that last minute against UNC, jaw dropped. My friend Sam was with me.

Duke basketball taught me that to love is to lose. To love something so much that you’re willing to sacrifice your time and energy (and, uh, grades, health, friendships and everything else tested during tenting). To love something so much that you feel every loss in your bones and win in your chest.

As so much ink in this publication has covered that I could hyperlink every word in this sentence with an example, perfection is elusive. But the ability to love something, as imperfect as it may be, is not.

When you are out of college, when you are old and washed up like me, when your frontal lobe is fully developed and when your friends are sprawled across the country, I promise you’ll miss those depression chicken tenders almost as much as the feeling of hot sparks off a flaming bench. You will recollect the slump of your roommate’s head on your shoulder as vividly as the loud cheers. You’ll recall crying both because the best thing just happened and the worst thing just happened. You’ll remember all the parts that sucked, and you’ll remember that you loved them too, at least sort of.

So, to all the freshmen reading this, keep your head up. Go hug your friends you didn’t know existed seven months ago. Take it from me: there will always be another game.

Hana Stepnick, Trinity ’23, is a speechwriter in Washington, D.C.

title: Linking lamentation with love
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
On the heels of Valentine’s Day, I’ve been thinking of the connection between love and lamentation.

The Hebrew prophet Jeremiah once said, “My joy is gone, grief is upon me, my heart is sick.” He’s living in a land of lament. Have you ever been there, to that land where lamentation is life? Jeremiah knows how to moan his mourning better than a blues singer. He releases the raw reality of his humanity. He’s honest with great pathos, which is an implicit challenge to a dishonest, detached, apathetic spiritual life that ignores grief and suffering and pain in the world. Jeremiah laments because he loves his people. 

If we’re honest, we could easily say, “My heart is sick.” You can be honest about how sometimes life sucks. You can face reality without putting on a façade and not shrink back from the jagged edges of life. You can scream into a pillow if you want and raise blues-inflected questions like “Why?” and “How?” You don’t have to rush to skip over the pain and agony of life and jump into celebratory bliss. So often you have to go “through,” just as the hymn “Amazing Grace” notes: “through many dangers, toils and snares.”

Because of this “through-ness” of life, I think we should love lamentation and not ignore it or lock it up in a desk drawer or barricade it in a closet. Rather, we should unleash it and free it from our hearts and vocal cords. 

As legendary preacher Gardner Taylor once said in an interview, “One needs in one’s diet more than candy.” Too much candy — only celebration — will give you rotten teeth. We need the fiber of lamentation in our spiritual diet.

We can learn this from St. Augustine in his book “Confessions” when he talks about how he didn’t shed a tear at his mother’s funeral. But the next day, he writes, “The tears which I have been holding back streamed down, and I let them flow as freely as they would, making of them a pillow for my heart. On them it rested….” 

His heart rests on a pillow of tears, a pillow of lamentation. He loved his mother so dearly that his expression of lamentation — his tears — was an act of love. 

The philosopher Nicholas Wolterstorff lost his twenty-five-year-old son many years ago in a tragic mountain climbing accident, and wrote the book “Lament for a Son.” “If he was worth loving, he is worth grieving over,” Wolterstorff writes. “Every lament is a love-song.”

Lament — if we practice it — can mean that we love deeply. Our lament can be a love song for those whose loved ones have been killed in the Israel-Palestine or Ukraine-Russia conflict, or for a nation gripped by deep polarization or for the environment that is being destroyed or for a friend we’ve lost due to a car accident. That’s why when Jesus wept at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, the onlookers said, “See how he loved him!” (John 11:35-36). 

Our lament is a sign of love. If we don’t ever lament, perhaps we don’t ever deeply love.

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: Why the UNC area studies closures matter to all of us
author: Anne Allison, Barbara Dickinson, Shai Ginsburg, Bruce Lawrence, Omid Safi, Kenneth Surin, Miriam Cooke, Charles Piot and Anne-Gaëlle Saliot
article_text:
In solidarity with our colleagues, faculty, students and staff at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC), we express our strong support for their efforts to preserve the vitality of six area studies centers currently slated for closure: the Center for European Studies, the African Studies Center, the Carolina Asia Center, the Center for Middle East and Islamic Studies, the Institute for the Study of the Americas, and the Center for Slavic, Eurasian and East European Studies.

We urge the UNC leadership to work directly with these area studies centers — together with the faculty, students, and staff who sustain them — to establish a durable, mission‑critical funding structure that will safeguard their work in these increasingly volatile times.

We take this position with the keen awareness, borne out by painful events at Duke and across the country, of what happens when such vibrant Centers are shut or restructured: the irreversible loss of accumulated knowledge and the abrupt abrogation of their educational mandate.

In uplifting UNC’s area studies centers now, we also affirm our own tightly intertwined interests. The relationship between Duke and Carolina has always been symbiotic — built on shared intellectual resources, complementary curricula, and longstanding collaboration. Together, we have worked to address each other’s gaps and limitations, maintaining academic continuity through various cutbacks. Should UNC discontinue its area studies centers, the crucial ligaments in our shared academic ecosystem would be cut. As a result, the global visibility and prominence of both institutions would be downgraded precisely in the areas where sustained expertise and outward‑facing engagement matter most.

In calling for these centers to be saved, we wish to underscore the outstanding, concrete benefits their work provides to students and faculty at both universities:

In an era marked by escalating conflict, volatility and deep planetary interdependence, it is highly alarming that academic centers devoted to rigorous regional scholarship would be weakened — let alone eliminated. Ending these centers would constrict the university’s global vision, impair its ability to respond to world events and strip students of the very capacities they were assured they would gain. Taken together, these actions constitute not just a rollback, but an unequivocal dismantling of the university’s own “Global Guarantee” when it is most sorely needed.

As we all know, it’s far easier to tear down than to (re)build. In order to prevent serious, irreparable harm — and in direct response to both the recent protests and the compelling advocacy of the invited student at the Jan. 22 Board of Trustees meeting — we ask that you pursue this course of timely due diligence:

Only by adopting a process that respects all stakeholders can the university embody the civic probity it seeks to instill — and only then can an institution whose motto is lux et libertas credibly claim to uphold its commitment to advancing the light of knowledge and the education of liberty. In writing this letter, we affirm our own stake in ensuring that such a process prevail, confident it will validate a change in your policy.

With this in mind, we now make public this appeal to the leadership of UNC, having invited all members of the Duke community — faculty, staff, students and affiliates — to lend their support by adding their signatures here.

Anne Allison is a professor of cultural anthropology.

miriam cooke is a professor emerita of Arab cultures.

Barbara Dickinson is a professor emerita of dance.

Shai Ginsburg is an associate professor of Asian and Middle Eastern studies.

Bruce Lawrence is a professor emeritus of religion.

Charles Piot is a professor of cultural anthropology.

Omid Safi is a professor of Asian and Middle Eastern studies.

Anne-Gaëlle Saliot is an associate professor of romance studies.

Kenneth Surin is a professor emeritus of literature.

title: Stuck on the surface: The issue with icebreakers
author: Sarah Pusser
article_text:
You’re new. Well, so is everyone else. It’s a classroom of maybe 20. A few words are exchanged with those sitting next to you: “Are you excited for the class?” “Where are you from?” “What are you studying?” It’s a precursor to a friendship or acquaintance, perhaps out of politeness or genuine curiosity. The teacher enters the class and announces an icebreaker activity to help everyone get to know each other better.

Some common ones you may hear in classes are: How many pets do you have? If you could have any superpower, which one would it be? What is your favorite movie/book? What is something interesting about you? (I don’t think this one needs much explanation for why it is my least favorite.)

The phrase “icebreaker” originates from the 16th century, when steamships were specialized to literally break up the ice in the ocean so as to keep the harbors clear and passable. They were used for polar exploration, carving new paths and turning the hidden familiar. But it wasn’t until the 17th century that the phrase began to be used in reference to the orchestrated mingling of strangers, gaining widespread popularity with uses in literature (Mark Twain’s “Life on Mississippi”) and in conversation by the end of the 19th century.

However, there are instances today where icebreakers are used before the ice has even frozen.

Think back to “The Duke Common Experience,” the summer reading every freshman is given with the intent “to be a common intellectual touchstone for Duke students that sparks engaging conversation in and outside of the classroom.” While I don’t think this is inherently a bad idea (as an english major, I certainly am not going to refute the idea of connecting a community of people over literature), I do think Duke missed the mark of utilizing the Duke Common Experience to create true friendships and connections. The University never integrated these readings into in-class discussions or orientation, which presumably would have encouraged insightful and personable discourse between new students.

Similarly, for the class of 2028, we were given the book, “All We Can Save,” a collection of “essays, poetry and art from diverse women leaders in the climate movement.” I think I can speak for many of us when I say I did not read the book, not because it was bad or its topic unimportant, but because I did not think assigning reading to freshmen before arriving at school was a sufficient way to foster meaningful connections. 

But what are the implications of these icebreakers, either before or upon arrival to Duke, for the student body? 

Icebreakers inherently imply that naturally occurring connections are too slow — that we need a way to speed them up. There are already many ways we cheat what should be organic relationships: social media, dating apps and now even AI are substituting natural connections for artificial ones. 

Duke’s use of icebreakers sets the precedent that mere surface-level connections are sufficient. But fostering truly deep and sustainable relationships requires time allocated each week for small-group discussion and vulnerability. 

Now, more than ever, people are scared of being vulnerable and answering (and asking) difficult questions. Merely asking students to name their favorite color can only allow for so deep a connection, and sets superficiality as the standard for getting to know each other. But in reality, any connection between people who are truly compatible will form naturally, regardless of whether or not they “break the ice” on the first day of class. 

Given the often intense social scene at Duke, which feels unavoidable when combining so many high-achieving students in one space, I understand the University’s desire to appear accommodating to students who may feel left out. And while I could go on about how the University is solely to blame, I can’t ignore the role we, the students, play as well. Many times I’ve found myself asking new friends questions that feel rehearsed, and therefore not personable nor meaningful. 

As the beginning of the semester drags into the dense, cold, not-yet-close-to-done middle, I urge Duke to think about how they can encourage faculty to facilitate more purposeful and natural connections between students, whether that be by encouraging vulnerability from the professors or genuinely thought-provoking questions for the students. 

And, as students, I hope that we can think about what questions we tend to rely on when first meeting people: “Are you excited for the class?” “Where are you from?” “What are you studying?” and think about how we can enhance these questions to go deeper and seek more honest, personable answers. 

Sarah Pusser is a Trinity sophomore. Her column usually runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: Why Duke missing the Playoff didn’t matter
author: Tate Arges
article_text:
Editor's note: This column belongs to a two part series about college football, with an emphasis on the coverage of Duke football. You can find Part One, “Why Tony the Tiger’s Sun Bowl Mattered” here.

On my flight home from El Paso after the Blue Devils’ Sun Bowl victory, I found myself wrestling with a strange feeling. Just 48 hours earlier, I had left Durham deeply disappointed. Disappointed about Duke’s season, about the bowl we were sent to and about being left out of the College Football Playoffs despite being ACC Champions. And yet there I was, in the skies above Texas, replaying in my mind some of the most joyful football memories of my life. And I kept asking myself a simple question: Why?

Why had I allowed a CFP committee held to no standards, bowl executives obsessed with ticket sales and an institution in South Bend feeling unjustifiably entitled to the Playoffs to define how Duke’s season went? 

I realized then that the core of my despair — and the true poison in this sport — is the Playoff-or-Bust mentality.

At its core, this mentality asks us to accept an impossible premise: that a 12-team playoff can meaningfully determine success in a sport with more than 130 teams. Even expanded, the College Football Playoff is structurally incapable of serving as a moral scoreboard for college football. When only nine percent of teams are allowed into the sole games we’re told ‘matter,’ the remaining 91 percent are implicitly told that conference titles, rivalry wins, development, and tradition don’t count.

This thinking is a fundamental distortion of college football history and what makes the sport special.

For over a century, there was no single, clear national champion. The title was a “mythical” crown, determined by various polls, systems and writers. Even after the BCS (1998) and CFP (2014) began, the NCAA still did not officially sanction either system. Go on any team’s Wikipedia page (including Duke’s own) and you’ll see sections dedicated to “claimed” and “unclaimed” national championships. Duke has 2 “unclaimed” titles in 1936 and 1941 — with the former being recognized by the NCAA as the champion for that year, even though we do not claim it. That kind of ridiculousness of having multiple champions every year was part of what made college football fun!

The CFP has replaced this rich, funny history with a single, cynical, media–fueled objective: make the playoffs or fail. But the damage goes deeper than just fan perception; it is fueling a reckless and unsustainable arms race. Because making the Playoffs has become the only acceptable metric of success, many programs now operate in a constant state of desperation. This culture has turned the offseason — and increasingly, the season itself — into a high-stakes auction house.

We now see programs, desperate to avoid the “failure” of an 8-4 or 9-3 season, attempting to lure away other teams’ players and coaches in ways that are frankly unsavory. The pressure to make the 12-team field has twisted the Transfer Portal and NIL into tools for predatory poaching. In 2024, we saw unprecedented movement, with over 2,000 players entering the transfer portal.While many athletes are simply maximizing their monetary worth, a significant amount of this movement is driven by big-time programs treating the rest of the college football world as a farm system. A system where they poach the proven contributors from “lesser” schools while simultaneously “cutting” their own underperforming players to plug holes for a desperate, one-year playoff push. Roster continuity, player development and loyalty have all become collateral damage in the panicked race to satisfy a committee’s December decision.

Duke has experienced the consequences of this culture firsthand. Miami’s coaching staff, eager to reload after a successful CFP appearance and having struck out in attempts to secure quarterbacks from other programs, appeared to successfully entice Duke quarterback Darian Mensah into breaking a two-year contract and entering the transfer portal. While Duke ultimately reached an out-of-court settlement with Mensah, this episode exposed the instability of the current landscape of college football. Seasons can now be unraveled overnight, not by losses on the field or injuries, but by programs plucking the best players from other schools before their seasons even begin.

The financial waste is even more staggering. Coaching buyouts have skyrocketed to the GDP of a small nation. In 2025 alone, schools committed over $228 million in “dead money” just to fire coaches. 

These are coaches who, in any other era of college football, would be considered successful. Some, perhaps, would have statues or stadiums named after them eventually. Look no further than James Franklin. This past season, Franklin was unceremoniously fired from Penn State midway through the year, less than ten months after leading the Nittany Lions to their first-ever College Football Playoff semifinal appearance in 2024. When the only thing that matters is a committee’s opinion in December, loyalty and program-building are traded in for short-term mercenary tactics. If college football’s soul is worth saving, the question is no longer whether it must change, but how?

We could spend endless hours debating systemic fixes to the CFP structure and College Football itself. 

However, these structural changes, while fun to think about, are complex, messy and require institutional agreements that the sport rarely achieves. The most simple, immediate, and powerful fix, requires no committee vote, contract renegotiation or act of Congress: what we need is for college football teams and fans to redefine what constitutes a successful season.

The core mandate for every program must remain the same: aspire to win the National Championship. Coaches, staff and players must operate under the belief that they can unlock each player's highest potential and compete for the ultimate prize. That ambition is non-negotiable. But we must separate that necessary ambition from the definition of a successful year. The success of a season must be a nuanced, earned achievement, not a binary "in/out" determined by a subjective committee.

For Duke, this season was an emphatic triumph because it achieved many of the meaningful, tangible goals within our reach:

The true failure is not being left out of the CFP; the failure is allowing that process to delegitimize a championship trophy that was earned on the field. To second-guess the joy that this season brought the players, coaches, students and fans. To forget that college football is supposed to be fun. The disrespect shown to the bowl system and the arrogant posturing of programs declaring certain games “beneath them” is a direct result of a broken system.

My feeling of defeat was a lie, a side effect of that broken and cynical system. But I refuse to be a part of that system anymore. Duke won the ACC Championship. Duke gave the people of El Paso an amazing football game that they will remember for years to come. The confetti was real. The joy with my dad was real. And no one can ever take that away from me or any other Dukie.

So I’ll be there again next season at Wallace Wade. And I hope I’m not alone. I hope that Duke can be the place where the culture of college football starts to change. A place where our students, alumni and fans know that a successful season isn’t decided in a boardroom, but on the gridiron. 

So let's fill Wallace Wade next season, all of us. Let’s host huge tailgates. Let’s make other teams HATE playing here. And let's show the world that at Duke, we are the only ones who define our success.

Tate Arges is a second-year graduate student at Duke Divinity School.

title: Just go for it
author: Alex Berkman
article_text:
When I started this column, I promised myself that under no circumstances would I write about myself, because opinion readers want opinions, not solemn introspection. 

Yet, over the past few weeks, I’ve found myself traveling the country for interviews that will likely determine the next five-plus years of my life: where I live, what I work on and to whom I become adjacent. So, God, it physically pains me to write this – but I’ve been reflecting.

I’ve always been a contrarian. Maybe that’s what happens when you’re a 5’10” white kid from Westchester, NY. I have no shortage of opinions, which makes me a great debate partner but an absolute pain in the ***. At parties, I dance absurdly among a sea of people committed to not moving at all. At the airport, my favorite hobby is yelling “Baaaahhhh” at the herd of passengers lining up at the gate half an hour before their group has even been conceived of.

For most of my life, this contrarianism felt unserious. But I didn’t realize until recently that it also completely shapes the way I make important decisions, causing me to trust impulse and curiosity over logic and consensus.

Beginning next year, everyone I know will be in New York. My family in Westchester, my cousins scattered across Manhattan, my high school buddies in Murray Hill and the rest of Duke starting their post-grad education at Goldman, McKinsey and you get the idea. It was an incredible opportunity to be near all the people I love.

So naturally, I passed on it. 

At Duke, pursuing a career outside of finance, tech or medicine is rare. For me, surrounded almost entirely by people headed into or already in those worlds, turning away wasn’t easy, but it felt right, and was a decision propelled by a curiosity that began years ago.

In high school, I joined my school’s research program, with admittedly very little expectation to become excited by science. My motivations, rather, were far more due to my being competitive than inquisitive. However, I soon found myself inexplicably drawn to HIV-1: its inherent yet sinister wit, its adaptability and its capacity to hijack host machinery for its own survival. At Duke, that curiosity only strengthened as I continued doing research in virology and protein biochemistry. And, with each experience, I felt increasingly confident that I wasn’t a fool for pursuing what I loved.

Here, prestige is loud, linear and constantly reinforced. We joke about Duke’s pre-professional monoculture, but for many students, that means forgetting the dream of becoming an artist, engineer or writer because the safer path is within closer reach. Just the other day, I overheard a student effortlessly transition from explaining her passion for Theater and Mechanical Engineering to why she was “born to be an investment banker.”

I recognize too that I am not a pioneer for wanting to be a scientist as a Duke student. There have been many before me, and will certainly be more after. I also know these words would carry more weight if they came from someone older, perhaps a couple inches taller and already certain of how things would pan out.

But man, I can’t help but feel sad watching so many curious, talented students push aside passion for practicality.

I recently read Jonathan Haidt’s “The Righteous Mind,” and one idea that has stayed with me is that most decisions aren’t made through careful reasoning. They’re made instinctively — the 99% — shaped long before we ever try to justify them.

We do it when we step in to defend a friend, when we pick Ginger and Soy over It’s Thyme and when we find ourselves pulled toward certain people, places or ideas without being able to explain why.

I get it. For decisions as serious as career moves, it is wise to be cautious. 

But sometimes it feels like we lean way too much into that 1%. 

I can say with absolute certainty that the times I have been the happiest, most fulfilled, whatever you want to call it, are the moments when I’ve trusted that feeling – when I listened to my gut over extraneous pressures. 

I didn’t logic my way into loving science, jumping out of a helicopter (sorry Ma) or leaving New York. Those choices felt right long before I could justify them. And until it bites me, I will continue to lean on this feeling. 

So, if you’re a freshman or sophomore scared of stepping off the ladder, don’t be. There’s another ladder waiting for you in a room full of infinite ladders. 

If something truly excites you, even when it doesn’t fit the dominant narrative, trust it. Trust the feeling.

And go for it. 

Alex Berkman is a Trinity senior. His pieces typically run on alternate Wednesdays.

title: In defense of snow days
author: Molly Huff
article_text:
Here’s how my average day has looked this snowy long weekend: I wake up at 11, trek through the snow to spend two hours at Marketplace brunch, watch Gossip Girl, stare at a blank Word document for an hour, call my mom, chat with friends until late at night and fall asleep reading. 

Over a leisurely coffee at Bella Union, I was talking to my friends about how terribly lazy I’d been. I did nothing particularly productive, letting my laundry and homework pile up without care. Deadlines came and went. My time went to waste. How am I supposed to make it through the semester if I can’t even stay motivated through the weekend?

Done with my complaining and halfway through a latte, I looked at my friends, deep into a conversation about nothing, laptops open in an unsuccessful attempt at studying, and realized — in the most sappy, teenage drama way — I had not been wasting my time this weekend at all. Sure, I wasn’t maximizing my time at school and work, but I was still spending my days valuably.

I fell asleep fulfilled and woke up rested for the first time since the start of the semester. I enjoyed days of beautiful scenery and played in some of the best snow I’ve ever seen. The Marketplace brunches that “wasted” so much of my time brought me closer to new friends. I read a book solely for pleasure. 

I spent my weekend collecting joy, doing things for me, yet felt like I should’ve been punished for my choices. Since when did the time we spend without a goal turn into something to be ashamed of — labeled as pointless?

Somewhere between childhood and college, we decided time must produce an output to be valuable — a paper, problem set, LinkedIn connection, or new skill. Otherwise, it’s time lost. It’s lazy. It’s unproductive. Time spent needs to be justified through a tangible return on investment.

At Duke, there is a constant need for forward momentum. You need to be rushing a club, taking the classes for your degree, looking for an internship two years in advance and doing everything to feel like you’re keeping up with your peers. 

This is important for our future, but so is time spent without a goal — on rest, friendship, love, health and inside jokes.

Decades from now, settled into whatever career we desire, we will remember the work it took to get there. We’ll remember studying, writing papers and showing up to lectures. It would be unfair and unreasonable to suggest otherwise. 

But first, before the thought of an Organic Chemistry lab crosses your mind, you will remember friendships, snow days holed up with freshman-year roommates and leisurely meals in the dining hall. These little moments, not designed to further any goal beyond our search for joy, will punctuate our lives and be the memories that have defined college. 

We should waste our time more, let the time tick away, doing whatever we want for no reason other than we want to.

Molly is a Trinity first-year. Her pieces typically run on alternate Tuesdays.

title: Remembering Deah, Yusor and Razan means facing what’s still broken
author: Fiza Khan
article_text:
Today marks 11 years since Deah Barakat, Yusor Abu-Salha and Razan Abu-Salha were mercilessly shot and killed in Chapel Hill on Feb. 10, 2015. While some, including Abdullah Antepli of Duke, have urged the public to consider motives beyond hate, our community has the responsibility not to let debates over motive eclipse the lasting trauma this violence inflicted on Muslim communities watching and on everyone who believes that safety should never depend on one’s faith or identity.

I was in fourth grade when the adults in my life made it clear that things had changed. 

I needed to be careful and think twice about my words and my actions — because my Muslim identity was no longer just a part of me, but something that could put me at risk.

At ten years old, I couldn’t understand what was wrong with being Muslim. At that age, being Muslim meant being nice to others, celebrating Eid and getting embarrassed when my dad would return to the grocery store to pay for something the cashier forgot to scan.

“But it’s now legally free!” I would argue.

“But God is watching,” he would reply.

To me, being Muslim meant mindfulness. It meant integrity. It meant doing the right thing even when no one else noticed.

I was too young to understand death fully, but their deaths still shaped my life. They came with warnings — reminders to limit my adventures, to be cautious with my words, to move more carefully through the world. I learned, quietly and early, that despite having spent my entire life in this country, I would always be a foreigner in the eyes of others.

More than a decade later, I still struggle to read about Deah, Yusor and Razan without feeling anger. Their story forces me to confront a hatred that I often naively forget exists — but it also reminds me of our responsibility to shape the communities we want to live in. 

Today, however, this sense of fear has not disappeared — it has evolved. That same lesson in vigilance follows me as I carry my passport card with me, not for travel, but out of precaution: a quiet preparation for the possibility of being questioned, detained or doubted simply because I look like an immigrant.

Deah, Yusor and Razan were students, artists and advocates. They lived lives devoted to service and contribution. Remembering them should not stop at grief or debate over motive; it should push us toward reflection and action. Toward asking what kind of world allows certain communities to be taught caution as an added burden to their identity. 

A few months before his passing, one of my favorite teachers shared something with me that I think of often:

“Your heart is a cup. You can choose to fill it with milk, or intoxicate it with wine.”

That choice — the agency to be better, to be kinder, to advocate for others — belongs to us. It is easier to close our eyes to injustice, to dismiss uncomfortable conversations or to claim neutrality. But refusing to acknowledge harm does not make it disappear. And continuing to harbor resentment and fear in our hearts does not protect us from our failures as a society.

At Duke, a university that prides itself on dialogue and leadership, remembering Deah, Yusor and Razan must mean more than annual acknowledgment. It means resisting indifference to issues relating to people of all backgrounds and identities. It means recognizing how rhetoric, silence and dismissal affect those society tells — explicitly or implicitly — that they must always be careful.

The mindfulness my father taught me as a child has grown into a broader sense of responsibility: to see, to speak and to act. Not only for the sake of morals and God, but out of sheer consideration for every member of our community. The choice of what we fill our hearts with will always remain ours, and so will the responsibility to act whenever any part of the community faces injustice. 

Fiza Khan is a Trinity junior. Her column typically runs on alternate Sundays.

title: Weekend at Duke quiet, unremarkable
author: Monday Monday
article_text:
Editor's note: The article below is satire.

This Monday, almost every Duke student reported that they can barely remember the events of the weekend and recalled only its general uneventfulness. The student body seemed generally unaware of the events of the weekend, if there were any at all. 

One sophomore told the Chronicle, “Let’s see, on Saturday, I guess I must have gone to breakfast and then maybe studied until 5? After that, it’s all just kind of a blur. Why, did something happen?”

Another said “Honestly, it’s been kind of boring; I can’t tell you why I don’t remember a single thing that happened. Weird.”

Interviews with professors and staff seem to reveal that last weekend might have been the most uninteresting and humdrum weekend on Duke campus ever. One professor noted, “Usually, the events of the weekend give me something to talk to my floor about on Monday morning, but, to tell you the truth, it’s actually been pretty quiet today.”

Another professor said, “It’s probably not important and, anyway, who cares?”

Some sources say they haven’t seen a Duke weekend this quiet since 2024.

Monday Monday is currently dealing with short-term amnesia.

title: Free honey
author: Anna Garziera
article_text:
I’ve just come back from abroad and found a lot of changes on campus. For instance, there are some strange conference pods on the first floor in Perkins that weren’t there before. Marketplace is no longer a construction site (and looks almost as good as it did my freshman year). It’s now Reuben-Cooke’s turn to be under the knife, and who knows when that will end. 

Besides the repainting of the Southgate bench and the new water taps at WU (which I hate), the biggest difference I’ve felt on campus has been not having to pay for laundry. 

With only my RA income to keep me going during the school year, laundry days used to be a little stressful. I didn't love paying separately for every batch. Most of the time, I didn’t separate my whites, colors or delicates and instead did one big wash per week. After fighting for years, Duke Student Government (DSG) finally got us our unlimited loads. 

At the same time, our tuition has continued to increase, estimated to hit the 100K mark in the next decade. This year, we saw the introduction of “laundry fees” that are meant to cover the cost of the new service. So while our laundry is certainly not “free” (nothing ever is), we now at least get to feel like it is. 

What this does is create a feeling of abundance. 

In some ways, Duke thrives on abundance. Every month, we see campus events featuring free swag, free food, free music, a huge venue and often, really good vibes. Think LDOC, the Centennial celebration, Countdown to Craziness, etc. There’s always a lot of leftovers. 

This same feeling of abundance is also reflected in the first-year experience of the buffet-style dining hall Marketplace. While some have thoughts about the food quality and long lines, I enjoyed Marketplace as a freshman. I found it liberating to be able to try new foods without having to like them. I really dislike wasting food, but I especially dislike it if I paid for it. Marketplace took that pressure off. In my freshman year, I tried okra and tempeh for the first time. 

Unfortunately, giving people unlimited access to a prepaid service can create huge amounts of waste. You can see this at the Marketplace dish line, where full plates of food are put up untouched. With our new laundry machines, this could mean more water usage, as students no longer feel obligated to stuff machines to the brim with every load. I know I’ll start separating my whites. 

But this isn’t necessarily a bad thing. You’ll get a better-smelling student body and fewer washers breaking from being overstuffed. 

At the same time, other Duke services are severely limited. I’m taking three humanities classes this semester, and I’m already worried about running out of black and white copies. We’re maxed out at around 140 pages per semester (double sided), and for someone who has to print a dozen readings per week, it’s not enough. 

Personally, I find it hard to believe Duke’s printing policy is an effort to save the environment. With the amount of water AI requires (it’s a lot) and Duke now paying for every undergraduate student’s ChatGPT subscription, it would be a little hypocritical of the University.

In fact, when it comes to black and white copies, I’m fairly sure most students walk out every semester with their printer balance largely untouched. Most classes are now laptop-friendly, and we’re all too busy to be printing stuff we don’t need. On the other hand, for those students who need to go over the print limit, a small surcharge on their Flex accounts won’t make them reconsider killing so many trees. So why bother?

I was at the gym with my friend last week and she wanted a smoothie from Red Mango. When I asked her which one, she said, “Strawberry, banana, yogurt, chocolate whey, honey.” I said, “Honey?”

The thing is, she used to hate honey. She only started liking it last semester, after putting it in her Panera Sip Club coffee to avoid paying for flavorings. Because syrup shots cost $0.69 each, but not honey. Honey is free.

You might have noticed the tension between how Duke tells us “there’s plenty to go around” and at the same time, forces us to count every pump of syrup in our coffee. We are being told one thing and shown another.

For some things, especially the needs of the everyday, Duke should lean towards abundance. (Think about how much coffee syrup we could afford if we just cut back on the QuadEX tote bags by 10%.) Abundance creates a feeling of comfort and lets you slow down. Not having to pay for caramel might seem trivial, but it’s at least one less thing on your mind.

We students constantly have a lot to stress about: exams, career choices, friend groups, sports clubs and our physical and mental well-being. Coffee flavoring should not be one of them.

Anna Garziera is a Trinity senior. Her pieces typically run on alternate Sundays.

title: Is Duke conservative? The New York Times and I disagree
author: Katelyn Cai
article_text:
In October, an article from The New York Times called Duke a “relatively conservative” campus. The journalist’s reasoning? Our student body’s lack of Gaza protests and our administration’s quiet rollback of DEI. 

Neither reason felt compelling nor accurate.

First, not a single student or faculty member was quoted in the piece to corroborate an outsider’s characterization of this campus. Instead, the article relied on the presence of protest, which is just one dimension of many that can define a campus political culture. 

Second, the administration is not the student body. And, the administration is not the faculty. Duke students largely self-identify as liberal or Democrat, at rates comparable to or greater than students at Harvard, the University of Pennsylvania and Vanderbilt. The majority of Duke faculty self-identify as liberal, at rates slightly below those of professors at Harvard or Yale. And, the administration is not the surrounding community. Duke is located in the most liberal county in North Carolina: Durham County. 

I’d instead describe Duke as an overwhelming liberal, if incrementalist, place. 

For better or for worse, students’ first instinct is never to protest. We didn’t erect an encampment in 2023 and protests against ICE have remained Durhamite-driven. But being an activist and being left-of-center are not mutually exclusive.

It’s a bit insulting to imply that the only notable form of political expression is on the streets. It’s also a bit problematic to imply that conservatives dominate campus politics, because they often feel uncomfortable speaking out in classes. 

It’s not implausible to consider why The Times might use protest as a metric for the political temperature at Duke. Not only did encampments across elite universities catch the national spotlight throughout 2024 due to the Israel-Hamas conflict, but American student activism has historically preceded political change: on the Vietnam War, on apartheid and on the Iraq War.

Duke’s protests, on almost any issue, are always muted at best. It’s likely a combination of factors. It could be how pre-professional we are. Nearly 30% of students who participated in a pro-Palestine protest lost a job offer as a result, and that’s a price not many Duke students, who feel intense pressure to be successful, are willing to pay. 

Maybe it’s how generally content we are. Duke has a strong sports culture (both watching and participating), a multitude of affinity groups and great weather; students here generally build strong social networks, one of the biggest resiliency factors against mental illness. Happy students are less angry about the wider world. Or perhaps it comes down to the campus design: we’re separated from Durham, which prevents community members from joining a protest. BC Plaza, our main campus crossway, barely has enough open space to stage anything; protests in Durham’s downtown, more spacious and far from West Campus, are much better attended. 

While these all may be true for other universities, Duke is unique in another way: we lack a centralized body for activism. We don’t have a long-standing social justice hub like UNC-Chapel Hill’s Campus Y, which has 30 student-led committees, nor a pro-Palestine umbrella organization like Columbia University Apartheid Divest, which united 120 student groups. Protest isn’t so scary when it’s done with others. But, when protest isn’t normalized or organized, and it has such high costs, why would students stand alone?

Sometimes, I’ve wondered in frustration what it would take for my classmates and me to stand up for something, anything. We seem apolitical, maybe deaf to the world. But we often express our political interest or allegiance in other ways. 

There’s political energy and interest at this school, even if it doesn’t manifest in protest culture. Public policy is — even if you exclude the future consultants — one of the most popular undergraduate majors. The Duke University Box Office regularly sells out tickets to political speakers brought to campus, like former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg or Representative Ro Khanna (both Democrats, I might add). 

Annika Aristimuno, President of Duke Democrats, noted that over 250 students attended a rally featuring Vice Presidential candidate Tim Walz.

“This was probably one of the biggest events, if not the biggest, in the last couple of years at Duke that was hosted or organized by a student group, not the university itself,” said Aristimuno. 

That energy is often directed toward liberal causes. A variety of issue-based student groups exist on campus, including Duke Beyond Borders, Duke Planned Parenthood Generation Action and Students Demand Action at Duke. 

That’s part of the reason some conservative students would also contest The Times’ characterization of campus. 

“The reason that I started Duke Republicans was because I was encountering a lot of students who were very conservative but never spoke out because of the fear of cancel culture, or they were afraid of retaliation by their professors,” said Trinity senior Zander Pitrus, former President and re-founder of Duke College Republicans (which actually did not exist on Duke’s campus between 2020 and 2024, if that speaks to Duke’s ideological skew).

Mischaracterizing the University as anything but left-of-center can make conservative students feel invisible and worry liberal prospective students about what they might encounter once they’re on campus. 

Labels, especially those given by legacy media institutions like The New York Times, are important. They can define how the powerful, including the President and the current administration, view this institution, and they can define how future students see this school. 

Journalistic outlets owe the public as close to the truth as the fallible human hand can write. Here’s my amendment to this draft of history: Duke should be rightly remembered, as the apolitical but liberal place it is, so that it can be rightly debated and changed. 

Katelyn Cai is a Trinity senior. Her column typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: Ridges of ice and what remains of 1984 today
author: Robert Wallace
article_text:
When the pogroms started in Nazi-led Germany in November of 1938, Adolph Hitler had been in power for five years. In 1933, President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor, after the once marginal Nazi party made political gains over a span of more than ten years. When Hindenburg died in 1934, Hitler proclaimed himself Führer.

Hitler and his party, systematically — in many cases using existing laws — demonized not just Jewish people, but Black people, Poles, Russians, Ukrainians, and many others, including the developmentally challenged. To them, these people were considered inadequate human beings. In fact, they were considered inhuman.

Make no mistake – History does repeat itself.

The Schutzstaffel (SS) initially was Hitler’s bodyguard, later evolving into his private army, essentially a paramilitary organization used to run concentration camps and intelligence activities. The SS had to profess undying loyalty to Hitler. By World War II, the SS had expanded to several groups, with hundreds of thousands of members overall. They were called upon for “brutalizing and murdering individuals in territories occupied by the Nazis”, and to run the death camps.

Later came the Geheime Staatspolizei, or the Gestapo, a group designed to go after Hitler’s enemies. It had various subgroups that specifically targeted Liberals, Catholics, Protestants, same-sex-loving people, anyone, in short, who opposed the goals of the Third Reich. Targeting to ensure the torture, imprisonment, and death of anyone who opposed them.

Make no mistake — Gestapo tactics can happen anywhere. 

Between semesters, I reread George Orwell’s 1984. What a profoundly prescient novel. The protagonist, Winston Smith, was eventually tortured by Big Brother because he dared. He dared to act against the government. He dared to read. He dared to love. Most of all, he dared not to believe the rhetoric: “War Is Peace; Freedom Is Slavery; Ignorance Is Strength.” He dared to believe that the government does not control speech. He dared to believe in truth. He dared to believe that history exists.

He dared to believe that the government doesn’t own the truth and cannot change it whenever it wishes. That alternative facts are not facts. It is, as Orwell pointed out, “doublethink.” Two plus two isn’t five. Yet this has become the goal today. To control us, by whatever means. To pursue power for power’s sake. Power that is often fueled by hate. This kind of power needs groups to terrorize. After it masters one group, it will find another. It has to. It can never be satiated.

Make no mistake — Hate is unsatisfiable. It is constantly hungry and must be fed.

Orwell’s vision is terribly disheartening. It left little to no room for hope — none, at least, that was seized by the characters. But it was there, latently. Like Steinbeckian hope, in the people. It took the form of large numbers. Tyranny thrives, as noted by Erich Fromm in 1984’s Afterword, on ignorance and despair. It condones inaction. 

Back in Michigan, when I was a child, I went ice fishing with my grandfather. We drove his Oldsmobile onto the lake and walked about twenty yards from the car.
