I watched my grandfather cut a two-foot diameter circle into the ice, and then, with a sharp instrument, pluck the thick round out of the frozen water. Though commonplace, I still marveled at the existence of an entire lake frozen underneath one continuous ice cube. My grandfather taught me a healthy respect for cold.

He said cold could be quiet, but not all cold is silent. 

Many years ago, when my grandfather was a child, he fished with his father on the same lake. A car went down that day, was sucked under the water like a predator taking a hapless victim. My grandfather said he and his father sat perched on padded stools, fishing silently. His father puffed on his pipe, sending rings of sweet-smelling tobacco smoke in the air, and sometimes he — my grandfather — pretended also to be smoking like his father, cocking his head back and blowing warm air into the cold. His father would smile at his miming son. 

There was another father and his son. They were fishing not more than two hundred yards away. In the cold quiet, their voices carried over to where they sat. But their voices were not loud. There was stillness about their voices. The car of this Father and son was not far from where they sat fishing contentedly, a lot closer than where their own car was. 

My grandfather said he would always remember the sound that cracked ice makes. It’s like the sound of lightning splitting the air. The ice cut a swath around the car like a moat, and it balanced there a moment, then fell into the water and was sucked below. The man and boy looked over at them; their frosty breaths visible even from where they stood. Simultaneously, they hung their heads.

Like something concrete and irrefutable, my grandfather’s father said, “They had parked over a pressure ridge.”

We are on that pressure ridge. We have to do something.

Robert Wallace is a first-year graduate student of liberal studies. His column, 'Telling Stories', typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: Facts, feelings and our failure to act
author: Devyn Deschamps
article_text:
Knowledge is power, a saying I’m sure many have heard once, if not many times, in their life. It’s a beautiful idea that with just intellect, one can control, transform and influence the world around them. To an extent, I do believe it’s true; if knowledge is a flower, then curiosity is its blossoming seed. As I’ve grown and learned about history, chemistry, mathematics and politics, I’ve felt as though my intellect can soundly guide my choices. 

In the last year, however, I’ve made a series of life-changing choices, some of which have been guided directly by rational thought, and others … Well, I’ve made many emotional choices. Even typing it out, I feel slightly ashamed. We’re taught that emotional choices are inherently irrational. The heart can be broken, the mind deceived, but facts? Facts are unchangeable, immovable, the end-all be-all. 

The Trump Administration and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have been using loopholes in recent Supreme Court rulings to reach their quota of 3000 immigrants deported each day. There are documented cases of United States citizens being detained and separated from their families based on racial profiling. That is not a baseless accusation, but a documented reality.

In September 2025, the U.S. Supreme Court made an emergency decision in Noem v. Vasquez Perdomo, allowing federal immigration officers to use race, language and ethnicity as sufficient cause to determine reasonable suspicion. Although Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh noted that ethnicity should not stand alone in this determination, ICE agents have surely taken it that way. 

For much of the United States’ history, the Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) has been regarded as the most impartial branch of government, an institution tasked not with politics but with reasoned interpretation of the law. Though no institution deserves blind trust, SCOTUS has long been viewed as the gold standard of legal reasoning. Its opinions, while technically interpretations, are often treated as the objective truth. When legal reasoning is elevated to unquestionable fact, the line between intellectual rigor and moral responsibility begins to blur.

This culture of intellectualism is especially visible at Duke. Although broadly applicable to many college campuses, grounding our opinions in logic has almost always been the way to win an argument, earn a grade and defend a paper. Even in social situations, we can take a step back and say, “Let’s look at this rationally.” This is what we were taught to be. Smart, analytical, problem-solving students who gather the facts and draw a conclusion based on such. 

What is often missing from the equation, though, is emotion. It isn’t even treated as a variable in the rising culture of intellect. More than that, empathy itself has been dismissed. Wearing your heart on your sleeve is bad enough; add to that trying to understand someone else? Out of the question. 

I wouldn’t go as far as saying Duke students are apathetic, but between overintellectualizing every emotion and being utterly infatuated with a pre-professional career, there seems to be no room to, for lack of a better word, feel. 

After relationships, we try to make our friends feel better by listing all the reasons, the logic behind why it was a poor fit or even how they are objectively better than their former partners. Often, we become so detached from our feelings that our way of processing anything is to observe the facts and try to act accordingly — “If my ex was such a loser, then I shouldn’t be sad that we’re no longer together.” No. Feel sad. Or angry. Or happy. Feel whatever crosses your mind. Immediately rationalizing every emotion defeats the purpose of being alive — to experience feelings fully, with as much depth as possible. 

While relationship endings are a common occurrence for students, the bigger issue becomes how this lack of emotion transfers to much larger global events. 

Not that I’ve been expecting a tidal wave of students to rush the streets of Durham, but Duke has been eerily quiet about ICE. It’s frankly disappointing. 

Duke students are not ignorant. If anything, we are exceptionally well-informed. And yet, knowledge has become a convenient excuse for inaction. Reposting Instagram stories condemning ICE costs nothing; it demands no emotional investment, no confrontation, no risk. This is not a failure of awareness, but of empathy. When facts are absorbed without feeling, they lose their power to compel action. The result is not neutrality — it is apathy.

This silence is made even more unsettling by proximity. The architect of much of this administration’s immigration policy, Stephen Miller, Trinity ‘07, is a Duke alumnus. And yet, Duke as an institution has offered no public condemnation, no acknowledgment, no reckoning. For a university that prides itself on moral leadership and global citizenship, this absence speaks loudly. If not now, when? If not here, where? 

Duke is nearly 20% international. Almost every student here knows someone who immigrated to the United States: a roommate, a lab partner, a friend. And yet we have somehow grown comfortable with a political climate in which immigrants are described by the nation’s highest officials as animals, as invaders, as something less than human. When dehumanization becomes routine, outrage should be instinctive. Instead, we scroll past it. The question is no longer whether we know what is happening, but whether we care enough to feel it. 

Facts alone will never be enough. History has shown that knowledge without empathy does not prevent cruelty; it enables it. If Duke students truly believe in using intellect to shape the world, then we must also allow ourselves to feel its pain. Change begins not when we see others as statistics, headlines or reposts, but when we recognize them as people who love, fear and hope as deeply as we do. Until then, silence will remain our loudest response.

Devyn Deschamps is a Trinity sophomore. Her pieces typically run on alternate Sundays.

title: My impossible plea: Zohran Mamdani for commencement speaker
author: Noor Nazir
article_text:
I did not think I would care this much about who speaks at a graduation I’m not even at yet. But I haven’t really stopped thinking about it since the Jerry Seinfeld fiasco. His appointment had landed as tone-deaf during a humanitarian crisis: it was a choice that alienated hundreds of students. In May 2024, about a hundred Duke students walked out of their own commencement ceremony. 

A commencement speaker is not just some ‘famous person’ who will get the crowd excited. This isn’t LDOC. It’s the last piece of knowledge a university chooses to leave its students with. It is a signal about what kind of leadership the institution wants to celebrate, and what kind of world it imagines its graduates entering. It’s a bare minimum expectation from the selection committee to center its students (all of them!) and not make a sizable part of the graduating class feel unwelcome at their own ceremony. 

When Seinfeld was named the commencement speaker of 2024, more than 34,700 Palestinians had already been killed in Gaza. Duke students partook in encampments across the Triangle alongside protests and demands for divestment.

Seinfeld has publicly shrugged at Palestinian suffering. Duke knew, or should have known, that this choice would land like a dismissal to the students who had spent months trying to make the University see them.

Since then, in fall 2025, he was invited back to an event sponsored by Chabad and co-sponsored by the Provost's Initiative on the Middle East, the Program in American Grand Strategy, Jewish Life at Duke, SSI, StandWithUS, and DiPAC. Here, he compared the “Free Palestine” movement to the Ku Klux Klan. Duke has since ‘supposedly’ distanced itself, claiming it does not endorse the remarks of invited speakers – but that disclaimer does not undo the harm.

Seinfeld is also not the first sign of Duke’s ignorance toward its students.

In 2022, Duke invited Mary Barra, the CEO of General Motors (GM) and now vice chair of Duke’s Board of Trustees, to be commencement speaker. The timing of that invitation came just months after Black-owned media executives publicly accused her of refusing to meet with any of them and published an open letter calling the company out for their systematic racism. The open letter didn’t arise in isolation; GM already had a documented history of discrimination allegations, including a 1989 class-action lawsuit and the 2018–2019 Toledo plant lawsuits.

I admit that Barra wasn’t personally responsible for every incident. Individual and corporate responsibility aren’t the same thing. But commencement speakers symbolize the institutions they lead, not just their personal resumes. When Duke chose Barra, it chose the leader of a company facing fresh, public accusations of racism.

Of course, not every choice has been like this.
Adam Silver, the 2023 speaker, and Grant Hill, the 2025 speaker, were both digestible picks. 

The overall pattern is revealing: Duke has historically chosen its speakers based on their image, not their students. Duke students deserve a commencement speaker who cares about people and their stories, someone who can offer real hope while still acknowledging the world we are walking into.

I’ve talked about it in my previous op-eds. Duke’s pattern is clear: image over people. But it does not have to be this way. There are leaders who center the voices Duke overlooks, and Zohran Mamdani is one of them. 

He went up against a political machine backed by billions of dollars and won. He didn’t tell people to “grind harder” or “chase the bag.” He didn’t promise that everyone could become a billionaire if they tried. He told a sitting President to “turn the volume up” on young people's voices, not down. Because they matter. 

His story, and the way he chose to tell it, is the kind of final message Duke should be willing to stand behind.

When I watched that speech, I cried. Thrice.

Not because of any policy detail, but because of how he talked about the young. In his victory speech, he walked out to “Dhoom Machale,” a Bollywood soundtrack that, on the surface, feels playful. But underneath, it was something else: an assertion that people who look like him, and people who look like many of us at Duke, belong not in lectured classrooms, but also “in the halls of power.” 

Which brings us to the obvious counterargument:
If Jerry Seinfeld was considered polarizing, isn’t Mamdani as well? Wouldn’t his presence make some conservative or pro-Israel students feel like Duke was taking a side?

Critics like Bret Stephens claim Mamdani is “frightening” because of his anti-Zionism, but that argument conflates the difference between criticizing a state and attacking a people. Stephens himself admits Mamdani has no record of antisemitism, writing “A good place to start is to concede that nothing in the public record suggests Mamdani is antisemitic.” 

The fear Stephens invokes relies on equating pro-Palestine politics with anti-Jewish hatred — an equation that erases the many Jewish groups who share Mamdani’s critiques of Israeli policy. Mamdani’s politics challenge systems, not communities; they do not tell any group of Duke students that their identities are dangerous. Seinfeld did. And that distinction is exactly why Mamdani’s presence would not be comparable to Seinfeld's. 

What Stephens ultimately resists is not Mamdani’s rhetoric, but the political imagination behind it, one that refuses to normalize injustice as the cost of stability.

Mamdani’s politics are certainly not “neutral,” but they don’t attack students for existing. They challenge systems — housing, policing, corporate greed — rather than delegitimizing communities.

Duke, however, almost certainly wouldn’t invite Mamdani. Not because he isn’t accomplished, or thoughtful or inspiring. But because he is not safe for the version of Duke that exists in the Allen building, where the selection committee likely meets. 

He does not flatter the powerful. He does not pretend that politics is disconnected from people’s lives. That is the kind of message many students are hungry for, but it is also the kind of message that makes people in charge uncomfortable.

And if we look at Duke’s recent history with commencement speakers, that discomfort of those in power has consistently taken priority over the discomfort of students who are already at risk, whether they are Muslim, Black, Palestinian or simply politically outspoken.

Perhaps we must reframe the question: Not “Who should speak at commencement?” but “Who is commencement for?”

Noor Nazir is a Trinity junior. Her columns typically run on alternate Tuesdays.

title: My connection with Jeffrey Epstein
author: Dan Ariely
article_text:
This statement isn’t an effort to minimize the seriousness of the acts at the center of the Epstein files, or to minimize the harm done to his victims.

It is simply to clarify the two interactions I had with him over several years.

The first time was shortly after I moved to Duke University, when I was looking for funding for my research lab. This meeting was not documented in the files. An alumnus suggested that I speak with Epstein because he had recently made a large donation to Harvard related to decision-making research. We met in Palm Beach, and I quickly realized that his interests did not meaningfully overlap with my research. I have never received funding from him.

During that meeting, Epstein told me about the accusations against him and said they were false. At the time, I believed him.

As a researcher who studies human behavior, I was curious about him, and a few years later, I met him again in New York. These meetings were always in the presence of others and focused on topics related to decision-making. Nothing in those interactions raised concerns for me or suggested that anything inappropriate was taking place.

I also encountered Epstein briefly at a professional conference, but did not have a substantive interaction there. While attending the conference, I sat near somebody who I believed was his colleague and had a short conversation with her that I found intellectually interesting. 

Afterward, I emailed Epstein asking if he could put me in touch with her, so we could continue that discussion. In that email, I described her as “very very smart” and mentioned that she was a redhead as a physical detail solely to help identify who I meant because I did not know her name. To the best of my memory, that introduction did not occur, nor did I ever meet her again.

In general, the contact I had with Jeffrey Epstein was infrequent, largely logistical, often mediated by assistants. I had no connection with his criminal activity, and was involved in no financial, professional or ongoing relationship. 

Dan Ariely is a professor of business administration.

title: A call to heal
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
Recently, I have been remembering the phrases “hurt people hurt people” and “violence begets more violence.” We see the incarnation of these statements sprawled out all over social media and on the streets of the United States, including in Minnesota. Archbishop Desmond Tutu, an influential figure in ending apartheid in South Africa, was precisely right when he wrote, “We busy, ‘normal’ people: we are sick … the litany of brokenness is without end.”

We are sick, not them over there, those people. But we. We are they. The sick ones. Perhaps physically, but most definitely socially. This sickness is infecting and spreading like a vicious virus of vitriol, making us all victims of the structural vampires of inhumanity. But how can we be made well again? 

Do we even want to be well? I ask this because I recognize that some cherish the hell of it all and that, for them, it works in their favor for promoting injustice and dehumanization. So where do we go from here? What is our ultimate goal?

I believe justice matters. I believe truth matters. But I also believe healing matters. We all come from different backgrounds, cultures, experiences, and religions (or lack thereof). Through my own religious tradition, Christianity, my imagination has been recently captured by a familiar “call story.” I’ve read it many times, but in 2026, I see something new.

In the Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 4, Jesus calls two sets of brothers to follow him. As fishermen, these men are not the upper echelon of their communities nor do they have a high socioeconomic status. When called, these brothers immediately leave what they’re doing without question. They don’t ask for a strategic plan or a job description or how many hours a week they’ll have to follow him or what their benefits are. They just get up and follow.

Right away, Jesus shows them their mission. It is a people-oriented mission — not thing — or program-oriented. They are called to people. But what freshly grabbed me this time in my reading was noticing to whom they went right away. They went to the sick, the afflicted, the diseased and those in pain. They are called to care for the sick. This is their very first move, indicating what their primary mission is. By following Jesus, they are undertaking an apprenticeship in healing.

There is also a call for us to be healers at this horrendous time in our country and world. Our wellness is inextricably linked to the depth of our connection with and care for those who are not well. This doesn’t negate the truth-telling and justice-seeking that needs to occur, but it does indicate an ultimate trajectory.

The Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King. Jr.’s question is still so hauntingly relevant: “Life’s most persistent and urgent question is, what are you doing for others?” How will you use your power? To dominate or to serve? Will you be a hurter or a healer?

 The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: Darian Mensah walked away from Duke Football, but fans don’t have to
author: Craig Principe
article_text:
When I heard the news that Duke Football Quarterback Darian Mensah decided to enter the transfer portal mere hours before it closed, I will admit that it hurt me deeply. 

I will admit, too, that I love Duke Football, which is why it hurt the way it did. Some might say I have no right to feel that way — after all, I am not on the team and had neither the skill nor ability to play college football when I was an undergraduate. But what I hate about the situation and what I feel entitled to judge him for as a Duke Football fan is how he conducted himself in making this decision. 

I do not blame Mensah for deciding to leave if he truly believed it was best for his future. But he could have made that decision a month ago and not told everyone he was coming back. Many of Mensah’s teammates and coaches were harmed by his decision in ways that no fan experienced. Some with options to transfer for better deals of their own were left without a choice, when several players undoubtedly recommitted to the team because Mensah recommitted to the team. The situation mirrors Coach Mike Elko’s departure, where it was not the actual decision to leave that made Duke fans so mad, it was the way he decided to leave and how that showed little respect for the players, coaches and fans. 

There may be college football fans who cheer the cutthroat financial decisions these athletes face, emphasizing the singular moral principle to “chase that bag!” But it is this mindset that allows traditional powerhouse football programs to utilize their football pedigrees and hegemony in the NIL/revenue-sharing arms race to put their programs in a superior position by exploiting rising, upstart programs. 

Like many college football fans, I am tired. Tired of loving a game and a team that seems to give so much only to then strip it away. Like so many things in society that seem to get worse every year — from our degrading sociopolitical norms to the cruel polarization causing people to find pleasure in others' suffering — perhaps it is easier not to care.

And after hearing the news about Mensah’s last-minute departure, it did indeed seem easier to just not care anymore. 

In that moment, I was convinced that the following morning I would box up all my Duke Football apparel: my #2 Connor Vernon jersey, my Belk Bowl shirt, my Chick-fil-a Bowl shirt, my 2013 ACC Championship game shirt, my 2014 Sun Bowl shirt … and mail it to Nina King with a note reading, “Thank you for some amazing memories, but college football just isn’t fun anymore.”

But I did not.

Duke Football is a true passion in my life and a joy that I have shared with my wife, also a Duke alum, for many years. As a freshman in 1998, I truly enjoyed going to football games with my friends, even though the team was not good. After a mediocre season my freshman year, there was hope that, with the hiring of Carl Franks, we would go “Airborne,” by focusing on offense and an aggressive passing attack. But Duke crash-landed, going 3-8, 0-11, and 0-11 the next three years. We could only dream of a quarterback and passing game like Mensah and Duke produced this year. 

As an assistant athletic trainer in my freshman year, I was at many football practices watching the struggles of players who were on one of the worst teams in Division I football. Many believed Duke should quit football altogether, but there were many more who believed Duke should fight for the program and its very distant past glory. People had hope.

That hope was first realized with the success of the Cutcliffe era and has grown since. Under Coach Cutcliffe, Duke Football achieved things it had not done in decades. Duke went to its first bowl game and achieved its first winning season in over fifteen years. In 2013, Duke finished ranked in the top 25 of the final AP and coaches polls and had its first 10-win season. In 2015, Duke won its first bowl game since the 1960 Cotton Bowl. Most importantly, though, Coach Cutcliffe altered the culture of the program, and that resulted in permanent change.

In the days that followed Mensah’s announcement, I asked myself, why? Why do you love this team and this sport? And why do you subject yourself to the great joys, followed by the inevitably greater disappointments of being a Duke Football fan? To read the current posts on X is enough to enrage a passionate Duke fan. People laugh and mock, as they have laughed and mocked for years. They say, “Duke has a football team?” or “Stick to basketball!” and other far worse, cruder things.

The 2013 Chick-fil-a Bowl loss, where Duke fought so hard and was so close to defeating Texas A&M (and Johnny Manziel), was the greatest live sporting event I ever attended. That was until this year’s ACC Championship game, where, after 27 years of rooting for Duke Football, the program finally won an ACC Championship. 

It was an extraordinary game and an extraordinary achievement … one that many honestly thought could never happen. It was an achievement built over decades with players and coaches who stood on the shoulders of those who came before them. It was built on dedication, heart, brotherhood, Coach Cutcliffe’s “Faith, Family, Future and Football,” Coach Elko’s G.R.I.N.D. and much more. 

But outsiders mock that achievement. They don’t understand what it means and what it represents: greatness and the perseverance of the human spirit. This is not an exaggeration. Rather, I believe this is the only reason we love sports so much. After all, it is “just a game,” yet we place extraordinary meaning in it.

Many people hate Duke Football for the same reason I love Duke Football. Because it is good — in the true sense of the word. Because it attracts quality players, coaches and administrators who are good and want to prove something to themselves and to the world. They want to show that they can build something great; that they can achieve greatness. That they can take a program that — like Indiana University — was once at the very bottom of Division I football to new heights. That they can change perception, can alter reality, can shape the future. 

But greatness cannot be achieved without struggle and adversity. Duke Football players are tough. They claw, they battle and they fight. But most importantly, they embrace the fight. When they get knocked down, they get back up, over and over again. They don’t quit.

Perhaps college football is indeed damned and in a faster-moving downward spiral at risk of imploding on itself. Time will tell. On Jan. 27, press releases confirmed what I had already come to believe: that Mensah will never wear a Duke football uniform again. That possibility is lost. What success our team could have achieved next year will never be known. 

Although I am glad that the University fought for whatever rights it had under its NIL contract — an uphill battle in the current legal landscape — some argue that by suing a player, Duke was only injuring itself, as players will not want to play for a school that actually expects them to act with integrity and honor commitments. I don’t think that is true. I think Duke will continue to find the right kind of football players for its program. Players who, when they say something, mean it. But the outcome of Mensah’s “decision” and this lawsuit don’t really matter fundamentally — it is just the next struggle to overcome.

There will always be haters who cannot stand to see a program like Duke Football rise from the bottom to reach the very top. The definitive answer to such doubters and haters was captured by Coach Cutcliffe in his pregame speech before the Belk Bowl: “Does Duke play football? You’re damn right we play football!” And when they do, I’ll be cheering for them.

Craig Principe, Trinity '02, is an attorney in Winston-Salem, NC.

title: On being far away
author: Ryan Growney
article_text:
I’ve been thinking a lot about my twin brother.

He goes to a different university, and this year is the first we’ve ever truly lived apart. It’s strange, not in any sort of overt way, but in the way that trickles down from the recesses of your mind when you’re in the shower or daydreaming instead of doing your homework. We’d shared a room for our entire childhood, but it’s not living apart that’s the weird bit — we’d already spent four years at the same boarding school with different roommates. Still, he was always nearby. I could always expect to see him during our weekly physics homework meetings or in passing at the dining hall. Always a crossable distance.

Now that we’re a plane ride apart, I’ve been forced to reconsider what that relationship looks like. What are you meant to do when you part ways, even temporarily, with someone you’ve spent your entire life with?

I had always wondered what life away from my brother would be like. I don’t mean this in a negative sense at all — he and I are different people, we always have been and both of us were interested in simply figuring it out on our own for the first time. Now, we’re both a semester and change into our first year of college, and until recently, I hadn’t thought once about that new reality. It was only during winter break, when he and I got to spend some meaningful time together again, that these swirling feelings bubbled up to the surface. 

Once we were back home, my brother and I easily fell back into the normal cadence of life with our parents. There wasn’t any difference between the person I saw making breakfast in the kitchen and the person I’d seen so many times in the past, no difference between how he talked or laughed. It was almost like we had never left, our lives having resumed after a brief intermezzo. Almost — but not quite.

He is very much still the same person, as am I, but there was space between us in the stories we told. It’s the space that comes with not having been there, the slightly far-away look of trying to imagine somewhere you’ve never been and people you’ve never met. I don’t blame him. I cannot. He goes to a different school; of course, he doesn’t have any idea what Marketplace looks, feels and smells like, or the taste of tea on a late night at Coffeehouse. 

The strange feeling is that he never will.

When a relationship defined by crossable distances is met with an uncrossable one, there are two considerations that are forced upon us. One is about you: how do I define myself when it’s always been in relation to someone else? The other is about them: how do I continue to be a good brother, friend, family member at a distance? 

These questions are terribly knotty. It would be difficult to discuss them in a book, much less an article. I don’t purport to know the answers. Maybe there are none. Yet, despite their indecipherability, these questions aren’t unique. They came up when I left my parents for the first time and went to boarding school, when I struck out on my gap year. But more importantly, they’re questions every one of us has to grapple with as we leave our families to come to Duke. 

When we become part of this community, we inevitably part ways with bits of who we are. My brother’s path and my own have taken on two different tracks since we’ve gone off to school. Neither of us would go back if we could. Even though it is our spaces diverging rather than our care, in the calculus of life, independence comes at the cost of identity. Inextricably tied up in who I was, to myself and the people I met, was always an element of “twinness,” and there’s no amount of texting or calling that can replicate that here. 

At Duke, I am not a twin. 

What’s missing is not content, but rather context. People at Duke can’t see the way my brother and I help each other with our physics homework anymore. They can’t see the nods across the dining hall. They can’t look to my brother to see me. Here, I am not a sibling or a family member. I am what people see from crossable distances — someone built on the jokes I make with friends, the interests I rant about to whoever’s ears are open and the accumulation of infinitesimals of action and belief.

I can’t understand my brother’s stories because I can’t hear the jokes he laughs at. I can’t know the feeling of late nights at his version of Coffeehouse. When you part ways with someone you’ve spent your entire life with, you miss what makes up “them.” You miss watching who they are change moment by moment, and you’re left to piece it together afterwards. Whatever we choose to call it, that deflating, wormy feeling is the price we pay for navigating this growth. 

I’m proud of being here at Duke every day. I wouldn’t trade it for the world. But I’ve been thinking about my twin brother a lot. I will never truly be able to show Duke who I am when he’s around. When I see him again, he will never truly understand what I mean when I talk of my experience here, nor can I place myself into the stories he brings back. Yet, despite this, I can’t wait to tell him everything.

Ryan Growney is a Trinity first-year. His pieces typically run on alternate Wednesdays.

title: Tips for Duke tenting: Testing, tent checks, sexual tension and more
author: Monday Monday
article_text:
Editor's note: The article below is satire.

As the Duke/UNC game gets closer and closer, Duke students will flood “K-Ville” as part of 10-to-12-person tenting teams to earn a coveted spot in Cameron Stadium as a one of the “Cameron Crazies.” Forget about paying $10,000 a year for a bed at Duke and instead, come sleep in a tent for six weeks! Below is your guide to everything you need to know about Duke tenting.

THE GAME

The Duke-Carolina basketball rivalry started around 1920 with the first Duke-Carolina game. Carolina is leading currently, with 16 consecutive wins between 1920-1928, when all the players were white and nets were five feet off the ground. However, the Duke tenting tradition only truly started in 1986. Meanwhile, instead of tenting, UNC students get tickets through an online lottery system, possibly to protect themselves from being identified in public as UNC basketball fans.

HOW TO TENT

In order to tent, assemble a group of 10 to 12 teammates, including a roommate with whom your relationship will slowly devolve over the course of the tenting season, two or three friends who are only free to stay in K-Ville in several 20-minute intervals during the week, those friends’ boyfriends/girlfriends who believe that they are being discreet about spooning in the tent, four to five people who your friends have talked about forever but whose names you can’t remember and at least one person with whom you have insane sexual tension, for the purposes of motivation.

If you’re black tenting (the most competitive level of tenting), at least 10 people will need to sleep in the tent every night, so consider lying to your team early on about your “violent night terrors” in order to be the teammate allowed to sleep at home. If you do end up staying in the tent, take up as much space for your sleeping bag as possible as a show of self-respect.

During these nights, checks will still occur via police siren and your group will have to leave the tent about three times in order to stay in line. It’s important to note that your Line Monitor hates you and will keep you from completing the check for as long as possible, to feel a sensation of control they lacked during childhood.

TENTING COLORS

Tenting is split into three colors, ranked by priority entrance into Cameron: “black,” “blue” and “white." Black tenters are required to complete a Duke trivia test in order to determine their order of entry in the stadium. Some questions in consideration for this year involve describing players' relationships with their mothers, their prom dates' astrological sign and finding a list of all medical procedures they've had.

Blue tenters will not have to take the test and will simply tent at K-Ville a week after black tenters, whereas white tenters will participate in the “Race to the Secret Spots.” In previous years, more competitive tenting colors than black tenters were available to students, but have since been discontinued; “gold tenters” were simply waterboarded by Line Monitors over the course of the tenting season in order to earn the coveted front row seats. While this is no longer an option, the Duke administration told The Chronicle that this practice was cruel and unusual and is now only used in extreme measures, such as against Pratt students.

But remember, no matter what color your tent is, all of the struggle that goes into tenting will be worth it under the lights at Cameron Stadium. Be proud to be a Blue Devil; after all, UNC students have to wait as long as we do for a losing game in a sport they’re bad at. DDMF!

Monday Monday is currently looking for the “f” in the word “Krzyzewskiville.”

title: Why Tony the Tiger’s Sun Bowl mattered
author: Tate Arges
article_text:
Editor's note: This column belongs to a two part series about college football, with an emphasis on the coverage of Duke football.

The first Saturday night of December was one of the happiest nights of my life.

In overtime of the 2025 ACC Football Championship, linebacker Luke Mergott snagged a game-sealing interception to win Duke our first ACC title since 1989. As he tucked that football into his chest and hit the ground, ending the game, it felt like the culmination of a lifetime of Duke football fandom. Sharing that moment with my father, tears streaming down my face as the confetti rained blue and white, felt like a dream. At that moment, I could not have imagined feeling anything less than ten feet tall ever again.

But by 5 p.m. the next day, I felt defeated.

Duke, despite being a Power 4 conference champion, was left out of the 12-team College Football Playoff. The committee's choice to favor a James Madison team, which boasted one of the least difficult schedules in the FBS and lost to the only Power 4 team they played, didn't shock me — what did, came during the ensuing Bowl Selection.

I had pictured a warm Florida weekend at the Pop-Tarts Bowl in Orlando, a uniquely entertaining game (who doesn’t want to see a human-sized Pop-Tart sacrificed to a gigantic toaster to feed the winning team?) against a highly ranked, yet beatable, opponent. While not the playoffs, this would still be a high-profile and prestigious matchup that would give our Blue Devils the opportunity to prove the CFP committee made a mistake. But that invite never materialized. Neither did one go to sunny San Diego for the Holiday Bowl or the easily accessible Mayo Bowl in Charlotte.

Instead, our Blue Devils found themselves destined for El Paso to play in the Sun Bowl. As the second-oldest bowl game after the Rose Bowl, the Sun Bowl has a history as prestigious as any non-New Year’s Six bowl game. But El Paso was neither the most exciting nor accessible location, and a matchup against an Arizona State team without its star QB was not the most enticing matchup.

The feeling of defeat was amplified by one of the biggest brands in college football. Notre Dame, having felt snubbed by the CFP committee, publicly declared their team would not participate in the Pop-Tarts Bowl, signaling without verbalizing that it was a “waste of time” and an “insult” to their program.

Here was one of the biggest brands in the sport sending a clear message: the bowl game I had looked forward to, the pinnacle of the postseason outside the CFP, was not worth a damn. And if that was the case, what did it say about the Sun Bowl that our Blue Devils were relegated to? In less than 24 hours, I went from the mountaintop to once again experiencing the deep-seated disrespect and defeat that Duke football had so often faced in the past. I questioned everything: maybe Duke shouldn’t have been in the ACC championship. Maybe this season was not the resounding success I had believed it to be.

Despite our disappointment over our bowl destination, my father and I found ourselves boarding a long flight to Dallas, and then another to El Paso, on the 30th of December. My dad had committed to following this team to every single game this season—from the epic showdown in Chapel Hill to the late-night kickoff in California—so he felt a quiet, almost weary sense of obligation to see the season through. We were going because we were “supposed” to, even if the excitement hadn't quite accompanied us across time zones.

We arrived with low expectations for the trip, for the Sun Bowl, and frankly, for El Paso itself.

But once we left the El Paso airport, we were blown away.

The entire city was buzzing with the energy for the game. At a local Walgreens, the clerk saw my dad’s Duke apparel and immediately engaged him in a five-minute conversation about the matchup. The hotel TV was a constant loop of “Sun Bowl traffic,” “Sun Bowl weather,” and “Sun Bowl preview.” On the morning of the game, my walk to the stadium took me past a sea of tailgaters—local El Pasoans unaffiliated with either school—who had turned the parking lots into a festival. There were more people outside of the Sun Bowl gates than I thought could possibly fit into the 50,000-seat stadium.

I have attended numerous bowl games and I have never waited in a longer line or seen a stadium look that packed. Most of those fans weren't Dukies or Sun Devils; they were El Paso locals. And tickets were so scarce that there were even people watching the game from the top of the mountains the Sun Bowl is nestled between.

The game itself lived up to the atmosphere. It was a display of offensive fireworks that wasn't decided until the final minutes when Luke Mergott snared another crucial interception to put the game away for our Blue Devils.

During our El Paso trip, we met a die-hard local Duke fan named Isaac who was able to shed light on why this experience felt so much different from other bowl games we had attended. He explained that to the people of El Paso, the Sun Bowl isn't just a game; it’s a point of civic pride. The event of the year. For a city of El Paso’s size, he noted a surprising lack of high-level sporting options. The Sun Bowl is the one day a year when the community can witness two winning, high-level programs face off on their own turf.

But Isaac told us something else that stuck with me even more. He explained that in a city with a Hispanic majority, the Sun Bowl is a cherished opportunity for the community to practice their own brand of hospitality. For El Paso, hosting the Sun Bowl isn’t just a business transaction; it is an invitation into their home. They aren’t just concerned with "filling seats"; they want to welcome fans into a culture that treats every visitor like family.

During that game, surrounded by thousands of people who treated this game as a celebration rather than just another obligation, I realized something.

The problem was never which bowl game Duke got sent to.

The problem was what the media and institutions have tried to get everyone to believe about it.

The current discourse around college football had convinced me that true joy requires validation from a committee, the media, or other teams. That championships need an asterisk if they don’t come with a Playoff appearance. And that seasons can be ruined by a television show in early December.

The people of El Paso didn't believe any of that. Our Blue Devils didn’t believe that. And after that day, neither do I. 

Tate Arges is a second-year graduate student at Duke Divinity School.

title: Why do peaceful protests succeed?
author: Brian Hare
article_text:
As we celebrate the life of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr, we are confronted with the reality of extreme political tension and violence. It is hard not to wonder how to respond. 

Just this month, after the fatal shooting of Renee Good by an ICE officer on Jan. 7, the governor of Minnesota, Tim Walz, held a press conference saying, “To Minnesotans, I say this, I feel your anger. I’m angry. They want a show. We can’t give it to them. If you protest and express your First Amendment rights, please do so peacefully as you always do. We can’t give them what they want.” 

But why not give them what they want? Aren’t peaceful protests just a relic of the past and tougher approaches needed for a new age? 

Together with my co-author Vanessa Woods, I argued in our 2020 book “Survival of the Friendliest”, that the answer requires understanding the nature of our species’ group psychology. Humans evolved to be attracted to and humanize those we see as similar to ourselves while having the potential to fear and deny humanity to groups we view as threatening. This plays out in two main ways that help explain the power of peaceful over violent protests.

First, peaceful protests humanize protestors. Showing one’s face while expressing non-threatening opinions in creative or even humorous ways, attracts others to your cause. 

Second, non-violent movements can grow large and draw on citizens from all walks of life. People, including women or entire families, are unafraid to join protests. A wider range of citizens recognize themselves in the protestors, even if they do not fully agree with their message. Acting together, these two factors work to protect and generate positive moral regard and empathy toward protestors by others. 

The nature of our evolved group psychology helps explain the consistent success of peaceful protests across time and culture, documented by political scientist Erica Chenoweth in her book "Why Civil Resistance Works". She analyzed more than a century of protest movements around the world and found that peaceful protests are twice as effective as violent ones in leading to meaningful societal change. Peaceful campaigns, she shows, are more likely to result in enduring democratic reforms and economic benefits for society.

According to Chenoweth’s analysis, violent protests, in contrast, quickly skew toward mask-wearing young men, who are viewed as threatening by most citizens. Protests remain small and are unsustainable. Many citizens who might otherwise agree with the views of the protestors, may not join but also quickly distance themselves from this group’s efforts. Those targeted by protests are now able to galvanize support for draconian security measures after characterizing violent protesters and their views as dangerous extremism. 

Violent movements, when they occasionally succeed, typically empower a different group that then adopts a form of repressive rule, essentially recreating what they fought against. A never-ending cycle of political violence ensues with everyone suffering. Or as Dr. King himself said, “force begets force, hate begets hate, toughness begets toughness. And it is all a descending spiral, ultimately ending in destruction for all and everybody.”

This reality can feel counterintuitive. Who has not imagined besting the bully? This is why so many great movies end with an aggressor getting what they deserve. Even Chenoweth shared that intuition. She originally predicted that political violence was the only effective approach to enact change before her own research found the opposite. 

But the implications from human nature are clear on our best response in these uncertain times. Peaceful protest will always be the more advantageous approach, across time and culture, because its strength comes from our species’ unique and universal need to connect and care for those we perceive as being like us. 

Whether we like it or not, we are all getting a lesson in group psychology and before the end of 2026 another key test is likely. Unfortunately, it seems to me that what is happening in Minnesota will not stay in Minnesota. 

The time for good trouble could be near. May we all show the incredible courage that the Duke community always shows by facing it peacefully. Our beloved community is counting on it.

Brian Hare is a professor of evolutionary anthropology.

title: The sun also rises: An ode to my time at Duke
author: Advikaa Anand
article_text:
When I first arrived to Duke, I quickly grew enchanted with Durham’s sunsets. Each evening would bring a vibrant painting setting the horizon ablaze with vivid hues of orange, pink and red. Over my 3.5 years at Duke, I beheld many of these glorious sunsets, but when I glance back at my camera roll, I do not retain very many images to look back on — because I was too busy basking in the moment to capture it. I feared that in the time it would take me to whip out my camera, the moment would pass and the sunset would flicker into cold night. 

Now that I have graduated, I must remain content with the memories I carved in my mind instead of striving to relive moments by sifting through albums. To savor the moment, I sacrificed permanence. 

The opportunity of graduating a semester early arose almost serendipitously: I sat with my adviser on BC Plaza, squinting at the planner on DukeHub, as the two of us noticed the overlap between my major and minor that would enable me to graduate in December. I smiled gleefully, seduced by the allure of brief freedom before I locked myself into my future plans permanently and organized the remainder of my time at Duke around this goal.

But now, as I have entered into what feels like a holding period of my life, that glee has shrunk to regret. Instead of relishing what I have gained, I am consumed by an overwhelming longing for what I have lost — lurking in Vondy to snag a table, weaving past the crowds during WU rush hour and lounging on Abele Quad’s benches with my friends discussing the same fifty scenarios over and over again. Seizing the future Duke promised me has come at the cost of moments like these.

For so many years, everyday life at Duke was my dream. Then, the dream came true. Now, dusk draws near and I wander aimlessly. I must brace to confront the dark stillness forcing me to examine who I am now that “Duke student” no longer shines upon me as my primary identity. That title gave me an anchor to ground who I was and what I was doing. Now that it has slipped from my grasp, I must redefine who I am.

For any individual who structures their identity around getting things done — and undoubtedly, I am one of them — this dilemma is destabilizing and disorienting. Who am I apart from what I do? This question haunts me every day. Often, though, I circle back to my time at Duke and find that while it might not resolve my quandaries, it does shed some light on an answer. 

During the fall semester of my sophomore year, I took Economics 104D (Statistical Foundations of Econometrics and Data Science) and Economics 201D (Intermediate Microeconomics I), both required for the Economics major, at the same time. As the courses progressed, I quickly realized that I had made a blunder: both classes presented challenging, unfamiliar quantitative material that demanded huge chunks of my time. Despite investing hours of studying, I barely made the average on both my midterms. I was crushed with disappointment: what did it imply for my intelligence that my efforts were not bearing fruit? Who was I without doing school right? 

After receiving those grades, I vowed to do something differently and refocused my studying on understanding the material rather than simply rote memorizing practice problems. As the intersections of supply and demand finally started to make sense, I reveled in the joy of understanding, and though my course grade was not ideal, the feeling of knowing what I was doing on the final exam lingered with me.


This experience at Duke taught me an important lesson — that when the external pillars of success upon which we stake our measures of self-worth rattle, we must turn inwards and find courage in the immutable qualities that make us who we are: our grit in the face of failure, resilience despite uncertainty, and willingness to choose optimism when wallowing in self-pity seems so tempting. Now, as I confront this crossroads in my life after Duke, this lesson feels more resonant than ever before. 

As I reflect on the close of this chapter of my life, I am grateful that though my time at Duke might be over, the memories I made and wisdom I gleaned will remain with me long after I walk at graduation. If there is anything I learned as an undergraduate at Sanford, it was to question traditional wisdom — not to dismiss authority, rather, to devise new possibilities. No matter where life takes me next, this commitment to rewriting narratives will stem from my time as a student at Duke, and in this way, the institution will forever have a mark on my story. 

These days, when I particularly languish for moments past, I find myself again glancing at the few pictures I have of Duke’s sunsets. Now, I realize something I didn’t quite grasp when I stared at the sky in awe — that splendid sunsets must fade into haunting nights. But I can walk through the darkness knowing that dawn will break and herald the morning. 

I will make it to see the sunrise because Duke taught me how. Until then, Duke University. Adieu. 

Advikaa Anand, Trinity '26, was an associate opinion editor and columnist for The Chronicle's Volumes 119-121.

title: Remembering King, remembering our humanity
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
This semester, I am teaching a Divinity School course on Howard Thurman.

Rev. Thurman was an ordained Baptist minister, served as dean of the chapels at Howard and Boston Universities, and was viewed as the pastor or spiritual guru for many of the Civil Rights leaders, including Martin Luther King, Jr., James Farmer and Pauli Murray. He also attended Morehouse College with “Daddy King,” Martin Luther King, Jr.’s father. Martin Luther King, Jr. was said to have carried Rev. Thurman’s book, “Jesus and the Disinherited,” in his briefcase everywhere he went.

Days after Rev. King’s assassination on April 7, 1968, Rev. Thurman said these words in memoriam: “[Rev. King] was killed in one sense because [hu]mankind is not quite human yet. May he live because all of us in America are closer to becoming human than ever before.” 

As we observe ongoing violence in this country and the world and experience political decay in human decency, we still see today that we are not quite humane yet. Hopefully, we are working on becoming more human by recognizing the worth and dignity of every person.

This is what Rev. King stood for. He believed that every human being mattered. He called for a “revolution of values” in which there would be a “shift from a ‘thing’-oriented society to a ‘person’-oriented society.” 

Money-oracy can destroy democracy and ultimately humanity. As Rev. King put it, “When machines and computers, profit motives and property rights are considered more important than people, the giant triplets of racism, materialism and militarism are incapable of being conquered. A civilization can flounder as readily in the face of moral and spiritual bankruptcy as it can through financial bankruptcy.”

This person-orientation, or what I call “a turn to the human,” is so critical for our times. To be human, humus in Latin, is to remember we are all “from the earth.” We are from dust, we are dust and to dust we will return. We find humble kinship at the site of dirt, and one day — whether we’re a president, prince, prophet or pauper — we will all end up in a box. 

This is the reality of our mortality. Thus, I propose we nurture what I call an “ethics of dust” in which we remember that we are all dust and will return to dust, and perhaps this honest memory might help shape our human encounters in the world. 

In Rev. King’s final chapter in what became his final book, “Where Do We Go From Here: Chaos or Community?,” he writes, “All men are interdependent ... When we arise in the morning, we go into the bathroom where we reach for a sponge which is provided for us by a Pacific islander. We reach for soap that is created for us by a European. Then at the table we drink coffee which is provided for us by a South American, or tea by a Chinese or cocoa by a West African. Before we leave for our jobs we are already beholden to more than half of the world.”

In other words, as gospel artist Hezekiah Walker has sung, “I need you to survive.”

Because of this human interconnection, Rev. King resisted the diminishing, dehumanization and destruction of the other. He recognized that we belong together. As the proverb says, “If you want to go fast, go alone; if you want to go far, go together.” As the wisdom of the old spiritual says, “Walk together, children, and don’t get weary.”

May Rev. King’s legacy live on, because all of us are striving to become more human together in recognition of our need to be the beloved community. As Rev. Thurman put it in remembering Rev. King, “It is the intent of life, that we shall all be one people. For better or for worse, we are tied together in one bundle, and I can never be what I must be until you are what you must be: for better or for worse, this is the only option. And to reject it is to reject life. And to reject life is…to make God repent that he ever gave us a chance to live …”

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: On fresh starts
author: Anna Garziera
article_text:
This has been the most emotionally exhausting year of my life. 

In 2025, I cycled through a whole bunch of friendships. I took on a new role as coxswain in my rowing team — something I’d sworn I’d never do. I got over some people and fell back in love with others. 

Half way through my semester in Berlin this fall, I decided I’d better come home early. I impulsively sent in my early graduation form — I’ll be walking this May. Relationships shifted, career goals changed. My puppy even started looking old. 

In a book about my life, I’d give 2025 its own fat chapter. Midterms. Heartbreaks. Root canals. Gradual ups and dramatic downs. I’d tell you I read the entire Harry Potter series for the first time. Or I might tell you about my trip to England, or that I took the LSAT twice. 

Maybe I’ll write that book one day, but not yet. For now, it feels good to just start over — turn over a new leaf, bury the past, as well as the hatchet — and enjoy the uncreased linens of the new year. 

2026. A clean slate. New Me.

Why do we feel this way? As college students, the rolling over of the new calendar year is not the only fresh start we get. Every semester, we have new professors and classes to look forward to. Each academic year brings new dorms, new roommates, new backpacks, new shoes. Some of us get a big reset with graduate school. But we also enjoy weekly resets. I know I’m always more productive on a Monday. 

I chase a fresh start with every book I read: Page one leaves all possibilities open. So does an “Untitled document” on Google Docs. I even feel a sense of renewal every time I hear “pens down” after a midterm. I tell myself that for the next exam, I’ll start reviewing even sooner. Crack open a new notebook. Uncap a new pen. 

A new dawn, a new day. Get an early start tomorrow: gym, shower and a 17-step skincare routine to “reset” your life. Rinse. Repeat.

But maybe, this isn’t the right way to go about it. 

I agree with you — it feels good to compartmentalize our lives into boxes. Big events. Days, months, years. We let it take over: The last digit of today’s date changes and suddenly, we feel invincible. 

I’ve always been a fairly harsh critic of New Year’s Resolutions. December 29th is not too late to start practicing a good habit. And yet 30% of Americans wait for drinks and fireworks to start eating healthier and going to the gym. Nothing else changes: not the temperature, nor their circumstances, nor their resources. Just the date on our made-up calendar. 

Fresh starts are powerful things. For a lot of people, COVID-19 gave them the permission to start over. You’ve heard the stories. Burned-out office workers quit their jobs. Couples decided to finally get married and start having kids. Families moved to new homes — including mine. 

This is all good, as long as it leads to positive change. But the same attitude can instead delay that change, or even ruin the progress we’ve already made.

It’s alright if this was you. We’ve all fallen victims to the same frame of mind. I’ve often felt my day was “ruined” if I hadn’t gone to the gym in the morning or studied at least three hours by noon. I’d let this drag my mood down and make me give up for the evening. But it’s silly to compartmentalize your life into “good” and “bad” days. 

The same goes with the new year. You shouldn’t let what went down in 2025 define whether you’ll be sorry or glad to leave it. Nor should you expect 2026 to bring radical change. You’ll still be the same flawed person, and you’ll be making the same mistakes. Maybe fewer — I’m not saying you’re a lost cause. But if you do change for the better, it won’t be because you have a fresh year at your disposal. It’ll have to come from within yourself. 

And if you do make the same mistakes, don’t let this define your week or month or year. Most likely, 2026 will be a mix of good and bad decisions, like every other year. And that’s okay.

It’s okay if the chapters of your life start blending or become incohesive. You’re allowed to start a new job mid-semester and re-kindle a friendship you thought was over without first seeing “a sign.” You’re allowed to get up at an uneven hour tomorrow and only go to the gym after class. 

This is your permission to give yourself a fresh start whenever you need it, not just at the popular temporal landmarks. You screwed up 30 seconds ago? That’s alright. Here’s your chance to try again in 3, 2, 1.

Anna Garziera is a Trinity senior. Her pieces typically run on alternate Sundays.

title: The LinkedIn doomscroll: Investing in your future or avoiding the present?
author: Devyn Deschamps
article_text:
Endless hours of polishing my résumé, refreshing Outlook and Gmail 30 times a day, scrolling through the infinite feed of LinkedIn and Handshake postings: searching, applying, refreshing again.

I’ve come to realize these habits aren’t just mine — they’re almost ritualistic among Duke students. As a school deeply ingrained in pre-professionalism and ensuring student success, it is no wonder we fall easily into the rabbit hole of "What will I do this summer?" Or "what am I doing after graduation?"

Even on a campus known for its energy and spirit, Duke students aren’t immune to the constant scrolling, texting, and dopamine hits that fill every spare moment. The difference? We’ve found a way to rationalize it — convincing ourselves it’s all in the name of our future.

Lately, my once high motivation for classes has vanished. My interest in the material is still alive; I continue to be challenged in different ways, yet the monotony of the semester has dulled the novelty of learning. So, as any burnt-out college student does, I distract myself.

These distractions, however, aren’t the socially nourishing ones, like spending time with friends, volunteering or pursuing a hobby, but something far more insidious: I entomb myself in the future.

At a school that almost sacrilegiously worships student outcomes, the LinkedIn obsession at first seemed like a Duke rite of passage. Expanding your network, finding jobs and curating your profile is, in a way, our generation’s introduction to the professional world. Meeting students with shared interests, sharing opportunities — undoubtedly valuable tools.

But somewhere along the way, the purpose shifted. Hitting the mark of 500-plus connections became a form of social currency. Competitive internships and scholarships stopped inspiring celebration and instead provoked a quiet, gnawing question: Why not me?

The cruel engine of social media has always been comparison. And lo and behold, the old adage holds true — comparison is the thief of joy. In many ways, the polished, prolific figures we follow on LinkedIn are simply the professional version of influencers on TikTok and Instagram.

And is that really harmless?

Frankly, no.

One night, I caught myself sitting in Perkins Library long after midnight — LinkedIn open, tabs upon tabs of applications half-finished. My coffee was cold, my mind numb. I wasn’t working anymore; I was performing productivity, convincing myself that my anxiety was ambition. The irony wasn’t lost on me: I was sacrificing my present to secure a version of the future that didn’t even exist yet.

Maybe what we call “investing in our future” is really just a way to feel in control. The moment we stop hustling, the stagnation gets uncomfortable. We start to ask questions we can’t answer — What if I fail? What if I’m not enough? It’s easier to search, apply and refresh.

In chasing these future ideals, we risk escaping the very experiences that make us the kind of people worth hiring in the first place. It’s easy to believe that our value lies in credentials, but a university is supposed to shape who we are, not just what we do. The most formative experiences —moments of curiosity, connection, even boredom — are right in front of us. Yet we spend them curating the image of a self we haven’t fully lived into yet.

Maybe that’s the paradox of being a student today: we’ve mastered how to optimize every moment except the present one. We know exactly what we should be doing, and yet we rarely stop long enough to ask why.

So maybe the question isn’t whether we’re investing in our future or avoiding the present. Maybe the two aren’t opposites at all. Maybe the truest investment in our future is learning how to be fully here, right now, before it all becomes another thing we scroll past.

Devyn Deschamps is a Trinity sophomore. Her pieces typically run on alternate Sundays.

title: Stop bragging about your private high school
author: Stella Kaye
article_text:
The move from my hometown to East Campus felt more like an extended season of Survivor on CBS than it did actual school.

It is pretty clear that from day one, there are a select few openings at the top of the social ladder and most people I ran into were fighting their way to the top — whether or not they realized it themselves. There’s this weird game of “Who do you know from this suburb of NYC or Miami?” And before too many days had passed, I realized perhaps I wasn’t so good at that challenge.

What I wasn’t expecting — likely the product of my ignorance and scarce knowledge on elite U.S. and international high schools — was that many of my new peers would, and still use the prestige of their private high school to give them a “leg up” in various social situations. 

It blows my mind how conversations on campus seem to be dominated by peers who attended private schools, when, according to the Duke Admissions Office, 58% of the class of 2028 actually attended public high school. It’s not that I don’t care about the fascinating field trip stories or Upper East Side “Gossip Girl” drama. And let me be extraordinarily clear: I don’t hate the elite private high school system. Despite the fact that I truly believe I am just as well-equipped to succeed in Duke classrooms as any peer who attended a private school, students like me are rarely encouraged to speak up due to our schools’ limited name recognition and financial resources.

I have also found there to be a strange misconception that all public schooling is the exact same. There’s the classic Hollywood depiction of a classroom, filled with students who would rather be anywhere else. Or the former gym teacher at the front of the room, executing a poor attempt at teaching algebra. But this worldview falls short in more ways than one.

The classrooms I was lucky enough to snag a seat in were filled with some of the most brilliant and engaged minds I had ever worked with, creativity that transcended what my imagination could see and teachers who pushed the limits and defied harmful stereotypes about public education. 

What I want to bring to light here is that there are thousands of incredible things I could say about my public high school (and I’m sure many other Duke students could as well) that I’m not being encouraged to say. So, if you’ll indulge me, I’d like to share a few aspects of my public high school that have really set me up for authentic and meaningful success here at Duke, starting with my teachers. 

Everyone has that one teacher they shared countless lunches and after-school conversations with. I was lucky enough to find several of those gold-star, one-of-a-kind mentors. My sophomore year chemistry teacher became the reason I even applied to schools like Duke. She worked tirelessly to make sure I knew my work was valued and that I was capable of achieving real success. “You can do this. Take a break and come back to it later,” she would remind me.

Even the most complicated concepts in AP Chemistry somehow felt like common sense when she was in the room. She trusted me, and that made me trust myself. Now, coming to a school like Duke, where brilliance is everywhere, I don’t see other bright minds as reasons to doubt my own abilities, but as more chances to grow and collaborate. The self-doubt still creeps in sometimes, but when I think back to those days in the chemistry classroom, I’m reminded of how far I’ve come and how much confidence I’ve gained in who I am as a student and a member of a community.

Right across the hall from the chemistry classroom was my choir teacher’s office. She taught me how to stand up for myself. She’d remind me that there’s no space in our lives for people who don’t value what we bring or what we believe in. When others tried to quiet me, she encouraged me to hold my ground — to sing with more confidence, to speak with more clarity.

It wasn’t just in hymns or a cappella rehearsals that she taught me to use my voice; it was in the everyday moments when choosing courage actually mattered. Since coming to campus, I’ve noticed that my voice shakes less when I’m called on in class or when I share an opinion that not everyone agrees with.

And those lessons didn’t stop with the teachers’ personal guidance. Instead, teachers carried them straight into the classroom. In classes like AP Literature, we were encouraged to re-enact classic scenes from Sophocles and Wilde — with full class participation, of course — and read poetry in the clock tower before hearing words of wisdom from our teacher.

In US History, we played a semester long game of Traitors, all for us to better understand the infamous Red Scare and its effects (my goodness, the teachers were creative!) And the students only became more engaged as the lessons lifted off the textbook page into engrossing conversations and hallway games. This creative mindset has done wonders for me as I begin my journey here. 

All this isn’t to say that I haven’t struggled at times during my first semester at Duke. I think almost every freshman has. But I think the main difference between those educated in the public and private school systems is that in public school, I was taught that unless I ask for help, I won’t get it.

This was not because my teachers didn’t care, but because in lively, crowded classrooms with limited resources, support often went to the students who reached for it first. Ultimately, self-advocacy is my most essential skill, and I have developed a strong ability to utilize my resources effectively. Coming to Duke, that habit has shaped the way I navigate everything from office hours to tutoring. 

So what is all of this ramble about high school for? We’re in college now! Well, at the end of the day, I believe wholeheartedly that each individual's educational background plays a large role not only in their higher education experience but also in shaping their character.

It’s time Duke students start paying more attention to those who were brought up in the public school system and acknowledge the strengths, perspectives and resilience that come from that background. There must be a clearer understanding that our experiences aren’t deficits, but instead simply differences, and often advantages, that deserve to be part of the conversation.

Stella Kaye is a Trinity first-year.

title: Middle East Studies are being marginalized nationwide. Duke is letting it happen here.
author: Leo Goldberg
article_text:
In the wake of Oct. 7, 2023, universities across the U.S. faced an explosion of political scrutiny regarding campus protests over Gaza. Intense pressure from both the federal government and donors over their handling of such unrest forced many schools to rethink certain academic policies and programs which quickly became drains on their reputations. Perhaps the biggest consequence of which has been the targeting of Middle East Studies programs across the country. 

Post Oct. 7, any association with Palestine, or the Middle East in general, became anathema in many circles in the U.S., producing a chilling effect on Middle East Studies at American universities. At Duke, despite largely avoiding the Gaza protests seen at other schools, a similar pattern has taken hold. No longer seen as politically and academically viable, Middle East Studies is being increasingly sidelined.

Over the last year, Duke has taken the following actions: the Persian language program was cut, denying students the ability to learn a critically important Middle Eastern language on campus. The joint Duke-University of North Carolina (UNC) Graduate Certificate in Middle East Studies has been “indefinitely suspended” after Spring 2025 and the gateway course for it (AMES 620S: Critical Genealogies of the Middle East) is no longer offered. The librarian for Middle East area studies was removed, forcing the South Asian area studies librarian to take over both regions, for which there was little or no consultation or communication with the faculty who actually teach in these disciplines and whose work is negatively impacted by such bureaucratic decision-making. 

To gauge how students have been affected by such actions, I spoke with Catherine Shaw, a sophomore who has to commute to UNC to continue studying Persian after it was removed from Duke’s language offerings. Shaw detailed numerous frustrations with this arrangement, of which she was given little notice, and which the University has been wholly unhelpful in solving. “There was the issue of figuring out [which Persian courses UNC offered] because we don't have access to the UNC course registration software,” Shaw said. “I just happened to have a friend who goes to UNC and asked him to send me a picture of all Persian offerings.” The commute is another issue. Taking Persian “requires taking the Robertson [bus to UNC], which adds 30 minutes in each direction, so it also impacts other courses I can take,” Shaw remarked. Enrolling remotely, despite the offer from UNC, was not an option allowed by Duke either. 

It’s worth noting that, despite Persian offerings, UNC has not been much better regarding the marginalization of Middle East Studies. It too is running scared from the field, with the University announcing its plans to cut all six of its area studies centers. Unlike Duke, though, it is subject to far greater influence from the federal government as a public institution. 

It is bizarre that Duke would discontinue Persian at a time when it is considered a critical language for national security, and US-Iran relations couldn’t be of greater importance, with our own president threatening military intervention against the Islamic Republic on behalf of the safety of recent anti-regime demonstrators. For a school that so heavily emphasizes public policy and dedicates an entire school to its study, Duke’s undermining of programs that would help produce good policy towards a region in desperate need of it is fundamentally counterintuitive.

For Duke, though, these cuts may tell a bigger story. As Middle East Studies has come to be seen as a political and financial liability, reducing its programs seems to be part of a larger public relations strategy which prioritizes protecting the University’s reputation and appeasing parties with stake in the institution who have come to view the field as ideologically adverse, and even dangerous. Although this process has been hastened since the fallout from Oct 7, it began several years earlier. 

In March of 2019, the Duke-UNC Consortium for Middle East Studies hosted a conference titled “Conflict Over Gaza: People, Politics, and Possibilities.” The conference was part of an annual tradition of holding a symposium whose purpose was to address an important issue in the contemporary Middle East. The 2019 topic was deliberately chosen to provide “sober, scholarly perspectives” on the contentious political and humanitarian crisis in Gaza, an issue with which we are all now, of course, extremely familiar. 

The event featured a range of cultural exhibitions including music, food, art and films from Gaza, with the purpose of illuminating a people whose culture is callously overshadowed by the political implications of their society. During the first evening of the event, an incident occurred in which Palestinian rapper Tamer Nafar encouraged the audience to “be anti-semitic with him” as he performed a song and “think of Mel Gibson” (a notorious antisemite) as they sang his lyrics. 

I dug for a long time to find the full video in context and from an unbiased source, but the best I could find was a clipped version presented by conservative documentary filmmaker Ami Horowitz in a video made for, brace yourself, The Daily Wire. From what I could gather from the video, the comments were made as part of a larger joke that was omitted, but they were disturbing nonetheless, and, indeed, quite antisemitic.

As one can imagine, already under intense scrutiny for its theme, the video caused an explosion of outrage which quickly had the entire conference flagged for its allegedly vitriolic anti-Israel bias. The scandal became so big that the federal government ended up stepping in and an investigation was opened by the Department of Education, then headed by the real-life airhead, Betsy Devos, into the use of federal grant money for the conference. 

After a sizable amount of national drama, the federal government ended up issuing orders to both UNC and Duke demanding they remake their joint Middle East Studies program over its “anti-Israel bias” and “lack of positive imagery of Judaism and Christianity in the region.” Duke and UNC also released public apologies and signed resolutions to rebaptize antisemitism in their anti-discrimination codes. The scandal left Duke badly burned, and, following the conference, Duke withdrew its name from the Federal Title VI Middle East Studies Consortium with UNC. 

The curtailment of the field at Duke has since persisted. In 2022, Duke appointed Eve Duffy to take over both the Duke Middle East Studies Center (DUMESC) and the Duke Islamic Studies Center (DISC) as "Interim Director.” Duffy is a higher education administrator who, while having an academic background in the German contexts of the Holocaust, did not appear to have any qualifications to run programs related to Middle East studies. Under Duffy, DUMESC and DISC were brought under one central “Global Affairs” office, presumably undermining their independence and giving the University greater supervisory powers over them. She left Duke when the Office of Global Affairs was closed as part of the first wave of downsizing in summer 2025. 

In all fairness, the consolidation did apply to all areas studies centers, too, and certainly hurt their respective autonomies.
