But it was especially painful for Middle East Studies, as Oct. 7 occurred in the midst of this bureaucratization which, as previously mentioned, created a unique dimension of marginalization for Middle East Studies.

It is also important to address that, in 2024, Duke did launch the “Provost's Initiative on the Middle East” (PIME) led by Provost Alec Gallimore in response to the hyper-tension of Oct. 7 on college campuses, the purpose of which was “to make space in the Duke campus community for rigorous and respectful debate.” The move, though, was largely performative, and heavily stressed “constructive dialogue,” which just seems to be code for controlling the narrative to avoid any actual protest. The initiative was also, of course, unveiled while simultaneously unraveling the programs that actually matter in promoting regional understanding, like languages and faculty. 

This would probably explain why, earlier this year, panicking from the outrage sparked by the infamous Jerry Seinfeld KKK incident on campus in September, the three heads of PIME hastily threw together a tepid response statement, “In defense of constructive dialogue on campus,” in The Chronicle on behalf of Duke which attempted to do damage control and pacify the student body. In reality, it did nothing to address the issues that actually matter to either side. Vacuous statements from the piece, such as “While there are people, perhaps a minority, who identify with the Free Palestine movement who are antisemitic and oppose Israel’s existence, there are those who are not and do not” reflect the total lack of understanding of the Middle East and its people which is desperately needed on this issue. 

And that brings us to now. As Middle East studies continue to decline, a new, very recent development has provided a hint as to where the University plans to take this moving forward. On Oct. 24, Duke released its new global strategy report, outlining its priorities for international involvement in the future. Outside of the astonishing amount of babble within it, the report’s emphasis on shifting international programmatic focus to health, climate and economic development in areas where Duke already has infrastructure sends a clear message: that actual cultural understanding of global regions through the humanities, of which there is a conspicuous absence in the report, is not a priority. 

I spoke with Catherine Mathers, professor of International Comparative Studies (ICS), on the latest report, which she described as “incomprehensible.” 

“I read [the report] and I don’t even understand it. It doesn't say anything,” Mathers said. “I asked [the administration] at the Town Hall, ‘I read this thing and I can't figure out what you mean by global. So, could you please tell me what you mean by it?’ And they said, ‘We can't possibly define it. It's too complicated.’ And [I thought], ‘that's your job!’ They're making financial decisions on where they're investing in terms of research, in terms of hiring, in terms of structural support. How can you make those decisions if you don't know what the vision is?”

The report is the latest indication that area studies and humanities are a sacrifice our university seems gladly willing to make in exchange for more expedient public relations. As Mathers said to me, “This is clearly a campus that is willing to compromise intellectually for maintaining good administrative relationships.”

At a time when a good understanding of the Middle East is absolutely paramount, Duke is cutting key programs in the field. While in the small, myopic world of Duke administration, the move may seem prudent, it is one that they will come to deeply regret. That much I can promise. Middle East studies are needed now more than ever, and if our university hopes to produce the next generation of responsible policy-makers and critical thinkers, on which it has staked so much of its reputation, they will need to take a long, hard look at where their priorities truly lie. 

Leo Goldberg is a Trinity sophomore. His pieces typically run on alternate Mondays.

title: Build back breakfast for new Devils
author: Anagha Gowda
article_text:
Marketplace: the world of fresh fruit and unlimited pizza. Every freshman appreciates Marketplace, and if they don’t, they eventually do as sophomores, juniors and seniors. Marketplace has long been the place of predominantly breakfast and dinner for freshman who are still exploring their habits regarding meals — whether it be loading up on breakfast, light snacking throughout the day or eating three meals a day. 

However, every college freshman has experienced large differences in their lifestyles from high school to college — the nights get later, classes get pushed back to the afternoon, and days start and end on a delay. 

Breakfast becomes quickly inconvenient and not worth the hassle. 

Marketplace is open for breakfast from 7:00-7:30 AM and then 7:30-11:00 AM on weekdays. For many students, the rush of the morning leaves them unable to attend these hours. Perhaps their first class is later or on West Campus and they cannot afford the time to swing by for a sit-down meal.

Skipping breakfast every once in a while can be a minor inconvenience. But the effects on the student body and their ability to work and learn effectively throughout the day are drastically affected. 

Research has found skipping breakfast, particularly in college students, to be significantly associated with other health problems, such as depression, decreases in happiness, increased stress, loneliness and a plethora of sleep-disruptive issues. Not only are students more at risk of digging themselves into a hole of significant health risk when they skip breakfast, but they have also been found to have reduced concentration within classes and exams and suffer from lower academic performance.

Connecting these findings back to Duke, what essentially has become the case is that Duke students, unable to adequately fit in breakfast while they are learning to build a new lifestyle, have been pulling themselves away from their best possible versions, physically, mentally and academically.

These are habits that become a staple even once they leave East Campus and eventually, Duke. Even if these same students do have opportunities to eat a good breakfast (whether that be when they have access to three meals a day at WU or they no longer consider adding what is more than crucial to their own wellbeing. 

Skipping breakfast becomes a cycle — a cycle where students who have the potential to be better are restricted to less because their bodies are not getting the adequate nutrition needed to succeed.

But what can Duke do to cut this cycle short?

Duke’s role as a university is completely unique in aiding the future generations of adults in crafting healthy and successful lives. By encouraging breakfast intake or making it more convenient, students may not neglect what could arguably be seen as the most important meal of the day. 

There are three easily foreseeable ways to do so:

The first: to simply extend the hours of Marketplace breakfast. Even an hour or two of extended breakfast (perhaps 7:30-12 instead of 7:30-11) could allow students to have the time to swing by, sit down and enjoy Marketplace’s world-famous omelettes. 

The second: to allow students to take Marketplace breakfast to-go. With the same compostable paper boxes used at WU, MarketPlace might entertain the idea of allowing students to pack their breakfasts into boxes and take them with them on the way to class.

The third: to expand equivalency options at WU. Many freshmen who have to rush in the morning to the 10:05 chemistry lecture in the far, far classrooms of Gross Hall may find it convenient to just pick up breakfast at CaFe or Panera on the way, rather than eating every single time (and easily getting bored with) Skillet. Having extra options in what they could eat for breakfast may encourage students to take advantage of equivalency. 

Duke students are known to be some of the hardest workers, the best and the brightest. I would say that Duke has the opportunity to foster these young minds beyond just classes – they have the opportunity to foster healthy adults whose habits allow them to harness their full potential. Potential only unleashed through the power of breakfast.

Anagha Gowda is a Trinity first-year.

title: Duke shows what not to do when feds come knocking
author: Dominic Coletti
article_text:
Duke’s fight against the Trump administration has a new front: employee speech. After the White House accused the school of maintaining unlawful racial preferences and cut millions of dollars in research funding as punishment, the University ordered its employees to keep silent.

In late August, Jenny Edmonds, Sanford School of Public Policy’s associate dean of communications and marketing, emailed faculty members that all requests about “Duke and current events” must go through the University’s PR office. She cited increased scrutiny on universities and their policies and admonished faculty to stay in their lanes, discussing only their research with the media. While Edmonds’s message was limited to the public policy school, faculty across the university got similar messages. President Vincent Price and Academic Council Chair Mark Anthony Neal praised the faculty, with Neal remarking it was “pretty amazing” that the Times received no comment from faculty members.

This kind of restriction is offensive to free speech principles. Students and employees of private universities — that promise not suppress speech — have a right to speak with the media on matters of public concern. At public schools, those rights are protected by the First Amendment, but at Duke, it is the University’s own promises that enshrine employees’ rights to speak freely, without fear of university retaliation.

Restricting their expression not only hurts these community members’ speech rights but also the rights of other concerned citizens to listen to expert opinions about the institutions they know best. And imposing a restraint — even an implicit one — on what employees can say to the media makes Duke a liar, belying its posturing as a university committed to open discourse.

Unfortunately, Duke isn’t alone in targeting speech to avoid political ire. Just ask student journalists at Purdue University, which broke off its longstanding agreement to distribute student newspaper The Exponent, citing a fear that others would conflate the paper’s positions with the university’s. Even though Purdue never cited the Trump administration’s campaign against higher education institutions, the insistence that honoring its agreement would constitute endorsing everything printed in a 135-year-old student newspaper suggests it, like Duke, wanted to make sure nothing its constituents said could draw unwanted government scrutiny.

And one can understand why Duke and Purdue felt pressure to censor their community members. There are countlessexamples of the Trump administration bringing the heat to universities, costing them hundreds of millions of dollars in funding. Outspoken students have even led federal officials to investigate — and pause funding for — major institutions. 

The fear that they could be next has not only chilled institutions; it’s led them to punish their own press corps and cut themselves off from other journalists. These responses, while noxious for a culture of free expression, may seem logical to administrators in the face of a government hellbent on attacking higher education. But even if such efforts seem like a good way to dodge pressure from Washington, universities are chilling speech that the Trump administration dislikes without the White House having to do anything.

But the Trump administration’s aggression can only explain so much. Some universities, like Harvard, have minced no words in rebuffing attacks on their institutional independence. Why not Duke? Purdue?

These universities are hurting their own case by targeting employees’ media comments. When they issue edicts restricting what employees can say, what this strongly suggests to an outside observer is that the university is in fact trying to hide something. It’s the higher-ed equivalent of Tony Soprano frantically stashing money in an air vent seconds before the FBI busts down his door. 

Suppressing student and employee speech instead of standing up for an institution's autonomy and legal rights will always be a losing battle. Harvard knew that, and has enjoyed numerous court rulings affirming its First Amendment freedoms. Duke and its peers are facing jarring federal overreach, and one can understand their fear. But in choosing censorship over principle, they hurt their students, their faculty and themselves.

Dominic Coletti is the student press program officer at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression.

title: Stephen Miller is dead wrong … About Christmas
author: Sherman Criner
article_text:
There are few alumni who attract such ire from the Duke community as Stephen Miller. Students loathe him for his brashness and nationalist policies; staff openly denounce his role in planning immigration raids across the country; and the Duke administration — well, to them Stephen Miller is something like the boogeyman to a small child tucked beneath the blanket, shuddering in abject horror and wishing he would “just go away.”

But before Miller rose to the highest heights of political power in the United States, angering nearly every political faction on his ascent, he was a columnist for this very paper. As an undergraduate, Miller wrote on a wide range of topics, often under hilariously terse titles like “Prejudice,” “Betrayal,” and “Persecution” — perhaps an emotional theme is already emerging. Other columns, to his credit, still resonate today, particularly those criticizing Duke’s lack of care for America’s cultural distinctives.

For all my agreements and disagreements with the many arguments Miller penned during his time in Durham, there is one column that stands apart — not merely because it is wrong, but because it illustrates a fundamental error at the heart of his brand of “national conservatism.”

In a Dec. 4, 2006, piece titled “The case for Christmas,” the future presidential advisor blasted Duke administrators for what he saw as a visible lack of Christmas spirit on campus. He amusingly suggested that “you’d probably find more Christmas decorations at your local mosque,” and he decried the fact that “there is absolutely no single logical reason why we shouldn’t have a Christmas tree on the quad and a Nativity scene in the Bryan Center.”

For a university like ours, which boasts both a Divinity School and a Trinity College, and in a country that Miller described as “settled and founded by Christians,” the prospect of a secular Christmas was, to him, unconscionable. Refusing to visibly celebrate Christmas would amount to ripping the very soul out of the community.

So one might reasonably ask: “Why, Ebeneezer, is it so wrong to put up Christmas trees to celebrate our national holiday?”

The answer is simple. It is wrong because we would be doing it for the wrong reason.

There is no such thing as a “national Christmas.” Christmas is not a political instrument or a cultural adhesive designed to bind together a fraying society. Its ultimate meaning does not change depending on which country one happens to inhabit. Strip away the Coca‑Cola polar bears and commercial kitsch, and the essence of the holiday remains constant.

That is not to say Christmas looks identical everywhere. Some societies reject it outright; others celebrate it imperfectly or inconsistently. But the holiday was not created out of thin air, try as corporations might to co‑opt it. Christmas was designated to celebrate something, and it is precisely that something that Miller either ignores or fundamentally misunderstands.

That something is, of course, the birth of Jesus of Nazareth, whom Christians call the Messiah, the “Chosen One.” Hence “Christ”-mas and the oft‑repeated phrase “the reason for the season.”

This reason is nowhere to be found in Miller’s proposal. He would have Duke adorn its campus with wreaths, ribbons and candles not to celebrate the miraculous birth of the Messiah, but to shore up national cohesion. Miller’s attempts to justify this move by claiming that “Christmas has come to represent and embody all that is good and righteous,” yet he never explains what he means by “good” or “righteous,” nor why Christmas should be the chosen vessel.

And, is any of this surprising? Miller does not believe the Christmas story is true. He is — or at least was at the time of writing — a “practicing Jew.” His column praises Christmas almost exclusively for its supposed social benefits, again without ever explaining what makes charity good or why loving one’s family is morally obligatory in the first place. 

At bottom, the Christmas narrative functions as a rhetorical device, a convenient bridge between Miller’s annoyance with Duke administrators and his broader grievance against the “secular left” for talking about justice while rejecting “the ultimate truth of goodness and morality.” In an irony he seems not to notice, Miller arrives at this critique of atheist and agnostic Americans only after spending an entire column watering down Christmas until its meaning becomes so general that anyone, of any religion or philosophical disposition, can get behind it.

Are you Muslim, Hindu, Christian, emotivist or just rolling the ‘ol ball up the hill Sisyphus style? Who cares. In Stephen Miller’s America, on Dec. 25, we all celebrate Christmas, not because it is true, but because it makes us feel good, however we define it.

There is no serious discussion in Miller’s essay of Jesus — his birth, his mission, his sacrifice or anything remotely relevant to why people instantiated Christmas as a national holiday. Apart from a passing request for a nativity scene, the only real mention of Christ comes in a joke about how “the messiah” has yet to arrive.

If none of what I’m saying is clicking, perhaps a metaphor will help. Think of one of those cheap red baubles we hang on a Christmas tree. If Christmas had never become a holiday, if there were no Incarnation to commemorate, no tradition of celebration, no tree upon which to hang it, would that little red ball inspire the same feelings, the same memories as before? Sure, someone might look at it and say, “I like that ball.” But that is not the same as saying it is a Christmas ornament.

The bauble only gains its meaning, its very status as an ornament, when it is placed upon a Christmas tree, in its proper context. Detached from the tree, it is just a glossy object, pleasant perhaps, but arbitrary.

Christmas, in Miller’s telling, is treated as that bauble standing alone. Severed from the event it commemorates and the truth claims that give it substance, it becomes a free-floating symbol, available for whatever political or cultural project happens to need it. He likes the story of Christmas because it offers Americans a common touchstone, but he empties that story of the very thing that makes it meaningful in the first place. Charity and love of family — two virtues Miller cites — became associated with Christmas because they were instructed by Christ.

The only thing that can make Christmas good is an understanding of, and belief in, Christ himself, otherwise we are just fooling ourselves.

Well, then, what do we do about Christmas at Duke?

By my lights, this debate admits of a fairly simple resolution. Either we, as a campus community, openly and unapologetically celebrate Christmas as a commemoration of Christ’s entrance into the world to save humanity from sin and death — or we discard it, superstition and all, into the dustbin of history. There is no squishy, Milleresque middle ground in which Christmas is retained merely for its vibes, its aesthetics or its capacity to generate vaguely warm feelings detached from any coherent account of goodness.

To repurpose a famous argument of C.S. Lewis, there is no room for a merely “good feelings” Christmas. One cannot celebrate something that is either knowingly false or believed for the wrong reasons. The holiday is, to paraphrase Lewis, either treacherous, true or trivial.

Though I, for one, would be among the first to argue that Christmas does indeed commemorate a true historical event, forcing others to celebrate something they not only disbelieve — but to do so for reasons immaterial to the holiday’s transcendent meaning — is just asinine. It is no secret that Duke has long since forsaken its Christian heritage. But that does not mean we can astroturf meaning by scattering religious symbols across campus and declaring “mission accomplished,” George W. Bush–style.

That path leads not to tradition, but to parody, an empty pantomime of faith, all aesthetic and no substance, not unlike the current administration’s tacky, ostentatious patriotism (cough, cough, Secretary Hegseth’s American-flag pocket squares, cough, cough).

So if a Duke Christmas is to mean anything at all, it must mean what it has always meant: a celebration of the most important birth in human history. Anything less is a farce.

Sherman Criner is a Trinity senior.

title: Rewritten: Honoring your inner child and an encounter worth remembering
author: David Goh and Jerry Wang
article_text:
The Chronicle had solicited submissions from alumni and current students for their rewritten Duke supplemental essay based on their time here. Read more about it here.

College admissions serves up a promise: “We’ve identified you as one with potential — here is your chance to be someone who matters.” 

My original Why Duke essay radiated that energy. I wrote about the pressure of team sports and how it had forged my convivial, fiery spirit. I imagined myself declaring, “Watch out, Duke, because now I’m coming your way.”

I really tried. I tried to see everything, do everything and be everyone’s inspiring team captain. I descended on the Club Fair like an interrogative tornado. Maximize exposure, maximize growth. I visited class after class and community after community, vying to find my fit and make my mark.

It seemed to work. In Marketplace lines, Wilson common rooms, and later on, WU, I found myself chatting with people I recognized from events or mutual friends, listening intently and taking pride in being someone who sincerely meant it when I asked, “How are you?” My calendar overflowed.

But eventually, the whispers began. “I don’t want to go to this lunch.” “I should have taken this class next semester.” “I can’t sleep.” “I can’t go on.”

And the voices were mine.

Sometimes you have to honor that scared, shy child inside. You gain more than you expect when you let others take the lead. By senior year, I learned to simply follow friends into the spaces they loved. Seeing Duke through their eyes taught me more than ambition ever could.

You don’t need to do everything; scrambling to fit obscures the view. Perhaps growth arrives when you finally sit still long enough to let it.

David Goh, Trinity ’25

Duke, more than any other community I’ve belonged to, challenged me, but probably not entirely in the ways that it intended. Yes, I was surrounded by whole new social circles that challenged me to leave my comfort zone. Yes, I encountered so many diverse cultures and perspectives that challenged me to open my mind that much more. And, yes, I was challenged by every midterm and final Pratt had to throw at me.

But, most of all, being at Duke challenged me to accept the life I wanted. And what I wanted wasn’t to go to medical school, to get a PhD, to be a start-up founder. It was not to pursue prestige, academic excellence or a top employer. I wanted a life that simply made me happy, with people who made me happier. 

By Duke academic standards, I probably came across as incredibly average. In four years, I stopped viewing this as a weakness and instead came to embrace the fact that I was average at what was still one of the top schools in the world. That was already enough for me. 

I will always be in awe of the ambition and perseverance of so many of the people I went to school with. These are my lifelong friends, and I intend to cheer them on every step of the way as they deserve to continue to climb. I’m so grateful to have been in those circles. And I’m equally grateful that I didn’t try to reinvent myself into something I wasn’t.

Jerry Wang, Pratt ’22

Rewritten is a recurring column of short reflective essays by Duke alumni and current students.

title: On the preventable Blue Devil pandemic
author: Anagha Gowda
article_text:
Freshman flu: the diabolical downturn of O-Week and FDOC season. Every single student has been warned over and over about the first sign of a college freshman: sniffles, dry coughs and nasal voices.

Now, it has long been known that freshman flu is a culmination of multiple factors — changes in climate, lifestyle and exposure to cold viruses all at once. Every student, no matter the strength of their immune system, is susceptible to some form of illness as they grapple with large changes in their life. 

While freshmen getting sick is the college story of centuries and cannot be prevented, at Duke, it quite often gets out of hand. Besides the freshman flu, bronchitis and even cases of pneumonia, strep throat have plagued East Campus for months. Even near the end of the semester, people continue to re-contract viruses they have already gotten. 

Part of the issue is being able to get access to health care at Duke. In a new environment, navigating a new healthcare system — whether it is figuring out how to schedule an appointment, taking a trip to the clinic itself or figuring out how to use your STINFs. 

What makes it harder is having little to no health resources on East Campus. Since freshmen have been shown to experience significantly more health problems than upperclassmen, this issue with combating sickness is increasingly exacerbated. Think about it: no campus health clinic on East. No place to buy basic viral medications. No supply of masks, disinfectant spray or wipes.

Students who are sick must go to West Campus to get into their appointments and must schedule those appointments multiple weeks in advance. Sometimes, students are not even diagnosed in person, but rather through a phone call that addresses their condition virtually. By the time they get through the process, the students have either overcome the sickness naturally (for much longer than they should have) or passed it on to at least three or four others.

East Campus is bound to become a beehive of viruses and bacteria. Freshmen cough on each other, pass around DayQuil and Claritin to try and fight it. Then, they get sick again because someone new coughed on them. And because the process of going to see a physician or a clinic becomes too much of a hassle to undergo, freshmen repeatedly just choose to thug it out as opposed to actually getting treated.

This is not to say that the Student Health Center on West Campus is not doing a good job, or that they are failing to care for Duke students adequately — it is to say that they do not have the resources to get adequately involved with each Duke student who needs care.

By expanding healthcare on East Campus, much of the spread of viral infections can be diminished and the healthcare responsibilities of the center on West Campus can be lessened. Rather than having to scramble to get treated, being able to speak to physicians and get over-the-counter medications close to the East dorms could prevent the spread of flu and colds among first-year students. 

It could be as simple as dedicating a small portion of White Lecture Hall or Marketplace (upstairs or downstairs) to an office that can address basic health concerns and give students the medications they need. Having access to information on handling your own health becomes increasingly important in an atmosphere where your decisions are completely your own and your life is in your own hands. 

Duke supplementing the living experience on East Campus with medical resources could allow students not only to take care of their health on campus now, but could also teach them crucial life skills in advocating for their health in the future. 

Health issues are an unavoidable part of the freshman experience; however, struggling with such issues is not. With even the smallest of efforts, what has become the overwhelming freshman flu can become nothing more than a small hiccup in a greater college adventure.

Anagha Gowda is a Trinity first-year.

title: Who are you now?
author: Fiza Khan
article_text:
When we first arrived here, most of us were just trying to do it right.

Taking the right classes, joining the right organizations, volunteering enough weekends — we’d become the people we were supposed to be.

Smart, capable, good.

Somewhere between what we planned and what actually happened, we changed — not all at once, but in ways that stuck.

It wasn’t just the work. It was the people.

The quiet ones who made us think harder, the loud ones who made us speak up, the ones who challenged what we thought we knew.

For some of us, that shift happened in moments we didn’t expect.

Like when you’re walking past a table in WU, rushing to get food before class, and you overhear two people arguing — not fighting, just genuinely wrestling with whether activism is best displayed through protests or working within institutions. As they push toward common ground, their conversation ends on a quieter, more subtle acknowledgement: that sometimes the hardest part isn’t speaking — it’s being heard.

Not a scientific breakthrough or sudden insight — just a small thing that stuck with you. And it wasn’t even your conversation.

Our time at Duke has been full of noise, involving elections, wars, social movements, conversations that start in classrooms and spill into the quad. And in the middle of all that, we’ve had to figure out who we are, even if no one’s grading us for it.

And, can’t sit through a campus protest, a student government debate, or even a late-night talk in the dorm hallway without realizing how much people here care — and how messy care can become and how messy caring can become.

There’s this idea that growth looks like confidence – like you’ll wake up one day and just know what you believe. But really, growth here has meant realizing how much we don’t know.

It means sitting in a seminar where your worldview expands just a little, or even arguing with someone who makes a good point you wish you hadn’t ignored.

Somewhere between East and West, between first-year ambition and whatever this version of us is now, things got multidimensional — and real. We learned how to have hard conversations — about race, privilege, politics, grief, burnout — and how to stay in them without shutting down.


We learned that silence is also a statement. And that sometimes, the bravest thing you can do is admit you’re tired.

And in the midst of all of that, Duke stopped being a backdrop and started being a mirror.

The people we’ve met here – professors, friends, the random person you sit next to in WU during rush hour — they’ve seen versions of us we didn’t even know existed.

They’ve seen us when we were in the midst of contemplation, when we were quiet for too long, when we finally started to understand what matters. Suddenly, we aren’t the same people who showed up with plans to “make an impact.”

And maybe, that’s the real Duke education.


Not the classes or the grades or the résumés, but what’s left after all of that fades — the small, hard-earned understanding of what it means to live among others, to listen, to keep learning even when it’s uncomfortable.

The first time someone challenged your worldview, it felt like an attack.

The second time, it felt like a question.


By the third, it started to sound like an invitation.

And then there were the quieter lessons — the ones that didn’t fit on a résumé.


Learning that service isn’t about pity but solidarity.


Learning that intellect means little without compassion.


Learning that some of the smartest people you’ll ever meet are the ones who admit they’re still figuring things out.

So, who are you now?


Maybe still changing.


Maybe still learning.


But definitely, just people — a little more aware, a little more patient, still figuring it out.

Fiza Khan is a Trinity junior.

title: The costumes we wear
author: Ashlei Tomlinson
article_text:
This Halloween, my friend and I — we’ll call her Stacy — decided to drive to Franklin Street. The drive, though slow, had its perks. There were no $80 rideshares, no sketchy detours, just "HOT GIRL" playlists. I’m talking Beyonce, Ariana Grande, Saweetie, Ariana Grande. Really, Ariana Grande ad infinitum, especially her “Positions” and “Thank U, Next” albums. 

Going bar for bar, we recited Ariana’s discography. That is, until the odd ‘eternal sunshine’ tracks played, silencing us. Silencing us as we glanced at each other. Silencing us as we subconsciously agreed to “Thank U, Next” over to the next song. That happened a few more times before I said:

“You know, I really miss Black Ari.”

Stacy, my very tolerant friend, understandably answered, “What?!”

Myself, an equally tolerant, albeit exasperated Black woman, replied again, “She was better Black.”

And I stand by that. A few self-tanners ago, Ariana’s music seemed to have a broader appeal or, at least, a broader platform, whereas her new releases, with the exception of the "Wicked" soundtrack, seem to have come and gone. Perhaps her past successes amount to ‘right place, right time’ metrics, her music befitting the culture psych-geist of the time. 

But, if that’s the case, we must ask ourselves how and why she fits the culture. To that question, I would answer her adoption of Black costume — affected ebonics, full-beats, long ponytails and all. These accessories made Ariana fabulous, but they decidedly seem borrowed from Black culture. And I say ‘borrowing’ here as a kindness, though I suspect she was more so taking from than giving to the Black community. 

“But wait,” Stacy said, “if you really do believe that, why would you have wanted her to keep being ‘Black’?”

Navigating a tricky turn, I reflected that, “sometimes, it feels better to hope you’re wrong even when you know you’re right.”

Countless artists — and I mean countless — found their start in Black-centric music. Look at established rappers like MGK or even up-and-coming ones like Ian, the 2025 XXL Freshman, for example. Both men found their start in rap but are now pivoting to country music, or what some would call ‘substantive music.’ 

Using their increasing celebrity, artists like these co-opt Black sound to build notoriety before ultimately transitioning into more respectable, though not necessarily mainstream, music. The refining epidemic, as I call it, is just so predictable. But I suppose it's better to be blissfully ignorant than to know that people treat Blackness as a stop on their final destination to their true ‘clean girl,’ ‘serious artist’ or ‘professional’ selves ... right?

But what does this have to do with Duke?

Why did my friend and I spend 40 minutes en route to Franklin Street discussing Black costume? Well, it seems Duke is falling prey to that very guise both within and without the context of appropriating Black culture. With that, I give you Exhibit A: the Duke “eco-warrior to econ” pipeline. 

What was your ‘Why Duke’ essay? What was your 250-word worth of passion? Did you promise to cure world hunger, to end systemic inequality, to keep ‘questioning’? How many stuck to those passions, if passions they were and not gimmicks to win over admission officers? I ask all this because it seems that, no matter the major, Duke students B-line to finance and consulting. 

The Duke Registrar found that 87% of students in the Class of 2025 stuck with their first major, with about 9.5% of students graduating with either an Economics A.B. or B.S. degree. Assuming comparable stats from year to year, we can look to the Class of 2024 Outcomes to see where the Class of 2025 might find themselves in the coming years. 

The Duke Career Center reported that 31% of seniors in the Class of 2024 entered economics industries, including finance, business and management consulting pathways. Again, if degree and career patterns hold, this would mean that about 20% of students in the Class of 2025 will enter econ industries without economics degrees. 

It could be that these Duke students have a change of heart upon graduation, finding a newfound love for economics. Possible, too, is that these same students feign revolutionary passion to gain access into Duke, only to shed that veneer the second another career — another identity — becomes more profitable. I’m more inclined to believe the latter, given the pattern of behavior Duke students nurture throughout their undergraduate degree. Which brings me to Exhibit B: the funniest guy on campus.

In early October, a Duke student posted this image on Fizz, presumably making a joke. The student suggested that the members ofDuke Students for Justice in Palestine (Duke SJP) were unemployed, or heading for unemployment, based on their participation at the “Name Reading and Die-in” vigil at Abele Quad on Sept. 24.

I understand that this joke might be too high-brow, so I’ve seen fit to break it down further: In this vigil, DSJP commemorates the lives of murdered Palestinians. In this post, the student implies that honoring the dead is tantamount to being unemployed. 

Whether you disagree with Duke SJP or not, the post, given this context, seems unequivocally flippant and dismissive of Palestinian lives and the Pro-Palestine movement at Duke. It’s so unserious. The person who made this post and the people who supported it are so unserious, not because their beliefs are invalid but because they try to repackage them as humor at the expense of another’s passion. It’s disingenuous. Meanwhile, when addressing an issue or event significant to them, many of these same people expect others to observe a gravitas that was previously denied to them. 

Sherman Criner best explores the irony of this imbalance in his column, ‘Duke students lack empathy,’ which unpacks Duke’s unsavory responses to Charlie Kirk’s assassination. And, all things being equal, I believe the two of us can agree that Duke students regularly don costumes, or caricatures of themselves, that are unserious and ready to be exchanged at their earliest convenience.

Whether it be unfunny ‘humor’ or econ-bait-and-switches, Duke students have a problem with being genuine. But are they at least self-aware? Do they realize that they co-opt social justice for admission and trade it for profit? That they demean the passion of others but disallow the same treatment in return? 

No, not exactly.

Of course, I’m not immune to this lack of self-awareness either. Every day, I have to remind myself that 1) all lived realities are not my own and 2) that it’s not for me to bastardize others’ dress and creed in bad faith. When I think that this is hard, I remind myself that it’s not. That it’s much harder to ponder whether blissful ignorance is better than admitting you are someone else’s costume. That it’s much harder for someone inveterately wronged to admit, “it feels better to hope you’re wrong even when you know you’re right.” 

We’ve cycled here through Halloween, Ariana Grande, Black costumes and Duke costumes — econ-pipelines, unfunny ‘humor’ and all. It’s fair to say this conversation escalated quickly, but not, I’d venture, without reason. Take it seriously.

Take this diatribe of mine as words of caution and the sundry of aforementioned vices as things to leave behind with Halloween. They’re scary for a reason. Don’t zip up costumes expecting, consciously or subconsciously, to drop them at a moment’s notice. Ask yourself: what are the costumes that we wear and where do we lie beneath?

Ashlei Tomlinson is a Trinity sophomore.

title: Duke, protect our research mission and workforce
author: Abhishek Chhetri, Aleksander Grimsrud, Cheyenne Lee and Hannah Soliman
article_text:
Recent federal cuts to science funding have caused unprecedented instability for researchers at Duke. Researchers are afraid to plan for experiments that take weeks to months when they could receive news of layoffs in a matter of days. We have had to work under constant stress regarding the security of our positions, with multiple researchers already having had to leave Duke. For international researchers, the stress is worse given that losing jobs will affect their legal status to remain in the United States, where many have been building lives for years.

Duke’s administration has responded by unveiling modest bridge funding opportunities thus far, but other research institutions have put their resources to use more fully and openly. 

Johns Hopkins, which has a similar endowment to Duke’s, provides substantial bridge funding of $100,000 over 12 months and pivot funding of $150,000 over 12 months for faculty who apply. This is beyond the year of support offered to PhDs and postdoctoral scholars to complete their programs. To support such efforts, Hopkins is tapping into its endowment. Meanwhile, Harvard and Yale offer up to 80 or 90% of funding lost from federal cuts, in an uncapped manner proportional to the original grant amount.

Inadequately responding will not only harm Duke’s own employees and researchers but also our ability to receive funding via future grants. After all, 38% of the University’s operating revenue came through grants and contracts, compared to just 15% coming from tuition. This revenue is earned by the hard work and expertise of Duke’s research staff, yet hundreds of these jobs and other supporting jobs have been cut over the last several months. 

With smaller labs, less research will get done, resulting in fewer papers, fewer projects and less preliminary data with which competitive grant applications can be written. Over time, these issues will compound, reducing Duke’s competitiveness.

In response, our research colleagues have been circulating an open letter to protect the University’s research mission and workforce. As of Nov. 15, over 650 researchers, including graduate students, technicians, postdocs and faculty, have signed on in support. We are asking the Duke administration to expand bridge funding to better support researchers by making up the gaps where federal funding has been lost. 

Duke’s administration possesses adequate resources and options to expand bridge funding. Over the last ten years, Duke’s endowment has grown to $12.3 billion for the fiscal year ending June 2025. While the endowment does have restrictions, nearly a third of it is “designated for unrestricted support of the university or one of its schools or budget centers.” Duke should utilize such discretionary portions of the endowment to help its research mission, while continuing to lobby for the restoration of federal grants. Additionally, living donors can be asked to lift restrictions they placed on their endowment contributions. 

Furthermore, when it comes to investment returns from the University’s endowment in the last decade, the numbers fare well against Duke’s goals and peer institutions. Last year’s returns alone may be sufficient to fund struggling labs in a way that is consistent with the University’s recent financial practices, which included designating around $820 million from investment returns to support operations in fiscal year 2024. Duke’s administration could also issue bonds, a measure it employed during the pandemic and one that Harvard is employing right now. Finally, it is worth noting that last month, Duke’s administration announced that it expects to operate at a surplus for the coming year.

On Oct. 9, we and other researchers who have been circulating the open letter delivered it to President Price’s office. On Nov. 4, Jennifer Lodge, the vice president for Research & Innovation, announced new bridge funding opportunities through the Office of the Provost. This directly responds to one of the key demands in our letter and we are heartened that the Duke administration is willing to work with us on protecting funding and research jobs. We encourage everyone in the broader Duke research community to continue to sign the open letter to show continued support for further efforts to protect Duke researchers.

By taking the opportunity to stand with researchers and our broader community, Duke’s administration can not only offer more stability to those of us in its research workforce, but also ensure that we work together to face these unprecedented challenges to higher education. Together, we can ensure that publicly funded research and scientific progress continue to grow. We urge the administration to consider the options laid out above and support its own leadership in research and competitiveness for grants by supporting the people who make it possible.

Abhishek Chhetri, Graduate School '20, is a research scholar in biochemistry.

Aleksander Grimsrud is a lab research analyst in hematology.

Cheyenne Lee is a postdoctoral associate in molecular genetics and microbiology.

Hannah Soliman is a former research technician in psychiatry and behavioral sciences.

title: My dad is the granite foundation of my flimsy cardboard castle
author: Anna Garziera
article_text:
I’m getting to that stage in life when all your friends start turning 21. Except for a couple of babies in the group, we will all soon be proper adults. If we wanted to, we could drive ourselves across the country, get married and even have drinks at our wedding, though we may not be able to book a hotel for the honeymoon. That’s a whole lot of independence. Sometimes, I wonder if I’m ready for it.

I turned 21 last June, and I don’t think I felt any different. Before the crucial birthday, I was a 5-foot-two child who still listened to One Direction and read the Twilight series at least once a year. After my 21st birthday, I drifted more towards Taylor Swift, but everything else remained the same. 

I’ve never been much of a party girl. In fact, the whole “being allowed to drink” thing didn’t make any difference in my life: My party animal spirit peaked at 16 and has since rapidly gone downhill. (Thankfully, I look almost the same as when I was 16, so I can post photos from parties from 2019 and no one will ever know the difference.)

I still live with my parents, and when I say this, I mean it to the fullest extent. When I am home for the summer, every morning I wake up to a bowl and spoon on the table, ready for my breakfast. I trail back upstairs, and find my laundry, done and folded, piled neatly on my dresser. My room is always magically clean, the fridge is always full, and when I come home after walking the dog, dinner is always ready. When I don’t feel like driving, I even steal the occasional ride. 

In other words, I’m spoiled rotten. While at Duke, as an RA, I’m responsible for the residents in my building, at home I’m barely responsible for myself. I’m somewhat saved by the fact that I’m not home a lot, so this pampering, while intense, is sporadic. But the fact remains. I’m 21 and still rely on my parents immensely. 

In a way, I feel this even more when I’m at Duke. I am blessed enough to be able to call my parents at any minor inconvenience. Any time there’s anything wrong with the car, I call my dad and ask him what to do. When I don’t know how long I should be cooking something for, I don’t Google it — I call my mom. I even ring up my little sister every two weeks and tell her to proofread my Chronicle article to make sure I didn’t make any blunders.

But at Duke, I don’t only rely on my parents via phone call advice. I also lean on a myriad of other people. 

First and foremost, I count on my friends. The especially lucky ones hear me knocking on their dorm room doors at two in the morning, in tears, telling them exactly why I can’t fall asleep. But even the others do their share of heavy lifting. From lending me their chargers to listening to me whine for two hours after my wisdom teeth removal, my friends are an integral and ever-present part of my life. I do everything with them: I row with them in the morning, have lunch with them in the afternoon and study with them in the evening. In their absence, my routine would feel broken and void.

To some extent, the same goes for my teachers. For most of my classes, I rely heavily on my professors to help me learn. I am extremely annoying to have in class: my hand is always raised. But I also regularly invite myself to office hours and pack emails with questions even on the weekends.

Take one step further and you’ll realize I even depend on people I barely know. This isn't unique to me. Just as I count on HRL staff to help with my RA programs, you count on the postman to deliver your packages to BC. You may think you got into Duke all on your own — but I’ll bet your high school coach’s advice also played a role.

For all the effort and time you’ve put into bagging all your proudest achievements, you will find you weren’t the only one who had a hand at it. 

In reality, we are not only products of our circumstances but also of our support systems. In other words, it’s not only the opportunities we encounter, but also the people we are surrounded by, who make a difference.

This will never change. I’m now an adult, yet I still heavily rely on everyone around me. As time goes on, I’ll start taking out my own spoon for breakfast and stop expecting to find the laundry neatly folded as soon as I get home. The people I rely on may change. Out of school, into a job, I’ll start asking my colleagues for help. After getting married, I’ll start calling my husband when the car doesn’t start. 

But don’t be deceived: getting older doesn’t mean you don’t need fewer people to help you than before. As a child, when you were sad and confused, you went to your mom. Now, you go to your mom, then your friends and finally your therapist. 

If my dad is the granite foundation of my flimsy cardboard castle, my mom is the super glue holding it all together. But it’s not only them. All of my achievements are a product of the people I have found on my path so far, who have helped me in one way or another.

Whose shoulders are you standing on? 

Anna Garziera is a Trinity junior. Her column typically runs on alternate Sundays.

title: MAHA at Duke? The truth behind TrueBlue
author: Adam Levin
article_text:
Although it was before my time, I still hear stories about the end of Panda Express: the iconic, bright, red-and-black logo replaced by the lifeless, corporate-slop-bowl, millennial-green of It’s Thyme. An affordable, hearty, protein-packed bowl starting at $8.90, replaced by a bowl that never seems to equal the sum of its parts, starting at $11.89. 

But as prices increased, the awards began flooding in. Last year, It’s Thyme received the FareCheck Gold Standard Award for safe, allergen-free dining — a day commemorated by Duke’s crack at a high-profile ceremony, including a ribbon-cutting, DJ booth and free merch. To be fair, there may have been a need for an allergy-free location on West Campus. And other opinion writers have lauded the location for ‘bringing back’ the natural state of human eating, reminding them of our ancestral days of “hunting, gathering or cultivating” (like the famously hunted, gathered and cultivated Pineapple Dole Whip). However, it’s unfortunate that opening It’s Thyme came at the cost of one of the only affordable locations left on campus. 

Yet this phenomenon is a pattern within Duke Dining. That is, introduce new, ‘healthier’ options at the expense of affordable, accessible options, hike prices and rake in the positive news coverage. In September, DukeDining committed to the TrueBlue initiative — agreeing to eliminate artificial sweeteners and food dyes across campus by 2026 and even suggesting that they would work to replace seed oils. 

Here’s the issue: while It’s Thyme may have had a less-than-perfect execution taste-wise and it may have contributed to the problem of Duke’s already exorbitant prices (the average food plan cost across the country is about $600 lower than Duke’s cheapest upperclassmen plan), at least it had clear, evidence-driven goals in mind. I don’t think it’s controversial to say that college students should eat more whole foods, fiber and vegetables. 

Conversely, the goals of reducing artificial sweeteners and food dyes have a much less clear impact on student health. Right now, the Cafe student store looks more like a Whole Foods than a college snack section — so let’s take the example of one of their new candy replacements, the Unreal brand gourmet chocolates. But if I choose to buy the Unreal brand knockoff M&Ms, am I really making a healthy choice? Unreal “chocolate gems” contain 140 calories and 14g of sugar per 30g serving.

Regular M&Ms contain 140 calories and 18g of sugar per 28g serving, a similar report for a candy that is around 2.5 times the price for a share-size bag (50 cents/oz for M&Ms vs. 1.28 cents/oz for Unreal Chocolate Gems). And while I might be reducing my intake of artificial dyes, I might inadvertently be increasing my intake of unsafe levels of lead and cadmium.

This scenario may sound unserious: after all, it’s just a pack of M&Ms. But over time, systematic replacements of our ingredients could have real impacts on students’ well-being. For example, replacing seed oils with olive oils could double the ingredient’s cost. As the same It’s Thyme aficionado noted in another column, rising Wu prices “contribute to a culture of ignoring breakfast, replacing meals with coffee, pushing off eating until work is done and choosing the cheap option over the more desirable one.”

But maybe, once we look beyond the beet-colored M&Ms instead of the red-dye-40-colored ones, the changes to our ingredients will be worth the cost. To address the efficacy of replacing food dyes, seed oils and artificial sweeteners in students’ diets, I spoke with Dr. William Yancy, the Medical Director at Duke’s Lifestyle and Weight Management Center.

He explained that while there is evidence to suggest the health benefits of reducing artificial sweeteners or seed oils in your diet, it’s still an emerging and controversial field of study. However, when asked about Duke Dining’s policy, he responded, “You have to be careful about eliminating… foods that aren’t clearly harmful either… it could be a problem if you outlaw them, and … we don’t have consensus on it yet.”

To his point, there’s also evidence that artificial sweeteners and seed oils can have real benefits. For example, the polyunsaturated fats found in seed oils are almost definitely better for your cardiovascular health compared to saturated fats like butter or lard. And there’s significant, albeit sometimes conflicting evidence, about the possible utility of artificial sweeteners for weight loss. 

However, instead of student health, Duke Dining’s changes seem entirely driven by political pressures and a quest for national attention. A “central part” of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. 's ‘Make America Healthy Again’ or MAHA agenda is eliminating seed oils, food dyes and corn syrups in our food supply. As a result, states and companies across the country have begun cracking down on these ingredients and Louisiana recently passed a bill with goals that are nearly identical to those of the TrueBlue Initiative. The Trump administration has also shown an unrestrained willingness to intervene in higher education — RFK Jr. has already begun directing medical schools to increase nutrition education. 

I’m not arguing that the federal government is forcing Duke to make these changes. But it’s naive to say this decision isn’t part of Duke’s strategy to avoid confrontation with the federal government and remain at the forefront of nutrition trends. 

And what will change once Duke successfully eliminates seed oils, artificial sweeteners and dyes? Even if the evidence is sound, the nutritional content of Duke’s menu might remain roughly similar. Yancy told me that while there isn’t a clear consensus on the harms of seed oils or sweeteners, there is consensus on what students overconsume in their diets: quick, easily digestible starches and sugars. No one is suggesting 86ing the Kraft Ice Cream Sandwich, the sugar-filled Cafe coffees or the Il Forno pasta, but those delicacies have a much more direct impact on our health than seed oils or dyes. 

So, what should Duke do instead? Well, Yancy argues that instead of just giving students the option to choose vegetables, there should be a greater emphasis on vegetables and protein in on-campus restaurants. I agree. While on-campus favorites Gothic Grill and Krafthouse offer a ‘side salad’, it often just looks like a collection of greens with a carrot or two thrown in for good measure. I’d suggest a more universal adoption of the Farmstead model: cooked potatoes, green beans, brussels sprouts and broccoli offered as sides instead of the current options —fries, alternative (sweet potato) fries or lettuce. 

Let’s skip the doubled ingredient price resulting from swapping seed oils for nominally healthier olive oils. Let’s keep options open for students, especially when we lack consensus on the impacts of restricting these options. Instead of following RFK Jr.’s favorite health trends, let’s follow the health guidelines of accessible protein and vegetables around campus. Let’s skip TrueBlue—and try TrueGreen.

Adam Levin is a Trinity sophomore.

title: Tilt at your own windmills
author: Robert Wallace
article_text:
It’s 1974 and I sit in my world literature class. The girls on the other side of the room cross and re-cross their legs. I am seventeen years old, and the teacher has yet to arrive. I chat with Johnny, my best friend, and with Gary, the friend whom I have kept in touch with my entire life. We talk about high school cross country practice that is scheduled to begin at 12:45, joking about how hard we plan to run, dreading the discomfort, wondering if we will be running long, doing a tempo run or repeats on the cinder track. All I can think about is the fact that I have to go to work after practice and how tired my legs will be.

I take out my book: "Don Quixote of the Mancha", and I start reading.

I’m about halfway through book one. I’m unsure what to make of the story; I don’t know if Cervantes is being serious or funny. Some of his phraseology seems a little off-center, quirky, and I wonder what readers in the seventeenth century thought about it. But it is those very sentences that often make me laugh, that even today bring a smile to my face, such as these in Chapter 12 when Don Quixote sits on the ground after another failed intervention “ … and there crammed himself with weeping … “ or this from Sancho Panza when speaking about his master, Don Quixote, and his love of Dulcinea del Toboso, “of whom his lord was enamored up to the livers.”

Mrs. Dempsey walks into the classroom. She is a petite woman. She has brown-colored hair, and she wears thick-rimmed glasses. Her eyes rise over the lenses when looking at us.

“For those of you behind in your reading you’re in luck,” Mrs. Dempsey says. “I’m going to give you time to read in class today. So pull out your books and start reading.”

Tom Selkow immediately reaches for his Cliff Notes.

“You need to read the book, Tom,” Mrs. Dempsey says.

Johnny snickers. He looks as happy as a termite in rotted wood.

“I’m just going to read a little in here first.”

“Read the book, Tom. There’s no enchantment in Cliff Notes.”

“Okay,” Tom says.

“Cliff Notes are an abomination,” Mrs. Dempsey says. “If you fail to read the book you’re missing out on magic and wonder.”

In reading Don Quixote for the first time, I had no idea, until years later, that I was reading something positively new. Perhaps Mrs. Dempsey mentioned that the novel was essentially the first one ever written, at least in the modern sense. But as a boy I don’t recall feeling particularly enlightened by Cervantes writing, although through the years I have come to realize how much is extraordinary about the Quixote. I don’t recall, in my world literature class, we read the second part of Don Quixote.

Published in 1615, the author in truly prescient form, though different from early nineteenth-century “Dear Reader” style, such as Austen, commented on his characters, themselves being aware that “others” have read about them. And it isn’t just this metafictional trick Cervantes employed that has made him copied by writers from all over the world. Cervantes was metafictional long before David Foster Wallace. Fiction by its very nature is an imaginary device whereby readers essentially “suspend” disbelief.

In Don Quixote, Cervantes sends his hero out into the world on adventures to save the world from injustices. Of course, what he surmises as wrongs are frequently misinterpretations, often due to misrepresentations of the people he meets. These misrepresentations, naturally, begin with him. One can imagine Cervantes sitting in a room somewhere, a candle burning well into the night, while he wrote feverously, unsure of what he was creating, but enjoying himself immensely.

"What is this crazy thing I am creating," I imagine him speaking out loud.

Of course Don Quixote isn’t solely about the madcap adventures of a demented middle-aged man and his robust companion. But this is what initially draws in the reader. Later, one understands there is social and political commentary and that one can read the novel on many levels, as satire, magical realism, adventure story or any number of other ways.

I read parts of Don Quixote every year. I’m reading it now, as I do most Decembers. As we approach the end of the semester, I urge you to pick up Don Quixote, and, while on break, go on an adventure. Most assuredly in the book, but perhaps in person. For at its heart, Don Quixote is about standing up for something. It’s about seeing injustices in the world and doing something about them. It is about helping others and calling out wrongs.

Now, as I give in to the memories of my world literature class more than fifty years ago, I chuckle at the boy I was, the man I have become and all the sad and beautiful moments in between. As a sixty-nine-year-old man going back to school at Duke, one of the essential joys of life has been reading. And Don Quixote is a book about reading. And rereading.

For without Cervantes’ novel, we wouldn’t have Mercier and Camier, or Huckleberry Finn, or James, or As I Lay Dying, or Frankenstein, or The Book of Disquiet (a book that never leaves my bedside table). We wouldn’t have Samuel Beckett, Mark Twain, Percival Everett, or Mary Shelley, or Fernando Pessoa. Or even someone as disparate as Clarice Lispector. So I urge you to read. Don’t skip the actual text. Don’t browse a cheat sheet. And write your own story. Don’t let AI do it. You have a unique voice like no other person.

You can go to El Quixote Festival NC for information regarding a local organization supporting activities surrounding Cervantes and other Latino literature. In the Harvard Classics translation by Thomas Shelton, Cervantes himself is attested to have said: “It is so conspicuous and void of difficulty that children may handle him, youths may read him, men may understand him and old men may celebrate him.”

Robert Wallace is a first-year graduate student of liberal studies. His column, 'Telling Stories', typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: Durham melts ICE, Duke should follow
author: Wendy House
article_text:
Last Saturday, Nov. 22nd, two of my friends got arrested. They had been protesting peacefully outside of Krome Detention Center, an institution famous for its inhumane living conditions in Miami, FL. A day prior, back here in Durham, hundreds of locals raised hell at CCB Plaza in an incredible display of solidarity with the immigrant community of our city. 

Federal Border Patrol agents arrived and began deporting and detaining immigrants in the Tar Heel State in Charlotte on Nov. 15th, expanding into the Triangle three days later. Over 30,000 students missed school in the Charlotte-Mecklenburg district, with other NC districts following suit with sweeping absences. Despite the barbaric language ICE uses to describe the people they target — “worst of the worst” or “criminal illegal aliens” — testimony shows that Border Patrol seems to rely on racial profiling to decide who they accost and abduct in the street. 

Since then, the Department of Homeland Security has detained at least 250 people across the state and intends to detain more. Local officials suggested activity was winding down after the 22nd, but immigrant rights organization Siembra NC warns of the deployment of over 50 additional ICE agents this week. 

If I may presume to speculate, though, it seems inevitable that the Department of Homeland Security will be forced to pull its satanic claws out of North Carolina — the state is unambiguously rejecting its slimy, kidnapping advances.

Since the confirmation of ICE presence, affected cities have been ablaze with resistance. “Operation Charlotte’s Web” has, ironically, been tangled up in countermeasures laid out by immigrant rights groups like Siembra NC. Early warning systems switched to watchdog duty (“migra watch”) as soon as they caught wind of the impending invasion, with Siembra’s Defensa Hotline collecting tips and notifying communities of confirmed ICE presence so they might prepare themselves. 

At the same time, average Joes are also taking up the mantle. Just last week, I covered my mentor’s shift at the lab to give them time to deliver groceries to Brown Durhamites unable to leave their homes out of concerns that they would be attacked or deported. Activists ride the bumpers of ICE trucks and honk warnings and high schoolers walk out en masse (including from my own high school!). Protests rage on as warning whistles chime out and churches overflow with attendees for volunteer trainings.

The message is clear: ICE is not welcome in North Carolina — anywhere in North Carolina. Our reaction to occupation has been allergic. I have never been prouder of my state, or my city. 

Say what you will about Trump. Anyone on any end of the political spectrum can appreciate that an organization which oversteps its normal boundaries of operation by well over a thousand miles to haunt a city — racially profiling its inhabitants and harassing them in the street to legally justify their residence in their home — has grown too big for its britches. Virtually everything about the way ICE is operating right now violates due process. It is unconstitutional and, yes, I’ll be the bleeding heart, it is ugly. Binding a man’s hands and then demanding he somehow offer ID? Outright fabricating “1400 criminal illegal aliens” allegedly sitting in NC’s jails in official DHS media? I can’t even compare ICE to the Gestapo, because there is nothing secret about what they do.

So, it is to the silver lining of my community I cling. Nothing quite brings folks together like vans trying to snatch your neighbors off the street. Not that I’ve ever been ashamed of where I come from; I still remember my offense freshman year at some of my peers’ reactions to Durham. Durham is a little dirty, but we protect each other. Southern hospitality isn’t all about manners and superficial niceties, it’s also about solidarity, a familial warmth that extends to everyone in your community without regard to color or creed; in the united local outcry for our immigrant neighbors, I think we’ve proven that as well as anyone could. 

You’re wondering what this mushy monologue has to do with Duke. A perfectly reasonable question. To start, I’ll remind you of a story that went somewhat viral here on campus: Luis Juaréz, the cherished “party bus” driver whom Duke failed to protect. 

Everyone knew and loved him. Even for those like me, too shy to have actually spoken to him, his bumping music was a sunbeam in an otherwise cloudy, mundane C1 ride. Having fought to come to the US from Honduras, he was an inspiration as well as a delight. The Chronicle aptly described him as “beloved by many.” His TPS status expired Sept. 8, and despite the agonized cries of all whose lives he enriched, Duke did nothing to stop it. 

Wait, though, guys! A university spokesperson said “[they] provided him with significant support and resources!” So did Duke give him an employment-based visa? Nope. Did he get to keep his job at all? Well, no. I guess the “support” they were referencing was mostly moral. Shake those pom-poms, Vince!

I don’t mean to make a mockery of Duke’s impotence to defend its immigrant workers. Well, maybe a little. What I mean to say is that Duke doesn’t have to compound this generational fumble with any others. Five Durham community groups, including Siembra NC and Durham Rising, held a press conference on Sept. 19 handing Duke one simple action to support immigrants: become a Fourth Amendment workplace. 

A Fourth Amendment workplace is one that adopts a policy of defense for its workers by informing employees of their constitutional rights during search and seizure procedures and maintaining an awareness that ICE requires a valid warrant to enter any private area. The city of Durham pledged itself a Fourth Amendment workplace ages ago; we’re behind as it is. 

I’m proud of Durham. I’m proud of my friends, the brave jailbirds Artivista Karlin and Abi Human, who drove all the way to Florida to scream and dance in outrage for the souls incarcerated and suffering at Krome. I just want to be proud of Duke, too. 

Wendy House is a Trinity sophomore. Her column typically runs on alternate Wednesdays.

title: The Android-iOS war at Duke
author: Kris Sun
article_text:
War! 

Chinese military tactician Sun Tzu once wrote that “the supreme art of war is to subdue the enemy without fighting.” Indeed, a war has been raging across Duke University. This war is nontraditional. It doesn’t consist of brawling and hellfire, but rather isolation and cultural sabotage. It is a war of attrition, hosted through our cellular devices.

The war is between Android users and IOS. The Samsung Galaxy versus the iPhone. Google versus Apple. 

What feels like 99% of the Duke student population versus me. I am on team Android. 

*sigh* 

Yes, I can hear your sigh of judgment. I myself am sighing. Because, despite the superb quality of my Samsung Galaxy S25 and its 256GB of pure awesomeness, I feel as though I’m an enemy sympathizer in a cold war between patriotic iPhone users and the ideologically incorrect Android-ers. And I feel as though Duke’s student population, whether aware of it or not, has gradually alienated us Android users.

I do not intend to argue that Android is better than IOS, or that my phone is better than yours (even though it is). Such fickle comparisons of blue-green text messages and camera quality have been debated and discussed for years, and are undeserving of an article in The Chronicle. What is deserving of coverage, however, is a thorough examination of how the culture of our phones represents a greater culture of how we dramatize unimportant differences. 

So, you may be asking, what difference does having an Android on an iOS-dominated campus truly make? To which I answer, the difference between having an Android or an iPhone is comparatively minuscule in terms of hardware and drastic in terms of societal acceptance.

Essayist Chuck Klosterman examines how certain cultural phenomena ingrain themselves into the popular zeitgeist, to the point that “ignoring a cultural phenomenon today may render you completely irrelevant in a few years.” His go-to example is Harry Potter: if you never read the books 10 years ago, then you’re just simply out of the loop. And every time someone shouts “EXPECTO PATRONUM” on Halloween night, you simply won’t appreciate it like the individuals who have read the books. I feel the same way towards Apple products.

The iPhone, iPod and iPad have all cemented themselves as cultural norms, which means that individuals who haven’t partaken in them are matter-of-factly culturally different. The terms “GamePigeon” and “AirDrop” are enemy codewords to my ears. As such, whenever someone says “I’ll AirDrop it to you”, I feel a sense of shame when I am forced to tell them that they can’t. Alternatively, I can only imagine the dismay one feels when requesting my location, only to receive a Google Maps link in return. I’ve certainly lost my own belongings before, wishing that someone could access my nonexistent AirTag.

Group chats are far worse. I can recall numerous experiences seeing friends’ faces drop in disappointment after adding me to a group chat, only to realize that they just permanently locked their social circle. In my experience, students at Duke sometimes treat creating a new group chat for an Android user as if it’s the equivalent of moving to a new house by burning down their old one. This imposed hardship has reached a point at which individuals have explicitly revealed that they chose not to include me in group chats solely due to the small technical differences between our operating systems. It cannot be that serious.

Another isolating aspect is the deliberate differences between mobile applications. Social apps like Fizz and Sidechat, exclusive to the App Store, have become a hub for exclusion in which Android users (or at least I) feel out of the loop with campus drama. My iPhone friends, more than once, have bragged about their Fizz comment blowing up, to which my only available reaction is a blank stare.

Simultaneously, new applications in development are almost always built with the iPhone in mind. Styl, a Duke-founded fashion app, started as an iOS-exclusive application. Even after being acquired by a larger app, GOLD, it remains inaccessible to Google Play Store devices.

If the Android-IOS War is the battle, then Duke has become the battleground. Beyond simple social stigma, I've begun noticing the sheer exclusion that Duke has created in its implementation of technology. Physics labs, for example, run on Mac computers, which has become highly problematic for me, a non-Mac user. There have been numerous occurrences where I’ve been stuck, troubleshooting methods to get my force displacement graphs from the computer to my phone, or struggling to print PDFs in the Link.

Perhaps the most alarming implication of this iOS bias is that it has slipped into our cultural mainframe so seamlessly that Android users simply accept that our phones lead to inequitable treatment. This became most apparent during the September 20th football game between Duke and local rival NC State, in which I had attempted to enter Wallace Wade Stadium, a digital ticket in my (Google) Wallet, only to be rejected by a staffer because my screen did not look like everyone else’s. I did not get to see the game that day. 

I don’t blame the gameday worker, nor do I fault the Duke community for its preferential treatment towards the iPhone. The reason why is open to speculation, but there are reasons to believe that the iPhone is as much a status symbol as it is a piece of technology. Owning an iPhone means that you belong to the elite iOS community, and that individuals who own Android products belong to lower rungs on the social hierarchy ladder.

We do the same as we judge each other for such fickle things as the quality of our clothes or the brand of our shoes. And so, the Android-IOS war is indeed a war of attrition and it’d be ignorant to ignore the domination of all things i-________ on college campuses. As an Android user at war, I’m constantly adapting and changing my tactics, whether I’d like to or not. It’d be much appreciated if I could do so without deliberate hostility from other fellow soldiers (students).

Rather, as society’s cultural preferences shift, it's crucial that we don’t alienate non-conformers. The trivial difference in our phone choice matters very little in the grand scheme of our social interactions. That is, until we treat these differences as more important than they actually should be made out to be. 

As Sun Tzu states, “There is no instance of a country having benefited from prolonged warfare.” So, while the Android and IOS operating systems continue their international battle for market shares, perhaps it would be more productive to just lay down our dramatic overreactions to different colored texts and give more flexibility whenever a fellow student can’t answer a FaceTime. 

To my friends plagued by my Android, I’m sorry that you have to create new group chats. But in a much more real sense, just make the chat and chill out.

Kris Sun is a Trinity sophomore. His column, ‘Multitudes,’ typically runs on alternate Mondays.

title: Duke students bring back insufferability this Thanksgiving
author: Monday Monday
article_text:
Editor's note: The piece below is satire.

In one of Duke’s most time-honored traditions, students flocked home to their families for Thanksgiving, inadvertently bringing back pretension, insufferability and the general elitism that only being a Duke student can provide. “Innocent families have never been exposed to this kind of group psychosis before,” say The Chronicle’s leading scientists, “It’s like how Columbus’ voyages brought smallpox, but more devastating.”

To research this phenomenon, Monday Monday listened in on Thanksgiving conversations around the country. In Chicago, Illinois, a Duke freshman was heard explaining to bored relatives that he was attending “the Harvard of the South” before attempting to steer the conversation toward the U.S. News & World Report College Rankings. With no natural defenses against the phenomenon, a cousin was forced to listen to a pretentious diatribe about “school value as an excellence indicator” until he called Duke a “shadow Ivy.”

It has also been reported that, in Phoenix, Arizona, a Duke junior was heard trying to convince an uncle to care about dining hall quality while completely sober. This same junior was seen trying to show people the r/Duke subreddit on his phone while several family members stepped out of the room to ‘take calls.’ At one point, the student threw a plate at an aunt’s newborn when she tried to toast her late mother instead of continuing to ask about the Ginger & Soy menu.

Scientists noticed that the most common symptom across the student body could be referred to as “ACC viral plague,” in which students, acting in what appeared to be a hive mind, commandeered living room televisions across America to watch Duke while trying to convince their families that Duke was going to be a No. 1 seed again after 5 losses. There is no known cure.

In an effort to combat this growing epidemic, Monday Monday recommends that family members of Duke students employ these common strategies that neutralize and neuter these students. The most commonly recommended approach is to position a family member from a more highly ranked university between the student and you, preferably at a school the Duke student applied to but was rejected from.

If no such family members are available, asking the Duke student if they have an upcoming internship can prove effective. If the student does indeed have an internship, ask which company and respond, “Not Google?” no matter their answer.
