If none of these methods work, we recommend disarming the student in either the head or torso, where it’s believed most of their vital organs are located.

Monday Monday is currently texting “Back at Duke University, which I attend!” to their family group chat. There is no reply.

title: Anticipating joy
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
Almost 2,000 years ago, a man in prison, the Apostle Paul, wrote in a letter, “Do not be anxious about anything” (Philippians 4:6). It’s as if he were peering two millennia into the future and reading our emails, skimming our social media posts or hearing echoes of our kitchen conversations.

We are often frightened and uneasy about the state of existential realities, living on islands of anxiety, isolated in and by our own fear in a vast ocean of incredible uncertainty. Scholars have written about how young people in our day have become more anxious due to the overuse of social media and overparenting. But in reality, all generations can become anxious by constantly devouring newsfeeds.

Anxious about where this nation is headed. Anxious about the state of the world as we look at Ukraine and Russia, Israel and Gaza and ICE agents roaming on the streets of America. Anxious about the environment and climate. Anxious about deep ideological and cultural divides. 

There is a folktale in which a grandfather is talking to his grandson about his feelings and says, “I feel as if I have two wolves fighting in my heart. One wolf is vengeful, angry and violent. The other wolf is loving and compassionate.” The grandson asks him, “Which wolf will win the fight in your heart?” The grandfather answers, “The one I feed.” 

Do we feed our anxiety? The answer is critical because we are what we consume.

We can hear “Do not be anxious about anything” repeatedly, but the longest road is sometimes the path from our head to our heart. Poet Mary Oliver captures our anxious plight in her poem “I Worried.” It begins:


"I worried a lot. Will the garden grow, will the rivers
flow in the right direction, will the earth turn
as it was taught, and if not how shall
I correct it?"

The answer to this question, and many like it, comes at the end of the poem:


"Finally, I saw that worrying had come to nothing.
And gave it up. And took my old body
and went out into the morning,
and sang."

We can worry endlessly, but to what end? A song-less life? Worry has no good outcomes and comes to nothing in the end. So why worry?

When we are anxious, we tend to anticipate trauma. In academia and beyond, there has been a rise in trauma studies and engagement with trauma theory, so we hear a lot about being “trauma-informed”— trauma-informed care, trauma-informed practice, trauma-informed systems and so on. 

While I understand the importance and influence of trauma on individuals and communities, this terminology can make it seem as if the whole story of humanity is trauma. Trauma is a part of human life, but it doesn’t have to inform your whole life because it is not your whole story.

If we prioritize trauma, this will lead to what Dean of Trinity, Gary Bennett, calls “anticipatory anxiety.” This means we live in anticipation of more trauma, thus creating more anxiety even before we actually experience what we anticipate. Put differently, anxiety is both a reaction to anticipated trauma and a creator of further anticipation.

This is where rats can help us. In a behavioral neuroscience research lab experiment at the University of Richmond, scientists created a rodent car from a plastic cereal container and discovered that rats could learn to drive the tiny car by grasping a small wire that acted like a gas pedal. After a while, the rats started to steer it with precision to reach their Froot Loop treat. 

As the experiment progressed, the researchers built rat-operated vehicles, ROVs, designed by a robotics professor, which were supposedly a rodent version of Tesla’s Cybertruck. These rats adapted to driving these mini cars, revealing how their brains can adapt to learning new skills (an example of neuroplasticity).

But there was something more than just the acquisition of skills that rose to the surface. One day, one of the scientists walked into the lab, and three driving-trained rats ran to the side of their cage, jumping up like a dog asking to go for a walk. This apparent expression of excitement prompted the scientists to shift their study to exploring how positive events, and anticipation of those events, shape neural functions. 

What they found was that rats who had to wait to receive rewards (like food treats) had a more optimistic cognitive style, performed better on cognitive tasks and were bolder in problem-solving. The scientists were learning that anticipation can reinforce behavior — even the very anticipation of a positive experience can create the emotion of that experience. 

For instance, the rats trained to anticipate positive experiences like driving were more likely to hold their tails high than untrained rats — straight up with a crook at the end like an umbrella — a posture linked to increased dopamine levels. 

And when they gave the rats the option to drive to their Froot Loop reward or walk a shorter distance to it, two out of three rats chose driving, revealing that the rats enjoyed driving. The conclusion was that planning, anticipating, and enjoying a ride has healthy benefits for the brains of rats.

The experiment revealed that there are benefits to anticipating the joy of things we love, even before experiencing them. So, instead of anticipating anxiety and trauma, how about anticipating joy? If these rats did, why can’t we?

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: Missing period products: Why Duke must provide this basic care
author: Aria Dwoskin
article_text:
Periods are — much to the frustration of women — a routine part of life. I got my first period when I was around 12, and understood innately that this was something I would be dealing with once a week, every month, for the next forty-some years of my life. This was a biologically inescapable, absolute certainty. 

Another certainty: periods require supplies. Many women use tampons and pads, often requiring several a day for several days. On average, an individual uses 22 menstrual products each cycle, amounting to approximately 11,000 over one’s lifetime. 

So why were there no tampons or pads in my dorm’s bathroom for two months?

The underfunding and chronic lack of focus on women’s issues is no secret — and this blatant neglect extends into feminine care. This is seen not just in the lack of period products present in public places, but in the price for them. The price of tampons and pads has risen faster than the price of food. In 2024, the price for tampons had jumped 36% and pads 41% since 2019, with both costing about $6.50 and $8.29, respectively.

Further, 18 states charge a sales tax on period products, including North Carolina, with a “tampon tax” of 4.75%. These factors compound to perpetuate period poverty, in which women cannot afford necessary menstrual hygiene products. In a 2019 study in Obstetrics & Gynecology, 64% of women struggled to afford period supplies, and 21% could not afford them on a monthly basis. 

People who menstruate are biologically required to manage periods for the majority of their lives — yet they are forced to pay high prices and taxes for the basic products needed to do so. As many women know, having these supplies on hand is essential, as bathrooms commonly lack period products. According to a national study commissioned by Free The Tampons, 86% of women have found themselves without supplies when their period started, and 1 in 5 low-income women has missed school or other events because they lacked period products. This, too, is the reality for many Duke students. 

It is no surprise that Duke University — like institutions across the country — is failing to prioritize consistent, accessible and free menstrual products for those who need them. But is that really so much to ask? 

53.7% of Duke’s undergraduate population is female, which amounts to about 3,502 students. And Duke requires these students to live on campus for three years, charging immense room and board fees throughout that time. Given that, is it too much to expect the university to provide free period products in our dorm bathrooms? And across all campus bathrooms?

I do not think it’s unreasonable to say that students deserve this basic form of healthcare. Especially when it has been recognized that Duke spends millions on "unnecessary renovations." Couldn’t a small portion of these funds be reallocated to support stocking menstrual products across campus? 

The irony is that my dorm bathroom was finally graced with a plastic box of free tampons and pads the other day — but not because Duke provided them. The beautiful, equity-driven and empowering student organization Progress Period has taken it upon themselves to fill this gap. In 2023, they partnered with Quad Council to launch an initiative supplying dorm spaces with free menstrual products. Through baseline and follow-up surveys, they found that after a three-month pilot in Few Quad, menstrual product accessibility reported a 133% increase, going from a 1.67 to a 3.9 rating after the pilot. 

I commend this organization, but I criticize the conditions that made their work necessary. Why should a student group be responsible for supplying basic health products to female students? Why can’t Duke, with a $12 billion endowment, award each bathroom a handful of tampons and pads? If a student club can fund and implement this initiative, surely the seventh-best university in the nation is capable. 

It’s important to note that some Duke bathrooms do offer free menstrual products, but access is inconsistent, unreliable and varies widely across campus. Progress Period revealed that this does not need to be the case; additional Duke initiatives and national efforts reiterate this. 

Take Duke’s Sanford School of Public Policy. Directors of Sanford Women in Policy raised a pressing question: why does the federal government require bathrooms to provide soap and toilet paper and not tampons and pads? Their effort was inspired in part by Scotland, the first country to make period products free for all students. They underscored the health risks of inaccessibility, which includes prolonged use and infection. To combat this, they partnered with Cora and piloted a month-long initiative stocking restrooms with menstrual products. 

And Sanford’s initiative isn’t new. Additional student organizations have also tried to tackle the issue. In 2017, after a pilot stocking the Bryan Center, Code Red and Duke Student Government placed free products in Perkins library and removed the coin requirement. The need was so clear that the products have remained there since. 

This pattern matches what’s happening across the country. 28 states and DC have passed laws supporting free menstrual products in school — though many fall short of actual requirements. In North Carolina, a 2022 grant program passed, providing funding to each school to purchase period products. Again, though, this is an optional endeavor, and does not provide the same offerings to universities. 

With growing government momentum, and implementation in K-12 schools, it is clear that now is the time for Duke to act.

We pay substantial tuition. We live in Duke housing. We use Duke facilities every day. In return, all we ask for is reliable access to tampons and pads. Surely a world-class university has the means to provide this basic health need. The question is whether they are willing to act.

Aria Dwoskin is a Trinity sophomore.

title: Duke, leave legacy behind
author: Harrison Walley
article_text:
I should preface this article by saying that I think I deserve to be at Duke, as do other legacy students here. I imagine that this article will get pushback from alumni and legacies, but I want to clarify that I am in no way saying that current legacy students are unqualified or do not deserve to be here.

There is, however, no reason that I should’ve gotten into Duke over non-legacy students who are more qualified than me — a demographic that I can only assume is quite large — just because I have family members who went here. Don’t get me wrong, I worked hard to get here. Duke was, in fact, the only college I ever wanted to attend.

Still, I also understand a harrowing truth: for every family of a legacy admit, overjoyed at the results of the college application process, there are qualified non-legacies who will receive rejection letters from Duke and wonder what went wrong. I distinctly remember the disappointment of a classmate at my high school upon hearing that multiple legacies got into Duke through the Early Decision application, while she didn’t. Neither the lifelong dream I had of attending Duke nor the work I put in to get here will ever erase the fact that I benefited from an unfair admissions system.

This is not a groundbreaking revelation. You’ve probably heard the argument to end legacy admissions repeated over and over again. From The New York Times to The Chronicle, people have been quick to express their concerns. I have, however, rarely heard legacies and alumni echoing the same sentiment from their unique perspective.

I’m disappointed. Though we are in a unique position to benefit from unequal, preferential treatment, we also have a unique responsibility to pave the path for new members of the Duke community, a goal that can only be realized if we call for the outright rejection of legacy preference.

Right now, Duke is continuing to stretch the past to justify the institutionalization of legacy admissions. In a 2022 address to the Academic Council, President Price stated, “We're an institution that was made in a family — the Duke family. We bear the name of that family. We represent family, we talk about family, so how does that translate into the way we behave? The idea that you would ban legacy admissions, or ban any particular factor as a consideration, is troublesome.”

Indeed, Duke University was founded by a family, but in what world does that justify the exclusion of some people in order to perpetuate a dynastic admissions process? The strength of a community like ours is its ability to grow, to branch out and to become diverse. President Price makes the mistake of conflating kinship with community. We are a community, not a literal family. The term “Duke family,” referring to alumni, current students and their kin, has been mistakenly used to harm the development of our community through legacy admissions.

Duke’s view on legacy admissions is clearly misaligned with the Office of Undergraduate Admissions’ mission statement, which states, “We consider each applicant as an individual,” and “We are committed to upholding and promoting Duke’s commitment to equity.” When the Duke administration is openly unwilling to budge on unfair and contradictory policies, alumni and legacies have a responsibility to step in. We are, after all, part of that extensive Duke family that the University loves to tote.

Alumni are pivotal to Duke’s operations, which can be a double-edged sword in the legacy debate. Universities like Duke may justify the practice of legacy preferences with a potentially substantial decline in alumni donations should legacy preferences be banned. On the other hand, alumni have a great amount of influence on the University and the policies it pursues. I hope that they’ll use this influence to pressure the University to remove legacy status as a consideration on applications.

It is not easy to reject the clear benefits of legacy preferences that our families will enjoy. I don’t know a single person who would say, “No, I actually don’t want to increase my brother’s chances of getting into Duke.” I am confident that alumni and current legacy students at Duke can recognize the unfairness in this practice and call it out, especially as college admissions become more competitive and legacy admissions gain more national criticism.

Other top institutions have seen opposition to legacy admissions from legacies. Promisingly, the Harvard Crimson, Harvard University’s student-run newspaper, surveyed its Class of 2027 and found that “55 percent of those with legacy connections to the College reported they do not support legacy admissions.” 

What legacies must remind themselves is that, unless they are a direct descendant of the Dukes, their relatives did not start as legacies. My mother was not a legacy when she got into Duke some 30 years ago. It is precisely because of Duke’s commitment to expanding to diverse backgrounds that she could get here.

Legacies owe it to the University and to hopeful applicants to recognize that, at some point, one of our relatives came to Duke for the first time in our family’s history. And from there, we must ensure that the same chances that our relatives were provided are given to every non-legacy who applies in the future.

With an administration that is so hesitant to positively impact its community and imbue fairness into its admissions process, maybe it’s time for Duke alumni to reconsider the dynastic legacy that they are leaving behind. And so, as someone who benefited from this lopsided system, I hope that others like me will push Duke to leave legacy admissions behind.

Harrison Walley is a Trinity sophomore. His column typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: Villages don’t build themselves
author: Molly Huff
article_text:
You’ve heard it before and you’ll hear it again — college is hard. Deadlines and work pile up, clubs and sports take our evenings. To top it all off, there’s the pressure to find a picture-perfect friend group — something straight out of “Friends” or “How I Met Your Mother.” 

Surviving and thriving in college is dependent on having a community; however, unlike our favorite sitcom, relationships like this don’t just suddenly materialize. We crave community, but we forget that it’s something that needs to be built ourselves, not received. 

We have all heard the saying, “it takes a village.” This four word mantra has been used to suggest that we, as humans, require a support system in life — whether that’s for raising children, managing work or navigating difficult life events. I believe this message is a fundamental truth of life. However, people often forget to have a village, we need to be villagers first. 

This means showing up and putting in the effort to build connections consistently, even when it gets hard or there isn’t a guaranteed return. It’s spending your time on others through actions as simple as listening instead of speaking, texting first, showing interest in others’ passions or offering a shoulder to cry on during a hard week. 

With college making all of our lives increasingly busy, it’s not always easy to do this. We get caught up in our work, deadlines and activities, forgetting half of the college is the social experience. It’s easy to put this half on the back burner and tell ourselves we’ll work on these connections when the time is right. But, to that I ask: When will the time ever be right? Will our lives ever perfectly balance? Who will still be there when the time is right if we don’t show up now? 

It might sound counterintuitive, but it’s at these moments when we feel overwhelmed that investing in relationships is most important. When we show up for others even at our busiest, we foster a community that will do the same for us. We risk losing this foundation of mutual support when we wait for what is convenient. 

A perfect community won’t just appear; it must be built. It takes someone showing up to lay the wood — despite busy lives and despite our hope that it will all fall into place effortlessly. Being a villager and putting in the work is undoubtedly a labor of love. But, no matter how hard it may be, that effort is the only thing that can bring us together despite our lives getting in the way. 

Earlier this week, I was talking about one of my friends from my orientation group whom I hadn’t seen in a while. We don’t have classes together — he’s in Pratt and I’m in Trinity — and our extracurricular interests don’t overlap; when I’m out hiking, he's dancing. 

I joked with some of my friends that even though I would say he’s one of the people I’m closest with on campus, he had recently gone “Hollywood” on me — now too busy to give me the time of day.

However, I began to realize that I hadn’t bothered to reach out and see what was going on in his life, to know why he had been so elusive recently. I wanted him in my village, for us to stay close and be there for each other, but when was the last time I reached out first? Have I ever asked how dance was going? Did he pass that exam two weeks ago? What classes is he going to take next semester?

I had spent so much time wrapped up in myself and my desire for a village that I neglected to be a villager. I wanted him in my life as a supporter, but I completely forgot to do the same for him. 

After realizing this, I sent a text:

“Hi! I’d really like to go to one of your dance exhibitions or competitions if you’re having one anytime soon. Miss you!”

He responded almost instantly — “YES, I’LL DO IT RIGHT NOW,” followed immediately with a link to buy tickets and, “OMG I’M SO HAPPY YOU’RE COMING.” 

Our culture promotes the idea that people should come to us, that if someone really wanted our company or support, they would ask without prompting — the viral TikTok philosophy of, “if he wanted to, he would,” for example. But people, just like my friend, don’t just go “Hollywood” or suddenly stop caring. Just like us, they’re caught up in busy lives, hoping for a reminder that someone still cares despite the distance. How often do we wait for others to make the first move and forget they might be waiting for us too? 

Take the time and make the effort to be a villager first.

If you do, your village will come to you. 

Molly Huff is a Trinity first-year.

title: A record shouldn’t be a life sentence
author: Lucas Barilovits
article_text:
North Carolina spends almost $55,000 a year — more than a teacher’s starting salary — just to put a person in a cage. Yet, the money is put to waste. The United States’ incarceration system is among the most flawed first-world intuitions ever. We incarcerate far more people than any first-world country, while also having high rates of incarcerated suicides, homicides and rapes.

The U.S. is torturing its own citizens for widely variable and targeted accusations. These people are then sent home, with a rap sheet, to intense stigma, little treatment and legal traps everywhere. Only half find any work in a year, and even then, the typical salary is in the low thousands. That’s not reentry, or a shot at a second chance; it’s a revolving door for failure. 

When records are cleared, the story changes. In a statewide study, people with expungements saw their wages rise over 20% within a year, driven by better job access and steadier hours. Additionally, their subsequent conviction rates were dramatically lower than similar people who didn’t receive the same services; As wages increase, future conviction chances continue to drop. Thus, the “clean-slate is dangerous” argument is completely backwards — denying second chances to our people is what is really dangerous.

Durham already has proof that this isn’t theoretical. Durham’s DEAR program — the city’s record-relief and debt-waiver initiative — and “Better Together” — a Duke, NCCU and UNC Law partnership with DEAR — have already delivered real results. An October 2023 event at Duke Law prepared 70 petitions to expunge 325 charges for 27 residents, and that is just a single day at Duke law. Those numbers translate into driver’s licenses restored, background checks passed and jobs landed.

The model exists; what’s missing is permanence, scale and a path beyond expunction for people the statute leaves out. With the scale of Duke Health (more than 26,000 employees) and Duke Law’s clinics, we can make second-chance hiring a standard. Implementing permanent expungement clinics, integrating treatment and reentry services and moving background checks to the post-offer stage would change the narrative.

But expungement usually takes years, and many people can’t get it at all. When expungement isn’t possible or is too far in the future, a certificate of relief is the next-best option. It doesn’t erase the case, but it tells employers and licensing boards to assess the person in front of them, not their past.

A certificate removes automatic “you’re barred” rules, requires boards to weigh rehabilitation and gives employers a state-law liability shield when they hire in compliance with it. In practice, it’s a judge saying: this applicant has done the work; consider them fairly. For assault-tagged or otherwise ineligible cases, it’s the difference between instant rejection and a real interview.

Many young adult minorities get targeted by cops, and then are forced to live with the “violent criminal” record forever. Across North Carolina, Black residents are arrested at approximately 2.3 times the rate of white residents, and in Durham County, Black people account for 69% of jail admissions, despite only being about 37% of the population.

Even in grade school in North Carolina, black children are about four times more likely to be referred to a juvenile court counselor, and thus, potentially taken to juvenile court. Systemic oppression continues to make the playing field far from fair, but with Duke Law’s political clout, and Duke Health’s massive workforce, Duke can be a place that creates massive change for people targeted by a racist system.

And this isn’t just a moral argument; it’s an economic one. The economic benefits for not just past offenders but non-offenders are profound long-term. If the goal is safer streets and a stronger economy, record relief is one of the most productive return on investment moves possible. When records are cleared, wages jump 22% within a year — people can finally access steadier jobs with more hours and roles that match their skillset.

As earnings rise, households spend more locally and pay more in taxes — growth that touches everyone, not just those with records. Additionally, rates of recidivism drop dramatically with proper treatment, employment and societal acceptance. A study in Michigan found just 7.1% of all expungement recipients are rearrested within five years of receiving their expungement, compared with 71% of everyone released from prison. Each avoided return to incarceration saves North Carolina over $50,000 a year — dollars we can redirect from cages to classrooms and clinics.

Giving employees with records a second chance is also good business for employers. A national survey found that 85% of HR leaders and 81% of business executives say employees with records perform as well or better than peers on reliability, retention and overall employee quality. Other peer-reviewed journals show longer tenure and fewer voluntary quits, with no spike in misconduct. At Johns Hopkins Medicine, nearly 20% of entry-level hires have records: a five-year review of nearly 500 such hires showed lower turnover over the first 40 months than their non-record coworkers. If one of the best hospitals in the world can hire at scale and show the benefits across the board, other industries can, too.

Duke is in a perfect position to do the same here. Duke Health can continue proving what Hopkins already proved: removing the endless hurdles past prisoners face and that hiring them helps everybody. Duke should create a single path — one page and phone number — to direct people to expungement, certificates of relief, license/ID help, background-check fixes and hiring within the Duke Health system.

If we want safer streets and less taxpayer money wasted to trap someone, we have to stop pretending a record is a life sentence. At Duke Law, provide a Reentry and Record Relief Fund to pay filing fees, IDs, court-debt relief and treatment slots; give core support to DEAR and partner nonprofits so legal help and treatment move together. 

Duke Law’s voice carries weight — use it to normalize certificates and make second-chance hiring standard practice. Duke can be the place that is progressive in a time of need while giving people their lives back. Helping to reintegrate people with records and change the narrative is the clear humanitarian and economical decision toward making our system better. We must do more to prioritize fighting the extensive systematic racism within Durham and the United States.

Lucas Barilovits is a Trinity sophomore. His pieces typically run on alternate Tuesdays.

title: How language at Duke has become a formula
author: Rohit Suresh
article_text:
“It’s easy to see that it’s optimal to Uber to the restaurant,” I heard someone say at Duke last week. Lately, I’ve noticed a strange trend among my peers at Duke. Students, mostly those studying a field related to math, will casually drop phrases that sound like they belong in a proof or an algorithm. I’ve heard everything ranging from a simple “therefore” to an elaborate “as one can easily show.” 

But it is not only math people. I have witnessed my friends in economics talk about how much they “discount” their future feelings as if their entire life neatly fits into an opportunity-cost model. Absurdly, these phrases come up even when we’re casually talking about what to eat for dinner.

Unfortunately, I’ve caught myself doing the same thing. Speech is contagious, and tools like ChatGPT make it easier to generate language that sounds polished. That polish, though, comes at a cost: our voices sound less human. 

The majority of written text I consume for classes, explanations of material or even things other people have written, read like they were passed through an ambiguity filter. Everything is neat and perfectly reasoned. At the same time, it is stripped of any real texture. Language has become optimized for clarity, not emotion. Naturally, the more I read it, the more I imitate it.

When I came to Duke, I knew some things about me would evolve. I expected my opinions to shift. I expected my academic interests to change. I expected my priorities to rearrange. But I did not expect my speech, something so core to me, to undergo any transformation. 

I figured if I took some “creative” classes through my T-reqs, I would have ample space to express my true voice. But increasingly, the attempt to make our language more exact also makes it less alive. The more we standardize the way we speak through academics and algorithms, the more we risk losing what it means to sound human.

But even in those classes, something has shifted. I find myself striving for precision in places which don’t need it. I superimpose streams of mathematical thought onto how I think about and interpret creative essays, abstract films and ambiguous poetry. The language of math has quickly and quietly seeped into how I process the world around me.

Watching this transformation of my language, I realized this is not just a quirk of my academics. Instead, it’s a view into how computers process language. What my peers and I do with major-speak, AI does at scale. Both take the unpredictable flow of language and condense it. The math student’s "therefore" and ChatGPT’s formulaic writing come from the same inherent desire to strip uncertainty. In both cases, we’re optimizing speech until it loses its heartbeat.

To take this to the extreme, I’ve also started to think like a Large Language Model (LLM). And I’m not alone. I form sentences that sound pre-written and bear resemblance to phrases I have read in class or from an LLM. There are times I speak where I find I’m not expressing a thought, but instead am recycling “correct” language patterns. I certainly did not think or speak like this before coming to Duke.

Part of me believes that the more we engage deeply in structured fields of study or work with LLMs, the harder it becomes to sit comfortably in ambiguity. Another part of me believes that it’s just easier and simpler to be precise than to speak vague thoughts.

Regardless, the creativity of language is collectively slipping away from us. The more we communicate through systems built on precision, the less room there is for surprise. Language is not meant to be spoken in patterns, but it is instead supposed to come with a constant element of surprise and interpretation. Our words have evolved to follow patterns as opposed to breaking them. Even in conversation, where words are quickly forgotten, people seem less willing to risk vagueness or absurdity. We speak in ultra-polished sentences that sound correct but have no heartbeat.

We, Duke students, need more self-reflection about the way we think, and speak. We need to spend more time letting our thoughts wander, writing things that don’t sound perfect and saying things that sound stupid.

There will always be nooks where precision is essential, but we should not let it spill everywhere. There is so much value in speaking with uncertainty, in saying something half-formed. If we can relearn how to be a little imprecise, we can rediscover what it means to speak as a human rather than a proof or a program trained to sound correct.

Rohit Suresh is a Trinity junior.

title: Fiber Arts as tools for resistance
author: Sam St. Lawrence
article_text:
When I first saw my mom and sister crocheting, I was immediately entranced. The methodical stitches and intricate patterns were fascinating combinations of artistic expression and mathematical precision. However, the fiber arts extend beyond mesmerizing beauty. 

Fiber arts encompass creative practices that use natural or synthetic fibers — yarn, thread, fabric and more — as their primary material. Crocheting, knitting and embroidery are among the most common examples, but the category extends far beyond them.

If you spend enough time on campus, you’ll likely hear stories of activism — calls for divestment, protests condemning genocide or historical movements like the Allen Building takeover. But most of these conceptions of activism and resistance are quite similar. While these have their advantages, activism doesn’t always have to take the form of rallies or occupations. How else might we engage? How can we cultivate a deeper, more diverse culture of resistance?

One answer is art. Fiber arts are ongoing acts of resistance; they are tangible responses to the conditions people find themselves in. Each stitch represents intention and determination—a sustained effort to make some new reality. Throughout history, fiber arts have empowered people, especially women, to take radical stances in the face of injustice. During the Pinochet regime in Chile, women created arpilleras — handwoven tapestries—to depict the violence of their everyday lives.

These tapestries enabled women to challenge social norms entrenched in machismo ideology and male superiority. In the United States, quilting has long been used in African American communities as a tool for resistance and communication. During the Underground Railroad, quilts were often used to relay vital information about safe routes and supply locations. 

Something often forgotten is that the clothes we wear are deeply personal — we’ve fooled ourselves into believing our connection to clothing is inconsequential. The rise of fast fashion has spurred the decline of handmade garments. Fiber arts, however, reintroduce slow production. It is a quiet resistance to expectations of disposability and speed in every aspect of life. It reclaims the intimacy of expression and honors the true cost of labor that clothing necessitates.

Beyond crafting things for personal use, fiber arts can also be used as public displays of resistance. One of the most notable examples of this is “yarn bombing”. Yarn bombing is a form of street art that combines protest, self-expression and community connection.

It involves adorning regular or dull objects with knitwork or crochet pieces. Yarn bombing transforms the mundane into something vibrant, forcing attention toward what we typically ignore. It reclaims public spaces, asserting that environments should reflect community creativity rather than corporate or institutional control.

Crafting doesn’t have to be loud to be important. Fiber arts are built on community. Traditionally, women’s crafts have been belittled and forgotten, leaving many people unable to understand their true impact. Knitting and crocheting have long been forms of expression and connection for women. Knitting circles, in particular, have served as spaces for storytelling and solidarity.

They transform isolation into shared experience and craft into collective power. In a knitting circle, stories can be spun like a ball of yarn. Lives come together, even when life itself feels like it’s unraveling. What emerges is not just fabric but care — a web of mutual attention that resists isolation. bell hooks once wrote that love is an action; perhaps knitting together is one of its forms.

Community is often about finding shared interests. For many people, fiber arts build community. Recently, I wrote a piece exploring how community isn’t created through institutionalizing interactions. But forming a knitting circle? That does. And at the end of the day, community itself is revolutionary. You might be surprised how quickly strangers become friends when you pick up a hook or needles — revolutions don’t have to start with explosions. Starting can be as simple as going to a workshop or putting up a flyer to form a knitting circle. Not only could you find a community, but you may find a new way to recharge beyond scrolling on your phone for hours.

At a school so caught up in hustle culture, participating in an activity that is slow and not possible to talk about on Linkedin, expands the horizon of what we think is worth our time. Especially in light of recent budgeting woes, outwardly showcasing our support for the arts is incredibly critical. So make a trek to the Arts Annex and check out their fiber arts kits! Sign up for the VisArts knitting workshops! Take classes that explore the importance of fiber arts and women’s crafts! Challenge yourself to make something that is not required of you.

In a world that thrives on disconnection, sustained connection is radical. Maybe it’s time we start recognizing fiber arts for the power they truly hold. We must learn that fiber arts teach us that patience is radical, creation is revolutionary and connection itself is a form of protest.

Sam St. Lawrence is a Trinity junior. Their pieces typically run on alternate Mondays.

title: Books are my love language
author: Anna Garziera
article_text:
I got a notification the other day: “Your screen time was up 261% last week, for an average of 7 hours, 15 minutes a day.” If you know me, you'll know this can only mean one thing. I’m reading again.

One thing about me is that I read on my phone. I have over 200 books downloaded on Apple Books, most of them classics that have long lost copyright privileges, but also a few modern ones I’ve picked up over the years. 

Most people aren’t fans of this and I understand. Reading is such a “pure” habit, one that seems “old-school” and in direct contrast with spending all day on your phone, rotting away on social media. Using the same cursed device for both activities feels like a sin.

One thing does save me from that. I don’t have any social media apps downloaded on my phone, so apart from opening up a book, my options are slim: updating my Linkedin profile, reading the New York Times or if I’m really feeling frisky, settling down for a game of Solitaire. As you can see, I don’t have a lot to work with. My Brontës and Cathers are by far the most exciting thing on my phone. 

One advantage of reading on my phone is, I get to have my books wherever I go. This is not to say I mind the burden of having to carry a paper book. I do still prefer paper books — getting to hold them, smell them — and I read on paper whenever I get the chance. But my reading spurts are simply too compulsive to make going to the library for every new book feasible. I only know what book I want to read next when I’ve finished my last, and if I don't have that book immediately on hand, I lose excitement really fast. Once that flame is extinguished, good luck lighting it again. 

Another thing I like about reading on my phone is that I get to take screenshots easily. I don’t know if you’ve ever tried to take a photo of a passage in a paperback, but it’s like taming a dragon. The book won’t stay open, the lighting is suddenly terrible and you can’t keep the book straight and take your hand off the page at the same time. This perk is important to me because I like to send to my sister any parts I find funny (and she likes to pretend she enjoyed them).

With all the good of reading on a device established, let me tell you about the bad. If you love reading as much as I do, you’ll find your screen time skyrocketing to unprecedented levels. If you thought you knew what mental fatigue was before, try diving into your favorite novel on a device that will let you keep reading exactly where you are, as the sun goes down and into the night.

Last Sunday, I happened to be curled up in my bed when I began reading “Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets.” It wasn't my first time attempting this tome. 

At the start of last semester, I read “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone” for the first time. It was transformative. Having partly grown up in England, I picked up on a lot of things that reminded me of my former home. From the way the characters talk, to how they dress, to the puddings that appear at the Start-of-Term Feast, everything seemed familiar. 

I devoured it in a day or two and immediately started what I thought was “The Chamber of Secrets.” After about 60 pages of not understanding what was going on, I checked the front cover, and sure enough, it was “Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows.” It’s easy to understand where the confusion arose. The thing with using Apple Books on your phone is, the book covers are really small. Both #2 and #7 Harry Potter books were green.

If I had taken out the wrong book from the library, this would have been a small disaster. As it was already evening, I would have had to wait a whole other day to go back to Perkins and swap it out. However, Apple Books was unshaken. I closed #7, opened up #2 and I was back on my roll.

“The Chamber of Secrets” made a lot more sense the second time around. I tore through around 80 pages that night before realizing I was headed towards a dangerous path. Only a week into the semester, I was already ignoring my homework in favor of running around Hogwarts with Potter. This made me feel guilty and I wasn't able to enjoy the book to its full potential. Therefore, last January, I abandoned the series.

Until now. I’m currently studying abroad in Berlin and there’s been a lot going on. My classes aren’t difficult, but all these “experiences” are making me tired. Anyhow, for one reason or another, I hadn't felt much like reading this semester until last week. After over two months of not touching a book, I knew I had to pick something easy to get back in the groove. I thought I'd give Harry another go.

I'm not here to write a “The Chamber of Secrets” review, but in short, I loved it. By Wednesday night, I had already started “The Prisoner of Azkaban,” which I finished on Thursday. I followed up with “The Goblet of Fire” on the weekend. 

When I told my friends and family about this new adventure, I got mixed reactions. The ones who had never read Harry Potter before were understandably uninterested by my newest reading quest. Others had only read the first one and were surprised I kept going. But by far, the reaction I got the most was, “Have you really never read it before?”

If there’s one thing I’ve learned from reading, it’s to look between the lines: in other words, “Aren't you a bit old for it?”

The reality is, it’s strange for a child not to have read Harry Potter. And it’s even more strange for an adult to pick it up for some light reading some random afternoon. 

Last year, I wrote on the importance of reading, and specifically, advocated that we read “below our reading level.” I argued that removing the friction that comes with reading difficult books can encourage us to read more in the first place, which is in itself an achievement. To move on to “college-level” books, there’s still time.

Today, I want not only to reiterate this message, but to add to it two things. First, don’t be afraid of starting your reading journey with something that feels easy to like. I’m grateful for everyone who has met my new Harry Potter pursuit with enthusiasm. Making me feel self-conscious for liking something that was not only written for 12-year-olds, but is also incredibly mainstream, would be unproductive. Not only would it fail to change how I feel about the series, it might also discourage me from reading, which in my opinion, is the worst offense.

Second, give reading on your phone a try. Again, you might be met with criticism. Like all things in life, reading online has its skeptics. I used to be one. But in an age where only 16% of adults in the U.S. read for pleasure — including magazines, newspapers and audiobooks — I don’t know if we can afford being nitpicky about the medium they read on.

Reading Harry Potter has already started to give me ideas. For instance, my rowing team just bought two new boats, which I think we should name “Firebolt” and “Nimbus 2000.” Some of my teammates might roll their eyes at this and that’s okay. Certain books aren’t for everyone. 

But that doesn’t mean they’re not for anyone — don’t limit yourself to what you can read or when you can read it. Before giving it a go, I didn’t think Harry Potter would be for me. I heard people saying I was too old for it and I believed them. But there’s nothing wrong with doing childish things. Go on — pick up exactly the book you want to read, and begin.

Anna Garziera is a Trinity junior. Her pieces typically run on alternate Sundays.

title: The real “utility” of a useless language class
author: Neel Dutta Gupta
article_text:
Prior to O-Week each year, orientation leaders (OLs) undergo training to better understand the role we must play in welcoming new students to Duke. This year was no different; around 200 upperclassmen (including myself) moved in early, excited to settle in and welcome the new academic year. Most of the training during the week focuses on understanding our roles as leaders and tips on how to ensure new students are settled.

But there’s also a session in which Duke academic administrators explain new program changes that have taken place for the year and provide us with instructions on how to communicate these changes. One of these changes was the foreign language requirement. 

Frankly, I remember very little of what was explained regarding the foreign language (FL) requirement in that session. I had to look it up recently to help myself gain a better understanding. The mechanics of the requirement will take me far too long to explain, but students now need to take a minimum of two foreign language classes prior to graduating. If they choose a beginner course, they must take three foreign language courses (disclaimer: do not refer to this article as a guideline for Duke’s foreign language requirement). 

What I took from this change was that the University wanted to increase the importance it places on Duke students learning another language. Since I’ve been at Duke, the FL requirement has been a large annoyance to some of my friends (with the exception of Pratt kids). Many of my friends complain that it’s a waste of time — an unnecessary impediment on top of an already rigorous liberal arts education. 

The requirement is a lot more comprehensive than other schools and is a pretty large undertaking to be reckoned with. But I would like to argue that this is not so much of an arduous requirement — rather, an opportunity to embody some of the school’s values.

To preface, I’m in Pratt, which waives the FL requirement, so I don’t have much of a leg to stand on in this argument. That being said, I strongly believe that there’s immense intrinsic value in learning a language other than your own. 

For me, language has always been a major part of my life. I grew up speaking English, learned Hindi from my parents and Mandarin from my peers. I “look” like someone who would conventionally speak English and Hindi, but not really Mandarin. As such, speaking Mandarin often elicited a unique reaction from many of my peers in Singapore. 

“你可以说中文?” — "You can speak Chinese?" is a reaction I have seen many times, yet still find hard to fully describe. Their response feels different from an ordinary conversation. I like to believe that most of our lived experiences can be captured in words if the writer thinks carefully enough about what they want to say, but this particular feeling always seems to slip away from precise description.

When you speak to someone in their own language, especially when it’s obvious you’re a foreigner, something shifts. Their face lights up — not because your grammar is perfect (it usually isn’t), but because of the effort itself. In that moment, you’re saying: I don’t assume English is the default or the language that matters most. Your language is just as important, and I’m willing to meet you there.

That small choice carries a quiet kind of respect and care that’s hard to translate, but impossible to miss. If the FL requirement can bring this experience to someone later in their life, I believe it makes the endeavour that students have to take worth it in the long run.

There’s another struggle my friends and I often talk about — seeing the utility of parts of our education once we begin to enter the workforce. While understanding the node-voltage method or the flux through a Gaussian surface may be interesting, it’s sometimes hard to see when I will ever use these ideas directly in my life. The usefulness of language, on the other hand, feels immediately clear. I’d like to share a story about my dad that proves this.

My dad studied computer science in college. Almost all of his classes were highly technical, except for a few outliers; one of them was German. Today, he remembers very little of that German.

A few years ago, my family was on holiday in Japan. Japan is famous for its communal baths, or onsens — large public spaces where people from the town or the hotel come to bathe and unwind. One evening, my father and I walked into an onsen where a Japanese man was already there, quietly enjoying his bath. We made eye contact and smiled, but it was clear we had no easy way to talk.

Then, suddenly, the man began speaking in German.

My dad’s face lit up. His German was rusty and broken, but it was enough. In that steamy little room, on the other side of the world from both our home and Germany, this “useless” college elective became a bridge. They exchanged a few simple sentences: where we were from, how long we were staying, how beautiful Japan was and the man’s whole demeanor softened. What could have been an awkward silence turned into a small moment of connection.

That German class didn’t help my dad write better code or optimize an algorithm. But in that moment, it did something much more human: it allowed him to meet someone in their comfort zone, to say without words, “I’m willing to reach toward you.” And that, to me, is the clearest kind of utility.

Duke prides itself on human connection; it’s the reason many of us choose to come here. We want a place where people are not only intellectually curious, but also willing to show up for each other, whether that means packing into Cameron Indoor Stadium for a basketball game, unwinding at a party over the weekend or staying up talking for hours. It is the reason I came to Duke.

If we take that value seriously, then I think it’s important to see the FL requirement in that light as well: not as a hoop to jump through, but as an attempt to extend this spirit of connection beyond English, beyond campus, and into the rest of the world. Maybe the requirement itself is not a perfect implementation, but the underlying belief — that learning a language other than your own can open you to other people’s worlds — is, to me, central to what it means to be a Duke student and, more broadly, to what it means to be human.

Neel Dutta Gupta is a Pratt sophomore.

title: Rewritten: The sellout arc and being who I am
author: Alec Higgins and Alexander Hong
article_text:
The Chronicle is soliciting submissions from alumni and current students for their rewritten Duke supplemental essay based on their time here. You can submit here.

In my original Duke essay, I wrote some boring preventive medicine pre-med starter-pack topic: trans fats, vaping, biochemistry. By freshman spring, I was a public health statistic. One of Duke Pre-Health Advising’s 30% casualties, doing my part to keep the attrition curve healthy.

I sold out. First software engineering, then yup — consulting. If my RBC interviewer hadn’t no-showed, I would’ve completed the trifecta of selling out by trying my hand at IB. No clue what an LBO is, and if you asked me to make a pivot table, I’d probably just ask Claude Code in Python.

Duke promises “leaders and innovators,” and to a concerning degree, we deliver. Everyone around me had ideas, ambition and initiative. But strategy without execution is just PowerPoint poetry at best — and an expensive brainstorm at worst. America wasn’t built by some superior public policy but rather by the ingenious blue-collar, lunch-pail, hard-hat grit of the working class.

My favorite professors got us to code iOS apps in Swift, build APIs and make HTTPS requests with CRUD — to make ideas real. I still use that every day. I loved the med school professors who never told me I was wrong, only asked me to explain my ideas and reasoning. That’s how my “wack” idea helped us validate plastic-eating bacteria. The ones too obsessed with their polymer research to teach? Bye.

Most of all, Duke taught humility. Going from top of my class to bottom percentile — that’s transformative ... and not in the inspirational LinkedIn way. It was my Dorothy moment: clearly, we aren’t in Kansas (a Georgia public high school) anymore. Doing grunt work during my summer consulting internship? More growth than any orgo class. Sorry, Mom, but I’d trade my 106 high-school average for my Duke transcript, alphabet-soup marks any day.

And tenting — the true Duke curriculum, which is why I saved it for last. Community buy-in and character development, even at the cost of 100k. It’s realizing your friend chose to tent with someone else because he was graduating early and wanted a better spot in Section 17 since we weren’t “hardcore” enough. So you bribe him by bringing a girl he’s interested in to tent.

He still says no — but their late-night K-Ville chats turned into dating, now 2.5 years strong (who’s counting anyways). It’s getting too lit at P-Checks and you finally have the guts to ask out that AB Duke scholar you had a crush on to make hotteok with you.

I came to Duke wanting to fix the world. I left knowing the real lesson was how to fix yourself — your ego, your expectations and that success is the colorful collages in your camera roll as much as it is the blue leather book they hand you. 

Who knew that was the best preventive medicine I was looking for in the first place?

Alexander Hong, Trinity '24.

I actually applied in 2009 for the Class of 2014 through the Common App, and the supplemental essay was optional for me. I grew up in California and knew next to nothing about Duke — I only applied because the supplemental essay was optional.

Eighteen-year-old me could not have imagined why Duke was such a good match. I was deeply insecure and closeted. While my academic learning was important, the personal development I experienced at Duke is what truly shaped who I am today.

For the first time in my life, I made friends I felt comfortable coming out to. Duke fosters a community where you can discover and reinvent yourself. While I cannot rewrite my essay, I can tell my younger self, “You’re about to make one of the best decisions of your life.”

It wasn’t an easy journey, and coming out to my freshman roommate (while sitting in the then AC-less GA dorm on East Campus) remains one of the hardest things I’ve ever done. Janie Long, the LGBT Center, my professors and my classmates gave me mentorship and friendship I never could have imagined.

My degree has opened fantastic doors professionally, but the personal growth I experienced is what makes Duke truly special to me.

Alec Higgins, Trinity '14.

Rewritten is a recurring column of short reflective essays by Duke alumni and current students.

title: The secret of the universe
author: Robert Wallace
article_text:
Let’s start with the personal. Writing honestly makes me feel stripped and exposed. But that is the kind of writing that I am personally drawn to. I write what I know, not because I like being vulnerable but because it might be something someone else finds meaningful.

When I was a boy, my father liked to sit at the kitchen table, smoke Camel cigarettes and listen to the radio. He loved to listen to baseball games from places in the country he knew he would never visit. He also liked to find stations that had radio personalities who told stories. It didn’t matter what kind of story. Any story would do.

I had problems sitting still as a boy, but I could sit and listen to the radio with my father. He liked to sit with his legs crossed at the knee, a cigarette in one hand. He would sit hunched over because often the sound coming from the radio was scratchy.

I couldn’t talk when I sat with my father at these moments, and, if I did say something, he would sharply go “shh,” and hold his forefinger to his lips. I loved it when my father would laugh. He had a cacophonous chuckle that didn’t seem to fit him right; it was high-pitched for a tall man.

My father liked to tape record his voice and he loved to tell his own stories.

In the summer, he liked to take his children to the lake. He used to stand in the water, his shins submerged, like a giraffe, all legs and neck, the thin torso holding the two together. He loved to put his children on his shoulders.

“Stand up,” he’d yell.

“No,” I said once.

He reached over his head and stretched his arms toward mine. I’m all hunched over; my legs shaking.

“When I let go, stand straight up,” my father said. “I’ll hold you by your legs.”

By the time I’m vertical my head was about ten feet above the water. I felt the heat of the sun upon my back. I could reach and touch the sky.

“One,” my father said, and he began to go up and down in the water. “Two. Get ready.”

As he dipped down for the last time, I began to lose my balance and started to bend my knees.

“Three.”

My father rose out of the water and launched me and for a second I felt like I was flying, but I forgot to extend my legs. I splashed into the water and came up grinning.

“That wasn’t much of a dive, Bobby,” my father said. “You can’t meet the world all balled up. Stretch yourself out next time.”

Life was serious to my father.

My father had big, calloused, thick-fingered hands with clear, clean nails that were bitten off at the end. Once he took me to an orchard — the rural part of Michigan was full of orchards — and I watched him take out a pocket knife and begin cutting away at one of his callouses, digging under the rough, hard skin. He had a habit of doing this while I stood beside him, quiet.

In that orchard, fifty-seven years ago now, he pulled an apple from a tree, and rubbed the apple on his shirt sleeve and the chest part of his shirt. He smelled the apple, cut it open with his pocket knife, trimmed away the skin into one long peel. He cut away the core and licked the naked apple. I watched his pink tongue go over the flesh; its thousands tiny taste receptors removing the surface juices.

My father once told me: “Your family is the most important investment you will ever make.”

From him I learned to throw a baseball. To comb my hair. To tell time on an analog watch. When my father cooked, he made eggs and spaghetti, just as I do now. From him I learned to be quiet and to listen. To tie my shoes. From my father, I learned to tell stories.

There are stories biding their time in each of us; stories that we don’t fully understand, or comprehend. But the impulse to tell them is potent and potentially transforming. I have, for the past several months, been sharing a number of personal essays in this column. The hope is that these stories touch a cord, a deep yearning, in your own life, thereby helping you to reflect on it, and maybe find some understanding or interpretation.

For I do not believe our lives are accidents. I believe that in sharing our stories about who we are, where we live, and what has happened to us — it connects us. It breaks down barriers of fear and mistrust. This is why we need newspapers and books. So if you ever felt you needed permission to tell a story, indeed any story, your story — I give it.

Telling stories has the power to save us.

As we approach Thanksgiving, take the time to tell a story about yourself. Tell your family about Duke. Tell them about classes. The professor you like. The one you don’t. Tell a story about a new friend you have made, the one whose smile is so large that it could capture the sun.

How, during a recent evening, while walking on campus, just as the sun was disappearing below a building, it brought back a happy moment during your childhood. Something your mother said, or your father, and it made you smile. Whoever you spend time with, tell them a story. And let them tell you one.

“Telling stories increases one’s love of the universe,” my father said.

And so it does. 

Robert Wallace is a first-year graduate student of liberal studies. His column, 'Telling Stories', typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: The Marriage Pact won’t save you
author: Wendy House
article_text:
Have you filled out the Marriage Pact?

That’s the question on everyone’s mind for the past week, it seems. Have you got your match? What are their initials? What’s their major? Got any idea who it might be? Aren’t you just chomping at the bit to know their name?

I won’t deny the premise is exciting. Come, ye hopeless student souls — we know you’ve already lost all hope of finding love yourself, so we’ll do it for you. The purported function of Marriage Pact is to set up a backup “safety” spouse in case one doesn’t organically fall into your lap in your four years at college, but we all know what it really is: a setup. Marriage Pact is your very own matchmaker, one that requires no asking around about any cute singles your friends might know. 

When I first heard that Marriage Pact would be rerunning this year, I was a little pessimistic. It felt like just one more way to gamify love in the 21st century, repackaging the same calculated compatibility promise of every dating app and sending participants careening toward disappointment. 

These days, it can be easy to feel like compatibility is naught more than a function of trait alignments — a multivariate analysis of personality type, interests, political beliefs, demographics and mutual attraction which governs the success or failure of a match. Social media and dating apps saturate us with an impression of unlimited choice, such that rather than make an actual move on someone, we flip through new crushes and profiles like a Rolodex. We act like dithering shoppers, indefinitely searching for something better around the corner. Indeed,data shows that participants in online dating disproportionately view it as a marketplace.

Forgive my waxing poetic, but love is no marketplace. It is many things: a choice, a compulsion, a commitment, a liberty, a delight or even a curse, but never is it mathematical. Love is associated with marriage — among other things, a financial transaction— so it is not above all practical considerations, but nonetheless I argue that to reduce romance to statistics is to neuter your ability to experience it at all.

To see dating as a matter of marketing or percent compatibility corrupts the entire endeavor with self-surveillance; in weighing potential partners against each other like products, you begin to see yourself as a product as well.

That’s not to say you shouldn’t ensure you and a potential mate agree on the big stuff before investing emotionally. Opposites attract, but similarities make a thing last. I only caution against allowing this fact to convince you that a “best” partner can be quantified or predicted. That fallacy is especially pertinent somewhere like Duke, because we’re all control freaks. Perfection on paper doesn’t create attraction or rapport; chemistry of the heart is no science.

It’s my opinion that this algorithmic love philosophy is in some part responsible for Gen Z’s decline in teen dating. In researching for this article, though, I discovered some good news: although matchmaking services like Marriage Pact do persist on college campuses, we're abandoning dating apps! 

Gen Z is losing faith in the intentions of dating apps to help us find love. They are increasingly seen as money-hungry vectors for “micro-rejections” which both erode one’s self esteem and create an addictive effect as more and more disappointment is accepted in exchange for that sweet, rare hit of reciprocity. User bases are getting disproportionately older; it seems the youth of today is turning to more old-fashioned methods of seeking out those elusive, amorous fireworks. 

To that, I say “hell yeah!” Having your matchmaking done for you is convenient, but it creates expectations for a chemistry that might not exist. Waiting on a meet-cute, while less immediately gratifying and perhaps more vulnerable, leaves less room for disappointment and opens the possibility of creating a new friend should sparks fail to fly. 

As a formerly single person, I know how it is. The mere effort of holding out hope to meet The One, or even just someone, can feel Sisyphean. Cracking open the door to your heart leaves you open to disappointment — even guarantees it— but it’s worth the trouble. The effects of education, career and wealth on happiness are all far eclipsed by that of marriage, despite what hustle culture might lead you to believe. 

I hope everyone marries their Marriage Pact match. I honestly do. Romance is a beautiful thing, and I think anyone capable of experiencing it should do so to the fullest, healthiest extent possible. Realistically, though, when the names are revealed and algorithmic compatibility proves itself impotent to predict real connection, I encourage all remaining starry-eyed singles to keep the faith. Keep looking. Delete Hinge. Pluck up the mettle to let your friends know you’re in the mood for love — I can personally attest to the efficacy of an arranged meet-cute. 

Don’t be embarrassed to seek more from your time at Duke than a network and glittering resume. College is a chance to, in the words of the great Henry David Thoreau, “live deep and suck out all the marrow of life;” and if love isn’t one of life’s greatest passions, I don’t know what is. 

Wendy House is a Trinity sophomore. Her column typically runs on alternate Wednesdays.

title: How do Australian Flying Foxes compare to Blue Devil Baseball and Softball players?
author: Aditya Baliga, Rose Cassidy and Wyatt Nowacek
article_text:
A platypus playing in the river, tree kangaroos hiding above and bats screeching overhead… this isn’t the Duke gardens! 10,185 miles away, three Duke students find themselves in Yungaburra, Australia. Our main focus: the endangered spectacled flying foxes (Pteropus conspicillatus), a species of bat which can be found roosting during the day in the treetops around the creek.

At dusk, nearly 5000 of these nocturnal mammals leave their roosting sites and congregate to feed on large fruiting trees about 20 to 30 kilometres away. They are generally back by sunrise, squeaking and jostling while finding the perfect perch. Flying foxes can hang effortlessly by their feet thanks to the tendons in their hindlimbs, which lock automatically.

An upside-down lifestyle presents some tough logistical issues, including giving birth upside down! Mothers catch their pups mid-air before they cling tightly to their fur. You might ask how hanging upside down affects bathroom breaks, but they have it figured out. They will often flip upright into a more vertical position so their waste falls safely, sometimes dangerously close to the onlookers.

While observing the bats, we noticed a pattern: bats can hang from either both feet at a time or from either foot individually. We began to wonder, do these flying foxes prefer to hang from their left or right hindlimb? And of course, the natural follow-up question, how would they swing if they stepped up to the plate? Halfway around the globe, Duke’s baseball and softball players step up to the plate swinging rightie or leftie. Do they have anything in common with the bats in the Burra? Perhaps a little more than you think.

We decided to try to find out whether our bats had a preferred "handedness” and surveyed 204 of them over two days. Asking them didn’t get us far, so we monitored each bat for 5 minutes to see how they shaped up. 

Most of our bats spent more than half of their time hanging with both feet, so we had to get creative in determining if they were righties or lefties. We decided that if they spent over a third of the time on just one foot, that would count as the individual’s dominant side. This design also allowed us to find the talented bats that could hang with either foot for over a third of the time: our switch hitters!

When it comes to our Blue Devils, the results are somewhat similar. The 2025 softball team was dominated by righties. The next most popular category belonged to players who used one arm for throwing and the other for batting, which we considered equivalent to our bats who had no preference. 

The 2025 baseball team was also rightie dominated, but less so. For both bats and Blue Devils, righties are more common than lefties, while switch hitters are a rare but exciting minority. 

While Duke Baseball came close to a College World Series bid in the 2025 season, and our Softball team made a 2024 appearance at the Women’s College World Series, spectacled flying foxes, do not have such a winning record. Between 2004 and 2017, their population fell by 75%. While previously listed as vulnerable, a major heatwave in 2019 wiped out more than a third of their population, which upgraded their IUCN status to endangered. 

Other common threats to this species include tick paralysis, cleft palate syndrome, cyclones, habitat loss and injury from barbed-wire fences. Motivating the public to conserve flying foxes is tricky, as they have a reputation for being noisy and social at night (not unlike Duke students at sports games). 

Despite the nuisance they may present, flying foxes are integral to the health of rainforests. They fly incredibly long distances per night, which, as fruit eaters, allows them to widely distribute seeds of important rainforest trees. In North America, bats help disperse and pollinate cacao, mango and agave, which is used to make tequila (a prized possession for Duke students.) 

Just as bats are key to their ecosystems, Duke athletes are key to ours. While they don’t plant fruit trees or eat insects, they are integral to our lives in other important ways. They create a sense of community and togetherness that couldn’t be replicated any other way. Without something to root for, campus can be a quiet and disconnected place; it just isn’t quite right.

Forests are like this when their bat populations decrease. We should show the same sort of community in trying to protect them that we do cheering on our Blue Devils. So when you see a bat in the Duke gardens, don’t be afraid! Just think of them as another part of our big Duke ecosystem that needs our love and support. 

Rose Cassidy, Wyatt Nowacek and Aditya Baliga are Trinity juniors.

title: Learning to listen in a world full of noise
author: Meena Puram
article_text:
In his Oct. 23rd talk at Page Auditorium, Percival Everett — the author of the Pulitzer Prize-winning book “James” — repeatedly speaks to his seemingly antiquated practices, including his abstinence from the internet and his tendency to use the public library for research. At one point, Everett was asked about his experience with painting, another art form that he currently pursues. 

“Do you hear music when you paint?” asked Deborah Rutter, vice provost for the arts, to which Everett replied, “I can’t listen to music while painting. It overwhelms me.” 

Despite this comment being overlooked in the interview, it struck me as particularly interesting. Everett spoke to the need for mindfulness in his creative process, an unbridled devotion to the work at hand, to the point where he cannot commit himself to any other emotion or experience. 

Upon hearing this, I thought about my own reading experiences, and how casually — almost instinctively — I pop in my earbuds and play classical music and movie soundtracks compiled into a playlist labeled “Study music.” In doing so, it begs the question of whether I’m giving either the music or the book the necessary attention they require. 

Yet I’m willing to bet that I’m not the only one who does this. Spotify and other music streaming platforms have turned music into a consumable product, a background noise to our everyday lives. In solitude, many of us are compelled to put on our headphones. Because, as the music streaming oligarchs have conditioned us into believing, noise is always better than silence. In submitting to this ideology, we risk losing the intimacy that comes with experiencing music as its own, profoundly emotional interaction between the musician and the listener. 

Unfortunately, the commodification of music presents itself in concert culture, too. We spend upwards of 200 dollars to see artists from a stage over 500 feet away, only to be surrounded by phone screens recording nosebleeds to post online, and thousands of fans screaming and, in turn, drowning out the voices of the artists themselves. 

Though I concede that these concerts are still sources of meaningful community, which is in and of itself a goal, our modern climate distracts us from that shared experience with the allure of aesthetics. After all, when was the last time you went to a concert, and did not post about it? Collectively, are we giving more thought to the “vibes” of the concert — the outfits and the social media potential — than to the substance of the performance itself?

All this to say, music, concerts and even artists themselves are being treated as products to be consumed rather than as art to be profoundly experienced. I worry that we, as readers, viewers and listeners, are forgetting the sacred practice of engaging with art to our fullest intellectual and emotional capacity. 

This issue has far-reaching impacts beyond the arts scene. Throughout his talk, Everett expresses a deep dissatisfaction with our modern political climate, but he constantly asserts that art has immense power in combating fascism. 

As he stated in his interview with Dua Lipa, “the art itself does the work in the world. It’s not complete until the reader comes to it,” a moment that was referenced in his talk at Duke. In other words, the meaning of literature is ultimately created through the joint labor of both the reader and the writer.

Yet we often fall short in taking on this labor when we passively consume art rather than intellectually engage with it. And, in turn, we fail to be participants in the type of change that Everett foresaw through his work. 

Enter: Duke CoffeeHouse, a building tucked into a crevice of East Campus, known amongst the student body for its “free coffee and good vibes.” The first time I went, two things stuck out to me. The beautiful wall decor and the sign that said, “If you come here to study, but not for the events, you’re missing the point.” But what is the point?

For me, this question wasn’t answered until I actually attended an event — the first CoffeeHouse open mic of the school year. I saw a local artist whom I would’ve never known of otherwise, and I saw my peers, whom I pass by daily, pour their hearts into original songs and covers. I realized, then, that the point is simply to be present, to be wholly enamored by the joy of creation and sound despite not being on stage yourself. 

I realized, then, that music is the most beautiful, not when packaged into a fully polished, pre-recorded track blasting into your headphones, but rather when you see, in real time, the resolution of a slight dissonance between the bass and the drums, the laugh of a singer in the middle of a lyric or the look passed between bandmates when a tune comes to a close. 

Moments like these make me understand where Everett is coming from when he says he can't listen to music while he paints. It helps me understand what it means to be devoted to the craft in front of you, even just as a viewer. If, in Everett’s words, “reading is the most subversive thing we can do,” then the importance of that devotion can never be understated. 

All this to say, moving forward, I encourage you to listen to albums cover-to-cover, just as intended by the artist, to go to live shows and put down your phones and read your books with nothing but indistinct chatter in the background. We owe it to our artists, we owe it to ourselves and we owe it to the world. 

Meena Puram is a Pratt first-year. Her column typically runs on alternate Tuesdays.

title: A purpose within
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
Content warning: This article contains mentions of suicide and death. If you or someone you know is having suicidal thoughts, call the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988.

At this point in the semester, as the clocks have been turned back an hour and the light fades earlier and earlier each day, it can feel like a heavy season. There are deadlines for projects, final exam preparations and crammed-in meetings before the holiday break. Life can be a lot, for everyone.

In this somber season, I am struck by the ancient words of Rebekah in the Book of Genesis (25:22) — “If it is to be this way, why do I live?”

“Why do I live?” she asks, not “how” should I live but “why.” Rebekah was barren, which, in a patriarchal society, was not a positive thing, as having children was thought to add value to womanhood. Her husband was a child of promise (Gen 21:1-7) and she was from good family stock (Gen 25:20), but even that was not an antibiotic against emptiness and disappointment. Privileged pedigree can’t prevent pain.

Eventually, she learns she’s having twins, but subsequently discovers that “the children struggled together within her” (Genesis 25:22). That experience is what causes her to ask the question that is still so relevant for our day — “If it is to be this way, why do I live?” Rebekah is caught in a web of suffering.
