First, the pain of barrenness. Then, the pain of the struggle between her sons, Jacob and Esau, in the womb, which anticipates the battle they will later have as men over their family’s legacy. It’s as if her suffering is inescapable.

You could almost hear Rebekah say, “My barrenness was broken only to create brokenness in my family? If I can never experience the fullness of joy, why live? Is there any reason for living if my struggle and pain never go away and every time I turn around there’s another problem? If I can’t escape the pain, what’s the point? Why do I live?”

Like a person contemplating ending their life as a means to stop the pain, Rebekah asks the question: “Why do I live?” When our pain seems to be in a perpetual cycle of suffering, we may ask this question. We know that life is not well-manicured and polished. We know that life is not perfect without struggle. The struggle is real within Rebekah, and inside us too. It’s there and cannot be denied. Suffering makes an indelible stamp on us and the whole world.

“If this is the path I must travel, why do I live?” we might think. “My child has cancer. My parent has dementia. I struggle with mental illness. I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate. Why do I live?”

Rebekah, like us, can’t make sense of her suffering, but her question gets to the heart of the matter—it gets to the “why” of our lives. It points to our purpose.

In this selfie riddled, technologically forward universe, it might seem that we live to see ourselves because it is all about the self. “See my new haircut. See my new outfit. See my bircher muesli breakfast. See my dog sleeping. See me with my dog. See my office.” It is a “see me” era and the technological gadgets have rightly been called “iGods” by Craig Detweiler.

iBook, iMac, iPod, iPhone, iPad — i. When Steve Jobs first introduced the iMac in 1998, he said that the ‘i’ stood for internet, individual, instruct, inform, inspire. If one bows to these iGods, it may feed into the overemphasis on “i.” Notice that it is a lowercased “i.” We have been reduced to a smaller size following these iGods, particularly the individual “i” that is consumed by selfies when we shouldn’t really be gazing only at ourselves. If we only do selfies, it fosters an i-world where our lives revolve around ourselves.

In contrast to the world of iGods, I want to suggest that there was something within Rebekah that was bigger than herself. When Rebekah asks, “Why do I live?”, a question that seems to be about herself as an individual, God tells her, “Two nations are in your womb.” Her sons, it turns out, will be the founders of the nations of Edom and Israel. She may not have understood what was happening, but entire nations were to be products of Rebekah’s life. Her life was more than her life. There was a larger purpose within her that went beyond her, a “why” that impacted the world. Her life mattered for more than she could even imagine. 

God’s response to Rebekah can be instructive to us when we consider her question, “Why do I live?” There may be much struggle and stress in your life these days, but you have a “why,” a purpose within you, that is bigger than you. Your life matters more than you can imagine. 

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: Only Duke male applying to Baldwin Scholars can’t take hint
author: Monday Monday
article_text:
Editor's note: The piece below is satire.

Duke’s Baldwin Scholars just dropped their female-only requirement for membership, meaning men can now join the prestigious undergraduate program once dedicated to promoting female leadership. While the move has stirred up controversy on campus over the supposed overreach of the Trump administration or the belief that spots for the women’s leadership program should be filled by women, there is one male student at Duke applying to the Baldwin Scholars who just can't seem to take the hint. In the words of Baldwin applicant and Trinity first-year Jake McCann, “Why is everyone looking at me like that?”

There are a lot of perspectives to hear about the new policies, such as those from Baldwin Scholars alumni, past applicants and diverse voices in general. However, in keeping with Duke’s new commitment to “Inclusive Excellence” — the approach that Duke has been using as a replacement for DEI and the policy responsible for the new Baldwin requirements— Monday Monday will only be reporting on this one guy in an effort not to discriminate against men. It’s time to hear all sides of the feminism narrative.

When McCann first heard about Baldwin’s updated membership requirements, he told The Chronicle he couldn’t believe his luck. “A program with research funding, specialized curricula and a built-in community of other motivated students? It’s like it was made for me.” When asked about his commitment to women’s leadership, McCann said, “I love when women lead. My mom led me in cleaning my room, doing my laundry and cooking all my meals for the entirety of high school, so I’m excited to hopefully replicate that dynamic with the girls in the program.” 

The Chronicle was also allowed a transcript of McCann’s Baldwin Scholars interview, where he was asked about how he engages with women’s perspectives on a day-to-day basis. McCann was recorded as saying, “When I tip at restaurants, I only give 75% of what I think the average guy would give to simulate the pain of the wage gap. I’ve also seen "Pride and Prejudice" — did you know the hand scene is improvised?”

McCann, while somewhat aware of the controversy surrounding the new policies, seems mostly content with his choice. “I’m not technically doing anything wrong,” McCann said, “And that’s like the only metric I’ve ever used to make decisions.” The Chronicle also asked McCann what he thought of “Inclusive Excellence”.

“Honestly, it’s working. ‘Inclusive Excellence’ is when I’m excellent and other people include me in stuff. I’m applying for a Pell Grant!” Jake McCann is rumored to be Vincent Price’s nominally but not financially estranged son.

As Duke continues to make changes to the last vestiges of DEI in its programs, curricula and infrastructure, stories like McCann’s are becoming all too common. Next week, we’ll cover male Pratt freshman John Hale, who is, to the dismay of his friends, rushing Illyria.

Monday Monday is currently believing women and validating their experiences, a true paragon of gender equality.

title: Landfills and Mobile Orders: What are we missing?
author: Anagha Gowda
article_text:
From Skillet $5 deals to Sazón bowls, everyone at Duke has discovered the food hack of the century: the incredible Mobile Order. Skip the line, grab your food and make your way to class— or Perkins or wherever you are headed. 

Mobile Order might be the savior of every Duke student’s hunger, especially following a lecture in Gross Hall or a lab in French Sciences. However, one common problem? By the time you get to it, the bottom of the box is damp and getting ready to give. 

Well, you think, that’s because it is made of paper. And even though it is made of paper, after eating, you throw it away in the trash. 

Duke has made active efforts in the past to maintain sustainable practices across campus. Whether it is the use of reusable plates in WU, the paper to-go boxes of every dining spot on campus or the assorted recycling bins lined up on the walls, it is clear that Duke holds its mission to create a greener campus. Duke even composts pre-consumer food waste, or any food that is not used at the end of the day, through compost contractors.

So, how did composting get so heavily missed with regard to Mobile Orders and WU?

Think about the capacity of students eating meals at WU during any given week. Each week, around 4800 undergraduates are eating three meals at WU every day and 1600 undergraduates are eating 1 meal for five days a week. That is approximately 41,600 meals being eaten at WU— at a minimum. 

Even if a tenth of those meals are eaten through the Mobile Ordering pathway (which I suspect is on the lower end of the spectrum), thousands of paper boxes have been going to the landfill as opposed to an area where they can be adequately decomposed. 

And that’s not considering the graduate students and visitors who eat at our world-class dining hall, or the students who decide to splurge on sweet treats.

Not only is composting post-consumer waste sustainable environmentally as a green campus, but it is also economically beneficial to Duke University as an institution. By adding a few composting bins and encouraging students to dispose of their Mobile Order boxes in the right place, Duke could save hundreds— if not thousands— on garbage disposal. With the right logistics, the compost garnered in these bins could be used in Duke buildings and around campus as fertilizer in both the Duke Gardens and the Duke Farm, cutting costs in multiple areas that could quickly add up.

This idea of composting and harnessing sustainable measures to make a real impact is not unheard of. The University of Michigan has composting measures that are available in over 150 different campus buildings and has ways for students to suggest composting bin locations. Brown University has had a similar composting program, taking its food scraps and creating fertilizer on campus since 2016. Georgia Tech also has composting available in every residence hall on its east campus and three of its dining halls. 

I mean, even UNC has composting efforts with their dining halls. I do not know how much longer we can take getting beaten by UNC. Even if it is about composting. 

Duke has made significant improvements towards becoming a more sustainable campus. However, those improvements require being followed through on, just like any other efforts to instill change in our communities. Having paper Mobile Order boxes means nothing if they are not being disposed of in a way that is good for the environment. 

Let’s make the Duke difference count. Or, in this case, let’s make the Duke difference compost. 

Anagha Gowda is a Trinity first-year.

title: The death of the essay
author: Evelyn Doan
article_text:
AI is shortcutting our writing competence. Depending on how we use it, it will either accelerate our writing or deprive us of our linguistic complexity, the very thing that makes us human.

Duke students like to be challenged, but we also want to obtain the highest grade possible in writing assignments. Oftentimes, AI can be used to increase the likelihood of the latter, and in Duke's embrace of AI, it can almost feel like a rite of passage in our work. 

Instead of aimlessly proposing that we cut out AI completely (because we are long past that turning point), let me show you the importance of intention behind writing and perhaps ways AI can be used without sacrificing our literacy intelligence.

The word ‘essay’ comes from the French word ‘essaie’ — to try, or attempt. Oftentimes, we ‘try’ in our essays in the hope of a good grade, long before we write for ourselves (and oftentimes we never even get there). Between the endless essays, discussion posts and Canvas reflections, our writing often becomes an act of survival rather than a means of discovery. 

Montaigne- the French philosopher who popularized the essay as the literary genre— wrote in his opening address of ‘Essays’ to the readers with the line, "I am myself the matter of my book." He traced out his thoughts as the subject and meandered along the paths of his consciousness. Attempting to sketch out his changes, doubts and confusion, he wrote not to prove a point, but to explore one. After all, writing, at its purest, originates from our own complexities.

If you have an opinion on a topic, if you are writing any piece at all— say a journal entry, a text, an opinion article— the act of writing should be how you discover your thoughts on that topic, like how Michael de Montaigne intended to.

Whereas we have retained the initial form of his essay, we have lost the narrative. The form has diversified and evolved, becoming more polished, but the motivation got lost along the way. 

This is because we have mistakenly prioritized the output of writing, rather than its cognitive process. If we avoid the strains of effort it takes to form our opinions on a subject, retreating away from genuine original thinking, we risk massacring the depth of our thoughts. If you want to understand how you feel about something, write about it. Foregoing any of the steps in between, erases the reward of learning. 

In our educational institutions, the typical essay writing has been drifting towards the edge of a precipice. Our much-discussed obsession with grades and the performativity of (elite) college culture made essay writing another purely outcome-oriented activity. Whatever the path— cheating, plagiarizing or perhaps most commonly and most insidiously just putting your mind on autocomplete for whatever your teacher expected— all that mattered was getting an A at the end.

Admittedly, I have plenty of fitting anecdotes where I have followed this same predictable pattern. Even in classes where our writing is supposed to be about our most personal feelings, I have found myself writing for the supposed ‘right’ answer. Hollowing out the bones of the words, so that it becomes nothing more than skeletons of paragraphs, forgetting the very purpose of self-reflection.

In this way, the essay transitioned from a form of discovery into a traded commodity. Homogenous paragraphs churned out like dull lightbulbs in a factory and handed over in exchange for a good grade. Now, AI has the same output-oriented mentality, producing the same product within five minutes. 

The essay was already rotten; now AI has put it in its coffin, so how can we revive it?

There are many ways students can use AI in their writing. Still, we need to make a conscious decision about whether to use it to shortcut our cognitive abilities or as a catalyst for creativity, allowing us to access worlds of knowledge within seconds and expand our thinking. These models are great for retrieving large swaths of anecdotes or sources (which, of course, need to be checked before use). They might be helpful as a sounding board, but once you start copy-pasting, think carefully about what you are outsourcing. 

There is no barrier to the temptation to integrate AI into our work, and frankly, I do not have a grand solution to prevent that desire. However, something larger is at stake here. The very structure of reality, how we grasp and understand it, is based on language. If we all converge our ideas into one unit produced from the same large language models, what sort of reality are we left with? 

When Montaigne said he was the matter of his essays, he did not just mean he was the subject; rather, the essays were, in a much more literal sense, him. They were not just empty squiggles on a page but the flux of a soul wrestling with many of the same concerns we all face today. 

To write an essay is to attempt; our motivation should be to explore our thinking and to reach personal conclusions about the subject. If we outsource this to large language models, we will become like them: empty, striving only to fill in the next word to appease our audience. 

Evelyn Doan is a Trinity sophomore. Her column typically runs on alternate Sundays.

title: Left, right or anyone in between: Here’s what we can learn from Kamala Harris's tour
author: Stella Kaye
article_text:
As the crowd files through metal detectors and settles into their seats, a wave of excitement hums through the air. There’s a shared joy here— one I haven’t felt since before the 2024 election. Tiptoeing down the row, I find my seat and crack open my notebook. “I feel better than I have in a long time,” I write, soaking in the laughter and buzz around me.

The 2024 election had wrung me dry. On November 5th, my friend and I baked Kamala cupcakes for our AP United States History class— red, white and blue with tiny “We Can Do It” decals. On November 6th, I walked into room 318 to find a pool of melted frosting and Harris’s face sliding tragically into it. “Shit.” I sighed. “This is going to be a long four years.” 

And that it has. It’s been a long four years. Except it hasn't even been a year– I begrudgingly have to remind myself of this several times a week. So when Vice President Kamala Harris announced she had written a memoir, it appeared like the liferaft I had prayed for was coming to save me, even if it was just temporarily. 

When the opportunity arose to pay forty dollars for a fifth-row ticket to her book tour, I didn’t hesitate. Hearing her speak, I was reminded of so many valuable ideas that had slipped away in the chaos of 2025. Harris’s message, though aimed at her base, carried truths that extend beyond party lines. Here are a few personal interpretations of some lines and lessons from Harris that I think everyone at Duke could use right now. Republican or Democrat, socialist or capitalist, anarchist or democracy lover. 

Lesson number one: High levels of success are not possible without the people beside you. Harris acknowledges that her success in politics is not only because of her ambition, but because of the support from those who stuck by her side: her “Dougie”, mentors, sorority sisters, the list goes on and on. For us, the friends who celebrate our ambition, the mentors who push us higher in our research, the quiet supporters who steady us when we flunk a test— they make every win possible.

We live in a culture that glorifies independence, but the truth is, every late night, every breakthrough, every “you’ve got this” text is part of a team effort. No one gets through Duke alone, and pretending we do only feeds the myth that success is solitary. The truth? Every achievement on this campus is a collaboration, even if only one name is on the first-place trophy.

Number two:We deserve more than the weight of others’ opinions. Harris has spent her entire career fighting off hate from constituents, co-workers and community members. While acknowledging that this too is hard for her at times, what Harris wants us to recognize is that we got to where we are for good reason— and we deserve to take up space. On campus, students are surrounded by some of the best and brightest the world has to offer. Overwhelmed with a combination of rigorous coursework and cutthroat extracurriculars, high-achieving students like those at Duke fall victim to imposter syndrome, feeling like they aren’t good enough, or that they don’t fit into the picture of an ‘ideal’ Duke student.

I certainly feel this at times. But students on campus can remind themselves that those who try to make us feel small often do so to feel taller themselves. What’s stopping students from embracing their own potential is often just the weight of others’ opinions— and that weight is entirely optional. We don’t have to shrink ourselves to make space for others, or to fit into someone else’s definition of success. At Duke, we are surrounded by brilliance, yes— but that brilliance exists in many forms, including our own. By remembering this, we give ourselves permission to aim higher, speak louder and step fully into the opportunities we are more than capable of seizing.

Number three: There is no job too big or too small to do; every job matters. Oh boy— Harris hit the nail on the head. On campus, it feels like a competition to land the “most impressive” unpaid internship, rack up LinkedIn connections and chase whatever looks best on paper. When we run towards the highest rank with the biggest salary, we gain the connections and credentials but lose our souls to the corporate machine along the way. The people who make the campus actually run— the Duke Dining workers, the janitors, the IT technicians— fade into the background, while others climb the ladder on their labor. We call them “support staff,” but they’re the foundation. Here’s the truth: the most essential jobs are the ones we overlook. The people who feed us, fix our Wi-Fi and clean our classrooms deserve more than gratitude. They deserve respect. 

Number four: misinformation ruins people; we need to make sure we’re working with the same facts. Harris spent 107 days fighting off some of the most bizarre accusations I’ve been alive to witness. From immigrants chowing down on dogs to transgender people committing school shootings at higher rates (both of which, by the way, are factually wrong), false claims were being thrown around like basketballs in gym class. This problem persists when the stakes are lower, too. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve had a conversation with a peer— sometimes even a professor— where false statistics are thrown out as evidence of why I’m wrong and they’re right.

On the other side of things, I’m guilty too: I’ve cited data about voter turnout and conspiracy-esque information I found in an Instagram post or Reddit thread without checking its source. The inherent problem with this lies within the erosion of trust, not only in one another, but in truth itself. When our arguments are built on shaky foundations, meaningful dialogue becomes impossible. Misinformation doesn’t just distort facts. It fractures relationships, polarizes classrooms and weakens our ability to solve real problems. If we can’t agree on what’s true, we can’t begin to disagree productively.

Last but most certainly not least, number five: It’s okay to protest andto dance and sing. Ah yes! Balance— Duke students’ weakest skill. Somehow, we’ve gotten caught in the cycle of doing things only because they’ll look impressive on our resumes. I’ve danced my entire life, yet since coming to Duke, I’ve taken a ballet class just once. I’ve forgotten how to make time for the activities that keep me sane: moving my body, connecting with friends at home, simply breathing. Everything feels impossible in the midst of our hectic daily schedules. But what rings so true in Harris’s words is that there is a way to do all of it— to pursue ambition without giving up the parts of life that make us feel human. So, let’s at least try. 

As the auditorium lights lifted and Harris walked off stage, I closed my notebook and sighed. Pages on pages of wise words that I couldn’t wait to share with anyone who would listen. Walking out of the theater, I thought to myself, “Maybe we’re not as divided as we thought we were.” If there’s anything to take away from these five lessons, let it be that, regardless of political affiliation, there are contested issues we can find common ground on. In fact, when we take the surface politics out of some of the most heated debates in American society today, I think we’ll come to find that there’s more we agree on than we don’t. And at the end of the day, that’s exactly how we will pull ourselves out of this polarized bubble we live in.

Stella Kaye is a Trinity first-year.

title: For when you're blankly staring in the C-1
author: Sarah Pusser
article_text:
I sit in the RDU airport, not surprised that my flight back to LaGuardia is delayed. They say the winds are too strong, and air traffic control is a “bug-mess,” whatever that may mean. My old yellow backpack from high school— which now serves as a weekend duffle— sits beside my feet, holding my jeans, sweater, socks and the empty space from forgotten PJs. I am spending a semester in New York City with the Duke in New York program, and came back to North Carolina to visit a friend for the weekend. Leaving this morning, it’s a 30-minute drive to the airport, where I now wait for three hours. The flight is two hours, then a 30-minute bus ride to a 45-minute subway ride back to my dorm. Six hours and 45 minutes total in transit. 

When I first got to Duke, I remember romanticizing the C-1. I think back to the strangers with whom I shared a 10-minute conversation, learning a few small details about them and then letting the conversation live on its own. There was something exciting about the forced proximity and how I was determined to engage with it. But patterns fell into place, and soon those C1 rides became some of the most detached moments of my day. Later in the year, I remember being surprised that I could watch an entire episode (sometimes more) of Severance in the moments walking to and riding the C1 from East to West. How can moving across one campus be so time-consuming? 

New York has been no different. I thought, given how compact the city was, and how relatively small it is geographically, I would be free of the long commutes. Turns out moving to a different city just introduces different problems. For example, now I know that taking the subway during a downpour is a big mistake— not that there are many other options. And people aren’t afraid to slam their bodies against the closing subway doors to shave off three minutes (something I haven’t yet adopted.) 

Usually, to fill the transit time, I play familiar music, something that’s already burrowed in my brain and find a safe space to rest my eyes (somewhere I’m not staring at anyone.) Or I’ll play Block Blast or do the NYT games, depending on whether I have cell service or not. Occasionally, I’ll just sit in silence and absorb the conversations and noises that surround me, but usually only when my headphones or phone have died. Around me, everyone follows the same pattern. A form of dissociation— silence— between the louder moments of their days. 

There is something frightening about this void of time. What exactly do we lose, and when exactly did we lose it? At first, I thought it was about phones— that we'd lost some pre-smartphone golden age of connection. But after talking with a Duke alum who graduated in the 80s, they told me no one talked on the C-1 then either. These moments of liminal time-passing are decades-old patterns, meaning this is about something deeper than technology. This is about the need to escape humanity. So how can we reclaim these moments? How do we feel purposeful in transit?

I believe there is something to purposeful observation, that is, looking at your surroundings and thinking about what you see, rather than just acknowledging it. For example, right now, as I look up from my spot in the airport, I only see one man who doesn’t have either headphones on or his phone in his hand. I recognize the jacket that hangs on the top of his suitcase.

My mother has one very similar. A dark, dark navy, with a beige collar and inside liner— the texture of a quilt, with three black buttons sewn to the front. He is wearing a bright pink long-sleeve shirt and looks content, and yet, almost confused. Almost everyone here looks content, despite the delayed flight. And as he stands among the rest of the crowd with their necks craned down, looking at their phones, I wonder when simply participating in an absence of something became resistance? 

But how do we let this practice stick with us? With small steps: finding one sight of interest per commute, spending one minute looking around before putting headphones in and letting yourself get bored, so you can think about what it means to be bored (and how much of a privilege it really is).

 What does this give us that dissociation doesn’t? While this moment won’t follow me to tomorrow, if I hadn't looked up from this screen, I wouldn't have seen the man in pink. I wouldn't have thought about my mother's jacket. I wouldn’t have realized how many of those around me were glued to their phones.

These aren't profound observations by any means, but they're mine— small threads connecting me to this moment, to my past and to the stranger across from me. This practice doesn’t have to extend into conversations, questions or eye contact— all things which can feel invasive— they just help add texture to lived moments, versus the ease of blankly passing time. 

With almost perfect timing, a woman has just announced that our flight is now boarding. I see the swarm of people pushing towards the front, and, for a second, they take their headphones out to listen for their zone to be called. Our ears are all collectively exposed to the bustling nature of the airport, and, though fleeting, the large body of people in flight DL1652 share a present moment in transit.

Sarah Pusser is a Trinity sophomore. Her column usually runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: Let's get lunch! (Not really.)
author: Katelyn Cai
article_text:
At Duke, we have an unwritten playbook for talking to your almost-friends, the people you see in class or used to hang out with during O-Week. 

Step 1: Complain about how long it’s been since you’ve seen one another. 

Step 2: Offer to get lunch. To catch up, obviously.

Step 3: Never grab lunch. Rinse and repeat. 

For too many of us, offering this empty promise of lunch is almost instinctive. It’s an easy “out” of the conversation, because you’re promising a “see you next time!” It soothes your guilt for falling out of touch or failing to deepen a potential connection, because you’re now “actively” trying in this relationship. 

But if neither of you ever sends a text to coordinate a time or place, you’re not trying. You’re performing friendship. 

Performing has long been a quintessential part of the Duke experience. A 2003 Duke Women’s Initiative report described how many female undergraduates feel the pressure to be smart, beautiful and popular: “effortless perfectionism.” While there are certainly still gendered dimensions to the problem, I’d venture to say nearly all Duke students feel an immense pressure to show up as our best, day in and day out.

We’ll chug caffeine to hide any trace of sleep deprivation, dress up just to go to class and downplay our half a dozen commitments like it’s nothing. I’ve never met a group of people who are better than Duke students at pretending absolutely nothing is wrong, ever.

In an effort to be our best in social interactions, we offer lunch because we think it’s expected of us. Never mind how disingenuous it is. 

I’ve offered countless lunches in my three and a half years at Duke and regretfully, have never even scheduled most of them. It’s not malicious. Almost always, the true culprit is my overwhelming schedule and workload.

Mathematically, we all only have five lunches a week (and even less some semesters, if my class schedule disagreed with my having friends). If I added meetings for extracurriculars, interviews for journalism classes, FLUNCHes with professors and research check-ins, I hardly had a single lunch left to give. 

I’ve loved every activity I’ve participated in college. But, I can’t deny I also listened to the nagging voice in my head that told me I needed to do more if I wanted a better resume or bigger impact. A full schedule might’ve quelled my career anxiety, but it came at the cost of investment in my relationships. 

Sometimes, at Duke, it feels like we don’t have the power to change anything. We can’t lighten our workload, because we’ll fall behind everyone else. We can’t send the scheduling text, because we won’t get a response back. But, the status quo only exists because we accept things as they are. What if we all decided to change?

For my senior fall, I decreased the number of courses I was taking so I could actually get the lunches I promised. I won’t be able to underload next semester, but I think this tradeoff (as there is with any decision) is worth it. I still don’t have a 100% scheduling success rate, but I’ve met some of my new favorite people: a fellow 9th Street Journal reporter to debrief hard stories with, a Bible study partner to worship with and a Pratt star to keep my Beli streak alive with. 

It’s unrealistic to assume we can always control our class schedules to reserve a “lunch period” or quit a commitment that’s become too much. When lunch isn’t possible, I’ll often offer a more realistic alternative: studying together. We might be sitting silently in the stacks, but at least we’re in community. And, if that’s too much, we should stop overpromising and simply offering nothing at all. 

When I’ve been overwhelmed this semester, I’ve switched my playbook for my almost-friends:

Step 1: Complain about how long it’s been since you’ve seen one another. 

Step 2: Catch up briefly. Genuine questions only. Part ways with a “see you around!”

Step 3: Run into one another again by chance. If I have time now, I’ll offer lunch. If not, I go back to Step 2. Rinse and repeat.

We’re told to go to a good college, not just for the quality of the education, but for the people we’ll meet. Let’s take the time to get lunch and actually meet them. 

Katelyn Cai is a Trinity senior. Her column typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: What does it mean to be informed?
author: Ryan Growney
article_text:
An incredible article was recently published here in The Chronicle called“Stop protecting your peace: Engage in politics.” It argues that just because we have the opportunity to disengage from the discomfort of current issues does not mean it is right to do so— we each have a duty to act. It is a well-worded and powerful call to action, but towards the end, the author states that we don’t need any fancy degree or even a personal motive to “stay informed.”

The phrasing invites some thoughts: is there a personal motive for staying informed? What does it mean to each of us individually to be informed? This article is just one example of a broader question, one too often ignored: what does staying informed really mean, and why should we strive for it? 

The short answer is that staying informed means understanding that we aren’t.

Right after that article was published, I was sitting in WU with a friend, and we got into a conversation about the question that would become this article— what is the right way of “being informed”? Being informed, for me, meant active engagement. It meant seeking out information instead of letting it come to you. My perspective came from the fact that most of the people I know are tuned out of current events, their news comes from overheard conversations or social media posts.

My friend, coming from a family whose TV is constantly tuned into the news channel and who regularly receives slightly fear-mongering emails forwarded from their mom about this or that crisis, had the opposite view. To them, being informed was selective; a glut of constant information only served to obscure the important pieces. About fifteen minutes after the conversation began, my friend looked me in the eyes and said, “I think we’re saying the same thing.” They were right. We disagreed on what being informed should look like, but we agreed why it was important.

“Stop protecting your peace” says we need to stay informed because, while we may not be feeling the effects of a particular issue, we know people who are. In as varied and broad a community as Duke’s is, we come into contact every day with people affected by decisions and problems that don’t affect us. We need to stay informed because it lets us understand, connect with and support the people around us. In other words, being informed is innately communal; it allows us to have empathy with those we interact with. 

While our definitions of what “being informed” actually may differ, my friend and I agreed on this point. In our separate ways, we each try to stay informed because it allows us to tap more deeply into the communities we exist in. Knowing what is happening more broadly lets us ask more meaningful questions. It lets us understand differing perspectives.

Being from New York, I try to stay up to date in New York politics because it allows me to understand the way my fellow New Yorkers see the world. Take the mayoral race that just concluded, for example. Simply knowing about it, I can ask about someone’s opinions at a high level. But being able to talk about particular policy points lets me understand what they value at their core. I don’t know everyone’s perspectives, I don’t know all of the details that inform those perspectives, but I strive to have the tools to find them. This is the “why” behind being informed— it lets us ask meaningful questions that elicit meaningful responses about differing perspectives.

Understanding why we value being informed, being informed seems to be less about information and more about being able to ask meaningful questions in the first place. Simply put, we strive to be informed to ask meaningful questions of the people around us, so being informed simply means understanding that we need to ask those questions in the first place. 

At Duke, we interact with a uniquely wide breadth of experiences and backgrounds, so particularly for us, it is important that we learn across a broader swath of ideas than most. We have the opportunity to interact with a veritable gold mine of passionate, engaged people with nuanced perspectives, and this community was founded upon the opportunity to learn from them. It’s in the Duke mission statement: the University promises to promote a “commitment to free and open inquiry” and “a deep appreciation for the range of human difference and potential.”

The reason we value universities, particularly top universities, is because they expose us to such a wide variety of perspectives. Duke is incredible because, in it, we are inundated with beliefs, ideas, information, perspectives and knowledge of a breadth and scope found hardly anywhere else in the world. Being informed here at Duke means giving ourselves the tools to understand each of those perspectives— that’s what we’re here for. 

We’re not expected to be knowledgeable about everything all the time, as my friend’s parents are. We’re not expected to be checked out. We’re expected to learn new perspectives. This is what being informed means. It means understanding that we don’t understand and embracing it. It means asking questions about the unique ideas and problems filling the minds of the people we worked so hard to be around. Nuanced perspectives require nuanced questions to elicit them. This is the implicit heart of“Stop protecting your peace”: being informed isn’t our burden, but the very thing we love about the community around us. 

Understanding “being informed” this way does not mean skipping out on the news. If anything, we should model ourselves more after my friend’s parents, because we need to ask thoughtful questions of the whole swath of people at Duke. However, for us, the news is not the end of being informed, simply the means by which we get there. In fact, it’s only one subset of the information we should be learning.

Books, podcasts, conversations, Wikipedia rabbit holes— all of these, and more, are places we should be learning about the problems that face the world today, because those problems affect the people around us too. This is what being informed is: a learning process. It’s a learning process that connects us to the people around us. It’s a learning process that helps us fulfill the goal of why we’re here at Duke in the first place. 

Ryan Growney is a Trinity first-year. His pieces typically run on alternate Wednesdays.

title: Rewritten: Delete later; Between expectations and needs
author: Heidi Smith & Madysen Rufener
article_text:
The Chronicle is soliciting submissions from alumni and current students for their rewritten Duke supplemental essay based on their time here. You can submit here.

The essays I wrote to get into Duke no longer exist. 

I love writing, and by that I mean I love writing about anything other than myself. So I wrote my personal essay in third person, and I wrote my “Why Duke?” about a girl I could eventually become. Years later, I’ve graduated, and I’m neither of those people. I’m pretty sure I deleted those essays as soon as I hit submit. I’ll probably delete this one too.

I remember fragments: something about an English major. Something about joining The Archive. 

I majored in cinematic arts. The Archive rejected me freshman year. 

Duke was not the place I wrote myself into. It was sharper, faster, more competitive. People spoke in elevator pitches: 

“What’s your year? Major? You don’t know? That’s okay… we can still be friends.”

I began to mirror them. I curated myself into someone impressive, someone who could go toe-to-toe with Oxford professors and live to write the tale (then delete it).

Ambition turned into performance because Duke rewards polish: the right answer, the right tone, the right kind of burnout. I played the game, and I hated myself for it. But underneath that exhaustion, I learned how to create things that mattered to me. Screenplays. Novels. A version of success that rewarded vulnerability instead of perfection.

Duke was the perfect fit for me because I made it fit. I made myself fit. Then I graduated; I stopped performing. But I still can’t imagine going anywhere else.

Delete.

Madysen Rufener, Trinity '25, is a columnist for The Chronicle's How To Duke column.

Despite the state of technology today, I was unable to unearth an exact copy of my “Why Duke” essay from six years ago— in my defense, the Common App has no retention policies, and I’ve since replaced my laptop. I have the vague memory of writing about why interdisciplinary programs like Bass Connections made Duke appeal to me, but, if high school me were being honest, I just wanted to get out of small-town Ohio, anywhere that would accept me.

After a fraught admissions season, during the onslaught of COVID-19, I eked into the class of 2024 off the waitlist. I did indeed do a Bass Connections project and ended up double-majoring in CS and English, doing research across the fields. Now that I’m over a year out— and I miss my college years dearly— it’s not what I intended to do, but what I happened into, that made my time at Duke.

Applying to The Chronicle's opinion department as a columnist because I mentioned it offhandedly to a friend who pushed the issue. Going all in for Club Running after my best friend forced me to come to practices. Reconnecting with old professors after some health issues that allowed me to realize how right the things they said were. Being utterly thankful that ChatGPT was released in my junior year, so I already learned how to think on my own.

What I got from Duke was not at all what I expected, but it was exactly what I needed.

Heidi Smith, Trinity '24, was a former Chronicle columnist for Volumes 117-120.



Rewritten is a recurring column of short reflective essays by Duke alumni and current students.

title: North Carolina Republicans choose Trump over democracy
author: Neil Sanderson
article_text:
Both chambers of the North Carolina General Assembly recently approved a new congressional map, with the new lines set to take effect for the 2026 midterm elections. The new districts, passed on party-line votes, are specifically designed to give Republicans an additional congressional seat, a reality that legislative leaders did little to deny. 

By once again engaging in the corrosive practice of gerrymandering, this time in an unprecedented fashion, state Republicans have chosen loyalty to Trump over loyalty to the very voters they were elected to represent. 

In fact, Senate Leader Phil Berger and Speaker Destin Hall explicitly framed the effort as a response to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s attempt to redraw California’s congressional districts to pick up additional seats for the Democratic Party. They also pitched the move as heeding Trump’s call to redistrict, with Berger saying it will help “protect President Trump’s agenda.” 

This comes at a time when North Carolina lawmakers still have not passed a budget, the effects of which are being felt throughout the state.

It’s a striking indictment of our leaders’ priorities that they rushed through these maps while pushing issues like ongoing recovery efforts and an impending Medicaid crisis to the side. What this latest effort shows is that appeasing Trump’s desires is apparently a bigger priority than the pressing issues people are facing. There are plenty of things state lawmakers could be doing, like adequately funding public schools and law enforcement, to name a couple. Instead, they’re depriving voters of their ability to elect the candidates they desire, tearing apart communities and adding confusion to the election process.

Alarmingly, the legislature’s actions represent North Carolina joining a dangerous race to the bottom on redistricting with nationwide implications for next year’s midterm elections. But even then, lines constantly changing like this is not normal — no state in the nation has seen disruption like North Carolina. Next year’s elections in North Carolina will mark the fourth consecutive election to take place under new districts, and the sixth of the last seven to take place under different district lines (2014, 2016, 2020, 2022, 2024 and now 2026).

In 2016, a federal court struck down North Carolina’s original 2010s redistricting plan as an unconstitutional racial gerrymander, a decision that was upheld by the Supreme Court. Later, in 2018, North Carolina was ordered to redraw its congressional map again by a federal court that found lawmakers had engaged in partisan gerrymandering. While the Supreme Court later decided it cannot rule on partisan gerrymandering claims, the North Carolina Supreme Court struck down the maps. 

Following the redistricting process after the 2020 census, Republicans passed another gerrymandered map, which was struck down by the state Supreme Court once again, in favor of a different map, which was in place for 2022. Under this map, the results reflected the state well: 7 Republicans and 7 Democrats were elected, and two races were incredibly close and hard-fought. 

However, in that very election, the court flipped to the Republicans, and the new state Supreme Court reversed their decision on partisan gerrymandering the following year, greenlighting a Republican redraw.

 In this manner, gerrymandering results in uncompetitive districts that suppress rather than engage diverse voices. Fairness aside, gerrymandering confuses and disillusions voters, particularly younger ones who are just beginning to be civically engaged. Consider the absurdity of this: Someone living in Goldsboro, about 80 miles southeast of Durham, will now have resided in four different congressional districts since 2020 alone. 

It’s worth acknowledging that gerrymandering itself is not a phenomenon unique to Republicans or to North Carolina. My home state of Illinois, for example, has maps drawn to heavily favor Democrats. But what is unique and without precedent is the president pushing legislators across the country to redraw their lines for maximal political gain in the middle of the decade — a process that, despite Berger and Hall’s assertions, started with Trump and Texas Republicans, not Newsom and California Democrats. 

What’s more absurd about this effort is that North Carolina is already incredibly gerrymandered, reflected in the lopsided partisan outcomes. Last year, Republicans won 10 out of 14 congressional seats, despite the state being split nearly 50/50 at the topline. Now, state Republicans are seeking to up that advantage to 11 out of 14. Further, the state legislators who just approved the new map were elected in gerrymandered districts themselves in 2024, when Republicans captured roughly 60% of the seats in each chamber despite losing the statewide popular vote. 

This effort is a reminder that threats to democracy may not always come in the form of people literally storming the Capitol — though, as we learned four years ago, they certainly can. These threats also come in the form of dark backrooms with cartography software and politicians too afraid of crossing the president.

It’s also a reminder of what’s so severely lacking in our politics today: courage. The fundamental problem, as I see it, is that there are simply too many people who are afraid of losing their jobs to actually do it. 

Under the current system, the incentives are stacked against courage and against listening to voters. Representative Ralph Hise actually claimed, “I don’t represent Democrats in the Senate,” in response to complaints about the lack of transparency in the redistricting proceedings. Hise’s quote is certainly concerning, but it speaks to a reality created by constant partisan gerrymandering. Representatives are simply not accountable to members of the other party; their only concern becomes winning a partisan, low-turnout primary election.

To be clear to Hise, though, you do represent (some number of) Democrats. More importantly, you represent North Carolinians and you represent Americans. North Carolina is part of a larger national battle, with states including Indiana, Kansas, Nebraska and Ohio considering redrawing their lines at Trump’s request following Texas, Missouri and North Carolina. 

The lesson here, on a basic level, should be not to succumb to threats. After all, state lawmakers are far from the only people under threat today. Look no further than our University, which has received threats to comply with the political preferences of the current government or risk losing even more funding.

Whether threats to democracy or threats to the independence of academia, we cannot let this zero-sum game continue. We must resist succumbing to threats and stand up to those who will justify any means to reach their desired ends.

At a moment when North Carolina Republicans should’ve drawn a line in the sand, they instead picked up the pen to draw their most egregious gerrymander yet. 

In this world, Trump’s will is seemingly a sufficient reason to upend elections in the search for pre-determined partisan outcomes, and it takes standing up to him to change that reality.


Otherwise, the question becomes, where does this end?

Neil Sanderson is a Trinity first-year.

title: I wrote this two months late: My hypocritical objection to flakiness culture
author: Annie Ming Kowalik
article_text:
This article, as suggested by its title, was penned two months late.

It’s late not because I was hit by the C1, or was stuck in a hurricane or was undergoing some grand existential reckoning. Honestly, I began because finally, after weeks of guilt (not enough to mobilize me, evidently), I felt as though I owed myself some honesty. 

This article was late because I lied and told myself I was too busy to write it. I penned this at 12:48 AM on a Sunday at the conclusion of a weekend where I could also have sat down and dedicated time at 2:00 PM instead. 

I told myself that I got overwhelmed, of course. Aren’t we all? I’m overloading, I’m a double major; I need a social life; I need a break, just one more day— into oblivion. I quietly moved the task of writing this lower and lower on my to-do list until it disappeared under a growing pile of urgent obligations and people I really do need to email back.

If that sounds familiar, it’s because it is. Every college student I know, myself included, lives in this constant state of semi-apology.

“Ugh I missed this, I’ve just been so swamped.”

“Totally my bad, this week’s just insane.”

“Wait, we have to get lunch soon. I’ll text you! x.”

These are word-for-word texts I have sent or received in the past couple of weeks. These phases have become a kind of social lubricant, smoothing over our collective flakiness. 

But, I think they also reveal a worrying shift in our collective values. Somewhere between our color-coded calendars, our overcommitted resumes and our 12-hour library days (I cannot remember the last time I didn’t get back to my dorm before midnight), we started treating our reliability not as a dependable virtue, but as a luxury to bestow only on the influential. Dependability is something given to professors, recruiters, or people who might one day write us a recommendation letter. 

We still manage to show up on time for that meeting that matters, the one with a title, a LinkedIn post or a line on a resume. We still find the time to charm new people by grabbing lunch, with rapid-fire responses that prove how on the ball we are. Yet, we’ll cancel on a friend who wanted dinner, or leave a message unopened for days. It’s hard to claim “whoops, sorry, I totally didn’t see this” when in reality our phones are glued to our hands, fingers tapping away at every notification except the one that would require real effort to answer. 

This isn’t entirelyour fault. Science does explain this behavior. Psychologists call it“attention fragmentation” — the chronic splitting of focus that leaves us constantly reactive but rarely present. As sociologist Jonathan Gershuny notes, “work, not leisure, is the signifier of dominant social success.” The busier we feel, the busier we believe we are, the worse we actually manage our time. As Time Magazine points out, busyness has become the new status symbol. People subconsciously associate busyness with status. Being unavailable signals importance. Reliability, by contrast, reads as a lack of ambition. 

It’s easy to see how this mindset bleeds into American work culture, too. The glorification of hustle, the long hours, the multitasking "do it all", primes us to measure worth in the scarcity of availability, scarcity of time and of presence of emotional availability. We prioritize the visible commitments and let the invisible, more enduring, more forgiving ones like friendship quietly decay. 

So what do we do about it? I don’t think the answer to that is some grand productivity overhaul. I can’t wake up tomorrow morning and decided to change all my habits for the better, immediately. Much like New Year’s resolutions, I fear that would lead to a couple days of vigorous improvement and a rather disappointing backslide come my next round of midterms. 

Rather, I think part of the solution is a smaller and much more uncomfortable choice: accountability. Our disrespect for each other’s time remains disrespectful even as we get unexpectedly busy. We must, at the very least, own this poor behavior. We must start treating our flakiness, our lack of communication, as a choice, not a symptom. When we say we’ll show up at a certain time, and arrive late or not at all, that’s not the calendar’s fault, nor that person who stopped us on the way to chat. It’s our own.

My mother (who called me out on my own flakiness, concerned I hadn’t penned an article this semester) likes to remind me often that “Sometimes the circumstances aren’t your fault, but your actions are always your responsibility.” I used to roll my eyes, but she’s right.

Whilst the culture around us isn’t our fault, we have a responsibility to own it. We cannot hide behind the schedules we chose for ourselves. If we value our relationships as much as our resumes, we need to start acting like it. That means replying when we say we will, saying no when we can’t and meaning yes when we do. 

Reliability is not a very glamorous thing. I have never seen it in the drop-down menu of the skills section on an internship application. It won’t win awards or go viral on LinkedIn. But in a culture obsessed with being busy— a culture we cannot help but get caught up in— just showing up, being honest and communicating well might just be the most surprising thing you can do. 

Let’s be on time, and maybe we’ll all stop pretending that only trying is enough. 

Annie Ming Kowalik is a Pratt junior. Her column, "The Tasmanian devil: An Aussie's experience in Americana," typically runs on alternate Mondays.

title: The Trump cuts have hit our clubs. Now what?
author: Kris Sun
article_text:
At most schools, starting a club is a finicky thing. The application process for a club at the University of California, Berkeley requires an orientation and multiple rounds of advisory meetings spanning up to three months. Northeastern University requires letters of recommendation from an academic department and a business proposal presentation to a board. Comparatively, starting a club at Duke University is simple.

Correction: was simple.

I came to Duke wanting to start a club. To be specific, a Duke branch of the Forward Party, a bipartisan national organization. Following Duke Student Affairs’ simple guidelines, I spent the first few school weeks garnering support from fellow students, cold emailing professors, and drafting up a Club Constitution. A few weeks later, everything was set. Only, when I clicked into the Duke Student Affairs page, I was met with the following message: 

"Based upon staffing changes and to provide better support to our current recognized student organizations, we will not be opening applications for new recognized student organizations in the Fall 2025 semester. We want to ensure we can provide a thoughtful and thorough review of new organization applications and will be best equipped to do so in spring semester. Please stay tuned in the early spring semester for more information about changes to this process."

The Trump Administration’s funding cuts have already bludgeoned Duke’s library systems, devastated our grant funding and steamrolled the Health System’s Medicaid reimbursements. Now, the Trump cuts have hit our club processes. Duke University’s response: firing staff and slashing funding.

Throughout the school year, I, alongside many other students, have watched as clubs have adjusted and adapted to our new funding deficit. I have spent the past few months exploring other methods for starting a club at Duke University. And through all of these compounding experiences, it's gradually become more apparent than ever before: the Trump administration has dug Duke’s club infrastructure a deep, deep hole. What do we do now?

After the roadblock of Student Affairs, I began researching further into this club predicament. Although my political club could no longer be housed under Student Involvement and Leadership, there were a few more methods I could try:

In my head, the most obvious first strategy was to email Student Affairs and magically convince them that my potential club was the last piece of the puzzle missing from the Duke University picture. Was it going to work? Probably not. 

But not for the reasons you would think. Student Affairs was one of many targets of Duke’s financial layoffs. Student Involvement and Leadership, the specific section of Student Affairs dedicated to club activities, once held dozens of staff members. It now has three, two of whom are graduate students. The activities, queries and questions of Duke’s 250+ clubs now flow through the inbox of one full-time worker. If I sent an email, it would likely have gotten lost among the hundreds of other club needs.

In fact, recent interviews with a variety of clubs (American Chemical Society, Black Student Alliance, Duke Club Taekwondo, the Duke Debating Society, Duke International Relations Association and the National Society of Black Engineers) reveal just how much recent personnel shifts have impacted club processes.

Duke Club Taekwondo, for example, noted that the downsizing of the Duke Recreation and Physical Education support team has led to response delays. The Duke International Relations Association (DIRA) also noted such deficiencies: when they submitted a question about merchandising, it was first routed to the one-person Student Involvement team, only to be rerouted to the one-person Office of Trademark Licensing. 

Meanwhile, the Black Student Association (BSA) is facing the wrath of Duke’s personnel losses. As a culture-oriented club, BSA remains highly connected to Duke’s Center of Multicultural Affairs, whose former Director left last Spring and was replaced by an Interim Director, who has also since left. The Center’s main page now lists zero staffers, and an official job posting has surfaced for a new Multicultural Affairs Director.

In sum, I don’t think an email to Student Affairs could’ve solved my club conundrum; they already have too much on their plate. 

I moved on to the second method: secure resources from an outside national entity. For a potential political organization, this option didn’t seem entirely far-fetched; many student clubs already do this(Alexander Hamilton Society, for example). Why couldn’t I do the same?

In fact, it seems that Duke’s clubs have gradually and increasingly begun seeking external funding. Club funding is allocated by the Student Organization Finance Committee (SOFC), the Duke Student Government’s club funding distributor. Only, I would argue that the Trump Administration’s funding cuts have ushered in new levels of financial hesitancy.

The BSA has reported hesitancy in event funding approval, including one outright proposal rejection. This sentiment is shared by the Duke Debating Society, which has already faced two SOFC Operational and Capital Fund(OCF) rejections. 

In remedy of funding pitfalls, many clubs have begun seeking alternative means of funding. The Duke Debating Society, BSA, and the NSBE have all separately reported attempts at diversifying their funding through business solicitations and sponsorships.

Given the experiences of other clubs, it seemed to me as though external support is a necessity to adequately fund a club. I contacted the National Forward Party, who agreed to provide funding and even worked to connect me with a potential faculty advisor (who said yes!)

Funding: secured. That resolved one of the issues of not having a Student Affairs-approved club. But it still didn’t help with the actual approval.

Option three: secure a club through department sponsorship. For a select few clubs, it is not Student Affairs that handles their administration and funding, but rather a Duke Department. The department provides all rules, regulations, and funding. In replacement of its abysmal SOFC funding, the American Chemical Society, for example, receives a significant portion of its funding from the Chemistry Department and Professor Charlie Cox’s personal Duke allotment. Both of these funding pools were thinned by the recent funding cuts. Similarly, the Center for Multicultural Affairs, whose Cultural Engagement Fund is dispersed to all culture-related clubs, seems to have taken on its own financial losses. 

Consulting with the national Forward Party once more, I continued my club search by connecting with a variety of Duke Departments. In total, I sat in meetings with three departments, all enthusiastic about my idea and shocked that Student Affairs was no longer accepting any additional club applications this semester.

The content of these meetings has been requested to remain private. Despite their enthusiasm, though, a clear consensus emerged that Duke's funding is no longer secure and that political action of any kind comes with unprecedented risk. It became clear that no department could reasonably and safely help with my club predicament.

This came as a big shock: Duke’s funding deficits resulted from federally-implemented political motives, and are now impacting the very politics of Duke itself, to the point where even a bipartisan club is unwelcome. Another newly forming bipartisan group, BridgeDuke, has similarly failed to get approved as a club. I’ve specifically chosen to give these professors anonymity because I fear the political punishment that could arise from their political opinions. And the ultimate unintended consequence: Duke’s nonpolitical clubs are suffering too.

In sum, I don’t think I’ll be able to bring a new club to Duke anytime soon. I blame the Trump Administration for unfairly positioning higher education at the cusp of his political agenda.

The Trump cuts have hit our clubs. So now what? Well, BridgeDuke, Duke’s unofficial bipartisan political organization, is pushing ahead anyway, even without the support of Student Affairs. I intend to similarly keep pushing for my club, even if it means that members will have to meet off campus. 

Another noteworthy similarity among my club interviews was that nearly every club recognized that Duke is both adapting and resisting. Duke Student Government has yet to pause its funding disbursement. A select few clubs and LLCs have even noted increases in funding. The Debating Society and DIRA are still attending competitions. Duke Club Taekwondo still managed to go on its yearly retreat. The BSA has an upcoming Halloween Party. Amid funding cuts, it seems clear that Duke’s club scene will pull through, even if my club won’t be an official part of it.

Kris Sun is a Trinity sophomore. His column, ‘Multitudes,’ typically runs on alternate Mondays.

title: More professors should ban technology
author: Samantha George
article_text:
I’ve been sitting towards the back of the same lecture hall every Tuesday and Thursday going on ten weeks now. Every day, as class begins and I settle into my seat, I make the same observation: no one is paying attention. 

Or, to be more precise, no one is paying attention to just one thing.

The rows in front of me are full of students flipping between tabs on their laptops, going from a homework assignment to a job application to Instagram back to the homework assignment at a comical speed. Or people are going multimedia, checking one thing on their phone, another on their iPad and then another on their laptop. All while the biggest screen, the professor’s lecture, looms in the background like the Netflix show you put on while folding laundry. 

We’ve weirdly normalized the phenomenon of letting our classes drift into the background, professors’ questions meeting long empty pauses, in the name of being teleported via our laptops and iPads to the timeless space that is All The Other Things We Have To Do.

I get it. I’m guilty of it, too. We’re busy college students with a lot to get done, which often requires taking advantage of every moment of our day.

But how is splitting our focus in class taking advantage of time? 

And when did paying attention to one thing become a waste of time?

At some point along our college careers, we’ve each observed, and likely adopted, the odd habit of doing work for other classes in class. It feels like the most productive option: to still go to class and absorb whatever you can from the lecture, but also check off those pesky things on your To-Do list. We halfheartedly take notes on a Google Doc while flipping back to the lab report that really has our attention. Or the Etsy shop. Or the sports highlights. 

But there are some serious hidden costs to this constant multitasking, or attempts to multitask, rather. You may roll your eyes or claim an exception, but over and over, the human brain has been shown to be incapable of multitasking. We simply lack the brain architecture to perform two tasks simultaneously — what we mistake for “multitasking” is really just our brains switching between one task and another.

To simplify the complex neuroscience, going from tab to tab on your laptop ignites these “switching costs” in your brain, which are basically the time it takes for your brain to leave one task and tune in to another. This switching is broken down into two stages: goal shifting (“I want to do this now instead of that”) and rule activation (“I’m now thinking about how this works instead of how that works”). Switching costs are higher with more complex tasks, meaning they take more time and energy. You can easily wash dishes while talking to a friend. But switching back and forth between a lecture and a homework assignment? That’s much more expensive for the brain.

With the explosion of digital media and the attention economy, media multitasking — the simultaneous use of two or more media streams or platforms — has become the norm. I can’t remember the last time I wrote a paper without listening to music or a time I didn’t check my phone while watching a movie. Can you?

Counterintuitively, several studies have found that people who engage in this type of behavior for hours a day (dubbed “heavy media multitaskers”) actually perform about the same or worse at tasks that require multitasking compared to people who engage less with multimedia usage. This shows that your ability to do two things at once doesn’t improve no matter how long you do it.

Perhaps even more concerning are the echoing impacts of media multitasking. One study found that heavy media multitaskers perform worse at single tasking, suggesting that even when you want to turn on your focus and “lock in,” multitasking bad habits can get in your way. This was most consistently observed with tasks requiring sustained attention, working memory and long-term memory — all skills vital to us as students. 

Now, I’m not crazy enough to think we’re all going to decide to shut out laptops in the epiphanic realization of multitasking being fake, even though we probably should. But that’s why I think more professors should take the option off the table to begin with and ban technology from classes.

Not only will more technology-free classrooms breed more respectful classrooms (it’s really awkward how we ignore professors in favor of laptops), but also, yes, better learning experiences for everyone. Isn’t it distracting watching screens scrolling constantly in front of you? Doesn’t everyone else doing other homework make you a little more likely to do the same? 

Plenty of professors are already doing this, too. The technology-free classrooms I’ve been in have always led to a happier, more community-driven class. Instead of individually typing away on our laptops, we whisper to each other in class. We engage more with the professor. And we leave class without that awful frazzled-brain feeling that comes from all those switching costs. Typically, all it takes is a few reminders from the professor for the rule to hold, especially once students start feeling the difference in the class experience themselves.

We signed up to come to this university to learn, and that all starts in the classroom. Whether it comes from the professors or students, I think Duke could use a little more focus on the big screen. We have the rest of the day to bounce between all our little screens, after all.

So, to the professors: make the case against technology to your classes. Encourage the use of pen and paper or exclusively notetaking software on iPads, and you might be surprised at how students respond after the initial moans and groans. 

And, to my fellow students: let’s be wise enough to work with our brains and stop trying to divide our attention endlessly during our classes. Duke’s hard enough — there’s no need to make it impossible.

Samantha George is a Trinity senior. Her column typically runs on alternate Mondays.

title: Library captures her
author: Robert Wallace
article_text:
An image that retains great clarity, in spite of all these years, comes back to her. She is a high school teenager with a job at the St. Louis Public Library. Standing among the books, looking at the colorful spines, the smell of the paper, she feels a sense of comfort, as if she belongs here. She carefully stacks them on the shelves.

Occasionally, she might peruse a title, rub her hand across a cover, feel its texture and heft. Outside, a fluke snowstorm could be hitting the streets of St. Louis, and she wouldn’t know it. Sometimes she wonders who might come along and pull the very book she has stacked on the shelf. She imagines them touching the same spine she has just felt.

That was the beginning of Arianne Hartsell-Gundy’s librarian career.

Hartsell-Gundy is now a librarian at Duke University. She has been at Duke for 10 years and heads the humanities and social sciences department for the library. Her specialty is literature. She thought she might become a professor but found the library — and not teaching — to be where she felt most at home.

“There's nothing more fun than somebody coming to you with some really interesting question, and having to try and help them figure it out. And having those kinds of conversations with somebody where a little light bulb goes off because they suddenly have a new perspective on their topic. It's a great feeling [that] I love,” Hartsell-Gundy says.

Hartsell-Gundy has a photo of herself, “that captures me,” where she’s maybe seven years old, sitting on the floor in a hallway in her grandmother's house with a teddy bear next to her and a book.

She recalls her first reading experience with nostalgia.

“I think it was probably a Dr Seuss book. If I go back further, I had gotten this illustrated fairy tale book [with] beautiful illustrations, like a golden book or something. I can see the cover in my mind. And I loved that book, I would just look at it anytime I could have a parent read [it]. I just thought it was beautiful. It must have been a Dr Seuss book, though, that I [first] read by myself. And I do remember how exciting it was, that it kind of all came together — it's like solving a mystery, all those letters I've seen on the page, this is what they mean.”

In academia, everyone needs a mentor. For Hartsell-Gundy, it was Professor Devoney Looser at the University of Missouri-Columbia. The professor’s name alone attracted her. She bonded right away. She taught Jane Austen courses, and Hartsell-Gundy fell in love with Austen. Interestingly, Professor Looser was a first-generation college student (like Hartsell-Gundy), and so she was one of the first people who stood up for her and gave her explanations about how higher education works. She showed Hartsell-Gundy how one can be, hopefully, a warm person in higher education, somebody who was thoughtful and caring.

Since then field of Library and Information Science has changed tremendously, and it continues to change. Much of the information searching is now done online. Duke has needed to adapt. A major renovation with Lilly Library, which Hartsell-Gundy is monitoring and is part of the planning committee, is in progress.

You can hear the excitement in her voice when she talks about it. Lilly will contain many new spaces, including a café and a lovely outdoor space right outside the café. Hartsell-Gundy believes students are going to enjoy the expanded options for places to study, along with spaces that will provide students with new ways to connect and collaborate. She’s very eager for students to be able to start enjoying the new space. It seems like everything is on track!

Still, there are concerns. AI is one of them.

“I don't know, yet, how AI is going to impact things. I still think that there will be a place for libraries and librarians, because I think you still are going to need someone to help you navigate the library databases. I do still think you're going to want some experts who can help you understand what you're to search, why to search, what you're doing, how to use AI and why to use AI. I'm not a doomsday person who thinks that libraries are going to disappear, but I do think they're probably going to change. We're going to have to adjust to some of that.”

For instance, bookstores haven’t disappeared. In fact, some have returned to more prominence. Hartsell-Gundy says she still enjoys “brows[ing].” And she prefers reading from a physical book. Others as well, at least faculty in the humanities. Serendipity apparently hasn’t died. During Covid, when the library was closed, faculty complained about not being able to browse.

Yet, and this gets back to the AI issue, Hartsell-Gundy does have concerns about students thinking critically, “engaging with the material.” Reading a book does that. “Wikipedia,” on the other hand, she says, “doesn't ever use any other kind of source, that's also kind of an issue because you're just getting a summary, you're not getting the actual thing.”

So what is Hartsell-Gundy’s favorite book?

“Persuasion by Jane Austen,” she says.

“I’m going to have to go with "The Sound and the Fury" or "Beloved,"” I say.

She nods. “I strongly believe that Beloved is the best American novel of the 20th century.”

We care about books and libraries because they are places that hold knowledge. They’re places where we go to learn. They’re places where you can touch the written word. They’re places that uphold and protect democracy. Most importantly, they’re places where librarians like Arianne Hartsell-Gundy work diligently every day to help others find information both online and in person.

As Hartsell-Gundy walks back to her office, passing the many stacks of books in Perkins Library, a story unfolds, of a young girl who once worked in a library in the Midwest and who loved books. It is that story which she sees as her responsibility now as a librarian to help students and faculty. “I love my work,” she says.

Robert Wallace is a first-year graduate student of liberal studies. His column, 'Telling Stories', typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: A realist’s case for frat reaffiliation
author: Wendy House
article_text:
Content warning: This article contains mentions of sexual assault and rape. 

Ask anyone who knows me and they could tell you how very much I detest frat parties. They are the nexus of all I despise: crowds, liquor and exorbitant noise. I find fraternities themselves cliquey and weird. I don’t want them around me; I don’t especially want them at my college at all. So, obviously, I never thought I would be making this argument: they should be on campus. 

In 2021, a faction of nine fraternities calling itself the Durham Intrafraternity Council broke away from Duke following the placement of restrictions that delayed rush to sophomore (rather than freshman year) and restricted eligibility for selective living sections to upperclassmen. Married to the unveiling of QuadEx, this appears to have been part of an attempted institutional divorce (or, at least, separation) from Greek life; one which has been a topic of much student criticism. Indeed, four years later — three weeks ago — DSG passed a resolution supporting reaffiliation of the estranged frats, demarcating a new endeavor to bring our boys home. 

The discourse about these decisions and their aftermath seems to mostly concern the social scene of it all. Duke feels that we’re over-reliant on frats to feed the work-hard-play-hard student culture we all know and love. Others argue that frats being off-campus fails to ameliorate this issue, and besides that, disrupts the communities around frat houses. I agree, but I think something is being lost in the hubbub of the affiliation-disaffiliation struggle — lost, or left politely unsaid. 

I still remember the first thing my best friend’s mom said to me when I was gushing about my acceptance letter. She warned me that girls get raped at Duke. 

She was right. Duke’s sexual assault rates for women were twice the national average in 2018. I would like to tell you if that has changed in the last seven years, for worse or for better, but Duke has failed to collect any such data. A Student Sexual Misconduct Annual Report conducted in 2020-2021 — whose scope was limited to cases reported to the Office of Institutional Equity — admitted the appalling fact that less than 10% of reported incidents even became formal investigations. 

What does this have to do with fraternities? As many as three-quarters of all college sexual assaults are “party rapes.” Fraternity-affiliated men are three times more likely than unaffiliated men to commit sexual violence. The correlation between Greek life affiliation and sexual assault is well-established; yet, it seems the burden of getting our frats in order through trainings and sober monitors is left to student organizations like SHAPE. That is, unless you count that nice consent-themed tote bag GVEO gave us during orientation! I’m sure that kept at least a few people from being violated.
