What it looks like to me, very frankly, is that frats operating off campus is a convenient setup for Duke: keep all the party hype with none of the onus that comes with such events actually happening under your roof. Indeed, Duke has a storied history with unbecoming Greek life headlines. Alpha Delta Phi was suspended in 2015 following rape allegations. Sororities announced an embargo on mixers with all-male fraternities in 2020 based on concerns about sexual assault. In 2012, a student’s life was cut tragically short in a drunk driving incident with a fraternity brother. These atrocities speak for themselves. There are more, but I won’t shell shock you or reduce these victims to statistics. The point is that it’s no wonder Duke wouldn’t mind driving frats off-campus with sudden aggressive restrictions.

Even as disaffiliation occurred in 2021, Mary Pat McMahon admitted that off-campus frats wouldn’t have access to “accountability structures set in place for recognized groups.” The last publicized discipline of fraternity chapters was in 2019 for hazing. You’d have to be naive to think nothing has happened since then to warrant bringing down the hammer again, yet it seems Duke has found the actions of its frats faultless, as they have remained ostensibly undisciplined. There is a cost to this false peace: security. 

Let’s all be serious with ourselves. We know frat parties are unsafe. They cannot possibly be made safer happening unregulated, off-campus, in a field with spotty service. Between the physical remoteness of party locations, the chaos of the party itself and the necessity of relying on frat-sanctioned buses for transport to and from the party, off-campus functions open a myriad of avenues for women to be lost in the shuffle. It’s already next-to-impossible to keep hold of your friend’s hand while trying to weave through that seemingly endless crowd of writhing bodies; must we add transportation to the list of vectors for losing track of who you came with?

Without a sexual misconduct climate survey to draw on, I can’t say with certainty what the effects of disaffiliation have been on rates of assault. What I can say is that our university absolutely, beyond the shadow of a doubt, has an obligation to protect its students. It cannot feasibly do so when its students are blackout drunk miles away from home base.

If frats reaffiliate, students have access to Campus Police and Narcan. As others have already pointed out, the watchful eye of the Duke administration is in and of itself an excellent motivator for frats to properly investigate and address misconduct. If the case continues to be that there are no appreciable consequences for letting party crime proceed unchecked, it will continue to proceed unchecked. Duke needs to get a leash on Greek life, and reaffiliation is the first step to that. 

I cannot overemphasize how little stake I have in the game of frats coming back on campus. When I told my friend I was writing this article, they called me a traitor to all introverts. Maybe I am, but if there is so much as a chance that the regulation and oversight which comes with frat reaffiliation could save one girl from possibly the most traumatic experience a person can suffer, I think we must pursue it with overwhelming zeal. Women have a right to drink, dance and enjoy themselves without a cloud of paranoia haunting their evening. Toward that end, I think the rest of us homebodies can afford to buy earplugs and suck it up. 

Wendy House is a Trinity sophomore. Her column typically runs on alternate Wednesdays.

title: Rewritten: More than a name, a canvas to shape and brownies
author: Maya Singla and Fiza Khan
article_text:
The Chronicle is soliciting submissions from alumni and current students for their rewritten Duke supplemental essay based on their time here. You can submit here.



If you had told me three years ago that Duke would make me the most homesick I’ve ever been — at times lost, overwhelmed, and tired — I would’ve pushed your words out my other ear. Three years ago, I wrote about research, coursework and Bass Connections.

No wonder this school waitlisted me. 

Duke is not just academics; it never was for me. Don’t get me wrong, it has one of the best Biomedical Engineering programs in the country, along with course material that can make your eyes light up (and just as quickly produce tears). But Duke was more than its name. It was a new coast, a new beginning — something to discover. 

And I did: from atop U-Hauls in barren fields, within the glass walls of the Rubenstein, in a dorm with my roommate and a dozen stink bugs, through the first snow and the last hour at Perkins. I found more than a name; I found a feeling, and I named it home. 

Sometimes I wanted to puke my guts up or sprint the 2,392 miles home. But without those moments, I wouldn’t have found my friends for life or learned that I can do hard, scary things. That I can dissect a frog leg, or perform on a national stage or TA a lab course. And perhaps most importantly, master the art of securing the perfect Marketplace brownie. 

Duke matches me because it embodies everything I value: uncertainty, excitement, magic, people and the chance to keep discovering (plus brownies).

Maya Singla, Class of 2027



As a dreaming applicant, I once wrote about my life at Duke as a Biology major doing research in the hospital and feeling at home among the students I saw during my childhood hospital visits.

Now, as a junior in the thick of midterms, I can confirm that reality looks a bit different. I chose neuroscience instead, drawn to how it connects the biological foundations of the brain with the psychology of human behavior. Along the way, I found a passion for global health research and discovered an interest in emergency medicine — something I might have never realized without Duke’s mix of research and hands-on experience. 

You can often catch me sprinting through the hospital — not for treatment this time, but because I’m late for my volunteering shift. I also never quite understood the meaning of “academic breakdown” until I became a full-time pre-med.

Still, Duke has been everything I imagined and more. I learned that my journey didn’t end with an acceptance letter — it began there. In time, I discovered that Duke wasn’t just a place to study, but a canvas I could shape — one where I could learn from countless populations and experiences, until I became someone my dreaming applicant self could never recognize. 

Duke, like any place, isn’t perfect. But it evolves — hour by hour — as its students, faculty, and community strive for betterment through knowledge, faith, advocacy, and research. And as Ken Jeong once said, “Duke is home.”

Fiza Khan, Class of 2027



Rewritten is a recurring column of short reflective essays by Duke alumni and current students.

title: Live a-humble
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
We can learn something new every day. 

This became crystal clear to me several years ago. A Duke senior was one of the scripture readers for a Sunday morning worship service in Duke Chapel. That morning, he was assigned to read a portion of the Gospel of Luke. We were doing what is called ‘a gospel procession;’ the music was played and a hymn sung as he and others made their way down the center aisle of the sanctuary to stand among the people. 

The music stopped, and it was time for him to announce the reading. He cleared his throat and instead of saying, “A reading from the Gospel of Luke,” said, “A reading from the Gospel of Duke.” 

Seriously, I thought it was my last day on the job! Who would have thought? A new book of the Bible discovered right here in Duke Chapel — the Gospel of Duke!

Though this was a slip of the tongue, it reminded me that there are many things in life we do not know of. We just haven’t encountered those things up to this point. You can learn something new every day because learning never stops — new information, new ideas, new knowledge, new techniques. Even when one thinks one has finally reached the mountaintop of intellectual discovery, there is always more. 

One example of this in the Bible is when a group of disciples in the city of Ephesus confess, “We have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit,” (Acts 19:1-7). They are disciples, serious religious people, yet still didn’t have all of the spiritual knowledge. They are humble enough to say, “We have not even heard.”

Their learning was unfinished and incomplete; they had a partial understanding because there was so much more to be learned. This is why a degree called “Master of Divinity,” a standard degree at divinity schools, can be misleading and make us think that we are to become masters rather than embrace mystery in what Duke Divinity School Dean Edgardo Colon-Emeric has called “the school of wonder.” 

In a university setting, you can’t learn everything there is to learn, but you do learn how to learn. This is why professors do research — to seek understanding. Professors realize that the more you know, the more you come to realize how much you don’t know. 

You don’t always have the answers, but perhaps you know where to find them. Or, you don’t necessarily know something, but you know who knows. There’s something about claiming to know it all that ironically suggests we don’t know it all. As the philosopher Socrates said: “The only true wisdom is in knowing you know nothing.”

We are not called to know everything but to keep asking questions, to keep seeking and being curious. Life has an inexhaustible curriculum, and there’s never recess. It brings new meaning to “continuing education.” At the age of 19 or 90, we can always grow, develop and learn. Implicit in this idea is that you shouldn’t be so sure that you are always right, which requires intellectual and spiritual humility. As the lyrics of one spiritual put it, we are to “live a-humble.”

This perspective could be helpful with all the talk about civil discourse these days.

It is not a matter of winning or losing a debate. It is the acknowledgment of how much we don’t know while also desiring to learn something new every day in the school of wonder. If we take this approach, perhaps we, too, will learn lessons we have never heard. 

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: Halloweekend Survey reveals Pratt students’ biggest fear is introspection
author: Monday Monday
article_text:
