title: 10 things to toss today
author: Anna Garziera
article_text:
Every late spring, students across campus are confronted with a demoralizing realization: They might be hoarders. The time comes to pack up dorm rooms and they notice the piles of books and laundry, which had been invisible to them until then. Cardboard box and brown tape in hand, they don't know where to begin.

It’s only November, and I am here to tell you that all is not lost. There’s still time to turn things around. Why wait for the spring to do a spring cleaning? Get ahead of the game and start decluttering while it's still manageable.

In this article, I will dive into your life, into your junk drawer, and propose 10 things in your dorm room you should consider getting rid of.

Anna Garziera is a Trinity junior. Her pieces typically run on alternate Sundays.

title: At the height of resources, facing burnout
author: Devyn Deschamps
article_text:
On paper, Duke students have everything they need to thrive. In reality, many are running on empty. Emotional exhaustion, fatigue, insomnia and a depleted attention span are all common symptoms of burnout. By mid-semester, these symptoms haven’t just reached Duke students — they’ve spread like wildfire.

Despite having every imaginable resource, students are increasingly using those tools as shortcuts rather than supports. The very platforms designed to make learning easier often end up eroding its meaning, fueling the exhaustion they’re meant to prevent.

So, has the college experience changed rapidly within the last decade? Are professors and curricula suddenly demanding far too much from their students? Realistically, no. Professors may tweak syllabi each year, but the core of higher education remains the same. The confounding variable isn’t instruction; it’s the students.

Duke offers a long list of amenities to undergraduates: free subscriptions to The New York Times, The Atlantic and The Wall Street Journal; the Duke AI Suite featuring Microsoft Copilot; and full access to all 24 Adobe Creative Cloud products (which I highly recommend, by the way).

In May 2025, Duke announced that all students would gain access to DukeGPT, a free, unlimited-use version of GPT-4o through a partnership with OpenAI. The original ChatGPT launched in November 2022, and after years of upgrades and innovation, the generative AI platform now boasts roughly 800 million weekly users. Three years later, it’s rare to meet a student who doesn’t use, or at least know of, ChatGPT.

It can be almost overwhelming to realize just how much access Duke students have. The pressure of being at a prestigious university is already immense — add to that the unspoken expectation to make the most of every resource, and those perks can start to feel less like benefits and more like burdens. Anxiety sets in as the question “What am I not doing?” becomes relentless.

In trying to keep up, many students begin to see resources not as aids to deepen their work, but as shortcuts to finish it. That shift, from using tools to support learning to letting them replace effort, sits at the core of modern academic burnout.

As overwhelm grows, so does dependence on technology. AI use has rapidly normalized, shifting from a novelty to a necessity. Two years ago, detecting AI-written work was straightforward. Today, the technology has evolved, recirculating and refining itself to outsmart detection tools.

Duke, like many universities, saw this shift coming. Their solution was to introduce a Duke-specific version of ChatGPT — a well-intentioned attempt to modernize and monitor. But in practice, the easy interface has lured many students into complacency: relying on the software not just to help, but to do.

While these tools appear to make academic life more efficient, they’ve also blurred the line between learning and outsourcing. With DukeGPT just a click away, many students feel pressured to constantly “optimize” their work, feeding into the same cycle of burnout these tools were meant to relieve. The ease of assistance becomes another expectation — to use AI for every task, to produce faster, better, smarter. What was designed to lighten the load often amplifies it.

At Duke, this tension is especially visible. Students swap prompt templates in group chats, use DukeGPT to generate reading summaries and finish assignments faster, but not necessarily more fulfilled. The more resources students gain access to, the less room they seem to have for rest, reflection, or true engagement. The abundance itself becomes exhausting.

The consequences extend beyond Duke’s campus. Nationwide, student learning outcomes are declining. The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), often called the “Nation’s Report Card,” tests fourth- and eighth-graders every two years and twelfth-graders every four. In its 2025 report, eighth-grade science scores fell four points since 2019 and twelfth-grade reading and math scores each dropped by three.

Of course, there’s no single cause. These cohorts endured COVID-19 disruptions, rising smartphone dependency and major shifts in education. Still, it would be naïve to ignore how AI subtly reshapes how students think, focus and learn.

Not all resources, however, have the same effect. A subscription to The New York Times encourages curiosity and critical thinking — skills that strengthen learning. But tools like DukeGPT, when used without intention, can dull those same skills by outsourcing effort. Understanding this distinction is key to addressing burnout: it’s not just the number of resources we have, but how they alter our relationship with learning.

There is a silver lining, though. If used intentionally, the resources Duke provides, including DukeGPT, can become powerful tools to prevent burnout, not cause it. The difference lies in how we use them.

Before introducing outside assistance, start with introspection. Take back your autonomy. The simplest organizational habits, like keeping a to-do list or breaking assignments into smaller tasks, can be transformative. Starting with approachable goals builds momentum and confidence, reminding you that productivity doesn’t always require optimization, just presence and consistency.

Duke students don’t lack tools; they lack time to pause. The irony of unlimited access is that it often clouds clarity. By approaching technology and resources with mindfulness, we can return to a healthier rhythm, one where tools like DukeGPT amplify learning, not replace it.

Ultimately, balance at Duke won’t come from another innovation or subscription. It will come from students reclaiming intention in a world that constantly rewards acceleration.

Devyn Deschamps is a Trinity sophomore. Her pieces typically run on alternate Sundays.

title: 80% of college is stuff you do not plan for
author: David Goh
article_text:
Visiting Duke as an alumnus is a real throwback — between nostalgic meals (including a coveted Marketplace swipe — thanks, freshmen!) I kept chuckling at the memory of my younger self drafting out my entire four years of courses before my first FDOC. From the clubs I’d promised to join in my Why Duke essays (only to find them long defunct on arrival) to the way I described Duke to skeptical Singaporean relatives as a “Methodist institution in America”, I was so sure that I could forecast and engineer my future college experience. Those were the days.

When everyone arrives bent on optimising their Duke experience, I now wonder: how do we try so hard and still fall so far? There’s something to be said for expecting detours — and letting others steady us when they come.

That notion would come as a surprise to the me of first year: who began college ready to optimise and maximise. I arrived with my three-year Math-and-Stats degree mapped out on a spreadsheet. By the first month, I’d appended a list of upperclassmen-endorsed “life-changing classes” I swore not to miss.

But four years will teach you that 80 percent of college happens outside any plan you make. In any given semester, maybe 20 percent of your time is spent in control: lectures you prepared for, assignments you anticipated, friends you see regularly. Then come the days your code throws inexplicable errors or you can’t get into a research lab — the sleepless, imposter-syndrome days that swallow you whole. Everyone knows that one innocuous task that cataclysmically overshoots the time you budgeted for it because you felt so close to getting it right that queueing for office hours just didn’t seem worth it.

By my final semester, my transcript was crammed with more courses than I needed to graduate, built on months of “I just need to finish this to get to what I want.” And I never touched that list of “life-changing” electives. So much for optimisation.

But the problem was not effort, nor the intractability of the liberal arts system. It was that we’re often blind to our own needs. Freshmen can pester seniors all they want for the best courses and hacks, but control is illusory. You’ll meet new friends, join new clubs and make tough calls you don’t yet have the perspective for. And when they don’t work out: you’ll crash out hard, having mistaken them for necessary steps toward your goals.

For most of us, admitting we need help is the hardest thing. Yet it’s exactly when we can’t help ourselves that others matter most.

In October 2024, I was hit with a spate of mental health issues and let two critical Computer Science 250D (Computer Architecture) assignments slip away. One day at lunch, I ran into Will Harris (T’26) and told him I was struggling. He was surprised — he was a TA for the course and knew I’d done well in the midterms. 

I vacillated, but he insisted that we sit together, talk through the work and map a plan to catch up. Most of all, he was there for me. Could Optimizer Freshman David have imagined that the redemption of my final semester from the abyss of the 80 percent would come from learning to accept help?

That moment made me wonder: if one conversation could turn things around for me, how many others might be waiting for such a chance encounter? What if the secret isn’t a grand mentorship program or perfectly timed office hours, but simply running into each other and checking in? 

Suppose every student occasionally reaches out to someone else, even at random, asking what they’ve been up to. Suddenly, the probability of being noticed during a crash-out period rises dramatically — a version of the bus-stop paradox, where random encounters often occur during the longest waits. Through these chance encounters, you reconnect with the very resources meant to help you. 

In a way, that’s the paradox: the more we try to optimize college, the more we overlook the human encounters that make it worthwhile. How much planning is right for you? My heuristic: as long as you go to bed happy, wake up happy and have a sense of direction, you’re optimising enough. In the meantime, never be too busy for people. Ping each other for a rose-bud-thorn; don’t be afraid to ask for help. And when you offer help, say what it’ll cost you — two hours, maybe — so they aren’t scared to accept. 

In the end, the real work of college isn’t about executing a plan flawlessly but about inhabiting the messy middle — the 80 percent no one prepares you for. It’s about being present, being available to others and letting them be present for you. That, after all, is what learning communities are for: the shared struggle, the reckoning, the part of college that truly sticks.

David Goh, Trinity '25, was a mathematics major at Duke.

title: Stop protecting your peace: Engage in politics
author: Molly Huff
article_text:
The social media craze of “protecting your peace” was designed with good intentions to prioritize mental health over taxing social expectations and set boundaries without guilt. However, when this innocent sentiment becomes an excuse to disengage from politics, we quickly fall into a culture of complicity. 

It’s no secret life is exhausting and, frankly, it can be mind-numbingly sad with an endless cycle of bad news. Every second it feels like another bombshell has taken what we have grown comfortable with and completely wrecked it. There will always be another war, another political debate, another tragedy. With this, it’s understandable to catch your breath and disconnect from the world now and again. However, choosing to withdraw completely to “protect your peace” is a privilege not everyone can afford.

Talking about conflict is incredibly hard, but living conflict is even harder. News stories on ICE raids, loss of healthcare coverage and death because of abortion bans are real-life experiences to someone else. For marginalized populations, politics is not an optional topic. Politics determine their ability to live and love freely, and, in extreme cases, their ability to exist. We leave these groups behind when we put on our blinders and only choose to look inwards. 

Our society has warped self-care and mental health into a way to escape this collective responsibility and our shared humanity — falling into the bystander effect. At the most basic level, putting aside political parties and disagreements, we can all agree that people should not suffer. Yet, we often choose to stay comfortable and not intervene, watching harm unfold like a bystander to a robbery in progress. 

We have the privilege of tuning out these issues and protecting ourselves from the discomfort of acknowledgement because of our Duke bubble. But it’s this passivity and our willful ignorance that have allowed our political culture to corrode. 

We complain “politics is too polarized” or “something needs to change,” yet we disengage from any efforts that might change this standard. What will address these complaints is action, discussion and debate. Democracy is built on engagement and activism. It requires informed citizenship, accountability and cooperation. If we all conform to the isolationism our culture promotes, we risk losing this foundation. 

Considering today’s climate under the Trump Administration, engaging in politics or speaking out can be incredibly scary for anyone in the country. For students here at Duke, this fear is enhanced due to international status, financial aid and free speech all facing uncertainty because of the administration's actions. 

In this, university academic freedom is undoubtedly under attack. What feels safe is to not say anything and ignore these infringements, simply hoping the storm passes over and leaves our house untouched. 

But, look at how this strategy is working for our Duke administration. Faced with funding cuts, lawsuits and proposals that undermine higher education, the administration has largely resorted to institutional neutrality. By abstaining from commentary or taking a political stance, Duke is effectively protecting the university’s peace over addressing the issues. This neutrality — or “strategically” ignoring issues, as President Price would argue — is simply a refusal to stand up for students affected by any one of Trump’s crusades. 

Price stated at an Academic Council meeting that he didn't want anyone to think “not talking loudly is, in any sense, an indication of complacency.”

However, I would argue that’s exactly what it is. Silence is not safety — it’s inherent complicity. 

Acknowledging this fact does not mean everyone needs to devote their lives to activism or pull a French Revolution; rather, I urge you to make conscious efforts to face hard truths rather than erase them for comfort. Talk to your friends, professors and your classmates. It doesn’t require a political science degree or a personal stake to stay informed. The point is to care consistently, not allowing issues to slip unrecognized or for our shared responsibility for others to be undermined. 

It's time to stop protecting our peace and care. 

Molly Huff is a Trinity first-year.

title: Duke has an accessibility problem
author: Suhani Karkra
article_text:
One of the things I miss most about home is my grandmother. This August, she braved swollen feet, chronic pain and a 6-hour plane flight just to see Duke’s campus. I was most excited to show her around, giving her a glimpse of my life for the next four years. 

However, as I tried to maneuver her wheelchair through mazes of stairs, sidewalks that close in and a ride on a golf cart just to get her to Marketplace, I quickly realized that she would never experience this space the same way I did. 

In that sense, Duke’s campus remains inaccessible not only to my grandmother but to so many others — people with disabilities or mobility differences, older visitors, injured individuals or even families with strollers. For a school that prides itself on who it includes, Duke’s vision of the “best and brightest” is restricted to only those who are physically able to cross its barriers. 

This problem is not a new one. In 2000, Duke settled a lawsuit with the U.S. Department of Justice in response to a complaint brought up by a student wheelchair user who graduated in 1997. The ruling held that Duke violated Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), which requires public places to be accessible to people with disabilities. Paying more than $25,000 in damages, Duke agreed to a list of 10 conditions, including providing accessible parking throughout campus and modifying building entrances.

Since then, Duke has made efforts to reform. For example, the Student Disability Access Office has been coordinating accommodations and providing resources, while the Duke Disability Alliance has been promoting awareness and education. Additionally, in 2021, Duke launched one of the nation’s first Disability Cultural Centers, a unique space dedicated to creating a safe environment and amplifying the work of disabled artists. These programs, as well as ADA accommodations like door openers, are a sign that Duke is at least making a gesture towards inclusion. 

However, those efforts are still not enough — 20 years later, many of its promises remain far from reality. Whether it is the steps leading up to almost every building entrance, the hike to reach Edens Quad or the narrow halls of Old Chemistry Building, Duke has failed to integrate accessibility in many aspects of its student life. For example, students are required to request ADA-compliant transportation for campus transfers two days in advance, which can be extremely difficult to coordinate given their complex schedules. 

As of Jan. 14, 2025, Duke has 10 pending lawsuits based on disability discrimination, one of the highest rates among colleges nationwide. Allegations include denial of benefits, disability harassment and retaliation. 

To confront these allegations, Duke should make decisions with disabled students in mind. Disabled students should have a voice in Duke’s policies, whether it is widening the sidewalks between East and West, improving the reliability of ADA shuttles or adding more ramps across campus. They must be centered in renovation and construction projects so that accessibility is built in from the start. 

Even as construction blares across East Campus, promising shiny new facilities and renovations, ramps remain unbuilt: a poignant reminder of who progress leaves behind.

For me, access is as simple as foregoing buying a bike or carrying my luggage up the stairs. But for my grandmother — and for students, staff and faculty with disabilities, access is a daily obstacle in a place that should be open to all: a contradiction standing in stark opposition to Duke’s inclusive rhetoric.

Editor's note: This story was corrected Thursday afternoon to remove two sentences incorrectly stating that Duke Student Government failed to approve a funding request to improve accessibility. At the meeting previously referenced, senators did not approve any funding requests after failing to meet quorum, but none of the outstanding requests were related to accessibility challenges. After publication The Chronicle found that sections of this column utilized artificial intelligence in a way that violates internal standards, which prohibit the use of AI for writing or refining articles. The Chronicle regrets the error.

Suhani Karkra is a Trinity first-year. Her column typically runs on alternate Fridays.

title: What activities should a Duke student take part in?
author: Ryan Growney
article_text:
How do we become the people we want to be? This is the question that Duke, and every university, is built to answer. It is the question that permeates each and every one of the systems in place here — not just classes, but clubs, sports, even social life. It is the question that brought each of us here, the motivation behind our drive for accomplishment. Most importantly, it’s the question that determines where we go next. 

There’s no doubt that Duke students are accomplished — acceptance to this school, as with any eminent university, requires it. When I talk to other members of the freshman class, I’m talking to valedictorians, team captains, presidents of clubs and companies. That breadth and scope of passion and commitment is what makes the Duke community so amazing.

It’s what drives each of us to do what we do best: go from class to class, club to club, event to event, filling our schedules with opportunities that purport to teach us the skills and give us the connections needed to fulfill our goals. Each of these opportunities are meaningful, there’s no doubt about that. But we often fail to ask if these are actually the fastest ways to become the people we want to be. Fundamentally, we, as Duke students, need to rethink the way we price the risks of the opportunities available to us.

At the most basic level, each of these chances to gain skills are simply risks. They are a grouping of probability-weighted outcomes that will either advance our chances of realizing our goals or not. Whether it is something as small as trying out a new tone in an essay or as large as learning an industry, we ante up the possibility of failure for our gains. This is not a new idea, nor is it a call to “be okay with failure,” but it leads to a question. At Duke, we have more opportunities than we could take advantage of in a lifetime, so how do we choose? What types of risk lead to the best probability of the biggest rewards? 

The obvious answer is that more risk means more reward. Choosing to pursue a particular major means you have the chance to fail again and again, in each class, on each assignment, but in the end, you are infinitely more adept at navigating a particular field. Similarly, the small risk of changing the tone of an essay only gives you the opportunity to fail on one assignment, and requisitely only gives you the possibility of a boost on that one assignment (and perhaps a tiny chance to find your “voice” if you were to become a career author).

But then why do we expect joining clubs to be an efficient pathway to our grandest goals? There is an asymmetry in our risk assessment; in the campus economy of achievement, there is no efficient market for originality. We inflate the price of affiliation and deflate the price of creation. We’re missing something in our usual assessment of risk.

What we’re missing is a different perspective on what effective risks look like. We’re missing a solid anatomy of the opportunities that help us clarify and advance our goals. When we join a club, change our essay tones, take hard classes, we understand the types of failure we are exposing ourselves to. That risk is not really a risk, as either outcome is expected and socially acceptable.

We know we could get rejected, we could not pass a class. Fundamentally, these are still safe bets, because we know what we stand to lose. By our previous logic, we stand to gain less from safe bets than from risky ones. The opportunities that connect us most directly with the goals we have are the ones in which we don’t know what failure looks like. 

I’m by no means saying don’t take hard classes or join as many clubs as possible. On the contrary, do exactly that. But we need to recognize the power of risks we often ignore. At Duke, we have a plethora of incredible, powerful opportunities to strike out on paths we haven’t traversed before. It is not by taking the risks we know that we grow, because the risks we don’t are the ones that have the power to change our perspective.

Previously, I’ve written about service and gap years and the power they both have to change our perspectives. They are perfect examples of this broader idea. Going on a gap year and participating in meaningful service are both opportunities in which we grapple with ideas and problems outside the bounds of the systems we know, where we expose ourselves to pitfalls and questions we don’t know the bounds of, and that is exactly what makes them uniquely powerful.

The Innovation Co-Lab is another incredible example. With programs like the DesignHub, each of us can collaborate with a specialized team of other students to design, prototype and iterate on solutions to any problems we can think of. Similarly, DukeEngage continues to be a bastion of impactful experience, offering the chance to engage in meaningful, on-the-ground work in a number of communities around the world. It’s easier than ever to take on unknown risks.

At its core, Duke lowers the barriers to these types of risk. It offers each of us the chance to pursue anything we want. We have the unique and powerful chance to take risks we don’t know and fail every time and still get back up again and continue. But the onus is on us to take advantage of them.

With all the incredible potential and opportunity around us here at Duke, it’s easy to fall into the risks we know. It’s easy to join that club because you know it will have some benefit and it’s okay if you don’t get in. It’s easy to apply for Scale & Coin because of the potential that someone in that network will help you get a job. It’s hard to start your own company, to make your own job, even here at Duke.

But the skills and experiences we value, the ones who answer our question of what it takes to be successful, are not easy to gain. They’re cultivated over time, through rapid iteration in success or failure. It’s our unique drive and passion, the constant forward momentum, that has brought us here. We need to recognize that this is a new place, a new chance. So reevaluate the opportunities you seek. Capitalize on the risks you don’t know. Your goals are more within reach than ever, so don’t slow down now.

Ryan Growney is a Trinity first-year. His column typically runs on alternate Wednesdays.

title: Look away, children are dying
author: Fiza Khan
article_text:
In public health, people often label some topics as "too controversial" to touch and dismiss others as "too political" or "too complicated." But the survival of children in conflict zones should never fall into either category, because the question of whether a child deserves medical care isn’t political — it’s moral.

Right now, in Gaza, children with congenital heart disease (CHD) face an impossible reality. CHD is one of the most common birth defects worldwide, affecting about one in every hundred newborns, with even higher rates in Gaza. In most parts of the world, a corrective surgery within the first few months of life can lead to full recovery. In Gaza, however, these same children are often left to die because they cannot reach the hospitals capable of saving them. Since October 2023, not a single child has been allowed to cross the Gaza–Israel border for treatment and no specialized pediatric cardiac surgical teams have been permitted to enter to care for them.

A child born with critical CHD shows symptoms soon after birth, including cyanosis, difficulty breathing, fatigue and early symptoms of heart failure. In most cases, surgery and proper follow-up care allow children to live normal, healthy lives. Behind every statistic is a child whose life could be saved with a single operation — a child whose mother paces outside a damaged hospital, praying that a border permit arrives in time. A baby who cries too weakly to be heard above the rubble — and that rubble is not just the ashes of Gaza, but the weight of political restrictions that prevent life-saving care. With restrictions that will cost them their lives, it is impossible not to feel the anger, grief and helplessness all at once.

Across the border, Israeli hospitals and international medical teams have treated Palestinian children for decades at cost (in partnership with NGOs who have helped facilitate travel permissions and raised the nominal fees requested) and many are still willing to provide treatment. But medicine doesn’t exist in a vacuum. War does not stop at the operating room door.

Even when Israeli hospitals are willing to accept patients, borders and sanctions make it nearly impossible for children to leave Gaza. Previously in Gaza, the difference between life and death was a matter of logistics — paperwork, crowdfunding, permission and crossing the border. And now, even that is impossible. Instead, parents watch their infants through the early tell-tale signs of CHD, watching them suffer until they eventually can’t fight anymore. A war stops for no one, not even children who are fading away day by day in front of their parents.

And no, this isn’t about taking sides. It’s about saving lives. Advocating for children’s access to healthcare — whether they’re in Gaza, Israel, Sudan, or Ukraine — isn’t creating hatred. It is a call for empathy in a world that cannot set humanitarian compassion apart from politics. It is demonstrated in the selfless actions of Israeli providers and in the NGOs that have historically carried out medical missions for this cause, but no longer can.

The global health community often talks about "health equity." But true equity isn’t achieved through slogans — it is achieved when access to care no longer depends on which side of a border a child is born on. The United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal 3 calls for “universal access to essential health services.” That promise rings hollow if it doesn’t include all children — even those living in warzones, unaccounted for.

The systems in place — UNICEF, WHO, Médecins Sans Frontières — continue to monitor, document and advocate. But surveillance is not enough when hospitals are destroyed faster than they can be rebuilt. What’s needed is not just aid, but insistence: that healthcare, especially for children, remains protected, neutral and accessible.

As I planned to write this article, I was warned about it being a "politically-charged" topic and how I should prepare beforehand. And yet, I still cannot see what is wrong with advocating for those children to receive healthcare. In an age where compassion is filtered through ideology, it can feel uncomfortable to care publicly about Gaza, since empathy can be misinterpreted as political bias. However, doesn’t moral clarity overshadow everything? How can we ignore the fact that children are morbidly dying not just in Gaza, but in conflict zones around the world, waiting for a heart surgery that could allow them to live a nearly normal life and live to a normal age?

An article in The New England Journal of Medicine recently reminded the medical community that war cannot be an excuse for withholding care. Medicine’s role is not to judge who deserves treatment, but to preserve life wherever possible. In Gaza, that ideal is being tested in real time. And at Duke, our courage to speak up and use the knowledge for the betterment of the world is our responsibility. Advocacy writing and talking to administration about the possibility of bringing patients here for treatment can help, but at the very least, we must be aware of this issue.

Some may argue that war causes healthcare to lose neutrality. But neutrality is what makes medicine sacred. Even in conflict, doctors and nurses cross lines, risking everything because a child’s pulse is louder than politics. Israeli physicians who have treated Gazan children know this truth intimately. So do Palestinian doctors working without anesthesia, electricity, or sleep, refusing to abandon their patients. Watching these acts of courage makes you realize that the human heart is more resilient than any border drawn by political sanctions- it transcends all.

So no, this is not a controversial topic. It only becomes one when empathy is politicized — when defending life is mistaken for endorsing a side. Advocating for a sick child’s right to care isn’t just activism. It is humanity.

Universities like ours have the privilege of distance — of studying crises rather than living them. But that distance also comes with responsibility. Through projects like Bass Connections and through the knowledge we gain on a daily basis as Duke students, we can turn research into awareness, awareness into advocacy and advocacy into action.

The children in Gaza don’t need pity; they need possibility. They need a world willing to see them not as future refugees or citizens of a war-ridden territory, but as patients. As children. As human beings whose lives have the same worth as any others. They need someone to be there, advocating for them to be able to cross the border, just to live a normal life. With the recent advent of a ceasefire, the time is now to act.

The corridor for international medical and humanitarian aid to enter Gaza is being opened; children with CHD need to be prioritized for the services they have been denied over the last two years. For many of the most critical defects, children become inoperable if their surgical care is delayed due to remodeling of the heart and lungs. The sad truth is, the window to fix things surgically has already passed for many of the children born in Gaza since the beginning of the war who were never identified or referred for care. If we fail to act now, that number will only grow. We cannot continue to look in the mirror every day and stay silent, or assuage our consciences by assuming that someone else will do the work. It is on us, every one of us.

Because hearts don’t wait for peace. Because no child should die for paperwork. And because saving a child’s life should never, ever be controversial.

Fiza Khan is a Trinity junior.

title: Can we talk about how we talk about food?
author: Samantha George
article_text:
Editor's Note: The piece below discusses eating disorders and restrictive eating. If you or someone you know is struggling with an eating disorder, please contact the National Eating Disorders Association help line for support, resources and treatment options.

“I can skip breakfast, but not lunch.”

“I haven’t worked out yet today, so I’ll have the coffee but not the bagel.”

“Ugh, I shouldn’t have eaten that, now I’m so bloated.”

I’m sure you’ve heard conversations like these around campus — I know I have. Conversations deflecting guilt or projecting worry, all centered around what we eat.

I often find myself surprised and slightly saddened by these nearly constant conversational run-ins I have with friends or overheard on campus surrounding these difficult relationships with eating. At Duke, we’re surrounded by some of the brightest young minds in the country. We’re a student body that’s ambitious, driven and ever-questioning. So how come our conversations surrounding food are often so unhealthy?

Rather than highlighting a weakness unique to our student body, the frequency of these conversations speaks more to the pervasiveness of the issue: that even as we are busy chasing dreams and careers, making friends and taking classes, many of us are still playing this silent game of minimizing our bodies and fitting a mold, which often impacts how we talk about the food we eat.

This hypervigilance towards bodies and eating is certainly more prevalent in my female friends, but not unique solely to them. It’s estimated that 9% of the U.S. population will have an eating disorder in their lifetime and 22% of children and adolescents worldwide show disordered eating.

Whether or not these food-centered conversations fall fully into the disorder category is hard to say, but their implication and frequency are worrisome nonetheless. Hearing how friends restrict food on days they don’t hit the gym, how they struggle to eat three meals a day without guilt or how they can’t enjoy dessert without worrying, it all hints to a bigger issue, and an issue we never really discuss aloud. 

The issue of body image and eating is a complicated one. Physical appearance is an unpredictable juggle of diet, genetics and lifestyle. And much of the culture surrounding body image is out of our control, with the fashion and beauty media we consume setting impossible standards which lead to body image and eating issues.

But one thing within our control is how we talk about food, especially here on campus where so many students live so closely together. It’s easy to fall prey to expressing guilt about eating. To eat the candy bar, but make a comment about how you really shouldn’t be. To talk about how you skip meals. To stand in line at WU and offhandedly comment how you could never eat that thing — just imagine the calories!

Instead of giving in, we should do the work to rise above the issue. It’s as simple as thinking twice the next time you feel the need to deflect a food-related guilt. Do it for your own sake, but also the people around you. When you say how you skipped breakfast or that you want the fries but should get the side salad instead, it is a sort of pollution that enters our student culture. Someone may hear you — a younger student who looks up to you, a friend who admires you or just a stranger passing by — and take it for the norm.

While changing the way we talk about food won’t topple the entire issue of eating and body image and overall health, it’s certainly a good place to start. As cheesy as it sounds, the change can easily start with you. If you stopped hearing other people talk this way about what they eat, would you maybe stop, too? I know I’ve partaken in this type of food talk just because I’ve heard other people speak that way. It’s almost like blending in with the crowd.

As an older sister and a friend who’s watched too many people fall victim to this unhealthy language, to the point they struggle with real body image issues, I’ve decided to stop partaking and start calling out the harmful ways we talk about food. Sometimes a simple “Why’d you say that?” is enough to make a friend realize how silly it is. Other times, setting the example is enough, by eating what you want without deflection. 

What you eat is part of a healthy lifestyle, sure, but so is how you talk about it. So, for goodness’ sake, have your cake and eat it, too. 

Samantha George is a Trinity senior. Her column typically runs on alternate Mondays.

title: The effort factor
author: Anna Garziera
article_text:
The other day, I was confronted with one of the harsh truths of my generation.

One of the classes I am taking this semester is “Economics of Environmental and Climate Policy,” otherwise known as “that easy elective” offered by Duke in Berlin. So far, our only assignment has been a 2-3 page proposal for our research paper.

Being the wonk that I am, I started working on it weeks before the deadline. On Friday, I was feeling calm, knowing I had already submitted my proposal, due Sunday. This could not be said for a majority of the class. The classic phrases were flying. “Have you started yet?” “What are you doing yours on?” And, worst of all, “I’ll just ask Chat to write it for me.”

This year, Duke is offering its students a free subscription to OpenAI’s AI chatbot ChatGPT. I should have seen this coming. With the recent introduction of AI-focused classes and the BS Concentration in AI and Machine Learning, a prepaid license to ChatGPT was inevitable.

I don’t think Duke endorses students asking “Chat” to write papers for them. Nevertheless, this generation’s reliance on artificial intelligence for schoolwork is undeniable. Some say it starts at the middle school level, with Gen Alpha. The first time I saw anyone seriously cheat using ChatGPT was when one of my friends let the AI chatbot write his final paper for English. He ended up getting a zero on it.

Regardless of the class policy, asking ChatGPT to write your paper isn't doing yourself any favors.

There are two good reasons I can come up with for why someone might ask AI to write their paper. (I’m sure ChatGPT could come up with more.) 

First, they think “Chat” will think up better ideas, or is a better writer than them. I find this a little sad. As an amateur writer, I can tell you that no chatbot-generated piece of writing will be as personal as one you wrote yourself. Your ideas will be more original and your writing will be, at worst, good enough. Certainly good enough for an econ elective. 

The second — and more likely — reason someone might “Chat” their paper is because they left the assignment for the last day, and now they don’t have time to do it. I don’t think ChatGPT is a better writer than me — but I can admit it writes faster. 

Procrastination is a big problem nowadays. As Duke students, we can see it all around us. I again find this use of AI extremely sad. By not having to write the paper, you essentially saved three hours which you used instead to “rot” in your bed. 

Let’s be clear: I’m not trying to criticize those who ask ChatGPT to write their papers, but to reassure the ones who do not. Your effort isn’t wasted.

I learned what effort was in my middle school PE class. We were doing the Pacer test for the first time. If you’ve never done it, imagine running across a 20m stretch at intervals marked by “beeps.” It’s easy enough, except each time the intervals get shorter, the beeps get louder and you get more tired and out of breath. Actually, it’s awful.

The first time I took this test was also the last time I liked gym class. I was red as a pepper and panting. The popular girls had coolly dropped out together at beep five and the boys were competing to see who could run faster. Everyone seemed more or less fine, except for a few stragglers like me.

I finished my beep test with a not-so-great score. Nevertheless, after class, my PE teacher came up to me and told me she’d noticed how much effort I had put into the test. I went home giddier than ever.

I’ve since put a lot of effort into a lot of things. I’ve put effort into some things that mattered: studying for my SAT, getting into Duke, maintaining long-distance relationships. But I’ve also put effort into braiding my hair and building the ultimate lego castle. Was that for nothing? Of course not. 

Effort is never futile. Even if it’s put outside of your grades or your resume. Even if no one sees it. 

Duke students, you are so lucky to have a head that works — use it.

Even if writing my own research paper gets me no better a grade than if I had asked “Chat” to write it for me, I’ll stick to it. My professor would probably not know the difference — but I do. 

Putting effort into things is how we grow. Not only will writing your own paper help you become a better writer (and dread the next paper a little bit less). It might also lead you to discover that you don’t hate writing so much after all. That’s how it happened for me.

And even more simply, effort has intrinsic value. Today’s work-shy culture turns away from this fact. But it’s true. It’s the reason you’d still prefer your mom’s disfigured, half-burned apple pie to Walmart’s. The effort she put into making it is what makes it taste good (as well as the butter).

This always happens when technology develops. A new machine can make something comparable to what we can make ourselves, but in a fraction of the time, at a fraction of the cost. Over time, we lose touch with how it used to be. How long has it been since you’ve held a hand-knitted blanket? Do you remember how warm it felt?

I don’t know whether artificial intelligence will soon replace the workforce as we know it. It’s possible. It’s scary, too. 

If in two years, all articles published by The Chronicle become AI-generated, I’ll be in mourning. ChatGPT might well become a better opinion writer than me. Maybe it already is. 

Yet, I don’t think its articles will be as valuable as the ones I wrote myself. The fact that I am taking time out of my Sunday to sit down and write this article is still worth something. Keep believing in it.

Anna Garziera is a Trinity junior. Her pieces typically run on alternate Sundays.

author: Aaron Siegle
article_text:
8,760. That’s how many hours there are in a year. When you think about it, that’s not that many hours, especially considering that we should be sleeping for 2,920 of them. Visualize 8,760 as roughly the capacity of Cameron Indoor Stadium (9,314), imagining that each seat is one hour in the year. Whenever I wonder where all my time has gone, I return to this image. Imperfect analogies like this one only begin to scratch the surface at the finiteness of our existence.

Acknowledging our impermanence puts the little things in context. That is not to say that we are trivial but rather, transient. Locked in the confines of the space-time continuum into which the universe corners us, we are forced to grapple with the reality of our smallness, not only as individuals, but as a society. 

This can be challenging, especially for a culture that prioritizes the individual, telling us that we can change the world if we are smart and driven enough. The undulations that we inevitably face throughout our daily lives suddenly turn into a gauntlet of life-or-death decisions. Thus, acknowledging our insignificance should be liberating, enabling us to find our clarity of purpose.

Even though Duke just recently celebrated its 100th anniversary, it can seem like the institution has existed since time immemorial. The stone that seems like it was sculpted out of the Earth’s crust and the monolithic administration and tenured professors who have occupied the same well-worn offices for 40-plus years make it seem as if this place has been around forever. 

A recent email from my neighbor back home put Duke’s “oldness” in context. He mentioned to me how he taught Duke President Vincent Price as a high school senior back in 1975 in Torrance, California. Like 2025, 1975 was a relatively crazy year with the end of the Vietnam War with the fall of Saigon, the takeover of Cambodia by the Khmer Rouge and assassination attempts on President Gerald Ford. Yes, we are facing unprecedented times now. But we’ve faced unprecedented times before.

Amidst the backdrop of an institution that appears to have been around for forever are students whose time in Durham will be quite brief. It’s cliché to say that the four-year undergraduate experience at Duke flies by. But four years is a lifetime compared to the mere 15 weeks that Duke Kunshan students get to spend in Durham. And this transience is a good thing – it would be a little concerning if we never graduated. 

Truth be told, you could spend a lifetime exploring Duke, dabbling in the various programs, student groups and research opportunities. But as every first-year finds out (usually the hard way) that difficult choices must be made — we cannot really be everything we want to be.

Given that time is finite, how then do we choose? On a personal level, how do we navigate the harsh reality that there are more things that we want to do than there are hours in the day? The answer lies in how we value our time, whether we think about it this way or not. By choosing to spend our time in college, we are making the implicit assumption that our education will be a stepping stone to a desirable career. 

In this way, we all have our own personal discount rates that show how much we value future experiences compared to present ones. While discount rates are often thought of in financial terms only, the reality is that we must make tradeoffs between the present and the future in every aspect of our lives – our relationships, our health and even our values are shaped by specific times and places.

The idea that we are constantly making choices about the present versus the future goes against the stereotype that Gen Z is only focused on the present: from recruiters getting blank stares when they ask, “Where do you see yourself in five years?” to kids thinking about life one TikTok post at a time. 

Yet looking beyond these viral moments, I see people at all stages of their lives planning for a future that they may never even experience, such as climate innovators creating new technologies that will allow us to adapt to a warmer planet. Young adults saving money to raise kids that have not been conceived. One common theme unites these examples of forward-thinking: looking past the present requires looking beyond ourselves.

In challenging times, we must see the larger picture. The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) nation developed the Seven Generation Principle, a decision-making philosophy that forces leaders to consider the impacts of their decisions seven generations from now. This approach seems radical and unrealistic in a world that is driven by quarterly earnings targets, mid-semester grades and weekly status updates. 

While these check-ins are an inevitable part of our modern lives, they too often function as idols – targets that we pursue with an unhealthy single-mindedness. Only when we put these intermediate goals in context will we find what is truly meaningful.

Aaron Siegle is a Trinity senior. His pieces typically run on alternate Fridays.

title: Duke needs to bring back its queer essay prompt
author: Aaron Dai
article_text:
This summer, amidst the chaos happening within higher education, Duke overhauled the list of supplemental essay questions on its undergraduate application. Among the three optional essay prompts that were removed or replaced, one explicitly asked applicants to share more about their identity in the context of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. 

The decision, likely spurred by the Trump administration's attitudes towards the inclusion of identity in higher education applications, not only marks the end of a decade-long tradition of inclusive admissions but also calls into question the legitimacy of Duke’s commitment to its LGBTQIA+ community. 

Duke first introduced the essay prompt in 2014, joining just three other schools at the time to ask about gender and sexual orientation — Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), University of Iowa and Elmhurst College. In a statement, then Dean of Undergraduate Admissions Christoph Guttentag said, “We wanted to make it clear to the applicant and everyone involved in the application process that diversity is really broadly defined and not just in terms of a box you can check, not just in demographic characteristics.” 

Yet, now that the essay prompt is gone, the University has made no move to supplement its absence. It feels like Duke’s earlier efforts were just another box to check.

Historically, Duke’s relationship with its own LGBTQ+ community has been strained at best and violent at worst. In the 1960s, 64 men were arrested on Duke grounds for the crime of “homosexuality.” As recently as 2015, then freshman Jack Donahue had the phrase “death to all f*** @jack” written across the wall of his dorm. The great irony of these grievances is just how entrenched they are with the University itself — all 64 men were arrested by the Duke University Police Department. The message left on Donahue’s wall was written by a fellow student. As Donahue said himself in his column in The Chronicle after the incident, “Duke has never been the paradigm of tolerance.”

I don’t believe it is a coincidence that the prompt on gender and sexual orientation was added just a year before Donahue’s incident. In combination with the national tension that came with the legalization of gay marriage that same summer, there’s an argument to be made that 2015 was just an abnormally turbulent bump on the path to progress. Even so, the lack of administrative action taken to both protect Donahue and prevent future students after the hate crime, spoke much louder than the statement they released afterwards.

In truth, the loss of Duke’s 250-word “queer” essay may be felt by some, but will otherwise go largely unrecognized by most of Duke’s applicants. It’s a simple numbers game — one that does not end in favor of LGBTQ+ students.

However, the principle of removing options for self-expression deeply worries me. In shortening the application length itself (now two essays instead of three), how will Duke ensure that its future generations are truly representative of the intellectual curiosity and diversity that the University prides itself on?

While the University could simply add the prompt back onto its list of essay questions, I echo the same concerns that Duke students in 2015 expressed about the release of a specifically “queer” essay prompt — creating the image that LGBTQ+ students deserve special recognition from other marginalized groups purely upon the basis of their sexual and gender orientation. Will LGBTQ+ students at Duke ever be able to find a middle ground between being a trophied token of inclusivity and being hate-crimed?

Even while writing this article, a question gnawed at my head. Shouldn’t I be grateful that it was ever there at all? That I, a member of the Class of 2029, made it through the gates before they got slammed in my face?

In considering this, I realized the basis for my dissatisfaction with Duke’s handling of this essay prompt: in a vacuum, the choice to add an “LGBTQ-friendly” essay is commendable. And after the Common App — the organization that provides applications for a large number of US universities ̦— rejected the notion of an LGBTQ+ essay in 2011, Duke’s choice was especially lauded. But when considering the University’s past treatment of marginalized identities, especially queer students, it becomes painstakingly clear that the essay decision was merely a band-aid for a wound that never healed and still bleeds. 

Now, as the national conversation again shifts to Obergefell v. Hodges, this time towards talk of its overturning, Duke’s decision to peel off its ten-year-old bandaid is a kick in the gut to students, like myself, who have come to believe that Duke is as safe and tolerant of a place as it advertises itself on the Common App. 

Duke needs to reconsider how it creates a truly diverse community through admissions, and that starts with simply allowing applicants to write more. Given the record-breaking number of applicants to Duke this past admission cycle, I don’t fault the Office for shortening the application. But I tend to question the legitimacy of Duke’s “holistic admissions” when I realize that they only end up reading about 1,200 words from each applicant. For context, the average person speaks about just under 16,000 words a day. While it’s not a clean comparison (quality is, of course, better than quantity), the question should still be raised about just how much an admission officer can understand about a student with just 8% of their daily word allowance.

While constraint and concision often create character, I can’t support concision at the cost of character. A fully open-ended, 250-word essay is one such option, but there are millions of replacement prompts that Duke could choose if it won’t bring back its “queer” essay prompt. In the end, 250 words are just 250 words. It is how students and the university act that ultimately determines if their words are truly worth their weight.

Aaron Dai is a Trinity first-year. His column typically runs on alternate Fridays.

title: Trick or Treat
author: Robert Wallace
article_text:
Somewhere near the end of “The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde” by Robert Louis Stevenson, Henry Jekyll awakens from slumber and finds himself turned into Mr. Hyde. But before he is fully aware of his transformation, he notices his hand “… in the yellow light of a mid-London morning, lying half shut on the bedclothes, was lean, corded, knuckly, of a dusky pallor and thickly shaded with a smart growth of hair.” Later, an almost continual ingestion of his potion was needed to restore himself from Hyde to Jekyll. “At all hours of the day and night, I would be taken with the premonitory shudder; above all, if I slept, or even dozed for a moment in my chair, it was always as Hyde I was awakened.”

At this point, Henry Jekyll’s nature has irreversibly changed: Dr. Henry Jekyll — his better self — has turned into Mr. Hyde, his worst.

Literature is replete with narratives about the dual personality of human existence — the good and bad sides of ourselves. "The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde" is the finest example of extolling this duality by suggesting that some may have a preference for the bad side. Jekyll pursued his negative side with vigor, even reveled in it, preferring the anonymity of his existence. After all, he could do whatever he wanted. He could get away with anything.

Most of us, from time to time, might wish to be someone other than ourselves. After all, the life we have chosen is often the one we continue living until the end. Yet, we all know that we harbor within ourselves a multiplicity of persons. We have our school or work selves, our family selves, our interpersonal selves and so many other selves. One could argue that these selves aren’t really differences in the truest sense, but examples of learned behavior, psychological adaptations necessary to survive a modern, ever-changing world.

Philosophy has argued for centuries whether there is an inner, authentic self, the “real” us. Sartre, for example, claimed “the appearance does not hide the essence, it reveals it; it is the essence.” As with most things, our being lies somewhere in the middle. We can only live inside our own minds, yet even knowing ourselves requires profound honesty.

As Halloween approaches, kids of all ages will dress up as scary figures, hiding behind plastic masks or painted masks that disguise their natural appearance. When one becomes unrecognizable, are we not in fact incognito? In the last section of the novel, Henry Jekyll recounts his confession: “Men have before hired bravos to transact their crimes. I was the first that could plod in the public eye with a load of genial respectability, and in a moment, like a schoolboy, strip off these lendings, and spring headlong into the seal of liberty. But for me, in my impenetrable mantle, the safety was complete. Think of it — I did not even exist!”

Back in the 70s, when I used to Trick or Treat in the quiet blocks of a small Michigan town, Halloween night mostly brought out homemade costumes, many of unsettling figures that were bathed in fake blood.

There was a boy who actually walked around with a real hatchet. He was dressed in clothes that were too big for him, and his face had badges of fake scars. I remember walking up to a house; he was right behind me. He was taller than me, and I didn’t recognize him—there was something unusual about his face that made his features look distorted.

Someone knocked on the door, and we sang in unison “Trick or Treat.” We offered our large grocery bags and watched the assortment of candy fall in our half-filled sacks.

“Who are you supposed to be? the woman asked, looking at the boy with the hatchet.

“A serial killer,” the boy said.

“Oh,” the woman said, unfazed by the hatchet. 

Of course, no one would allow anyone to go out on Halloween night now with a hatchet in their hand. Yet, with the recent shooting at a bar in South Carolina, where four people were killed, we see that people do walk around with guns, and they do kill people in mass. Some don’t even hide their face.

It seems, in fact, that they want to be seen. It seems we talk about how horrible it is, yet we do nothing about it. It is as if we have accepted not only tragedy, but the circumstances under which they occur, and, although I choose to believe in the goodness of people, sometimes Hyde’s adage in his letter of confession does ring sadly true, “I hazard a guess that man will ultimately be known for a mere polity of multifarious, incongruous and independent denizens.” 

Robert Wallace is a first-year graduate student of liberal studies. His column, 'Telling Stories', typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: Celebrate … Everything, even grief
author: Lauren Haigler Henderson
article_text:
Today, Oct. 23, marks fifteen years since the death of my best friend, Drew Everson, while I was a senior at Duke University. Ten years ago, Drew's roommate, Pat Rutter, urged you to celebrate ... while you still can. Five years ago, Pat and I encouraged you to celebrate ... friendships. And today, I invite you to celebrate … everything, even grief.

My name is Lauren Haigler Henderson. Over the past fifteen years, I have learned to celebrate everything, including my grief after Drew's untimely death.

Why should I celebrate grief? The simple answer is that for me, embracing my grief has helped me become the woman I am today. Grief can tear your world apart, but you can also use grief to rebuild it. 

As open conversations about grief have finally become more accepted, I have come to see my own grief as a kind of superpower. I know I can overcome difficult times and terrible things. I have transformed one of the hardest experiences of my life into a source of strength. Grief became the catalyst that allowed me to face my mental health challenges for the first time with courage and conviction.

I struggled with anxiety and depression for years before Drew’s death, but I only managed it just enough to get by. The overwhelming grief I experienced after he died made just getting by unfeasible. It caused me to finally earnestly seek the treatment and support I had avoided for so long. Grief has also allowed me to support friends and family experiencing grief. 

And it has given me the honor of keeping Drew's memory alive for all these years.

From the absolute devastation of losing my best friend at 21, I learned to enjoy life. I learned to live it to its fullest, laugh more and love harder — like Drew did. We, somewhat irreverently, started saying "Live, Laugh, Love ForEverson," after Drew died, but I have truly taken that motto to heart. 

I celebrate whatever it is I want to celebrate. I try not to take myself too seriously. I prioritize time with the people I love. I tell my friends and family how much I love them. I profess what they mean to me more often. I find some hope in the many sorrows of our lives. It is because of my grief that I can do all of these things

Can I always use my grief as a celebrated superpower? Absolutely not. There have been many dark, hopeless moments and plenty of tears. Even as I move forward, there are many memories, what-ifs and thoughts that I still grapple with — how Drew died on his way to see me, how I didn’t get to tell him how much he meant to me or how we were supposed to get old together. I can never fully accept that everything happens for a reason. 

A friend once told me, "Grief is the biggest catch-22 there is in life. For me, it's having every happy moment punctuated by the whisper of a thought, '... but I wish you were here.'" In every milestone that he hasn't been there for, my grief is still ever-present.

Shortly after Drew died, another friend advised me that there would come a day when I woke up and Drew would not be the first thing I thought about and I would be so mad at myself. She gently explained to me, “That’s okay.” When that day came, I was mad at myself, but I also knew it was perfectly okay that Drew is not always top of mind. 

I take comfort in knowing that while life moves on without Drew, he is still with me. Always. To quote the legendary Miss Britney Spears, "I'll be here for you now and forever ... When you need someone, you just turn around and I will be there." That was Drew for me in our life together and he has remained that way even in his death. 

And every so often, he is still with me in my dreams. His initials and a quote of his, “so join me every day in celebrating,” are tattooed on my ankle. I have become “Viking Girl” in Cameron Indoor Stadium to honor him as Viking Guy (and shame UNC fans who make fun of me). I pack one of his shirts in my suitcase for every trip I have taken since he died. A LiveForEverson bracelet was sewn into the back of my wedding dress. I talk about him as often as I possibly can.

If you know me, you have heard of the one and only Drew Everson. Every year, I join with friends on the anniversary of his death — a day we have come to call Drew Day — to celebrate a life worth celebrating and to reframe our grief. We honor him by doing the things he would have loved — going to an Usher concert, sharing queso and scotch and reminiscing about the good times we shared, like the 2010 National Championship — even as we continue to grieve.

There is a saying that we all die twice — once when our bodies give out and again when our stories are no longer told. I will continue to share Drew's story until my body gives out. 

But how can his story apply to your lives as Duke students who have never heard of him — or me — until now? I hope you can embrace your grief and celebrate it wherever and whenever you can. I cannot tell you the right or wrong way to grieve. What I can tell you is that while you will never be over your grief, you can move through it. It takes effort, but it is worth it. 

Everyone must find their own path through grief, but here are a few suggestions. Remember that grief can come from many different experiences, not just the death of someone you love. Treat grief like a lifelong relationship — learn to work with it, not against it. Do not minimize your grief — ride the waves of emotions as they come. Talk about your grief and call it by its name — you have probably noticed that I have used the word "grief" many times, intentionally avoiding a synonym. And most importantly, ask for help — you don't have to do this alone. 

Life is full of loss, struggle and grief. However, my hope, today and every day, is that your life is full of celebration. As I found fifteen years ago, life is short and you can't take it for granted. In 2009, Drew implored Duke students to enjoy life while you still can and that "whatever you do, don't ever, ever take life too seriously." 

In words that are still true to this day, he also reminded us that: "What it all boils down to is finding ways to enjoy each and every day ... It's fun to love life. So join me every day in celebrating whatever it is you want to celebrate." On this Drew Day, I celebrate the life of Andrew Ryan Everson, the profoundly positive impact he had on me, the friendships forged and strengthened in his memory and the grief that has become my lasting superpower. 

[P.S. 27 years ago today, the aforementioned legendary Miss Spears changed the music industry with the release of "... Baby One More Time." Today is also the first day of my Scorpio season, National Horror Movie Day, Mole Day, TV Talk Show Host Day and iPod Day. So go blast “Baby One More Time”, watch Jennifer's Body with your fave Scorpio and a chemist; and then listen to Kelly Clarkson on an iPod (even if you didn't get one from Duke like the Class of 2008).]

Lauren Haigler Henderson, Trinity ’11, is a grants manager for a social justice nonprofit.

title: BookTok: A literary marketing echo chamber
author: Sarah Pusser
article_text:
Who does not love fall at Duke? Leaves spilling onto the sidewalks in front of the Chapel, warm drinks from Bella Union, cooling winds in the Sarah P. Gardens; it feels like second nature to grab a blanket, a sweater and a good book to curl up with. Wanting a new story that can capture that same all-consuming awe of their favorite reads, students pull out their phones and type, “Books to read if you love ____.”

As if by magic, dozens, if not hundreds, of videos, lists and articles await, trying to sell them their next favorite book. How perfect?! Right? Well, not quite … 

Last semester, while sitting in a creative writing class, one of my classmates brought up her experience with what felt like reading a “knock off.” After having fallen in love with Donna Tartt’s “The Secret History”, she was looking for more books that could capture the same “dark academia” ambiance that Donna Tartt crafts so well. Soon after, she happened upon a recommendation for M. L. Rio’s “If We Were Villains” and bought the book, only to find that the two were practically identical.

“The Secret History” is a phenomenal read. Following the lives of six college students studying Greek at a small elite university and their grappling with the death of one of their friends. Having enjoyed the book and hearing about my classmate’s story, I decided to look into “If We Were Villains”, to see how truly similar the two novels were. Just reading the synopsis on the back of the book seemed to be proof enough — another group of students at an elite conservatory, enduring rivalry, performance and a fatal ending.

M. L. Rio’s book was a huge success, with many readers saying they preferred “IfWe Were Villains” over “The Secret History”, due to its more accessible writing. But what does this mean for the future of reading (and writing)? A prioritization of marketability over originality, quality and merit.

Now, this is not to say that this is a new idea. Comparison titles — or “comp titles” — have frequently been, and still are, used to pitch books to publishing houses, as a way to help agents, publishers and editors understand the author’s intended genre and audience. 

What’s troubling is now that we see comp titles spilling over into social media as a reader-facing marketing strategy, where millions of book lovers go to make their decisions on what to read next. Authors now face pressure to conform their narrative voices, themes and even story lines to mimic successful novels. Just like how M. L. Rio’s “If We Were Villains” became successful in part due to its recommendation from Donna Tartt’s “The Secret History”, other authors may see this path to success and begin tailoring their work to fit within this narrow marketing world.

As for the specific downsides to this cycle of marketing, for one, is that it inhibits the literary merit of newer books. The goal of these books is to follow trends, meaning that authors are writing on a tight timeline, often leading to lower-quality and less nuanced novels. By practically feeding ready-readers books that are easier to comprehend, challenging syntax, vocabulary and storylines that improve consumers’ cognitive development — the gifts of many books — are lost.

Another issue with the emphasis on marketability is the limited market this presents to emerging authors. According to Circana Bookscan, a point-of-sale tracking service that monitors U.S. print book sales, approximately 59 million print book sales were attributed to BookTok in 2025, having increased from 46 million copies in 2023. This means that BookTok accounted for roughly 8% of all print book sales in the U.S. in 2024. Through this enormous impact, BookTok’s influence pressures newer authors to contort their own narratives to those that they know will sell.


Lastly, readers are now being marketed books that do not expand their literary diversity.

Not only does this further reinforce the echo chamber of consumers buying only books with which they are familiar, but it also limits the discovery of other authors and genres that readers may otherwise have found enriching and novel. The beauty of buying a new book shouldn’t be knowing how the story will unfold; it should be that we don’t know. It should be the lure of discovering something new. 

Listening to a new narrative voice. Approaching a perspective you never knew you had missed. Laughing, crying, thinking, dreaming, because of something you could never expect.

Given the consequences of constantly buying books that reinforce the algorithmic echo chamber, it feels crucial to "do our part" and discover books differently — both for the future of literary culture and for the diversification of our own reading lives.

So, in order to find yourself a proper book that is refreshing, engaging and "new new new", here are some ways you can go about acquiring an enriching read just in time for this fall’s cozy season:
