title: When Duke chose courage — and must again
author: Tate Arges
article_text:
On a crisp fall day, the Board of Trustees of a small Southern college gathers for an emergency meeting. Their task is an unpleasant one: to decide the fate of a young professor whose comments in the media had ignited a firestorm of controversy.

He had made remarks about a prominent public figure that many found to be offensive. Politicians and community leaders demanded that the college terminate his employment. Some donors threatened to pull their support. Local media outlets began to attack the college. The future of the school itself seemed to be at a crossroads.

The professor, although he stood by what he said, regretted the trouble his words had caused for his school. He told the Board that if they requested his resignation, he would comply. The meeting stretched late into the night, as the trustees debated whether or not to make the request.

The year was 1903.

The professor was John Spencer Bassett.

And the school was Trinity College — the institution that would one day become Duke University.

Bassett’s offense was writing about race, an explosive topic in the Jim Crow South. In an essay for The South Atlantic Quarterly, he praised the Black educator and civil rights leader Booker T. Washington as “all in all the greatest man, save General Lee, born in the South in one hundred years.”

That single line was enough to spark outrage. Politicians in Raleigh called for his immediate dismissal. Jospehus Daniels, editor of The News & Observer, denounced Bassett and Trinity as threats to the “Southern way of life.” Parents were urged to withdraw their children, while prospective students were warned to stay away.

So, on that chilly night, Trinity’s trustees seemingly faced an impossible choice: protect their professor — or protect their school.

At 3 a.m. the next morning, they made their decision.

They chose courage.

The Board refused to request Bassett’s resignation and voted to keep him. In doing so, they affirmed that the pursuit of truth was more important than public approval or political safety. What became known as “The Bassett Affair” is now remembered as one of the finest moments in Duke’s history.

I’ve been thinking about that chapter in our school’s story a lot this year — and what it means for Duke now.

Once again, Duke faces pressure from powerful forces demanding silence or compliance.

The Trump administration has not been covert in its attacks on higher education. Its newly proposed “Compact for Academic Excellence” offers universities an unsavory deal: federal funding in exchange for ideological conformity. The Compact would bar institutions from teaching “objectionable political topics”, restrict diversity and inclusion programs, and even cap international student enrollment. Schools that refuse to sign risk losing access to federal research funds. Schools that agree are promised preferential treatment when it comes to receiving those funds.

So far, Duke University leadership has not announced whether or not it intends to sign this compact. And it’s true — our University has already suffered deeply under this administration’s policies. Federal investigations into the University have been initiated. In anticipation of future cuts to our school’s funding, we have had to say goodbye to beloved faculty and staff whose positions are no longer sustainable.

These losses are real. They are painful. And they are human.

But in 1903, Trinity’s leaders also faced threats from powerful forces. They, too, were warned that courage and academic freedom would cost them dearly. Yet they stood firm. They refused to sacrifice truth for comfort, or integrity for security.

It would be a disservice to our community, a disservice to those we’ve had to painfully part ways with, and a disservice to our University’s legacy for Duke to sign this compact.

While defending the principle of academic freedom, then Trinity President John C. Kilgo wrote that the ideal was so essential to a university’s DNA that “no dread of unpopularity, no fear of small attendance, no criticisms and even hatred can divert it” from upholding it.

Kilgo was not alone in his conviction. Writing to trustee Benjamin Duke in 1903, Walter Hines Page — a Trinity alumnus and patron, journalist and future US ambassador — urged the Board to see the controversy surrounding Professor Bassett not as a crisis, but as a defining opportunity for the school. He called it “a great chance to speak out for freedom and [to] help Trinity so much.” The backlash, he said, was nothing more than “a blind howl by those who think they can rule North Carolina.”

Page then asked a question that still echoes today:

“What if the fools criticize it? What if even some good men criticize it? What if half the boys are withdrawn? Nothing better could happen. What is a great college for? Isn’t its main purpose to be a place for absolute freedom of thought and speech? For every boy that may be withdrawn, the college will get a dozen a few years hence, when men come to their senses. For every man who takes offense, a hundred better men will be pleased and will rally to you.”

Page understood what some of Trinity’s own trustees could not — that courage rewards you in ways that fear never can. And his words eventually proved to be prophetic.

Trinity’s leaders were warned that refusing to fire Bassett would destroy the college. Instead, the opposite happened. Enrollment grew. Trinity gained national recognition with many praising the small Southern school’s integrity. And when President Theodore Roosevelt visited the campus two years later, he lauded the Board’s decision saying:

“You stand for academic freedom, for the right of private judgment, for a duty more incumbent upon the scholar than upon any other man, to tell the truth as he sees it, to claim for himself and to give to others the largest liberty in seeking after the truth.”

The board’s courageous choice transformed a small Southern college into an institution worthy of national respect. It was a decision that became a cornerstone in Duke becoming the elite university that it is today. It was not only morally right — it was strategically wise. And the same will be true today.

When President Vincent Price recently told an audience that Duke’s current strategy was to “lay low” to avoid drawing further ire from the Trump administration, it may have sounded prudent. It may have sounded “safe”. But what the brightest students and faculty around the world are looking for in the institutions they hope to attend and work for is not silence or safety. They are looking for leadership. They are looking for courage.

They are looking for universities that defend the freedom of inquiry even when it is inconvenient, that stand firm against the abuse from powerful forces, that will say with courage and clarity that “our values are not for sale.”

Yes, this kind of defiance will invite retribution. The Trump administration will undoubtedly seek to inflict as much financial pain as it can upon schools that resist its agenda. And that will lead to more losses in the short term. But to paraphrase Page’s wisdom, for every donor that withdraws, a hundred better supporters will come to our aid. For every unjust attack we endure, a generation of scholars will be inspired — and they will come to Duke.

The same principle that proved to be true in 1903 will also hold true in 2025 and beyond: courage attracts excellence. Fear and silence drive it away.

If Duke stands strong while others sign away their autonomy for financial convenience, it will become a beacon for the most gifted students, the most visionary researchers, and the most brilliant faculty. They will come here not because Duke is safe, but because Duke is free. They will come because they will know that this university will not forsake or silence them when the political winds turn cold.

Now is the time to seize that opportunity. 

Now is the time to remember who we are.

We are Duke.

In 1903, Trinity College chose courage.

In 2025, so must Duke.

Tate Arges is a second-year graduate student at Duke Divinity School.

title: Respect versus renovations: the Price is wrong
author: Wendy House
article_text:
If there’s one thing every Duke student loves to hate — other than a Tar Heel — it has to be renovations. They are the bane of our existence and the object of almost no desires. I, along with many peers in the Class of 2028, will tell you that renovations made my time on East Campus truly kafkaesque. I cannot articulate, in language appropriate for publication, the exponential irritation of having to walk into a chain-link hamster track just to exit my dormitory. It feels like not a day goes by that our gothic paradise isn’t marred by gaudy orange machines. 

What I think makes Duke’s construction addiction especially absurd is that it’s so very … frivolous. Much or most of it is superficial. Repaving decorative roadways, “modernizing” our impeccable vintage buildings and expanding libraries which seem to have never suffered from overcrowding, seem like inadequate reasons to inconvenience hundreds of people every day for years at a time.

It’s minor irritations such as these that really get my gears turning. If Duke pours hundreds of millions of dollars into purely superficial upgrades — low-priority stuff— surely there’s nothing more important being neglected in the budget. If we’re burning cash on aesthetics, it should be safe to assume that issues of real substance are already provided for; for pointed instance, employees and students.

It should be, but it isn’t. In fact, Duke has not taken care of nurses, service workers, and graduate students since the moment wages began failing to meet the rising cost of living in Durham around the mid-2010s. 

Other Chronicle authors have covered the Duke-Durham relationship with incisive clarity. Depending on who you ask, it is one of love, of hate, of parasitism or of beneficence. Duke maintains it gives back through taxes and community programs, while members of said community respond that Duke dodges taxes while exploiting Durhamites for insufficiently compensated labor. A coalition of said community members, Duke workers and several Durham and NC labor unions, Durham Rising, has recently stepped up as a fiery champion for a $25/hr minimum wage and respect for workers’ right to organize. 

Sunrise Duke, a student organization dedicated to advocacy for migrant and labor justice, has collaborated with Durham Rising toward the achievement of these goals. I interviewed their president, Artivista Karlin, to get down to brass tacks on the mission.

She began by addressing the strain of federal financial attacks on higher education: “Of course, it’s horrific that Duke is facing federal funding cuts … However, what we’re seeing is that instead of prioritizing Duke workers and the people who make Duke function, the University’s administration and President Price are… shifting the burden of those federal funding cuts to Durham workers.”

She emphasized that the voluntary separation incentive program (VSIP) and layoffs have had deleterious effects on workplace standards. “Now service workers have to work 3 AM shifts … they have to work unbelievable hours and do a lot more work for … a wage that doesn’t provide affordability to live in the city of Durham.” Compensation was already inadequate prior to the reduction in workforce, and now service workers are forced to take up the mantles of their fired colleagues. 

She concluded that “Duke University has a responsibility to pay its workers a livable wage, to treat [them] with dignity and respect, and ensure [they] are able to live in the community that they’re a part of.”

As for the facts, Durham Rising appears to be right about the cost of living in Durham. The Living Wage Institute at MIT puts the living wage here at $25.55/hr for a single adult without dependents. The News & Observer gives $26.00. Even compared to the city’s measly estimate of $19.58, Duke’s $18/hr minimum wage still comes up short. Durham has been slowly succumbing to gentrification for the last decade or so — the displacement of historic communities is an active and ongoing process perpetuated by this cost of living inflation. 

As a native Durhamite, I’m more than a little embarrassed to say that I was largely unaware of the gravity of the situation prior to this semester. “Gentrification” to me meant a Starbucks popping up on Ninth Street; it was a vague feeling of cultural sapping, devoid of clear shape. Even now, I certainly won’t go grandstanding as if I can speak for the city.

All I know is this: Durham used to be pretty cheap. It’s not anymore. I think my neighbors deserve to stay here. If Duke workers are mustering the bravery to come forward and argue for fairer treatment, I think we ought to believe they’re being treated unfairly. I think we ought to show some solidarity to the people who feed us, who keep our residential spaces clean, who heal us and who maintain our status as a world-class research hub. I think working people ought to be paid such that they can live in the city where they work. Is that so radical to say?

According to the Duke administration, yes! Despite over 10,000 signatures from community members and employees, there had been nothing but radio silence from them to address the demands for an increased minimum wage and the right to form unions — until Thursday. 

About a month after Durham Rising’s rally calling on the administration to recognize the 'true' founders of Duke on Founders’ Day, the Office of Community Affairs got off its behinds to hold an Academic Council meeting. They made some fairly big moves, which I won’t disparage: the creation of an online database tracking Duke’s “local collaborations, volunteer opportunities and grantmaking” as well as a Center for Community-Engaged Scholarship which hopes to promote the view of Durham as a partner, rather than a needy vampire to Duke’s glorious wealth. These seem like pretty good ideas. There’s only one problem — the council managed to completely dodge every one of Durham Rising’s demands. 

There was no acknowledgement of Duke’s prohibition of unionization. There was no acknowledgement of payments in lieu of taxes (PILOT), which Duke does not make despite enjoying $50 million in property tax exemptions, and which many peer institutions (such as Harvard and Cornell) give to their cities. President Price actually managed to refer to the $25/hr minimum wage as a “[call] to just hand them the money.”

I can’t say I’m completely surprised. I’m sure to someone whose salary is in the sextuple digits, seven extra dollars an hour is just money. To the rest of us, though, it’s a living. It’s the difference between living in your home, where you grew up, where your parents and grandparents lived and loved and fought for their rights, and being ousted.

It is a slap in the face to all Duke employees, union-affiliated or not, to refuse to even recognize Durham Rising’s advocacy as a motivator for these actions. I cannot fathom a clearer way to articulate that service workers are subhuman to the Duke administration. “Here, you filthy animals, take this conciliation prize and stop yammering.” It is unreasonable. It is unbecoming of an institution determined to tout itself as “honest, credible and reliable in [its] words, behaviors and actions.” I frankly don’t think we’ve seen the likes of this blatant disregard for labor rights since the Gilded Age. 

I’m not an accountant nor an Econ major, but it doesn’t take one to run the math. If President Price can blow millions on beautifying an already beautiful campus, he can afford to pay his workers. At the bare minimum, he can spare some overpriced time to look Durham Rising in the eye and explain his decisions. Or perhaps I should be less scathing; maybe Price is just allergic to the proletariat. 

Wendy House is a Trinity sophomore. Her column typically runs on alternate Wednesdays.

title: Rethinking mandatory service — What a new era of youth service could look like
author: Stella Kaye
article_text:
In an active warzone, no one asks who you voted for, the chromosomal makeup of who you love or if you believe in God or not. That’s how Secretary Buttigieg described his time in the military during a recent visit to Duke. Speaking to a crowd of Gen Z students — some eager, others disheartened — the former Transportation Secretary discussed how his time in the armed forces instilled the merits of empathy and care in ways he had never seen before. Buttigieg even rolled out a plan in 2019 to expand national service programs, aiming to create over one million service jobs by 2026. “You shouldn’t have to go to war in order to have that kind of experience,” said Butiggeg in an interview with Politico. 

Carrying out acts of service has long given humans a sense of pride and gratification, knowing they are doing good for their community. In fact, volunteer and service work has been proven to be extremely beneficial to one’s mind and body, with results such as increased self confidence and happiness, combined with lower levels of depression. For college aged youth, combatting high stress levels with dedicated service time could prove extraordinarily useful for long term stamina and mental health. 

Buttigieg’s plan aimed to employ around four million high school graduates in service jobs each year. As ambitious as that sounds, I believe four million is not enough. If we want Gen-Z to bridge the longstanding divides and disconnections felt in America, we need to think bigger. It’s time to bring back community service for every young person. Not simply picking up trash on the first Saturday of each month — although I’m not trying to discount efforts for cleaner neighborhoods — but instead, consistent and diligent service, aimed to close the ideological gaps that are tearing our country apart. 

So, let’s get practical. If we agree that trash pick-ups once a month aren’t enough, and that real service must be immersive and transformative, what should the structure look like? I propose a model centered on higher education and early adulthood, one that balances service with personal growth, while ensuring every young person contributes. 

Those who intend to enroll at higher education institutions (i.e. university, trade and technical school, etc.) should be required by the college or university to serve two service periods in order to complete their degree. The first placement would be six months sometime in the first two and a half years, followed by several semesters in class. University curriculum should remain closely aligned to the current requirements and systems, focused on a liberal arts education for students in the arts and sciences, and an alternative curriculum for those in engineering, business or other specialized programs. Later on in their academic career, students would take part in a second placement; another six months doing more specified service based on their educational work. These placements could be in public service, nonprofit work, environmental projects, disaster relief, education support or local government. For those not choosing to enroll in higher education, they would participate in a more flexible, mandatory twelve-month service before the age of twenty-five. Additionally, NCAA athletes and those in research-intensive programs or other special circumstances, could complete a year of service post-graduation instead. 

The goal of these service requirements isn’t just participation — it’s transformation. The true success of such a model depends on institutions that already value character development and civic engagement, such as Duke University. Duke has a longstanding commitment to critical thinking, fulfilling civic missions, interdisciplinary collaboration and character formation. Mandatory service would allow for the integration of these lessons across a variety of fields specific to Duke’s commitments. 

Let’s start off with how we could best place emphasis on critical thinking in this program. Duke, and most major universities, aim to produce problem-solvers. Service placements would give students real contexts for applying theories. From tutoring young students in reading and math, college aged individuals would be able to take what they learn in labs and lectures and guide the next generation of leaders. While cleaning rivers, lakes and hiking trails, students could apply chemistry and life science concepts, working to preserve the natural world and land in the United States. 

Once we become world class thinkers, we need a cause to put these new ideas towards. Many universities already promote civic engagement, ethics and global citizenship. Through working in criminal justice reform efforts or reentry programs, social science, law and sociology, students could take a more hands-on role in the visions of the world they dream up in papers. 

Historically, service has exposed students to different sectors, encouraging cross-disciplinary thinking. For students studying in Pratt (or other engineering schools), an initial placement in sustainable engineering or infrastructure repair could connect theory to community impact. Working alongside public policy students or environmental scientists, engineering majors would see firsthand how technical design intersects with social and environmental needs. Similarly, humanities or social science students might join projects that rely on data analysis or technology, bridging the gap between qualitative insight and quantitative skill.

Finally, service would cultivate resilience, adaptability and a sense of purpose —values universities often claim to foster but rarely nurture. Through immersive service experiences, young adults would learn to navigate discomfort, build empathy and lead with humility. These lessons extend beyond a classroom transcript; they become the foundation for thoughtful citizenship and lifelong civic engagement.

Universities like Duke often praise the value of service, yet treat it as an extracurricular rather than a core part of education. That gap reveals a deeper problem, where commitments to service seem symbolic, rather than systemic. If every young person in America had the chance to learn through service, the effects would extend far beyond college gates. In a nation struggling with division, loneliness and distrust, service offers something rare — a shared purpose. It’s not just about what students gain, but what we all stand to rebuild together. 

Stella Kaye is a Trinity first-year.

title: The Chronicle is soliciting submissions for "rewritten" Duke supplements
author: Shambhavi Sinha
article_text:
In celebration of the variety of experiences and people that belong at Duke, we are planning to run a series of rewritten Duke supplemental essays, soliciting responses from current students and alumni. 

The Duke supplemental essay has traditionally been required for all prospective undergraduate applicants and is a critical part of the admissions process. But words and actions diverge. How has your Duke journey deviated from your perception? Have you been rejected from the club you wrote about? 

Have you found yourself in a completely different place than you imagined? Now that you have attended, or are attending Duke, would you go back and change your essay? Now is your chance to!

We want to hear this and more from your submission — how Duke has been different, and if you were to write this again, what you would write about? We want to hear the positives, the negatives and everything in between. We’re looking for candid and thoughtful reflections on your time at Duke. 

If you are interested, please respond to the prompt below in 250 words and send it to opinion@dukechronicle.com:

“What is your impression of Duke as a university and community, and why do you believe it is a good match for your goals, values and interests?”

Shambhavi Sinha is a Trinity junior and opinion editor of The Chronicle's 121st volume.

title: Bill Belichick to become Duke assistant coach after dropping UNC
author: Monday Monday
article_text:
Editor's note: The piece below is satire.

In an unexpected but completely understandable turn of events this morning, head football coach for the North Carolina Tar Heels Bill Belichick has announced his resignation from UNC, saying at a press conference, “I just really miss winning.” In explaining his future plans, he said “I’m excited to announce that I’ll be taking on the role of assistant football coach at Duke, a job I’ve wanted for a long time.”

It’s not hard to understand why Belichick is making the switch, with his 10-month stint at UNC seeing some of the worst games of his own career and a terrible season so far. Reflecting, Belichick said, “I think the team and I just never hit it off. I’ve never had to explain that, in order to score, you have to get the ball into the end zone, but, at the end of the day, they are UNC students, so I can’t say I’m surprised.” On his future here at Duke, he told The Chronicle, “It’s a great opportunity; why try to build a winning program over there when they already have one here?”

News of the switch is already circulating among Duke staff. “Belichick said he’s assistant head coach?” Manny Diaz, Duke football head coach, told us, “No, no, no, I told him he could be the assistant to the head coach. I’m not trying to throw the season, you know?” During this interview, Belichick was seen trying to move into assistant head coach Gabe Infante’s office. 

Nina King, vice president and director of athletics, told The Chronicle, “To be honest, he’s mostly here as charity. I mean, clearly, we’re doing fine without him, but having to pretend that you think UNC is a winning team for almost a year is something no one should have to go through. Bill still thinks the UNC-Clemson game was ‘kind of close’.” 

While many are concerned about where Tarheel football can go from here, Lee Roberts, chancellor of UNC, assured The Chronicle that they’ve dealt with complete and total failure before. “So what if we’re worse than Duke at football. Yes, that’s a minor hiccup, but at least we’re better at basketb— Oh, they’re above us in the preseason poll? Hm. Ok, well, at least our academi— What was that? Oh. Well, at least our Confederate statues were up for longer — another day, another win for UNC.”

What Belichick’s future here at Duke will entail is still up in the air, but he’s assured us that he sees a long and prosperous future as a Blue Devil. “What really attracts me to this program is the players here at Duke. I mean, to meet these 19-year-old kids and build a relationship with them into their early 20s? There’s no better feeling in the world.”

title: Fix me
author: Luke A. Powery
article_text:
Okay, enough is enough. It is time to check yourself before you wreck yourself. It is time to recall the words of the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.: “There is some good in the worst of us and some evil in the best of us.”

That may be a hard pill to swallow, but the truth can be hard to accept, even though ultimately it will set us free.

These days, those words of Dr. King may be difficult to digest with all of the showboating, name-calling, fight-picking, hating and so forth happening in this country right now. And these actions often occur toward “those people,” that is, people who aren’t like us in thought, behavior or beliefs. But enough is enough. 

When was the last time you looked at yourself in the mirror? When was the last time you said aloud to God or a therapist, “Fix me.” How about that for a change? A change may come when you change, not when someone else changes!

Jesus was right — “Why do you look at the speck of sawdust in your neighbor’s eye, but do not notice the log in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3). We often see the problems created by others or when something doesn’t seem right with other people or different groups. But can we see when we are wrong in our thinking or acting? Are we humble enough to accept that we may need adjusting as well?

I am not saying to let injustice roll down like water over us and to be silent in the face of horror, but what I am saying is to check yourself before you try to check someone else. Evaluate your life and behavior. Instead of judging another, judge yourself. Focus on you with a microscope. 

Get to the point of saying, “I need to fix me. Work on me. Better me.” What can I do to help myself become a better person — more loving, more joyful, more peaceable, more faithful, more gentle and more self-controlled? In a time of ongoing inhumanity, how can I become more human? What can I do to fix me, to be more just, merciful and humble?

In a fairly recent New York Times op-ed, David French wrote a piece called “There are Monsters in Your Midst, Too.” We don’t normally think of our monsters. Instead, we point at the monsters we see among others. But if we slow down and “see one’s self pass by,” as Howard Thurman once wrote, we might see ourselves honestly and recognize we need to work on ourselves too.

Let’s shift our gaze away from always looking at other people and what we think they’re doing wrong and take some time to study ourselves in order to better ourselves. And maybe, just maybe, through our change, we might become the change we desire in the world—even the change we’ve been waiting for.

The Rev. Dr. Luke A. Powery is Dean of Duke University Chapel. His column runs on alternate Mondays.

title: Duke: Reject Trump’s higher education compact, immediately.
author: Leo Goldberg
article_text:
In June, amidst the Trump administration’s ongoing attempt to hijack American higher education and debates about the extent to which Duke should allow this to happen, I wrote an article in The Chronicle titled “Duke: Forget institutional neutrality and join Harvard’s lawsuit against Trump.” Given the latest development of the Trump administration’s war on higher education, and our University’s demonstrated willingness to be bullied into losing such a war, I think it’s time for round two. 

On Oct. 14th, the Trump administration extended its offer of a “Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education” to all American universities, after initially piloting the proposal to nine of the nation’s “top universities.” The compact pledges to prioritize federal funding to schools that comply with certain ideological and policy demands, and now, our own school is faced with the choice of how to respond.

In the first comments Duke has made, President Price announced he is choosing to “strategically” ignore the compact and follow our University’s typical pathetic playbook of offering wishy-washy words of condemnation while publicly doing nothing. But if our leaders had any spine at all, they would have unequivocally rejected this latest stunt at federal appeasement. Putting the political aspect aside for a moment, from a professional standpoint, the compact should be rejected for its gross inconsistencies, blatant contradictions and embarrassing display of sophomoric idiocy. 

The compact is 10 pages of clumsily thrown-together dictation, comprising 9 pages of actual content followed by a tenth one that is completely blank. There are one-sentence paragraphs, one-paragraph sections, empty threats and bizarre citations. It uses the language of fake eloquence and the appearance of confidence to poorly disguise its incompetence. 

Among the biggest demands is the abolition of identity-based considerations in both the admissions and hiring processes of universities, as well as the capping of international enrollment to 15% of undergraduate student bodies and 5% from any one country. Under this umbrella of “DEI” initiatives, whether national or international, I want to provide a small bit of commentary. 

I never really had a strong opinion either way on the issue, but prior to college, I was vaguely anti-DEI, probably as a result of my deep dislike for the toxicity of identity politics. Since arriving at Duke, my thinking has shifted. 

I cannot quantify how much my growth as an intellectual and human being has been spurred by interacting with the many different types of people here. The diversity of individuals on campus is astounding. The next time you are in a large lecture hall, take a look around at the students you see. In the same class, there may be someone whose grandparents survived the Holocaust, and another whose were beaten in the Civil Rights Movement. You can hear from the perspectives of a Brazilian, an Italian and a Korean in the same classroom. Cultural access to the entire world is available in the people sitting right next to you.

It is truly one of the most remarkable things to live in a country which offers an education like that. Nothing can convince me that that isn’t worth having, and I hope I can say I attend a university that feels the same and would, without hesitation, rebuke the demands of a president who encourages them to get rid of that in exchange for a higher slot on the lottery machine.

What is most concerning, though, is the stipulation that foreign students will only be allowed into American universities given they hold the correct political views. According to the compact, only students who are “supportive of American and Western values” will be welcomed. Apparently, we must “screen out students who demonstrate hostility to the United States, its allies, or its values” in order to “prevent [university] services from being used [for] the financing of terrorist activities.” Ah, yes, silly me. How could I forget that al-Qaeda’s main base of operations is the Duke Chapel?

To translate, what this means is that universities that agree to the compact will now have their admissions patrolled by the thought police. Any views that dissent from Big Brother’s fabrication of “American and Western values” are to be excised. This is, of course, antithetical to American and Western values, which the compact invokes, and is certainly awkward to explain in conjunction with the compact’s second heading, which claims to promote a “Marketplace of Ideas and Civil Discourse” on campus. 

What the compact is really about is forcibly wrenching universities to the political right. We are witnessing an attempted state-run ideological transfusion of higher education for purposes of propaganda. The administration uses the strategy of accusing the political opposition of doing that of which they are guilty to shield their own underhandedness. In this case, the institution is meant to feel liable for political indoctrination it is not committing in order to repent for this fabricated transgression by “revising governance structures as necessary to create such an environment, including but not limited to transforming or abolishing institutional units that purposefully punish, belittle and even spark violence against conservative ideas” (The stylistic and grammatical blunders continue). 

This self-pitying statement is meant to shroud yet another attempt by this administration to usher in a fascistic model of government. Not to exhaust the analogy between Nazi Germany and the Trump regime, which has indeed often been mis- and over-used, but the scheming to turn higher education into an impotent mouthpiece of the state, as Trump is doing, was likewise a central strategy of the Third Reich. 

The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum describes in detail the blueprint used by Hitler to turn German universities into propaganda outlets, and below are just a few examples worth mentioning:

“The new Nazi government began an effort to completely reorder public and private life in Germany. The Nazi regime quickly targeted German universities — among the most elite in the world at the time — for restructuring according to Nazi principles.”

“After purging Jewish and ‘politically undesirable’ faculty, the regime then targeted the student body with the ‘Law Against Overcrowding in Schools and Universities.’ As German authorities continued to "Aryanize" German universities, Jews increasingly lost the opportunity to teach or study. Many non-Jewish Germans sought to benefit from their persecution.

“Political concerns increasingly influenced the way professors and students worked and studied. The practice of denunciation illustrates the danger posed to both students and faculty if they failed to follow new ideological norms. Those willing to voice support for the new regime — whether out of enthusiasm or practicality — often received promotions or other rewards. Meanwhile, many others quietly accepted the new policies and passively benefited from the persecution of their Jewish peers.”

“Professors' academic careers became vulnerable to the whims and wishes of the Nazi state. While only a small minority of professors had been Nazi Party members before 1933, several prominent professors quickly voiced their support for the Third Reich. In the new German university, political loyalty was valued over academic ability in the assessment of students and in the selection and promotion of professors.”

The parallels make themselves. Remove the words “German,” “Nazi” and “Jewish” and replace them with “American,” “Trump,” and “leftist/minority,” and you don’t have to change a word. 

The obligation of our University and others now is to do everything in their power to resist the current administration by maintaining a staunch defense of their independence and autonomy. The compact makes clear when it says, “ academic freedom is not absolute.” The Trump administration wants to systematically dismantle one of the most reliable forms of dissent and free thought from the inside out in order to synthesize an ideological makeover of the United States.


Schools like the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Dartmouth and the University of Pennsylvania have already bravely rejected the compact, with others likely to follow. We must do the same. Duke has done an incredibly disappointing job thus far in taking a stand against the greatest threat American universities have ever faced. We tried at first to avoid the administration’s wrath by keeping a low profile. It didn't work. It’s time for the University to go on the offensive for a change and show, for the sake of its principles, that it will no longer be bullied by America’s biggest straw man.

Leo Goldberg is a Trinity sophomore. His pieces typically run on alternate Mondays.

title: Go ahead and take that ‘undeserved’ break
author: Harrison Walley
article_text:
You’ve survived the midterm season. Perhaps the first thing you thought was, “I deserve a break.”

You absolutely do! But the word “deserve” can be dangerous. Deserving something implies that you did something to earn it. You deserve good grades because you worked hard. You deserve to get into an organization on campus because you went to all of their events. But there should never be a feeling of working to earn something as basic and necessary as rest.

As we end our first cycle of midterms, I have found myself reflecting on the immense stress that I’ve faced this semester. I’ve dealt with anxiety from the frequent national news updates reporting crisis after crisis, the pre-professional culture at Duke, my coursework and my own fear of failure. After speaking with friends and clubmates, I realized that these stressors were not unique to me. 

The culture at Duke can be overwhelming, and that may be an unfortunate consequence of being a top-10 school in the country. In writing this article, I am not aiming to fix all the problems that I’ve faced this semester. I am writing because the people whom I care about — and probably most students at Duke whom I don’t even know — need to hear a three-word message: “Take a break.” 

I’m not talking about a post-midterm reward like fall break. I’m not talking about a ten-minute run to WU as a reward for finishing an essay. I’m not talking about any type of break that you’re taking as a reward for completing a task. I’m talking about the “drop everything for an hour because I really need this” breaks, the “I have an essay due in a few days, but let’s see if my friend wants to hang out” breaks and the “this club isn’t good for my mental health, let me drop it” breaks, too. Unlike seemingly everything else at Duke, breaks are not something that you need to earn. Taking care of yourself shouldn’t be contingent on the finalization of an assignment, but I’ve so often found that Duke students — including me — have put their health on the back burner for the sake of the grind. 

I know that people will object to what I’m saying. At a competitive university like Duke, it’s easy to feel the dread of falling behind when you take time for yourself. When it feels like your value is founded on how much work you get done, breaks begin to seem like a reward and not a necessity. We have become so used to the incentive of immediate success that pursuing anything else feels like a waste of time. And when we take breaks prior to our achievement of success, the fear that we are falling behind becomes a sharp reality. 

Yet when you take a step back, I think that these worries become misguided. By next semester, will you remember the extra 30 minutes you spent calculating optimal bundles in preparation for your Econ midterm? Will you remember the hour-long Model United Nations training session that you attended? In a year? By the time you graduate? 

I barely remember the extra time I spent studying for midterms last week! I do, however, remember the time that I went to Wilson to play basketball with my friends. I remember staying up to play games with my roommate as we momentarily forgot about midterms. I remember making fun plans for fall break. These breaks lasted only an hour or two, but I felt rejuvenated for many hours afterwards.

Naturally, the opportunity to unwind looks different for each person. I feel privileged that I could even consider taking lengthy breaks amidst this hectic midterm season; many Duke students do not have the liberty to take hour-long breaks. Regardless, I think that everyone is entitled to some rest, even if it comes in shorter forms. A 2022 study shows that even a 10-minute break, something that I think we can all find time for, can improve well-being. 

Duke is full of 10-minute activities! Take a short walk to the Chapel. Sit on your dorm’s bench and see how beautiful Durham can be in the fall. Go grab a cookie from WU (or from Trinity Cafe if you live on East Campus). Do some exercise in your room. Play a quick video game. Throw a Frisbee or a football on the quad. Learn the names, numbers and positions of players on the Men’s Basketball Team in preparation for tenting in the spring. 

I know that there are people who cannot take these breaks without thinking about the studying that they’re missing out on. I get that feeling, too, sometimes. During my freshman year, it was impossible to get out of the mindset that I would fall behind if I rested. However, in ignoring my mental and physical health, I allowed my academic life, the very thing I was trying to protect by refusing to take breaks, to suffer from burnout and stress. As I’ve transitioned into my sophomore year, I’ve realized something: I have done myself a great disservice by refusing to take breaks, to find little moments of solitude where I could free myself from the pressures of college life and counteract the burnout that so many Duke students face. 

When I think of Duke, my mind often instantly jumps to academics. But the lessons that we pick up outside of class should be just as important as the ones we absorb during lectures. At a university where academic anxiety is the norm, I understand the reluctance to take a break. Still, despite the popular notion at Duke, not everything needs to be earned to be legitimate. 

Harrison Walley is a Trinity sophomore. His pieces typically run on alternate Thursdays.

title: All your friends look just like you
author: Katelyn Cai
article_text:
“So, do you have any non-Asian friends?”

The question caught me off guard. It was freshman year winter break and my hometown friends were doing a “friend tour,” flipping through our camera rolls and lore-dropping on our new college friend groups. 

At first, I was upset — was she accusing me of being prejudiced somehow? But when I scrolled through the photos myself, I saw what she meant. Every smiling face beside mine was South or East Asian. They were all children of highly educated immigrants, mostly from competitive high schools in the suburbs on either of the coasts or in university towns. We were similar in race, culture, socioeconomic status and political affiliation … Just like the majority of my friends from Arizona. 

My friends looked just like me. But, your friends also look just like you.

At Duke, we self-segregate disturbingly early. Even during O-Week, we often recreate the environments we grew up in, whether it’s the New York City private schools kids, Miami Catholics, Indian immigrants, or black Southerners. 

It’s uncomfortable for me to write so crassly, as if I can reduce people to their identities. Because I can’t. But, at a University where so much of the student body and faculty critiqued the end of affirmative action and our lack of socio-economic diversity has brought national scrutiny, we shouldn’t only point to systems or institutions and say: “You, amorphous entity, you change!” 

Because we, Duke students, need to change too. 

On the surface, our in-group preferences make sense. College is a disruptive experience — you move hundreds (or thousands) of miles away from home, leaving behind your support system while adjusting to a totally new rhythm of life. It seems natural to seek out comfortable and familiar relationships to ease that transition. Some research has also shown that minorities can prefer same-race peers as a result of perceiving a white dominated world as hostile. 

And, it’s not as if Duke students are the only “offenders” in creating homogenous social spaces. Other writers at Columbia and Yale have opined about this same problem. 

That’s probably because for many of us, self-segregation was exactly what we grew up with. The Urban Institute found that the average white American lives in a neighborhood that is 75% white and 8% black, while the average black American lives in a neighborhood that is only 35% white and 45% black. It’s the result of decades of redlining and racialized policy and we’re still living with the social consequences of the post-Jim Crow era today. 

I grew up in the only Asian family in my neighborhood, but went to a public STEM charter high school, which was overwhelmingly Asian. When I got to Duke, I felt like I only related to other Asian kids, and in the race to make friends as quickly as possible, I latched onto them.

If our priors are formed on homogeneous communities, we unconsciously select for the same communities when we arrive at Duke. Our new (but suspiciously familiar) friends can relate to our family upbringing, high school drama and favorite childhood TV shows. We often fail to recognize what else and who else might be out there when we’ve already found people who understand us. Content, we then reproduce those homogenous communities in the social communities, spaces and organizations that we run. 

So many of the selective organizations at Duke don’t just select for qualification (because we have way too many qualified applicants!), but also the ever-vague “fit.” Fit makes sense, because you want your club to maintain its distinctive social qualities — that’s your sell, over any other club. 

But, when your idea of “fit” is based on who is like you (and this is true more often than we’d like to admit), Duke’s clubs then tend to reinforce social segregation. I can guess which formal is who’s, based on a cursory glance of who’s attending; it shouldn’t be so easy to put any organization into a box.

We’re also a student body that seems allergic to hard conversations. We hardly protest and we certainly don’t want our friendships to be full of strife. Our friendships also often fail to cross class lines, because it’s uncomfortable to talk about what we can and can’t afford, or to change dinner plans because one person is paying for student loans and another isn’t. 

So, the wealthier rush Greek Life, paying over $1,000 a year for membership, while students on financial aid gravitate toward Student Organization Finance Committee-funded clubs. While the latter still attracts students from across the income spectrum, the strenuous rush processes of certain selective clubs favor people whose parents have consulting jobs or whose siblings already attended Duke — yet another unspoken class cleavage in the Duke social ecosystem. 

Wealth isn’t a bad thing; but refusing to acknowledge its influence on campus life is.

We live in a pluralistic democracy that relies on cross-cultural, cross-class and cross-partisan unity to exist. The American Experiment can’t continue to exist unless we learn to live with each other; in a year of immense violence and polarization, it seems like we can’t. 

Duke isn’t perfectly reflective of America or the world, but it’s one of our best training grounds to practice welcoming, affirming and co-existing with all kinds of differences. By making different choices about who we befriend and how we recruit club members, we can change this campus and this country, one friendship at a time.

Today, I make intentional choices to find and create spaces where multiculturalism and economic diversity can thrive. I was an orientation leader and Community Coordinator for Project BUILD, which focuses on both community service and (surprise) community-building; I dance with the multicultural Defining Movement; and I report for The 9th Street Journal, getting me out into Durham’s diverse neighborhoods.

I didn’t come to college to find the same people I could’ve grown up with; the world is too big and beautiful and vast. I want new friends, not old mirrors.

Katelyn Cai is a Trinity senior. Her pieces typically run on alternate Thursdays.

title: Salud, dinero, amor — and what else?
author: Anna Garziera
article_text:
Your first sneeze in Spain will earn you a blessing to your health: Salud. 

But unlike in most counties, where subsequent sneezes simply earn you additional blessings for your well-being — which you clearly need, by the way — in Spain, the blessing changes with the second and third sneezes. After "Salud" comes "Dinero", and last, "Amor."


If you remember anything from your high school Spanish class, you’ll know these translate to “Money” (or “Wealth”) and “Love” respectively. (Don’t ask me what happens after “Amor,” at the fourth sneeze. I can only suggest you look into a Costco pack of Claritin and retire indoors for the season.)

I think about this fact often. Not only of the first three blessings, but also of the hypothetical fourth one. What more would I ask for? Fame? Fortune? A bigger pool? 

I’ve written on the importance of being thankful for what you have several times in the past two years. I am a simple girl and don’t mind recycling my article ideas. But still, this is a little different. Today, I’d like to point out that we should not only recount our graces but also limit our wishes. And this time, I don’t mean our physical wishes. I mean that we should limit our goals.

That’s right, you heard me. Here I am, telling you the opposite of what you’ve been hearing your whole life: Don’t dream big, dream adequately. 

Hearing this from a fellow Duke student might seem strange. After all, we all got into Duke thanks to our ambitions, our “extraordinary” work ethic and achievements.

And if you knew me in person, this would seem even stranger. I am a very ambitious person. I constantly have too much on my plate: I overload every semester and am unsatisfied by anything below an A. I wake up to row at 4:45 a.m. three mornings a week, but will not give up my nine hours of sleep. 

Yet, I am convinced a lot of you do the same. Duke students are prime-time over-achievers. We want to be the best academically, athletically and pre-professionally. Yet still go to basketball games every Friday. Yet still go to parties every Saturday night.

We are constantly reaching for the top rung. In every area of life, it feels like nothing but the best will do it for us. 

And we are a bad influence on each other. I’m only researching highly ranked grad schools because everyone around me seems to think nothing less is worth it. I only want an internship with Goldman Sachs this summer because all my peers seem to have one. I don’t even like finance.

We are a self-feeding ambition monster. Within this environment, it’s hard to take the advice, “Be driven, but not too much so,” to heart. 

But realistically, overzealous goals will only leave us unsatisfied. Let’s go back to the three Spanish blessings. I sometimes think of these as the three core goals that humans have shared for centuries: Health, Wealth and Love, not in order of importance. All else is arbitrary. And mind you, “Wealth” doesn’t mean Elon-Musk-levels of wealth. Only wealth enough to live comfortably. Wealth enough to manage.

Aim low, achieve high. That is what my best friend wrote in my yearbook in the eighth grade. Looking back, he was right. This life motto, though simple, unlocks one of life’s greatest secrets.

Perhaps it’s not only the height of our goals that matters — it’s the quantity. We should aim to have fewer goals. Don’t accept offers for two summer internships and also try to squeeze in a boys’ trip in the last week of summer. Don’t fill your schedule with meetings, clubs, coffee chats, office hours, study groups and pickleball and still expect to have time for self-care. At the start of the year, you believed all of this was manageable. You wished for all this, but are now enjoying none of it. 

It’s time to come to terms with this and adjust accordingly.

Here’s my promise to myself: My senior year, I’ll do it differently. I’ll be content with taking easier classes and getting only six hours of sleep when we go rowing at five in the morning. I’ll be satisfied with less than 10,000 steps and a two-step skincare routine.

By adjusting our goals to be fewer and simpler, we won’t be kept from achieving good things. We’ll even be able to better channel our efforts. The only difference is that we’ll throw in a sprinkle of humility and a dash of reality-check and stir it well into our humble broth. 

I’ve been thinking of a poem that illustrates this point well lately. In “Oh Me! Oh Life!” Walt Whitman despairs of Life’s suffering and seeming futility. He is full of self-doubt. He asks himself what he is alive for, what his eyes should crave, what his goals should be — questions we sometimes ask ourselves as students at Duke: What am I doing here? What should I aim for? 

Whitman all but dampens these questions with his last stanza: “That you are here — that life exists and identity, / That the powerful play goes on and you may contribute a verse.”

Anna Garziera is a Trinity junior. Her pieces typically run on alternate Sundays.

title: What does a gap year actually do?
author: Ryan Growney
article_text:
Most people have heard the spiel about gap years. It usually goes something like this: “Everyone should take a gap year! It’s a way for you to experience the world, explore your interests and yourself and mature as a person” (whatever that means). It’s not wrong. But it misses the point. By assuming growth is automatic, it strips away the nuance that makes a gap year so powerful.

Duke already offers opportunities to travel, to learn, to meet people and grow — and you don’t have to take time away from classes to do it. What a gap year offers is a testing ground. It’s a deliberate exposure to systems — social, cultural, ideological — outside the traditional structures we spend our lives until high school living in. Everyone should take a gap year because, when done intentionally and effortfully, it does “change your perspective” — it takes abstract knowledge and applies it, asking you to discover how to achieve on your own terms.

At dinner with a friend late in my own gap year, I was struggling to articulate why my gap year was so special. I met some amazing people, had some fun experiences. But what did it offer? I felt like a different person, but how? Talking through all this, she mentioned a phrase that I’ve been using ever since: “action potential.” 

To the biology students who hear that phrase and think about voltage changes powering muscles and neurons, bear with me. Action potential is a measure of the probability of meaningful success. It has two parts: one, the set of opportunities available, and two, the ability (and willingness) to seize them. It is a combination of adaptability, agency and confidence in how we act. It asks us, “what degree of impact can we make and how able are we to make it?"

We already view the world through the lens of action potential, albeit subconsciously. Take Duke, for example. Each class we take, we take it to gain experience grappling with ideas and problems that we expect will be useful in our future. We expand the breadth of actions we can take, gain the ability to play in fields we couldn’t have before. We also increase the degree to which we can impact those fields.

This is also true for our communities. We meet people, make friends and network so we can rely on and tap into a source of power to create change around us. Friends, clubs, sports: each of these activities are places to expand our opportunity to engage with new ideas and skills. Be it academic, athletic, social, personal — at a fundamental level, what we do at Duke is build action potential through well-defined structures. 

The question is, what happens when we get rid of those structures?

In the thirteen years from kindergarten to twelfth grade, you try to learn what the world is. You take classes on history and math and writing, meet friends and lose them and explore innumerable ideas for the first time. But you have yet to test them. What skills actually matter outside of these structures? What ideas? What is the tangible value of what you’ve learned? What does increasing your action potential look like?

The million-dollar question is no longer whether or not you can succeed in a system, but whether you have the tools to build one for yourself. It doesn’t matter what you do. Whether it’s travelling the world, working close to home, reading a bunch of books or pursuing a passion, an intentional gap year forces you to find an answer. It forces you to find what it takes to do well within the facets of life you value, what it takes to motivate yourself and to chart a path forward. It forces you to find opportunities and learn how to seize them. Rather than learning to thrive within a system, you have to create one.

Each and every person here at Duke is intelligent and driven. We’ve been able to excel within the systems we’re used to, but those aren’t the systems that will always be there. A gap year, at the fundamental level, is a testing ground. A gap year asks us what it means to do well in the world. It teaches us not just to pursue our goals, but how to do so, how to create systems rather than act in them. It teaches us what increasing our action potential means in the larger world.

Duke gives us all an incredible opportunity to learn, grow, think and connect. It gives us the opportunity to achieve our goals and become better friends, learners and people. It gives us the tools to maximize our impact in the world. But we have to know how to use them. Everyone should take a gap year because it does exactly that — inform our actions. Because it forces us to confront the hard questions: what does it mean to be autonomous? What does it mean to thrive in the real world? How do we pursue our passions and realize our goals? Everyone should take a gap year because it redefines growth, not as finding ourselves, but as finding what it means to act powerfully. 

Ryan Growney is a Trinity first-year. His pieces typically run on alternate Wednesdays.

title: Hard times
author: Robert Wallace
article_text:
They didn’t used to be this visible.

Decades ago, before deinstitutionalization, many were in state hospitals. Warehoused some would say. They walked along fences, their fingers grabbing the chain links; sometimes they might give a full-throttle shake as if they were imprisoned.

And who’s to say they weren’t?

Then, if society didn’t know what to do with someone, they stuck them in the hospital. Some might say that being in the hospital was better than being unhoused and on the street. Perhaps. Perhaps not. We know that some were forgotten and left in hospitals for years.

Once, as I walked along Main Street, I stopped and talked to a man who sat in a small chair tucked inside the alcove of an empty storefront. He was a very large man. His beard was large and unkempt, streaked with gray. It was a sunny day but quite cool; yet he sat in his chair, wearing only a short-sleeved shirt. He watched the people passing him; his look neither intent nor dreamy. Most passersby ignored his request for change.

I handed him a couple of dollars and kneeled on the cold sidewalk.

“How are you?” I asked.

He grunted but didn’t say anything.

“What’s your name?”

“It’s a secret,” he said.

“Fair enough,” I said. “Mine name is Bob.”

“Good to meet you Bob.” He held out his hand, and I shook it.

“I’ve been thinking about the universe a lot,” he said.

“Oh.”

“It’s all a mystery, you know.”

“What?”

“Everything.”

As I stood up, a city bus roared by, a plume of smoke following in its wake. 

“I ride the bus a lot,” the man said.

“Yeah,” I said. “You got a place to stay?”

“Yes, but I’m not telling you.”

“Have a nice day,” I said.

According to the latest point-in-time numbers, Durham has 415 persons experiencing homelessness. 172 persons are living on the street. The number of unhoused children increased by 58%.

Houselessness is a complex problem, but the results are devastating. In and of itself it is a health problem. The report shows mental illness or substance abuse is on the rise among the unhoused. We know that people experiencing homelessness are less likely to be receiving needed health care, increasing the likelihood of early death, including infant mortality.

Durham’s Continuum of Care is comprised of social service providers, nonprofit homeless providers, mental health agencies, law enforcement, housing developers, formerly unhoused people and many other agencies and organizations, all designed as a “Network” approach to reducing the unhoused. Duke also sponsors a Health Summit through Duke Community Health. In 2024 the focus was on building an equitable path to sustainable food systems.

Hard Times, Dickens’s 1854 novel, elaborated on the struggles of the common mill workers. He had empathy for them because when he was young, his own father had been put in debtors’ prison and Dickens had to go to work in a factory to support the family. The experience affected him his entire life. He knew firsthand the cruelty of the work, the poor pay, the decrepit working conditions. Bounderby, a middle-class character, tried to come across as a pick-yourself-up-by-the-bootstrap sort of fellow (he wasn’t). If I can do it, you can do it, he essentially claimed. It is such a mean-spirited attitude. In America, that attitude has always been around. It does a disservice to the people who each day do work that most of us wouldn’t do.

I think, sometimes, we forget how hard life can be for some. For many.

Before I came to Duke University in the liberal studies program, I spent thirty-five years as a social worker. Everyday I saw people who were experiencing homelessness, hungry, scared, struggling in many areas of life. So many had small children. And each year I saw society becoming less and less willing to help. Government spending dwindling to the point that food stamps could hardly by a few loafs of bread.

It pains me to see us as a country becoming less caring, victimizing the unfortunate, one-hundred-seventy years after the publication of Hard Times. How is it that after so much time, much hasn’t changed? There are people even calling for the death of people experiencing homelessness! Think what is being said here: “You have no home; therefore you should be put to death.”

We are failing so many people, so many families. People are being picked up by masked individuals and carted away as if they are cattle.

Medicaid is being cut. Public health services are being cut. The people who work in Public Health are being demonized. Vitriol and hate are becoming more and more acceptable. With cuts in the support system, I fear it is only going to get worse for so many.

Maybe what we need is a 'Health Summit on Empathy and Kindness'.

When I see a homeless person on the street, I give. I don’t ask questions. I don’t judge. I don’t assume anything. I don’t know their story, although I’m willing to listen. I also refer them to services for help.

Robert Wallace is a first-year graduate student of liberal studies. His column, 'Telling Stories', typically runs on alternate Thursdays.

title: Institutionalizing community will not solve our community crisis
author: Sam St. Lawrence
article_text:
Duke spends significant time, energy and money on institutionalized community events, and yet loneliness persists across campus.

Duke presents a glimmering campus of strangers anxiously anticipating your imminent arrival. But once the confetti settles, who’s left to help you pick up the mess you made? There’s no shortage of community events on campus at any given time, but why do so many of us still feel so lonely? Obviously, our primary job as students isn’t just to have a grand old time, but community does soften the blow of a bombed midterm. Throughout my time at Duke, I’ve talked to a lot of people: students from all kinds of backgrounds, staff who have become close friends and faculty who’ve offered guidance. I’ve heard a few things over and over: I’m so busy. I wish I had more friends or saw the ones I have more. What the hell am I going to do this summer?

Some of these are facts of student life. However, I don’t think loneliness should be a fact of life. Connection has become easier, and community-building programs have increased too. If you talk to alumni from 30 years ago, they wouldn’t have a clue what QuadEx is, what your O-Week group means or who your Blue Devil Buddy would be. If the infrastructure exists, why does loneliness persist for so many? Well, because institutionalizing community cannot solve the community crisis — meaningful connections form organically, not through forced programming.

To be clear, this isn’t just a Duke problem. Loneliness, especially for young people, is rising everywhere. About half of U.S. adults report experiencing loneliness, with the number even higher among young people. Further studies have found that as many as eight out of 10 people ages 18 to 24 report feeling lonely. So while Duke cannot hope to solve this problem alone, the University’s response highlights the difference between more spending and more connection. 

I first realized the discrepancy between Duke’s community programming and the reality of loneliness in my search for queer community. I followed the rainbow brick road to the Center for Sexual and Gender Diversity (CSGD), but it left me unsatisfied and pessimistic. I was certain there were queer people at Duke, but I struggled to find uplifting queer spaces on campus. I realized the problem wasn’t just about queer community, it extended to affinity spaces more broadly. Eventually, I did find people I connected with, but it wasn’t through any Duke-approved official space. 

When you first get to a place like Duke, the instinct is to cling to people like you: international students finding each other, minority students connecting over shared culture, queer students seeking safety and so on. These spaces can be valuable, especially at the beginning. They can facilitate friendships, but fail to continue being a fully supportive, value-based space. Quickly, you realize that an institution with such a grim history isn’t going to be a groundbreaking avenue for solidarity. Although Duke recently began offering Cherokee language classes and approved a Native American Studies Initiative, Duke continues to fail to acknowledge its history as a boarding school for Cherokee students and calls for a Native American and Indigenous Studies minor consistently falls on deaf ears. 

Soon, you learn that if you make too much noise, want to be subversive or try to talk honestly about the darker parts of identity and belonging, Duke suddenly isn’t such an ally. Duke’s history is full of examples of half-done allyship. A recent example includes Duke’s failure to understand the critical importance of immigration issues to Hispanic communities, going as far as threatening retaliatory action for holding a press conference to support a beloved bus driver. This isn’t to say affinity spaces aren’t necessary — they are, and their presence is a net good. But expecting them to fulfill the same emotional role as organically formed communities will only set you up for heartbreak.

And it isn’t just identity spaces where Duke falls short. Career spaces raise a different but equally frustrating set of challenges.

I’m majoring in economics. If I told you nothing else about myself, what would you guess I want to do? It’s okay if you say finance or consulting or IB or quant — all those things you hear about all the time and might not understand (me neither). I’m used to hearing that, even from academic advisers, other economics students, professors and basically everyone I talk to. But as someone who very much does not want to do those things, I wanted to find other people like me — and I had no idea where to start.

So I did what everyone told me to do: I signed up for peer mentorship programs, I joined events and clubs geared toward econ majors, I applied for programs that were supposed to point me in the right direction. I did everything Duke had to offer for econ majors. Long story short, I was confronted, once again, with an overwhelming amount of information about a field completely unrelated to what I want to do.

If affinity spaces show how Duke struggles to support who we are, career spaces reveal how Duke struggles to support who we want to become. And in both cases, the institutional community ends up narrowing, not expanding, our options. 

It wasn’t until I started organically meeting people by talking to researchers involved in projects I care about, running into familiar strangers at unrelated events (from hobbyist clubs to casual social events) and ultimately going beyond what made sense that I found genuinely helpful advice and support.

Duke infrastructure is great if you are a standard student (whatever that even means), and it will drive you crazy if you’re not. At a school as pre-professional as Duke, I have definitely felt like a failure when pursuing a nonstandard career path. Duke career assistance, like all forms of institutional assistance, is based on an arbitrary model that malfunctions at the slightest deviation from the standard student mold.

Not only is this frustrating, but given how powerful social pressure is as a motivational tool, this oversight can in turn force more people to conform to these standards — people who might otherwise have done incredibly cool and unique stuff. It’s like how freshmen arrive at Duke wanting to make the world a better place and somehow end up working at one of the Big Four because, well, you gotta get that bag first and THEN we can do good … right?

This shows that institutional programs only work if you fit the mold they expect. For anyone outside that mold, they reinforce exclusion rather than solve it.

Career programming wasn’t the only place I felt boxed in. Even in the most basic part of college life, where we live and who we live with, Duke’s version of community felt more like an obligation than a connection.

I am by no means the first to critique QuadEx, and many people have written better, more fleshed-out arguments that are worth your time, but I would be remiss to exclude the most glaring flop of institutionalized community on campus. QuadEx refers to the current housing system in place for undergraduates. It is built on the premise of connecting East and West Campus residential buildings to create one, overarching community. It replaced the previous model of housing that was built on an amalgamation of student-run organizations (Greek Life, Selective Living Groups, etc.). 

Budget cuts are nothing new, and if you run a student organization, you’re certainly no stranger to seeing approved funds shrink year after year. But if you’re looking for money, might I suggest QuadEx? Although the attendance at most (if not all) events I’ve been to looks grim at best, there seems to be a never-ending list of programs meant to build up the Quad community. As someone who lived in West House and now in Wannamaker, I quickly realized that QuadEx isn’t really about fostering true community. Hailing from the Quad half the size of the others, I’ve struggled to get a roommate, had to show up at other Quad events because Wannamaker couldn’t host our own and sometimes been straight-up forgotten.

There is no opt-out and there was no opt-in. Duke has monopolized housing, leaving students, especially those in smaller quads, with little to no choice.

So what are we to do? Surely there has to be something better than eating all of our meals alone and crying about how bad QuadEx is. The answer isn’t easy — it means we have to put ourselves out there. It means sending texts to acquaintances for dinner, even when you don’t know what you’re going to talk about. It means showing up to events where you barely know anyone and keep showing up because friendship is really just repeated exposure. It means getting involved in things you truly care about to find the people you will soon truly care about too. It means realizing that you aren’t alone and lots of people feel lonely, but you need to be the one to take action. Experiment with settings, activities and expectations. Try what I did and have open office hours in your dorm (people will show up!). And if organizing is too much for you right now, come say hi to me! I’ll give a tarot reading to just about anyone, so find me on BC Plaza with a deck of cards and a friendly face. 

True community is slow, imperfect and inconvenient — but also deeply worth it.

Sam St. Lawrence is a Trinity junior. Their pieces typically run on alternate Mondays.

title: On Tylenol, autism and medical anti-intellectualism
author: Wendy House
article_text:
As I’m sure many of you already know, the White House recently graced us with a claim which has simultaneously generated anger, celebration and an exorbitant amount of memes: Tylenol causes autism. Or, to be specific, the use of acetaminophen (the active ingredient in Tylenol) during gestation is causatively linked to autism in the offspring.

This claim was immediately disputed by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. All studies to date on this possible linkage have been correlative, so purporting a cause-and-effect relationship is a misrepresentation of the data at best and a lie at worst. 

I don’t want to spend my esteemed readers’ valuable time contesting the validity of the ostentatious declarations made by the current administration. Everyone everywhere is doing that already. I want to argue a different point. 

Even if it were true, even if pregnant people capitulating to the need to relieve the pains and fevers of childbearing was the root cause of this “autism epidemic," there is a simple truth that trumps the whole debate:

It doesn’t matter. It just does not matter. 

So, autism diagnoses have risen. This is stale news. This has been confirmed by experts to be due to a widened diagnostic criteria and improved public health services, which allow autism to be detected during wellness visits. This “epidemic” is made up of increased diagnoses for those with lower support needs who would have gone undetected previously. The number of autistic people with higher support needs, who may need constant or near-constant care, have intellectual disabilities or have limited communicative capacities, has increased “minimally, if at all.” The actual proportion of those meeting the modern-day criteria for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) has probably remained near-constant since the diagnosis was created. In sum, there is nothing causing a hike in autism, because there is no hike. 

The “autism epidemic” is a non-problem. Autism has always existed and it always will. To throw precious resources into trying to prevent its very genesis is not only futile but grossly wasteful when you consider that funding for research aiming to eliminate autism could instead go to research aiming to allow autistic people of all support needs to live in dignity and comfort. It could go to research assessing how best to accommodate those newly incorporated into the diagnostic criteria. It could go to literally any research on any real problem. 

Instead, taxpayer dollars are being squandered on a whodunnit-style goose chase for the “cause” of the very natural, even healthy, diversity of human cognition. Or maybe it would be better compared to a witch hunt, where we ravenously sniff out new reasons to pick apart and castigate the actions of expectant mothers and prove once and for all that women are the root of all evil. Sorry, was I not supposed to say that part out loud?

These bold, glitzy claims belie the true state of American medicine under present federal policy. You might get the impression from such open aggression against disorder and (perceived) disease that research into cures of all sorts is flourishing under the Trump administration — or at least that it is interested to an appreciable degree in the health of the country it serves. 

As many of you have doubtless noticed, this is not the case. I know this is not the case because everywhere I turn, medical research is being gutted by federal funding cuts. I know this cannot possibly, even a little bit, be the case, because I — we — are seeing the effects of this rabid, unprecedented anti-intellectual streak right here at Duke. 

First, a primer for the unfamiliar. Previously on we’re-all-gonna-be-poor-and-die: the Trump administration is attacking National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding. In late February, it began by terminating funding for DEI-related projects. As of April, the NIH had cancelled about 770 grants related to (in order of greatest to least fraction) HIV/AIDS, transgender health, COVID-19 and climate change. 

Down here in Durham, Duke shuttered the Inclusion, Diversity, Equity, Advancement and Leadership in the Sciences (IDEALS) office of the School of Medicine, which funded career-building resources like the BioCoRE program. This was done without consultation with any relevant parties. The director of BioCoRE, which helped PhD students from underserved backgrounds gain career skills, had to pack up her things the very same day she learned the program was ending. In May, the Duke Consortia for HIV/AIDS Vaccine Development was terminated by the NIH. No, not trimmed. Not scaled back. Terminated. They were given a little over a year to secure private funding or set their affairs in order and die quietly.
